View image in fullscreen Michael Carrick looks on from the touchline during the Manchester derby. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

City now have 12 points, second only to Arsenal on goal difference, while United have only four points and are 13th. “We will get there, I’m convinced of that,” Carrick said.

“We haven’t got as many points as we wanted and we should have. We’ve got to accept that and take that. It doesn’t change us moving forward and our hopes for the season and what we can achieve as a team. We’ve made really good strides over a period of time and we will continue to do that.”

Carrick was asked about the pre-game protest against the club’s move to eradicate ticket touts that some believe to be draconian. United said on Friday that 685 accounts had been subject to a ban and 464 supporters had received a reduced sanction or final warning.

Carrick said: “The details in terms of all what goes behind it, I’m not always in line to get to the bottom of it, but I definitely appreciate the supporters.

“If they do feel [unhappy] in certain ways then, of course, we want to try everything to make them happy. That’s part of performances on the pitch and off the pitch. That’s obvious. They’re a huge part of this football club. They’re everything for this football club.”

Inside the stadium The Red Army hung a banner over the tunnel that said, “The Way You Treat Us Is A Disgrace.” All usual banners were removed from the Stretford End.

Sports.title: Ludek Miklosko, former West Ham and QPR goalkeeper, dies aged 64
Sports.content:
The former West Ham and QPR goalkeeper Ludek Miklosko has died at the age of 64. Miklosko, who won caps for Czechoslovakia and Czechia, had cancer.

Miklosko joined West Ham from Baník Ostrava in 1990 for £300,000 after a trial and helped the club win promotion to the top division in his first season. He left in 1998 having made 373 appearances, joining QPR, initially on loan. Miklosko ended his career there in 2001 and returned to West Ham, where he worked as a goalkeeping coach until 2010.

He later worked for a sports agency before taking roles at Baník Ostrava as a board member and sporting director.

View image in fullscreen Ludek Miklosko made 373 appearances for West Ham. Photograph: Tony Marshall/Empics Sport/PA Images/Alamy

West Ham said Miklosko would “for ever hold a special place in the hearts of the West Ham family”. The club described him as a “beloved, inspirational goalkeeper and gentle giant of a man”.

Miklosko played 40 times for Czechoslovakia and twice for Czechia in an international career that began in 1982. He said in 2024 that he was withdrawing from cancer treatment.

His son Martin Miklosko said in a statement shared by West Ham: “We are heartbroken at his loss, but take huge comfort from the immense support he received from all of you, along with the knowledge that he is now at peace and no longer suffering.

“Dad simply loved West Ham United, and especially hearing his name sung loud and proud at every game. The club, and its fans, were and always will be a part of our family, so thank you all from the bottom of our hearts.”

Sports.title: The Hotspot | South Korea pushes for football season to make winter switch after unbearable summer
Sports.content:
South Korean football is trying to find the goldilocks time to play the K-League. Winters have long been too cold and, increasingly, summers are too hot. This may be the Land of the Morning Calm but, for much of the time, the weather can be pretty extreme.

Last week a survey revealed that more than 70% of 29 respondent coaches in Asia’s oldest professional league support a shift from the traditional March to November schedule to one that matches the European format, which starts in late August and has a winter break.

It is an old debate that has intensified of late along with the summer temperatures. The city of Yangsan reached 42.5 Celsius on 2 August, the highest since records began, and Seoul recorded 17 consecutive tropical nights, so defined when the temperature does not fall below 25 degrees.

Fans fainted in stadiums and coaches bemoaned the quality of play. It looks like it is only going to get worse. A December 2025 report from the Korea meteorological administration (KMA) found that temperatures in the country had risen 0.9 degrees from 2020 to 2024, a worrying amount given that the increase over the previous 100 years had been 1.9.

South Korea’s Pro Footballers Association (KPFA) called for a change. “The K League must transition … to protect players from the worsening climate crisis and punishing summer heat,” it said in a statement. “And to maintain the league’s leadership within Asia and its global competitiveness.”

Players believe that aligning with the European season will not only be beneficial for their own and fan welfare, but also helps in terms of buying and selling players. Japan has just done this. The J League followed the same schedule as Korea until this year but has just kicked off the new season.

View image in fullscreen A person carrying an umbrella walks past a spherical digital display showing 38 degrees Celsius during a severe heatwave warning in Seoul on 7 August 2026. Photograph: Kim Soo-hyeon/Reuters

Japanese fans and media have long lamented the relatively small transfer fees they receive for their growing number of talented young players. Having the same three-month summer transfer window as Europe should make a difference. It also puts the league in sync with the Asian Champions League, which made the same transition in 2023.

For Korea, which has a 38-game season, the problem is a winter which is harsher than Japan’s for a greater proportion of clubs. It is not much fun sweltering in a stadium in summer but then neither is watching games at sub-zero temperatures. The KMA said that since that early last century, summers have become 25 days longer with winters 22 days shorter. If this trend continues, then the mid-season break will not have to be as long as once thought, but a midsummer pause could be lengthy.

View image in fullscreen Roberto Firmino of Al Ahli lifts the 2025 Asian Champions League trophy. The tournament was switched to an autumn to spring schedule in 2023. Photograph: Reuters

A change could come sooner rather than later and it does not need to be that disruptive. The J League employed a self-contained mini-transition season from this February to May before the World Cup. The 2030 tournament may provide the perfect time for Korea to follow suit.

China has the same schedule as Korea and a similarly harsh winter in some parts, and sweltering summers in most. It is an issue here too. It helps that there are just 30 games in the top tier there and that, given the country’s size, there is more flexibility around fixtures with games at the coldest times able to be held down south.

It may depend on how the J League does financially. Despite concerns over the impact that lengthy mid-season breaks have on matchday revenue as well as interest from fans and broadcasters, officials in Tokyo said before the new season started that they expect record revenues. If so, it could be that, as much as the fainting fans and perspiring players, that makes the difference elsewhere in the region.

Beyond football, the Indian Premier League, the most lucrative competition in the cricket world, is also considering changing its (March to May) dates. “Weather is another challenge that we are facing now, with May getting very hot,” the IPL chair, Arun Dhumal, said in June. “We are also looking if we can find a window from February to April and then later in the year,”

Likewise, the Tour de France has much to think about after a summer disrupted by blistering heat and wildfires. It became so bad that fans were asked to stay away from the final legs of the race for their own protection.

View image in fullscreen The Tour de France and the Tour de France Femmes may have to rethink its July schedule in the coming years. Photograph: Jean-Christophe Bott/EPA

“We’ve never experienced anything like this,” Yvon Ledanois, sports director at XDS Astana, told RMC Sport. “It’s not just that one day it’s very hot and the next day we have normal conditions. No, it’s extremely, extremely, extremely hot every single day.”

It does not seem as if a move away from July, when the event has taken place for 120 years, is on the cards just yet but a change in times of races to avoid the hottest parts of the day may not be far away. In Korea and elsewhere, flexibility in the future is key.

Sports.title: Arteta embraces perfect storm to play the victim in game of his own making | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
A gentleman is never rude unintentionally, only by design. Nobody really knows who said this first. But it could easily be a line from the Elite Football Manager’s Guide to Press Conferences (Premier League edition). Because nothing happens by accident in these spaces.

Every word spoken in front of the board covered in adverts is metered and planned. A manager is never angry, or concerned, or even charming unintentionally. The game is the game, but so are all the other bits spilling out either side of it.

It was hard not to think about this while listening to Mikel Arteta talk about the penalty awarded to Sunderland at the Stadium of Light for a perceived act of grappling on Dan Ballard by Ezri Konsa. This is said with genuine professional respect. As everyone who has ever done a podcast knows – and this is, let’s be clear, everyone – there are lost Amazonian tribes discussing Girls season three in their own dark corner of Spotify – there are moments when you just have to flip the switch, up the energy and turn on full clip‑this‑bit‑up‑please‑Dave sincerity mode.

Arteta did this beautifully in the moment, appearing genuinely struck by what he was saying, radiating wounded integrity, like a disappointed junior headmaster appealing for the return of the school minibus keys.

Let’s be clear though. Arteta is not “very worried” about all this. He’s not “sad” or indeed, as he later emphasised for good measure, “really sad”. He’s not concerned solely with “protecting the game”, speaking here for all of us, just a fan of football.

Come off it. This is a manager we know to be obsessed with the most marginal of gains, to micro-plan the micro-details. As is all elite sport now. There has been talk of rowing coaches installing fibreglass toilet seats at their training hubs having calculated the average athlete spends 20 minutes in there and this is all key glute management time. Arteta loves this stuff. There’s no way Ben White isn’t sat fiddling with his phone at the training ground on a gold-standard Easy‑Cup Mega-Soft Evacu-Throne.

So it is with his public statements. This will have all been gamed and contingency‑planned in advance. And for hard, rational, tactical reasons, because this is how the game is played and run now. So what does it mean?

View image in fullscreen Ezri Konsa is penalised for a contentious foul on Dan Ballard in the box. Photograph: MI News/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

There are three things we know for sure. First, Arteta was right. This was a bad refereeing decision. Most obviously it was factually wrong. Ballard very skilfully pulled Konsa down on top of him, while simultaneously feigning shock that such a thing could happen.

It was doubly bad because the referee’s response was pre-planned, flagged by the early-season chat about refereeing in a more interventionist fashion. Go into any situation with a voice in your head, a vaguely worded mission to fulfil: this will skew your judgment.

The second thing is that referees are not biased. They’re just not very good. Two things have happened to them. First, the barrage of information to be absorbed in real time during a game is now utterly mind-boggling.

Most referees are not from a high-pressure data-processing background. These are not military pilots or traders on a currency floor. Less than a quarter have an academic degree. The task is beyond them. This is not a slur or an insult. It’s a simple description of what is happening, as supported by the evidence.

This is doubly annoying because referees have become fundamentally confused about their role. Referees are not ringmasters, or curators of the spectacle. They don’t get to decide what our sport should look like. Pro Ref is a private company with no locus standi to rule on the aesthetics of football. A referee should exist at the very edge of the spectacle. You’re not a local government planning officer with a mandate to decide which double-glazed French doors are or aren’t in character with the neighbourhood. Stop getting football not just wrong, but wrong.

View image in fullscreen Mikel Arteta has a word with the fourth official, Elliot Bell, at Sunderland. Photograph: Scott Heppell/Reuters

But Arteta was also ready for this. Arsenal’s coaches will have known this would happen at some point. That press conference response was already in the chamber. Arteta may even have practised his sad-not-angry face, his key lines.

And this would be the correct thing to do. None of this is breaking the rules, just as Arsenal are not a dirty team or a bunch of cheats. They play the game that is being presented to us, a sport that is being made to operate at the edge of its own ludicrously micro‑analysed rules on small issues of physical contact.

Arteta’s Arsenal have been masterful at finding advantages in this. Defenders are very good at playing with the ball at their feet now. Defenders are not selected for their ability to resist physical challenges. It is logical to exploit this, just as it is logical to seek to protect your ability to do so by speaking in public about how the rules are applied. This is why Arteta is good, and why he wins.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

It is also true that this has created a strange environment. The tone of the wider Arsenal fanbase is another element here. There is no one type of football fan. All human life is here. But the fact remains, the loudest voices in the online Arsenal hive mind, even the atmosphere in the stadium is unique in its absolute conviction of victimhood, of conspiracy, of a galvanising sense of adversity.

There is no other ground where every single refereeing decision, even the who-knows 50-50s, is so violently and eloquently disputed. There are supporters who seem to spend most of the game up on their feet in a state of performative, weaponised indignation, whose entire interaction with the spectacle is an attitude of aggrieved injustice.

This makes sense, too. It speaks directly to the game we have created. Aggrieved middle-aged rule pedantry. This is the new cauldron of hate.

View image in fullscreen Set-piece grappling was a theme once more in Arsenal’s win at Sunderland. Photograph: Ian Hodgson/AP

Is it based in reality? Not perhaps on the outline numbers. Arsenal have been awarded more fouls than any other team this season. Only six teams last season had more fouls awarded against them, and the same the year before. They had the fewest yellow cards last season. They haven’t had a single red since they had six of them in 2024‑25.

Still, certain key incidents continue to grate and fester. There was the incorrectly denied penalty claim for Bruno Guimarães at Aston Villa. The balls-up with VAR lines against Brentford in 2023, which, if it really was deliberate conspiracy-cheating, was the worst, most public attempt at deliberate conspiracy-cheating ever conceived.

There is discontent at the way some rules seem to be applied more severely to Arsenal, the silly little stuff like delaying or fiddling about with restarts. But then again, if you make the game about that, if you plan to play on the margins, and successfully so, more stuff might happen in that place while you’re doing it.

Arteta has also played the role of arms-length rage conjurer expertly, has gone from rarely commenting on referees to heartfelt and carefully targeted critic. The Sunderland penalty award was a first opportunity to unload on the refereeing backlash to Arsenal’s tactics, to launch his pre-prepared defence; and to point out something demonstrably true. Referees have lost control of this, because the game has got beyond them.

In many ways this was a perfect storm for Arteta. Not just a decision that didn’t matter, because the penalty was saved. But a decision that was clearly incorrect too, a chance to get your lobbying in while very obviously in the right.

There will be more of this as the season plays out, as Arsenal work to preserve the advantages they have made for themselves in close quarters, tactical attack and defence. Factor in that masterful turn at a press conference j’accuse, and Saturday was a significant win in more ways than one.

Sports.title: Lewis Dunk’s showstopper helps five-star Brighton to rout 10-man Coventry
Sports.content:
The bare facts are bleak: Coventry City are only the second team in Premier League history to lose their first four games of the season ­without scoring a goal. “And yet …” will be the enduring message from Frank ­Lampard to his players.

And yet they have caused prob­lems for opposition teams. And yet they have already faced three of the top flight’s European contingent. And yet they are not altogether playing that badly – the Brighton goalkeeper Bart ­Verbruggen being named player of the match can attest to that. But Coventry des­perately need a point, or even a goal, to give their ­confidence a much-needed boost. It does not take long for a promoted club’s relegation fears to turn to reality.

Goals from Charalampos Kostoulas, Malick Yalcouyé, Lewis Dunk – especially – and Yasin Ayari were all moments of individual brilliance. But there was also a sense of Coventry self-destruction, with no complaints from Lampard over Taiwo Awoniyi’s red card for an elbow into Maxim De Cuyper’s face, nor the penalty conceded by Bobby Thomas for Pascal Gross to score the ­visitors’ third. There are also legitimate questions to be asked of Lampard’s decision to maintain an attacking approach even after the sending off.

“It’s a difficult scoreline and it’s not easy at home,” Lampard said. “The first half was pretty good, we created some chances, better chances and we had them under a lot of pressure. Then a mistake to make it 2-0 and the red card makes it very difficult.

“It feels very difficult to take the result, but a lot of circumstances that you can reflect on and say: ‘If, and if, and if.’ We need to be honest about that – we need to take chances in this league. It’s not a nice feeling.”

The scoreline certainly lent weight to Fabian Hürzeler’s insistence that Brighton have no attacking concerns despite Danny Welbeck’s summer departure. Brighton have scored more goals and created more big chances than any other club in the Premier League this season – indeed, they have never started a top‑flight campaign with more goals.

“It’s not about having one good goalscorer,” Hürzeler said. “It’s about the flexibility of having many goalscorers and a lot of players who have this desire to score. We were very efficient today and quite ruthless at the right moments in front of goal.”

That was certainly true, beginning with a moment of mastery from ­Kostoulas to break the deadlock, when the Greek teenager showed great poise to control an aerial ball with his foot, nod it between two defenders and then fire into the bottom corner.

That Brighton were not already behind by then was thanks to ­Verbruggen, who produced two excellent saves to deny Jack Rudoni, when palming a volley and a header to safety.

Lampard publicly urged his ­players to “have belief” during the half‑time interval, but then followed two ­minutes that instantly extinguished Coventry’s hopes.

View image in fullscreen Frank Lampard endures another glum day in the Premier League with Coventry. Photograph: Mike Egerton/PA

First came Brighton’s second goal, when Yalcouyé was played in behind the Coventry defence, and the Ivorian’s pace kept all at bay before calmly slotting past Carl Rushworth.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Moments later, the hosts were reduced to 10 men. At first glance, contact appeared accidental between Awoniyi and De Cuyper. But, to the refe­ree Tony Harrington’s credit, he spotted the Nigerian had led with his elbow, prompting a straight red card. To compound matters, the stadium announcer chose that period to tell fans that train cancellations meant there would be no departures from the stadium for 90 minutes after the final whistle.

Thomas’s challenge to bring down Kostoulas inside his own box was as clear a penalty as will be awarded all season and Gross duly stuck the spotkick into the bottom corner.

By the time Dunk sealed the rout with the finest strike of his career – smashed into the top corner from 35 yards – the mass exodus had already begun. It was an outrageous hit, with Dunk saying: “I shocked myself, but it was lovely.”

That was followed in injury time by another excellent finish, this time from Ayari, curled from range into the ­bottom corner.

The only other team to lose their first four Premier League games without scoring were Crystal Palace in 2017‑18. Palace finished 11th that season, but need to pull the emergency Roy Hodgson cord. ­Coventry will hope he is not required here.

Sports.title: Lauren James revels in free role as Chelsea show ‘respect’ by scoring five past Manchester United
Sports.content:
A swaggering Chelsea cast off any suggestion that they had lost the ability to kill off games, putting five goals past a worryingly lacklustre and lackadaisical Manchester United.

Sonia Bompastor, the Chelsea manager, said: “When you have the opportunity to really hurt a team, the best way to respect them is to score as many goals as you can, to create as many opportunities as you can.

“Of course, it’s never easy to see the other team or the other manager concede five goals because if I was the other team, I would be really sad. For me, showing respect to the opponent is having that desire and mentality to score as many goals as possible. That’s the difference between the great teams and the good teams.”

United’s players and fans may have preferred disrespect if that is the case. Instead, it was another bruising result for the new manager, Eva Olid, and her side after an underwhelming performance in their 2-1 defeat against London City Lionesses in the opening game of the season.

Olid needed a result to give her some breathing room and her team some confidence, having had just three weeks to get used to one another before the start of the season, and this early into a project there has to be some grace.

For their opponents this game had been talked about as something of a must‑win after the Blues were held to a 1-1 draw by Aston Villa on the opening weekend despite dominating that match.

View image in fullscreen Keira Walsh scores Chelsea’s side's second goal from the edge of the box. Photograph: James Gill/Danehouse/Getty Images

To some extent the concern over Chelsea’s profligacy did not need to be too deep. They were at their creative best against Villa and were without the injured centre-forwards Melvine Malard and Mayra Ramírez while Aggie Beever-Jones, who led the line against the Midlands side, had not scored in the Women’s Super League since September 2025. The off-target Beever-Jones was relegated to the bench for the trip to United. Instead, Lauren James and Sjoeke Nüsken worked away interchangeably up front.

The visitors were similarly fluid in other areas too, and that flexibility was super effective. Chelsea were unpredictable and James’s free‑to‑roam role put their star talent at the centre of everything.

Lucy Bronze’s marauding forward yielded the opener when she sent a looping ball over the top and Dominique Janssen should have been first to it, but the United defender misread the fall of the ball and a stalking Wieke Kaptein nipped it away from her. The Dutch midfielder squared to Nüsken who fired in from close range.

The second goal, which eluded them against Villa, arrived just over 10 minutes later. A diving header from the new recruit Andrea Medina cleared a cross whipped in from the left but the hard-working Bronze was there to meet it, clipping it into the path of Keira Walsh, who took a step and powered in from the edge of the box.

The hosts’ heads dropped, which left their manager unhappy. “In football we know anything can happen,” Olid said. “You can be losing 2-0 and can end up winning. I don’t like the heads down. Heads up and we have to continue. Everything is about confidence.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

A very brief brighter spell for United after the break was snuffed out by the visiting team and James finally got on the scoresheet after the hour, latching on to Walsh’s defence‑splitting pass and shrugging off Janssen before sending a low drive into the net.

Chelsea’s fourth goal rubbed salt in for a very wounded United side. Janssen, under no pressure, failed to respond to an ambitious burst from Kaptein and the Chelsea midfielder pickpocketed the centre-back and slipped the ball wide to the onrushing Ellie Carpenter, whose first effort was kept out by Phallon Tullis‑Joyce but her follow-up found the net.

Bronze then added to United’s misery during the final minute of added time, hammering the ball in after Walsh knocked a corner back into the melee in the six-yard box.

It became a training exercise for Chelsea and the hosts failed in their attempts to limit the damage. Things look as if they will get worse for Olid’s side before they get better, with a trip to the Emirates Stadium to play Arsenal coming up next weekend, but Olid said she will not divert from the style of football she wants the team to commit to playing.

“If you start changing, then you are never going to build what you want to build,” she said. “It’s a process. I know it’s so hard, the process, because this beginning is hard. Nobody wants to lose games, but we have to be faithful to what we want to do, because I think that long term will give us the wins.”

Sports.title: WSL roundup: Arsenal rue misses in Palace draw, Manchester City crush Villa
Sports.content:
Arsenal were left to rue 30 missed chances after dropping points in a 0-0 draw against Crystal Palace at the Emirates Stadium.

The Gunners hit the target nine times and had almost 80% possession but could not convert their superiority into goals. Promoted Palace put on a resilient performance, with the goalkeeper Pauline Peyraud-Magnin batting away attempts from Alessia Russo, Chloe Kelly and Mariona Caldentey to earn another clean sheet.

The reigning champions, Manchester City, continued their winning start to the campaign with a dominant 4-1 victory against Aston Villa. Jade Rose broke the deadlock for City in the early stages, tapping home after Akane Okuma failed to claim a corner. Assisted by Khadija Shaw, Mary Fowler doubled the advantage with a low-driven strike into the bottom-right of the net.

Amalie Vangsgaard gave Andrée Jeglertz and his players a fright after converting Chasity Grant’s pass in the 42nd minute, but Shaw returned to the scoresheet after half-time to restore the two-goal cushion. City wrapped up the victory in added time when Lauren Hemp’s strike was deflected in by Mathilde Harviken.

View image in fullscreen Khadija Shaw scores Manchester City’s third goal in their 4-1 win at Villa Park. Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/Action Images/Reuters

Brighton came from two goals down to snatch a last-minute equaliser at Birmingham City. The promoted hosts took an early lead through Oceane Hurtre, who capitalised on a lapse in concentration from Caitlin Hayes before running into the box and slotting past Chiamaka Nnadozie.

Lily Crosthwaite made it two in the second half with a low driven shot across the goalkeeper, but Brighton gathered momentum when Olivia García came off the bench to close the gap in the 77th minute. As Birmingham attempted to hold on for the win, Kiko Seike raced into the box with just a few seconds remaining and made the most of a small gap between Sophie Baggaley and the near post to score.

At Goodison Park, Charlton fell to a 1-0 defeat by Everton following an own goal and two red cards. After a goalless first half, things quickly went downhill for the promoted side when Ashleigh Neville saw red for a high boot which caught Ruby Mace. With 13 minutes of normal time to play, the visitors found themselves behind when Holly McNamara’s cross deflected off the leg of Leighanne Robe and into the net. In the latter stages, Charlton went down to nine players after the substitute Hawa Cissoko received two yellow cards in quick succession.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Liverpool came from behind to earn a 1-1 draw against Tottenham thanks to a 60th-minute header from Aurelie Csillag. Spurs took the lead just before half-time when Signe Gaupset’s effort was deflected in off the foot of Liverpool’s Sam Kerr. The hosts levelled things up at the hour-mark after Csillag got in front of Lize Kop to head home Fuka Nagano’s cross.

Sports.title: Coventry told to worry about Derby points record as Frank Lampard’s problems exposed
Sports.content:
Coventry have been warned they are already staring at a rock bottom Premier League finish after their 5-0 thrashing by Brighton.

Frank Lampard's side saw their dreadful start to life back in the top flight continue on Sunday, as they fell to a fourth defeat in four league games.



5 Frank Lampard has endured a nightmare return to Premier League management so far

After Charalampos Kostoulas' opener put the Seagulls 1-0 up the interval, second-half goals from Malick Yalcouye, Pascal Gross, Lewis Dunk and Yasin Ayari condemned Coventry to a crushing defeat.

It marked a new low for the Sky Blues, who have now lost their opening four league games in a season for the first time in 107 years.

The result leaves Coventry rooted to the bottom of the Premier League table having conceded ten goals and scored none.



Having sealed a long-awaited return to the top flight by storming to the Championship title last term, Lampard's side were tipped to have the best chance of avoiding relegation out of the newly-promoted teams - ahead of Ipswich and Hull.

However, four games in, Coventry's tough start sees them languishing bottom of the trio, with the Tractor Boys sitting ninth on six points while Hull are flying high in third place.



Coventry labelled 'crap'

With Coventry already facing an uphill task to stay up, talkSPORT's Sam Matterface, Alex Crook and Troy Deeney have offered a bleak verdict on their chances this season.

With the Sky Blues yet to register a single point, the trio raised the question of whether they could beat Derby County's lowest-ever Premier League points tally of 11 points from the 2007/08 campaign.



Discussing their latest defeat on the Premier League All Access podcast, Crook jokingly called towering defender Lewis Dunk's long-range screamer for Brighton an ominous sign.

He began: “I tweeted to say, ‘When Lewis Dunk sticks one in the top corner from 30 yards, you know you're going down’."

Ex-Premier League striker Deeney was in agreement, who delivered a stinging assessment on manager Lampard and his side's displays.

5 A number of Coventry's players are plying their trade in the Premier League for the first time, with Ephron Mason-Clark and Jack Rudoni working their way up from non league Credit: Getty



5 Lampard's side fell apart against Brighton after Taiwo Awoniyi was sent off in 53 minutes Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

Deeney chimed in: “Four games in and he's already relegated them.

“Do you know what? I'm going to be fair and I think you should join in with me on this - are you going to admit that Frank has lied to us?

"He told us this team was going to be good, they were going to be pragmatic, and they're crap.”

Presenter Sam Matterface was more balanced in his assessment, who insisted Coventry showed some promise when they were narrowly beaten 1-0 away by a strong Manchester City side.



He levelled: “I think you'll find last week they were excellent at Manchester City and they could have got something out of that game.”

Summer recruitment criticised

Despite his earlier defence, Matterface then claimed Coventry's summer transfer business puts them at an instant disadvantage.

5 Forward Loum Tchaouna joined Coventry after scoring twice for a relegated Burnley last season Credit: Getty

The Sky Blues splashed out £136m on new signings in a bid to strengthen ahead of their Premier League return, although few of these players bring proven top-flight experience.



Midfielder Caleb Yirenkyi joined the club as their record signing from Norwegian outfit FC Nordsjaelland - having never before played in England - while Loum Tchaouna was signed for £20m off the back of relegation with Burnley last term.

Elsewhere, Ethan Pinnock signed from Brentford having struggled for minutes in recent years, and Matterface insisted this is not enough.

He said: “The recruitment has been limited and I think they spent mid money on players who are on the fringes of Premier League teams.

“Like Tchaouna is probably a really good Championship player - I'm not sure he's destined for the Premier League. Pinnock has passed his best in the Premier League. I think that's the sort of player that they spent their money on."



With Coventry reportedly boasting the Premier League's lowest squad wage bill at an estimated £42m per year, Matterface insisted this leaves them almost destined to rank lowest in the table too.

5 Lampard has been warned he will struggle to keep Coventry up in their first Premier League season since 2001

The presenter added: “The issue is that Coventry have spent money on fees, but they're not spending as much on wages as Hull are and as much as Ipswich are. I think if you look into it, that's definitely the case.

“And the problem is if you've got the lowest wage bill in the Premier League - which they have - you're probably going to finish bottom of the table. I think they probably will.



"I think that Frank really would love to be able to play some sort of progressive style of football like they did last year in the Championship, but actually has tried to play a more pragmatic style in order to try and get points.”

Having labelled Coventry a doomed side, Crook asked if unwanted history beckons: "Do we think they'll beat Derby's points record?"

To this, Deeney admitted: “It’s not the worst shout.”

Matterface refused to write them off just yet though, as he snapped back: “Come on? It’s four games in.”

Sports.title: ‘Bully’ – Roberto De Zerbi cannot keep making scapegoats as Tottenham reign predicted to unravel in weeks
Sports.content:
‘Bully’ – Roberto De Zerbi cannot keep making scapegoats as Tottenham reign predicted to unravel in weeks

Roberto De Zerbi's reign at Tottenham has been predicted to be a short one as his side continues to struggle.

After a 0-0 draw with Everton at the weekend, Spurs are one of only two Premier League sides yet to score a goal with one game until the international break.



5 De Zerbi ran onto the pitch at the end of the game to slate Mathys Tel Credit: Getty

De Zerbi appeared to lose it after the match when he went onto the pitch to publicly berate Mathys Tel, leaving the Frenchman stunned.

The Italian made some bizarre claims in his post-match press conference about how he would be the best manager in Serie A

Tottenham backed De Zerbi in the summer with a whole new rebuild and several big-money signings.



However, talkSPORT's chief football correspondent Alex Crook, ex-Premier League striker Troy Deeney, and talkSPORT's lead commentator Sam Matterface believe that things could start to go very wrong at Tottenham.

Speaking on the Premier League All-Access Podcast, Crook said: "I think this is going to unravel pretty quickly for Tottenham and Roberto De Zerbi because he's already getting his excuses in.



"I think he mentioned the number of passes they played, the number of opportunities they had, and he was basically saying, 'well, it's not my fault my team can't put the ball in the back of the net. We kept a clean sheet, therefore, I've done my job.'

"But he is already passing responsibility. He is already outing players like Tel.



"I don't think this is going to last very long."

Deeney then added his thoughts.

"What he is already doing is laying into everybody else, the media the fans and saying, 'there's your problem, it's not me'.

5 Spurs have just two points from their first four games in the Premier League Credit: Getty

"He stinks to me as a bit of a bully, to be honest.

"Richarlison, who I am not the biggest fan of, is not the same kid I knew at Watford, but he'd been doing alright now.

"He has a bit of fight about him and puts his body around and maybe get a goal.



"Now, he's not even in the squad, so Richarlison was a problem, and you made him look silly.

"Now, it's Tel, and it's so cheap and easy to find one person and say, 'you're the problem.'

"What about [Mateus] Fernandes? The kid you spent £85million on?

5 Tonali, among most of the new Tottenham signings, has had a slow start Credit: Getty

"He was f****** mint again, wasn't he?

"[Sandro] Tonali, who you spent £100m on. Can he pass it and dictate a game?



"What about the winger you brought in [Savio]? Or are you going to just let [Omar] Marmoush keep shooting from 65 yards, so at some point, it's got to be with the lads.

"I think his ability to self-harm and self-sabotage is going to be the unravelling of this over the next four to five weeks."

Defending De Zerbi

It is still relatively early on in De Zerbi's Spurs tenure and he has been backed to turn it around.

Spurs fan and talkSPORT regular Ricky Sacks said: “I think we will come good. I think you have to bear in mind De Zerbi, when he first started at Brighton, he didn't win his first five. Lewis Dunk said it takes around five to 10 games to really understand what De Zerbi ball is.



“You have to bear in mind, we're playing a different style of football with De Zerbi this season in comparison to last.

“We are trying to gel in nine to 10 new faces. That is going to take a bit of time.”

Fiery De Zerbi

De Zerbi has left both of his last two managerial roles with Marseille and Brighton and Hove Albion by mutual consent, but that doesn't tell the full story.

The Italian's time with the Seagulls saw them qualify for Europe for the first time.



But after being thrashed 4-0 in the last 16 of the Europa League by Roma, De Zerbi called out the owners for not strengthening the squad.

In that previous summer, Moises Caicedo, Alexis Mac Allister and Robert Sanchez all departed.

And in an interview with the Daily Telegraph last year, the former Sassuolo gaffer revealed his thoughts on that summer.

He said: “That year after finishing sixth, the squad should have been strengthened as they did the year I left.



5 De Zerbi's time at Brighton was very up and down Credit: Rex

“We reached a point where after qualifying for the Europa League, I didn’t understand what the next step forward was.

“And you can offer to double my salary, but if I can’t see a dream or goal to achieve, I can’t give my all as I would like.”

“I would lose motivation and a purpose I always had in football.”

Many Brighton fans also felt he downed tools in the second half of the 2023/24 season.



At Marseille, De Zerbi's whole time was fiery before it came crashing to an end earlier this year.

He left in February following their Champions League exit and a 5-0 thumping to Paris Saint-Germain.

Spurs then opted to make a move for De Zerbi, who kept them in the Premier League.

And they've since handed him a war chest to strengthen the squad, but the results and goals aren't there.



The Italian was blaming, in part, issues in pre-season for their sluggish start.

“I said we started this season late for many, many reasons; too late,” he said.

5 Maddison has struggled with injury issues at the start of the season Credit: Getty

"Many players at the World Cup, many injuries, many problems in Australia. Micky van de Ven suffered an injury in Australia. Domi Solanke the same. James Maddison the same. Mateus Fernandes suffered an injury in Australia. He lost 15 days and it’s not so quick.



"Sávio and Marmoush, they came 10 days ago. I started to work with this [whole] group not last Thursday but two Thursdays ago. So, I think we have not the right physical condition yet.

"We played very well in the first 30 minutes and then maybe the energy, maybe the fact we didn’t score … maybe we lost in some players a little confidence. We have to be not positive but realistic."

Next up, they host Aston Villa on Saturday lunchtime, live and exclusively on talkSPORT.

Sports.title: Man United deserved to lose against Man City as five players called out including ‘cheat’ Bruno Fernandes
Sports.content:
Man United deserved to lose against Man City as five players called out including ‘cheat’ Bruno Fernandes

Gabby Agbonlahor believes Manchester United got their just desserts against Manchester City, especially Bruno Fernandes.

Fernandes was at the centre of controversy in the first half when his theatrical reaction to a kick from Phil Foden got the City star sent off, even though replays suggested it was the United ace that instigated the red card.



2 Foden had never been sent off in his senior career up until Sunday's derby Credit: Getty

But City would have the last laugh courtesy of Erling Haaland, even if refereeing governing body Pro Ref admitted his goal should not have stood.

Pro Ref's verdict unsurprisingly caused uproar among United's supporters given they were beaten by what has now been deemed an illegitimate goal.

But Agbonlahor felt the Red Devils should be looking in the mirror rather than stropping about over a retrospective decision.



Gabby Agbonlahor's brutal verdict on Manchester United's performance

"You lost the game because Fernandes didn't turn up, [Matheus] Cunha didn't turn up, [Bryan] Mbeumo didn't turn up," Agbonlahor said on talkSPORT Breakfast.

"[Diogo] Dalot was horrendous and right-back, [Patrick] Dorgu is not a left-back.



"You lost the game because when you went up a man, for 70 minutes, you decided to sit back. You decided not go to go for it.

"How can Manchester City be the better team with 10 men? You lost the game for different reasons.



"You didn't turn up, the occasion got to a lot of the players, not because of the goal that shouldn't have been given."

Agbonlahor then tore shreds off Fernandes, who he believes should have been sent for an early shower as well.

Gabby Agbonlahor rips into Bruno Fernandes

"At the end of the day, Bruno Fernandes is a cheat," Agbonlahor said.

2 The Red Devils skipper's alleged deception couldn't help his side win Credit: Getty

"He's an outstanding player, but he's a cheat.

"You've kicked Foden twice on the floor, which should have been a red card to you.



"Then Foden's lashed out a tiny little bit and you're rolling around when you're not hurt.

"A proper referee goes over and says, 'You two, cut it out.' A yellow each, play on. It's never a red card.

"That's why you get your karma. Maybe the goal that should've been disallowed on Haaland, is the karma you sometimes get in football for the red card to Phil Foden."

The defeat was United's second of the Premier League campaign, having lost on the opening day against Hull.



Michael Carrick's side will now look to bounce back when they host Brighton on Wednesday in the third round of the Carabao Cup.

Sports.title: Colin Cowherd joins owners club with surprise $450m Premier League team after MLS failure
Sports.content:
NFL media personality Colin Cowherd has purchased a stake in Ipswich Town after previously trying to invest in the MLS.

Colin Cowherd has been successful in his second attempt in expanding his portfolio into soccer.

Front Office Sports reported that Cowherd has acquired a minority stake in Premier League side Ipswich Town.



4 Cowherd has purchased a stake In Ipswich Town F.C. Credit: Getty

The size of the holding is unknown, but Ipswich have a reported valuation of $450 million after an ownership restructure late in 2025.

"Reached by phone, Cowherd confirmed that he became a part-owner in the team. His late mother, Patricia, was from Leicester, 120 miles away…" the outlet reported.

"A spokesperson for Ipswich said he wasn't able to comment on any individual investment arrangements."



He later told the outlet that he has previously tried to purchase a state in a Major League Soccer (MLS) team, but nothing panned out.

Cowherd is the host of 'The Herd' on FOX Sports one, and is a regular contributor to the network's NFL Kickoff show.



He made his name as a radio host, but has also recently expanded his business empire.

His podcast network at The Volume has grown immensely, and the 62-year-old has recently explored a sale that could coup nine figures.



Many A-list sports personalities host podcasts on Cowherd's network.

This includes Indiana Fever star Sophie Cunningham, Richard Sherman, Nick Wright, and former MLB players David Ross and Anthony Rizzo.

His co-host on 'The Herd', Jason McIntyre, is a minority owner in Liga MX's Nexaca.

4 Ipswich are one of England's most historic clubs, having played at Portman Road since 1884 Credit: Getty

4 Cowherd (L) has previously attempted to purchase an ownership stake in the MLS Credit: Getty



Cowherd joins a unique list of other Ipswich minority owners, that includes 44-time award winner Ed Sheeran.

New Orleans Saints wide receiver Marques Colston and former Miami Heat forward Udonis Haslem also have stakes in the soccer club.

Ipswich were founded in 1878, joining the football league in 1938.

In their first season in in the top flight (1961/62), they won the league title. They have won the FA Cup once in 1978.

They were an inaugural member of the newly-minted Premier League in 1992.



However, after relegation in 2002, the club spent the next decade-and-a-half in the Championship Division, culminating in their demotion to League One 2019.

4 Sheeran, who is a die-hard Ipswich fan, is also a minority owner Credit: Getty

They have yo-yo'd between the Championship and Premier League in recent seasons.

Time will tell if 'The Herd' begins featuring regular updates on Suffolk’s favorite football club, but Cowherd has officially put his money where his mouth is.
