“If the government has ‘overwhelming evidence,’ why did the same government that arrested her file a Bill of Information to admit her to bail?” he asked. “Is the government now acting as both prosecution and defense in the same case?”

He further questioned whether Taylor had been considered a flight risk and whether authorities had first invited her for questioning before carrying out what he described as a highly publicized arrest.

Cephus said he was particularly troubled by what he characterized as the government’s public-relations campaign following Taylor’s arrest.

“Government apologists went on air saying, ‘Jewel should confess, the evidence is overwhelming,’” he said. “Confess to what?”

According to Cephus, publicly declaring a suspect guilty before trial undermines the justice process.

He compared the situation to “catching a man, beating him, calling him a ‘rogue,’ and then demanding that he confess to being a rogue,” arguing that such treatment amounts to public humiliation rather than justice.

“This is a serious misstep in the ARREST Agenda,” he said.

‘Let the Court Determine That’

Cephus stressed that his criticism should not be interpreted as opposition to the government’s drug campaign or as a declaration of Taylor’s innocence.

“I am not asking for an apology for the allegations linking her to drugs. No, far from it,” he said. “Let the court determine that and let the chips fall where they may.”

Instead, he said the President should apologize for what he considers the government’s treatment of Taylor as though she had already been convicted.

“I am asking for an apology for the manner of treatment meted out against a former Vice President,” Cephus said, criticizing what he described as a “near-naked spectacle before television cameras” that portrayed Taylor as though she were already condemned.

“For treating a former Vice President like a convicted criminal awaiting execution before trial,” he added.

Cephus also invoked a previous conversation he said he had with Boakai during the Alexander Benedict Cummings trial, when Boakai was Vice President.

According to Cephus, Boakai had then emphasized the importance of having people around the presidency who would tell the President when his actions were wrong and prioritize truth over friendship.

“Mr. President, you owe Madam Jewel Howard Taylor a public apology,” Cephus concluded. “And I mean it.”

World.title: Liberia, Morocco Deepen Military Ties as AFL Secures Commando Training, Vehicles and Air Wing Support
World.content:
MONROVIA — The Armed Forces of Liberia (AFL) is moving to deepen military cooperation with Morocco, with Chief of Staff Major General Davidson F. Forleh securing commitments for commando training, military vehicles, training equipment and support for Liberia’s efforts to establish and operationalize an Air Wing.

Major General Forleh is in the Kingdom of Morocco on an official visit from September 6–14, 2026, at the invitation of the Royal Moroccan Armed Forces (FAR), as Liberia seeks to translate the two countries’ military cooperation agreement into concrete programs and capabilities.

According to a release from the AFL, the visit is focused on strengthening bilateral defense relations and implementing the Liberia–Morocco Military Cooperation Agreement signed in Rabat on October 21, 2025.

The agreement provides for cooperation in military training, exercises, technical assistance, military health, and the exchange of experience and expertise. It also establishes a Joint Military Commission tasked with identifying priorities, coordinating implementation, and developing a structured framework for military cooperation.

Morocco Offers Training, Equipment Support

One of the immediate outcomes of General Forleh’s visit is Morocco’s commitment to facilitate commando training for an AFL composite company-sized element in Morocco.

The training is expected to expose Liberian troops to advanced individual and collective training, fieldcraft and operational techniques, according to the AFL.

Morocco has also committed to providing four vehicles, including a command vehicle, along with training aids and selected equipment to strengthen the AFL’s training and operational capabilities.

The measures form part of a broader package of cooperation encompassing professional military education, specialized training, military exercises, technical assistance, equipment support and personnel exchanges.

Support for AFL Air Wing

During the first phase of the visit, the Liberian delegation toured the Royal Moroccan Air Force Inspectorate, Air Transport Base and Royal College of Higher Military Education.

The engagements focused on professional military education, aviation and air transport capabilities and institutional development.

Of particular significance to Liberia is Morocco’s commitment to support the AFL’s efforts to establish and operationalize an Air Wing, including the training and development of qualified personnel.

The Royal College of Higher Military Education also indicated its readiness to provide opportunities for AFL officers at appropriate staff and higher defense education institutions.

High-Level Military Talks

On Tuesday, September 8, Major General Forleh held high-level discussions with General of Army Corps Mohammed Berrid, Inspector General of the Royal Armed Forces and Commander of the Southern Zone, at the FAR General Staff Headquarters in Rabat.

The discussions centered on practical modalities for cooperation in military training, exercises and exchange visits, consistent with the October 2025 military cooperation agreement.

The Liberian delegation subsequently visited the 1st Parachute Brigade and Mohammed V Military Hospital to examine operational training, military health capabilities and potential areas where Moroccan expertise could contribute to AFL capacity development.

Military Health Cooperation

Military health has also emerged as a key area of bilateral cooperation.

During the visit to Mohammed V Military Hospital, AFL Medical Command Commander Major Dr. Albertha Clark briefed Moroccan authorities on the state of Liberia’s military health services, including existing capabilities and key challenges.

The discussions identified opportunities for training and exchanges involving AFL medical personnel, technical cooperation and arrangements for specialized medical referrals.

The initiative is expected to strengthen the health-support component of military cooperation between the two countries.

Maritime Security on the Agenda

The AFL delegation is also scheduled to engage with additional Moroccan military institutions, including the Royal Military Academy in Meknes, the Royal Moroccan Navy Inspectorate, the Royal Moroccan Naval Academy and other naval facilities.

The engagements are expected to explore cooperation in maritime security, naval operations, professional military education, technical training and the development of Liberia Coast Guard capabilities.

The Royal Moroccan Naval Academy has served as a venue for professional maritime training and engagement with international naval partners.

Turning Agreement Into Action

A central objective of General Forleh’s visit is the establishment of a structured mechanism to implement the 2025 military cooperation agreement.

The Joint Military Commission is expected to serve as the institutional framework for converting areas identified during the visit—including command and staff education, commando training, air capability development, maritime training, military health, exercises, equipment support and personnel exchanges—into annual cooperation programs.

Such programs could include agreed priorities, training quotas, timelines, focal points and responsibilities for both countries.

The AFL said the approach is consistent with discussions between the two military leaderships, which identified training, exercises and exchange visits as immediate areas for advancing bilateral cooperation.

Delegation

General Forleh is accompanied by his Military Assistant, Lieutenant Colonel Francis O. Gbodi, and Major Dr. Albertha Clark, Commander of the AFL Medical Command.

Liberia’s Ambassador to the Kingdom of Morocco, Joseph Johnson, has also participated in the engagements.

The AFL says the visit represents an important step toward transforming Liberia and Morocco’s longstanding relationship into measurable military capability, professional development and improved operational readiness for the Liberian military.

The cooperation also opens opportunities for sustained institutional engagement between the two armed forces.

According to the AFL, the support being extended to Liberia is being provided pursuant to the High Royal Directives of His Majesty King Mohammed VI.

World.title: Liberia: Africa College of Bishops Ends Liberia Meeting, Calls for Bigger Church Footprint Across Africa
World.content:
Monrovia — The 2026 Africa College of Bishops Meeting of The United Methodist Church has concluded in Liberia with bishops from across the continent renewing their commitment to expanding the Church’s mission, strengthening institutional sustainability and partnering with governments and civil society to address Africa’s social and development challenges.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

The five-day gathering, held in Monrovia from August 31 to September 4, marked the first time Liberia hosted the Africa College of Bishops, bringing together active and retired bishops and other senior church leaders from across Africa.

Held under the theme, “Deepening Ecumenical Engagement, Expanding Continental Influence and Strengthening Institutional Sustainability,” the meeting focused on the future of The United Methodist Church in Africa and its role in promoting peace, justice, reconciliation and sustainable development.

At the conclusion of the meeting, the bishops issued a statement anchored in Isaiah 54:2: “Enlarge the site of your tent… lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes.”

Regionalization Taking Root

The bishops said the Church’s regionalization process is now taking effect across Africa, allowing United Methodists to conduct mission and ministry in ways that better reflect local contexts while maintaining connections with the worldwide denomination.

They said African regions are updating their Books of Discipline and establishing judicial courts as part of the transition.

The bishops also recognized the continued role of United Methodist general agencies in supporting the Church’s mission and maintaining connections across the denomination.

Several major denominational institutions provided updates during the meeting, including the General Council on Finance and Administration, Global Ministries, United Methodist Committee on Relief, United Methodist Communications, the General Commission on Religion and Race, Wespath and Africa University.

New Bishop Expected for West Africa

The bishops also celebrated what they described as continued growth of The United Methodist Church in Africa, pointing to plans for the election of a new bishop in the West Africa Regional Conference in December 2026.

According to the statement, the additional episcopal leadership is expected to help address the vast geographical responsibilities of the regional conference, which encompasses Liberia, Sierra Leone and Nigeria, as well as mission districts in Senegal and Cameroon.

Guinea-Bissau, the bishops said, is also in the process of formally rejoining the West Africa Regional Conference and is expected to become part of the Sierra Leone Conference.

Discussions were also held on the feasibility of adding more bishops in Africa during the next quadrennium.

Bishops Push Wider Ecumenical Role

The gathering reaffirmed the Church’s commitment to ecumenical engagement, particularly on issues of peace, reconciliation, violence and public health.

The bishops said United Methodists across Africa continue to work with other Christian denominations and ecumenical organizations to confront major challenges facing the continent.

They specifically cited efforts to end wars and violence, promote peace and reconciliation, and respond to pandemics, including Ebola outbreaks in parts of Africa.

The meeting brought together prominent Liberian Christian leaders, including the President of the Liberia Council of Churches and keynote speaker, Rev. Dr. Samuel B. Reeves; Roman Catholic Archbishop of Monrovia, Most Rev. Gabriel Blamo Snosio Jubwe; and Bishop of the Episcopal Church of Liberia, Rt. Rev. Dr. James Bombo Sellee.

Africa Eyes General Conference 2032

The Africa College of Bishops also received an update on preparations for the 2028 United Methodist General Conference.

The bishops welcomed efforts by the Commission on the General Conference to ensure that African delegates can participate fully and effectively in the global gathering.

But they went further, urging the wider Church to consider hosting the 2032 General Conference in Africa.

The call could give the continent a greater role in shaping the future direction of The United Methodist Church as its membership and influence continue to expand across Africa.

Backing AU Agenda 2063

The bishops also expressed support for the African Union’s Agenda 2063, “The Africa We Want,” saying its objectives are reflected in development and social initiatives being pursued within various United Methodist episcopal areas.

They called on African political leaders to champion equality, justice, peace, reconciliation and the wellbeing of citizens.

The Church, they said, remains committed to partnering with governments, civil society, ecumenical institutions and local communities to help build a peaceful, just, prosperous and sustainable Africa.

Call for Accountability

On church administration and finances, the bishops highlighted what they described as increased giving and apportionment contributions across their episcopal areas.

They also commended support for the Regional Conferences Theological Education Fund.

At the same time, they urged United Methodists to maintain high standards of accountability, transparency, generosity and responsible financial management, stressing that resources entrusted to the Church must be properly managed in support of its mission.

Liberia Receives Special Commendation

The bishops expressed profound gratitude to the Government and people of Liberia for hosting the historic gathering.

They said Liberia occupies a special place in the history and mission of The United Methodist Church in Africa, making the country an appropriate setting for the meeting.

During their stay, the bishops interacted with President Joseph Nyuma Boakai Sr. and former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, Africa’s first elected female president and a lifelong United Methodist.

The College also commended the Government of Liberia, ecumenical partners, United Methodists, the Liberia National Police, development and institutional partners, sponsors, media organizations and individuals whose financial, logistical, moral and spiritual contributions helped make the gathering possible.

Host Committee Closes Its Mandate

The Special Committee established to host the meeting also formally concluded its mandate, expressing appreciation to all individuals and institutions that contributed to the event.

The committee was headed by Cllr. Amb. Medina A. Wesseh, Chairperson; Cllr. Ruth Jappy-Samukai, Co-Chairperson; and Jeremiah S. Swen, Secretary.

As the bishops returned to their respective episcopal areas, they said they were leaving Liberia with renewed commitment to the mission of Jesus Christ, stronger fellowship and a shared determination to “enlarge the tent” of the Church’s mission across Africa.

World.title: Liberia: Tweh Backers Fire Back at Snowe, Reject Claims of ‘Politicizing’ Liberia’s Defense Ministry
World.content:
Monrovia — A group of former and incoming staff members associated with newly appointed Acting Minister of Defense Cllr. N. Oswald Tweh has mounted a strong defense of the former Minister of Justice and Attorney General, rejecting Senator Edwin Melvin Snowe’s decision to oppose Tweh’s confirmation.

The group’s response comes after Senator Snowe, a ranking member of the Liberian Senate, announced that he would vote against Tweh if his nomination comes before the Senate when lawmakers return from their current break.

President Joseph Nyuma Boakai recently reassigned Tweh from the Ministry of Justice to the Ministry of Defense as part of a broader cabinet reshuffle.

Snowe, in a Facebook post, criticized Tweh’s tenure as Minister of Justice, accusing him of contributing to the politicization of Liberia’s justice system.

The Bomi County senator said Tweh’s record raised concerns about his suitability to lead an institution responsible for the Armed Forces of Liberia (AFL).

“I will vote against his confirmation,” Snowe declared.

According to Snowe, Tweh’s tenure at the Justice Ministry “too often reflected political considerations” rather than the provision of independent and objective legal advice to the government.

He further warned that leadership at the Defense Ministry must protect the professionalism, discipline and political neutrality of the military.

“The military is one of our most sensitive national institutions and must remain professional, disciplined, apolitical, and firmly committed to its constitutional responsibilities,” Snowe wrote.

He argued that any leadership that could introduce politics into the military could threaten its cohesion, professionalism and institutional integrity.

Snowe said his opposition was not personal but based on his assessment of Tweh’s public record and his constitutional responsibility as a senator.

“I do not believe Cllr. Tweh’s record as Minister of Justice inspires the confidence necessary for this responsibility,” he said.

Tweh Supporters Reject Snowe’s Claims

But the group defending Tweh has strongly rejected Snowe’s characterization of the former Justice Minister’s tenure, describing the senator’s allegations as exaggerated, unsupported and potentially damaging to Tweh’s reputation.

The group said it was particularly concerned by Snowe’s claim that Tweh “politicized” the Justice Ministry and could potentially “contaminate” the Defense Ministry by politicizing the Armed Forces of Liberia.

It accused the senator of making serious allegations without providing evidence.

“What we find interesting is that, among the many things he cited, the Senator’s major claim is that the former Minister of Justice ‘politicized’ the Ministry of Justice, and therefore he is unfit to lead the Ministry of Defense,” the group said.

The statement argued that Snowe cited no independent studies, authoritative sources or empirical data to substantiate his allegation.

The group also challenged Snowe to present his evidence during Tweh’s confirmation hearing rather than making what it described as a public case against the nominee through social media.

Defense Group Challenges Snowe on Military Authority

The group also disputed Snowe’s suggestion that Tweh could use the military against political opponents if confirmed as Defense Minister.

According to the group, such an argument demonstrates a misunderstanding of the operational structure of the Armed Forces of Liberia.

It argued that the Defense Minister primarily exercises civilian administrative and policy leadership, while the military’s operational affairs fall under the authority of the Chief of Staff.

The group specifically pointed to Major General Davidson Fayiah Forleh, Chief of Staff of the AFL, as responsible for the day-to-day operational affairs of the military.

It maintained that the country’s defense structure, including the role of the military leadership, is governed by the 2008 National Defense Act.

The group further argued that Liberia’s military has undergone significant professionalization since the end of the civil war and the signing of the Accra Peace Agreement.

It said the AFL has evolved from its wartime history into a professional force with specialized units and greater adherence to rules of engagement, international law and military standards.

The statement also highlighted the role of international partners, particularly the United States, in Liberia’s Security Sector Reform process.

According to the group, international investment and oversight make it unlikely that the AFL would be transformed into a political force for any government official.

‘Tweh Upholds Rule of Law’

The group also defended Tweh’s record as Justice Minister, arguing that his commitment to applying the law without political favoritism may have contributed to the criticism against him.

It accused Snowe of implicitly advocating selective justice by objecting to the prosecution or legal treatment of politically influential individuals.

“The erstwhile Minister of Justice and now-appointed Minister of Defense refused to play by those rules but upheld legal sanctity,” the group said.

The supporters argued that Tweh’s legal background and experience make him qualified to lead the Defense Ministry.

They specifically highlighted his legal education at Harvard Law School and his years of legal practice.

“As someone who obtained his degree from Harvard Law School, Minister Tweh, more than anyone else, knows that the legitimacy of any law in any national jurisdiction is based on impartial application,” the group said.

Call for Senate Confirmation

The group is now urging the Liberian Senate to reject Snowe’s objections and confirm Tweh when his nomination reaches the chamber.

It described Tweh as “supremely capable, competent, and morally upright” and said his leadership could strengthen civil-military relations and improve conditions for members of the AFL.

The group said Tweh, if confirmed, would prioritize the welfare of military personnel, modernization of the armed forces and improvements to social services at military barracks.

It also said his leadership could improve conditions for military families and strengthen the broader relationship between Liberia’s civilian authorities and its armed forces.

“We, therefore, thank the President for the appointment of Minister Tweh,” the group concluded.

World.title: Liberia: How Sen. Moye Helped Steer Unity Party Lofa County Through Years of Division and a High-Stakes Leadership Contest
World.content:
VOINJAMA, Lofa County — Long before the first ballot was cast last week, the Unity Party’s county convention in Lofa had already become a political test. The question was not simply who would emerge as chairman. The bigger question was whether the party, after years of internal disagreements, competing claims to leadership and politically charged confrontations, could finally conduct an election without tearing itself apart.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

For weeks, political tensions had been building among rival camps. Names, loyalties and competing interpretations of the party’s internal rules had created an atmosphere in which even an ordinary county convention carried the possibility of becoming another divisive episode in the history of the Unity Party in Lofa.

Then came Senator Prince Kermue Moye Sr. The Bong County senator was appointed and confirmed to chair the convention, placing him at the center of a political process that required more than simply organizing voting.

He had to manage competing personalities, conflicting interests, and a party membership divided over who should control its county structure. When the process finally ended, the result was strikingly different from what many might have feared.

Lofa Superintendent J. Lavelah Massaquoi was elected chairman of the Unity Party Lofa County Chapter, defeating Voinjama District Commissioner David Mawolo by 85 votes to 50. More significantly, the election was conducted peacefully.

For Unity Party supporters who have witnessed years of internal wrangling, the peaceful conclusion has become the defining feature of the convention. It was, according to accounts from party supporters, the first smooth county convention in Lofa in approximately 15 years.

That makes Senator Moye’s assignment more than another entry on his political résumé. It places the senator at the center of what supporters describe as a possible turning point in Unity Party politics in the county.

The Tension Before the Vote

The disagreement was rooted in competing claims over the legitimate leadership of the Unity Party structure in Lofa. At one point, two parallel political structures reportedly emerged within the county. One was associated with William Akoi Eesiah, while another was aligned with David Mawolo.

The situation reportedly intensified during this year’s July 26 Independence Day celebrations in Lofa. Representative Thomas Fallah was said to have traveled to the county and provided financial support to Akoi to celebrate with Unity Party partisans.

Akoi reportedly carried a letter from National Chairman Luther Tarpeh authorizing him to act on behalf of the party. For supporters of competing camps, that development raised questions about who had the authority to speak for the Unity Party in Lofa.

Mawolo, who had served as Vice Chairman for Mobilization, argued that the party’s ascendency provision gave him grounds to assume leadership of the county structure. His position became part of a wider debate over succession, authority and the interpretation of the party’s internal rules.

They were unfolding in a county where political relationships are often closely connected to family, community and district interests. A dispute over party leadership could therefore quickly become a dispute involving larger political constituencies. That was the environment into which Senator Moye was brought.

The Choice of an Experienced Hand

Senator Moye was not entering unfamiliar territory. He had previously chaired the Unity Party’s National Convention on two occasions and had played important roles in the party’s national political campaigns. His political experience includes the convention process that produced Joseph Nyuma Boakai as the Unity Party’s standard bearer in 2017.

He later served as National Campaign Chairman during the 2023 presidential election, when the Unity Party defeated the incumbent Coalition for Democratic Change and returned to national power. That history helped explain why he was entrusted with the Lofa assignment.

But national political experience does not automatically translate into success in a county where political disagreements have become deeply personal.

Senator Moye’s challenge was to ensure that the convention did not become a contest in which the winner inherited a divided party and the loser rejected the process. The credibility of the process was therefore as important as the outcome.

His role required balancing the competing interests while maintaining enough authority to keep the process moving. It also required allowing the delegates to make the final decision. That distinction became important when voting began.

Five Districts, One Verdict

Delegates from Lofa’s five electoral districts participated in the convention. The election was conducted from the district level through the county level, creating a process intended to provide the new leadership with a broader mandate across the county.

When the county chairman’s votes were tallied, Massaquoi emerged ahead. He received 85 votes. Mawolo received 50. The margin was substantial enough to establish a clear winner. But the numbers tell only part of the story.

The more consequential development was what did not happen afterward. There was no major confrontation. There was no immediate collapse of the party structure into rival camps. Instead, the convention ended peacefully.

That outcome has become a source of pride among Unity Party supporters who remember the previous difficulties associated with county-level party elections. It also gives Senator Moye a political achievement that cannot be measured solely by the final vote count.

The convention’s peaceful conclusion gives him an opportunity to pursue that reconciliation from a stronger position. Had the election ended in confrontation or competing claims of victory, the new leadership could have inherited another prolonged crisis.

Instead, the convention has created an opening for the party to begin rebuilding its internal relationships. This could become one of the most important consequences of Senator Moye’s intervention.

Beyond Senator Moye’s Home County

The political significance of the convention also extends beyond Lofa. Senator Moye represents Bong County, but his role in Lofa places him within a broader Unity Party effort to stabilize its structures ahead of future electoral battles.

The Unity Party will eventually have to defend its governing record and organize for the 2029 elections, according to Senator Moye. That, he said, requires functioning county structures.

It requires local leaders who can mobilize supporters. And perhaps most importantly, it requires party members who believe internal elections can be settled through established processes rather than political confrontation.

The Road to 2029

With the convention behind them, attention will gradually shift toward the next political cycle. The 2029 elections are still ahead, but political parties rarely wait until an election year to begin preparing.

For the Unity Party, the task will be to translate organizational stability into electoral strength. Lofa will be part of that calculation.

A party divided into parallel structures will struggle to campaign effectively. Whether that foundation becomes a political advantage will depend on how the party manages its internal relationships from this point forward.

For Senator Moye, Lofa represents another chapter in a political career increasingly associated with difficult Unity Party assignments. He has already operated at the national level as a convention chairman and campaign leader. But the Lofa assignment offered a different measure of political skill.

World.title: Liberia’s Electoral Success Strengthens Democratic Consolidation Across AfricaNaymote Executive Director highlights four post-conflict elections, peaceful transfers of power, and lessons for credible elections ahead of 2029
World.content:
Liberia’s transition from civil conflict to four consecutive competitive elections and two peaceful transfers of presidential power was highlighted as a significant success story in Africa’s democratic journey during the second quarterly convening of the FixPolitics Africa Conference.

Speaking under the theme “Credible Elections in Africa: Lessons from Cape Verde and Liberia,” Eddie D. Jarwolo, Executive Director of Naymote Partners for Democratic Development, presented Liberia’s electoral experience as an example of how repeated democratic practice can gradually strengthen constitutional governance and public confidence. Since the end of its civil conflict, Liberia has held four post-conflict general elections in 2005, 2011, 2017, and 2023. These elections have helped normalize the ballot as the legitimate route to political authority and demonstrated that political power can change through constitutional processes rather than violence.

Liberia’s democratic journey has produced important milestones. Ellen Johnson Sirleaf was elected in 2005 as Africa’s first elected woman president and re-elected in 2011. In 2017, George M. Weah was elected in a process that resulted in Liberia’s first transfer between elected presidents in more than 70 years. In 2023, Joseph N. Boakai defeated the incumbent president, producing a second consecutive peaceful democratic transfer.

Jarwolo emphasized that these repeated elections have strengthened democratic consolidation by creating a pattern in which citizens vote, institutions administer political competition, disputes are addressed through legal mechanisms, electoral outcomes are respected, and power changes hands peacefully. “Liberia’s greatest democratic success is not simply that elections have been held, but that repeated elections have increasingly established peaceful political competition and constitutional transfer of power as the accepted democratic norm,” Jarwolo said.

The 2023 elections offered one of the strongest demonstrations of Liberia’s democratic resilience and consolidation. The elections involved 2,471,617 registered voters across 2,080 voting precincts and 5,890 polling places, within a competitive political environment of 46 registered political parties. Women constituted 50.06 percent of registered voters, underscoring their significant role in Liberia’s electoral democracy.

First-round voter turnout reached an impressive 78.86 percent, reflecting strong citizen participation and commitment to democratic choice.

These indicators, combined with competitive elections and the peaceful transfer of power, demonstrate how sustained citizen participation and respect for electoral outcomes continue to strengthen Liberia’s democratic culture and constitutional governance.

The presidential runoff was decided by only 20,567 valid votes. Amb. Joseph N. Boakai received 814,481 votes, or 50.64 percent, while incumbent President George M. Weah received 793,914 votes, or 49.36 percent. Despite the extremely close result, President Weah conceded after progressive results covering 99.8 percent of polling places, before the final official declaration by Liberia’s National Elections Commission (NEC).

His timely concession reduced uncertainty, eased political tension, and reinforced Liberia’s constitutional transfer of power.

This peaceful outcome was particularly significant because the same two political leaders had competed against each other in the 2017 runoff. In 2017, Weah won decisively. In 2023, voters reversed the result and elected Boakai. Both outcomes were accepted.

This demonstrated that Liberia’s electoral system could produce genuine alternative in power through the ballot.

“The real strength of democracy is revealed when elections are close, political power is at stake, and leaders and institutions still respect the rules. Liberia passed an important democratic test in 2023,” Jarwolo emphasized.

Jarwolo stressed that Liberia’s electoral progress is a product of shared democratic ownership, built through the collective actions of citizens, institutions, political actors, civil society, and the media. Citizens demonstrated strong commitment to peaceful political participation, while election administrators managed nationwide polling and strengthened transparency through electoral safeguards and tallying processes. Political actors largely relied on constitutional and legal mechanisms, and civil society provided independent scrutiny through domestic election observation and public reporting.

The media and fact-checking initiatives further strengthened access to credible electoral information. Together, these efforts reinforced public confidence, strengthened the legitimacy of electoral outcomes, and demonstrated that credible elections are a shared national responsibility rather than the achievement of any single institution.

Jarwolo also recognized the contributions of the National Elections Commission, civil society, domestic observer groups, the media, political parties, ECOWAS, the African Union, the European Union, UNDP, and other international partners that have supported Liberia’s democratic progress over successive electoral cycles.

Another important success story highlighted during the presentation was the contribution of political education and youth leadership development to Liberia’s democratic consolidation.

Through the Young Political Leadership School Africa, political-party youth training, civic education, public-interest media, citizen engagement, and democratic oversight, Naymote has supported young people to move beyond being campaign mobilizers to becoming informed leaders, observers, advocates, and democratic decision-makers.

Jarwolo noted that strengthening democracy requires more than effective electoral institutions. It also requires citizens who understand democratic values, demand accountability, engage in public institutions, and contribute constructively to political processes. “Institutions alone cannot sustain democracy. Political education and civic participation help build the democratic culture that allows institutions to work and enables citizens to protect democratic gains,” he said. While Liberia’s achievements demonstrate important progress, Jarwolo cautioned that democratic consolidation remains unfinished.

Challenges include delayed electoral reforms, outdated constituency boundaries, late financing for the National Elections Commission, weak campaign-finance enforcement, misuse of state resources, barriers affecting rural voters and persons with disabilities, misinformation, and limited political representation for women and young people.

He, therefore called for early action ahead of the 2029 elections, including completing legal reforms, updating constituency boundaries, ensuring predictable financing for the NEC, strengthening political-finance oversight, promoting inclusion, and investing continuously in civic education and information integrity.

Jarwolo concluded that Liberia’s experience offers an important lesson for Africa: credible elections are built over time, not only on election day. “Liberia’s democratic progress shows that repeated credible elections, peaceful transfers of power, responsible political leadership, informed citizens, and strong institutions can gradually transform a post-conflict society into a more resilient democracy. But the 2029 test begins now.”

Eddie D. Jarwolo is a governance, leadership, and electoral expert with over 20 years of professional experience. He holds a master’s degree in public Sector Management and several international professional certifications. He is a trained ECOWAS Long-Term Election Observer and a certified BRIDGE facilitator, with extensive experience in democratic governance, elections, civic engagement, and leadership development.

World.title: Lwandamina names Chipolopolo squad: Chama, Mumba miss out
World.content:
Captain Fashion Sakala will lead a 27-member Chipolopolo squad named by Coach George Lwandamina for Zambia’s back-to-back 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers against Algeria and Togo this month-end.

Lwandamina unveiled the squad at a media briefing in Lusaka, expressing confidence that Zambia will excel in the AFCON qualifying campaign.

Zambia will face Algeria on 25 September in Algiers before hosting Togo on 29 September at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium, Ndola.

Besides Saudi Arabia-based captain Sakala, other key names include Lameck Banda- recently moved to Libya and Gamphani Lungu – Orlando Pirates, South Africa.

Missing from the squad are inform and local star Ackim Mumba of Red Arrows, Tanzania based Cletus Chama, winger Lubambo Musonda, enterprising Joseph Sabobo Banda, South Africa based keeper Toaster Nsabata and midfielder Kings Kangwa, who is suspended.

Panathinaikos midfielder Kangwa will miss both games as he serves a four-match CAF ban imposed after an incident involving match officials during Zambia’s final group-stage match at AFCON 2025 against Morocco.

Coach Lwandamina says the team is ready for the challenge.

“We also played Argentina, so we measured our prowess, so we understand what is ahead of us,” Lwandamina said.

He added: “Zambian fans have an obligation to support the National Team.”

Zambia is in Group I alongside Algeria, Togo, and Burundi.

The 2027 AFCON will be jointly hosted by Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda under the banner TotalEnergies AFCON Pamoja 2027.”

Top two teams in nine of the 12 groups will qualify automatically.

In Groups D, H, L – where the three host nations are – only one slot will be available.

FULL SQUAD

GOALKEEPERS

Victor Chabu (Nchanga Rangers), Lawrence Mulenga (Power Dynamos), Luka Mainza (Red Arrows) Willard Mwanza (Power Dynamos)

DEFENDERS

Mathews Banda (Bohemians Praha, Czech), Owen Mwamba (Red Arrows), Obinno Chisala (Al Merreikh, Sudan), David Hamasenya (Slovan Liberec, Czech), Dominic Chanda (Power Dynamos), Tinkler Sinkala (Zanaco), Ricky Chanda (Nõmme United, Estonia) Fredrick Mwimanzi (Zanaco)

MIDFIELDERS

Owen Tembo (Power Dynamos), Wilson Chisala (Power Dynamos), Joseph Liteta (Cagliari, Italy), Miguel Changa Chaiwa (Hibernian, Scotland), David Simukonda (El Gouna, Egypt), Given Kalusa (FC Muza), Pascol Phiri (Al-ittihad Alexandria, Egypt)

FORWARDS

Gamphani Lungu (Orlando Pirates, South Africa), Lameck Banda (Swehly, Libya) Fashion Sakala (Al Fayha, Saudi Arabia), Patson Daka (Hamburg, Germany), Kingstone Mutandwa (Serviette, Switzerland), Albert Kangwanda (Young Africans, Tanzania), Eliya Mandanji (Red Arrows), Chanka Zimba (Unattached).

World.title: Treason Case Detainees Mark 40 Days Without Court Appearance
World.content:
Director of Public Prosecutions Gilbert Phiri says the State is still investigating treason suspects being held at Mukobeko Maximum Security Prison in Kabwe, as pressure mounts over the length of their detention. In an interview in Lusaka on Friday, he said the delay in taking National Reconciliation Party for National Unity and Prosperity presidential candidate Brian Mundubile, his running mate Makebi Zulu, prominent Lusaka businessman Harry Valden Findlay and others to court for treason was because law enforcement agencies were still building their case.

The Director of Public Prosecutions said law enforcement agencies had the mandate to investigate cases and should be given space to do so without undue pressure. He appealed to those concerned over the prolonged detention to exercise patience, arguing that investigators needed adequate time to conclude whether a prosecutable case existed at all.

“Some investigations are complex. The mandate of investigation is with law enforcement agencies and this process sometimes may take time, but it must be respected, and the space and opportunity must be given for them to inquire, and this is for the betterment of you, myself and the public in general,” he said.

Mr Phiri explained that police and other agencies needed to compile a docket that has to be vetted before any matter reaches court, a process he described as systematic in every jurisdiction, including the Western world. He said investigations sometimes end without a case if evidence proves insufficient, and that this conclusion cannot be reached without first being given the space to operate.

“So, all these processes take time. In every society, including the Western world, there are these processes that take time before a matter can go to court,” he said.

The family of Harry Findlay, however, says it remains deeply concerned that he has spent 40 days in detention without being taken to court, while his health continues to deteriorate. They said the allegations against him should not deprive him of his constitutional rights, including the right to have his case determined fairly and without undue delay.

“It has now been 40 days since Harry Findlay was arrested and yet he has not been taken to Court. Whatever the allegations against him they do not take away his constitutional rights. He has the right to be taken to court and the matter determined fairly and without delay,” the Findlay family said.

The family added that despite his serious medical condition and deteriorating health, he had not been taken to hospital and continued to receive treatment at the detention facility. It said it had exhausted all avenues available to it through the law and was now awaiting the court’s decision on its constitutional petition.

Political analyst and former detainee Muhabi Lungu drew parallels between his own treason trial three decades ago and the current case, warning that Zambia risks sliding into what he termed authoritarianism if detainees are not brought before a court. He recalled his own experience in the “Black Mamba” case, in which he said a judge at the time had told the State that suspects charged with serious offences must still be brought to court promptly, describing that as what due process means.

International observers have echoed some of these concerns, with the United Nations urging Zambia to uphold human rights and judicial independence, while the African Union has warned that prolonged detentions without trial undermine democratic legitimacy.

Both the DPP’s office and the concerned parties agree on one point: the matter now rests on the courts and the pace of the ongoing investigation, with all sides awaiting the next procedural development.

World.title: Al Merrikh coach hails Chipolopolo’s Chisala
World.content:
Al Merrikh coach Darko Novic has heaped praise on Chipolopolo midfielder Obinos Chisala after the Sudanese side eliminated Power Dynamos from the CAF Champions League at the preliminary stage.

Al Merrikh beat Power 1-0 in Ndola on Saturday to complete a 2-0 aggregate win and advance to the second preliminary round. Chisala started both legs.

Speaking at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium, Novic described the former Zanaco man as a key part of his team.

“Obino is one of my favorite players and one of the important players in our squad,” Novic said.

“From last year when I came to Al Merrikh I have been putting him in 100 percent. I use him any time and I also use him on the right back when I’m in problems,” he added.

Chisala joined Al Merrikh in January 2025 from Moçambola club Costa do Sol. The coach says the Zambian’s versatility has been vital.

Novic wants more goals from the midfielder.

“His technical aspect is very perfect. The only thing he is missing is scoring goals from that position,” the Serbian tactician said.

Chisala is part of the Chipolopolo squad for this month’s 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers against Algeria and Togo. He also featured for Zambia at the AFCON in Morocco earlier this year.

The Al Merrikh coach also pointed to Power’s main problem.

“Power Dynamos didn’t score and that is one of their problems. Last season if you count their goals in the Champions League, it was three or four in the group stage,” Novic told reporters.

World.title: K24 Million Disbursed To Youth-Led Businesses Through Imisepela
World.content:
More than K24 million has so far been disbursed in funding youth-led businesses on the Imisepela application, with about 2,300 people securing employment through the platform since its launch in March this year.

Special Assistant to the President for Finance and Investment Jito Kayumba said the initiative was helping young people access funding and employment opportunities.

He told ZNBC News that the platform was also offering an opportunity for business and skills development masterclasses, adding a training dimension to the funding support already being provided to young entrepreneurs.

Mr Kayumba said the programme was ongoing and was ensuring that youths were empowered, positioning Imisepela as a continuing rather than a time-limited initiative.

He also dismissed allegations that the programme was no longer operational, saying such claims had been made by people whose applications were unsuccessful because they did not meet the required criteria.

The clarification comes at a time when Government-backed youth empowerment platforms have faced public scrutiny over transparency and continued functionality, making Mr Kayumba’s intervention a direct rebuttal to that narrative.

With more than K24 million already disbursed and thousands of young people reporting new employment through the platform, Imisepela is being positioned by Government as a practical delivery mechanism under its broader youth economic empowerment strategy.

The masterclasses referenced by Mr Kayumba suggest the platform is intended to go beyond simple disbursement of funds, aiming instead to build the business and skills capacity of young entrepreneurs so that funded ventures are more likely to succeed and sustain employment over time.

For young Zambians who have already benefited, the figures represent tangible proof that the platform is functioning as intended. For those whose applications were unsuccessful, Mr Kayumba’s explanation places responsibility on eligibility criteria rather than any failure of the programme itself.

Attention will now turn to how quickly the remaining funds are disbursed and whether the number of jobs secured through the platform continues to grow as more youth-led businesses come on stream.

World.title: Government Shifts Focus To Delivering Growth For Ordinary Zambians
World.content:
The United Party for National Development Government is preparing to shift its focus from stabilising Zambia’s economy to ensuring that ordinary citizens feel meaningful growth in their pockets, Moomba Member of Parliament Fred Chaatila has said.

An economist by training, the lawmaker said the second-term agenda would centre on accelerating economic activity, creating decent jobs and raising household incomes through increased investment in productive sectors.

He tied this directly to the Grow Zambia Agenda, President Hakainde Hichilema’s framework for expanding economic opportunities, saying it would ensure that gains recorded during the first term translate into tangible improvements for ordinary Zambians.

Greater emphasis would be placed on sectors capable of creating employment and generating wealth, particularly agriculture, mining, manufacturing, and small and medium-sized enterprises, the Moomba MP added.

The first term’s economic stabilisation, he argued, had laid a foundation on which a more productive and inclusive economy could now be built.

“The focus now should be on making sure that ordinary citizens begin feeling the economic gains that have been recorded,” he said.

Growth should not be measured merely by macroeconomic indicators, according to the lawmaker, but should result in increased investment, more employment opportunities, improved household incomes and better public services.

Agriculture, he noted, remained critical to the country’s economic transformation because of its potential to create jobs, enhance food production and provide income opportunities for millions of citizens.

Mining and manufacturing were also singled out as key drivers of expansion, with increased activity in both sectors expected to stimulate value addition, investment and employment.

The renewed mandate given to the ruling party, Mr Chaatila said, offered an opportunity to consolidate progress made during the first term while addressing the economic challenges still affecting ordinary Zambians.

He said the second term should therefore be defined by greater productivity, increased investment and inclusive development.

Zambians were urged to support initiatives aimed at growing the economy, with the lawmaker stressing that sustainable development could only be achieved through cooperation among Government, the private sector and citizens.

A growing economy, he added, required collective responsibility: Government creating the right policy environment, businesses investing, and citizens participating productively in economic activities.

The ultimate measure of economic success, Mr Chaatila concluded, should be improved living standards, particularly through better incomes, employment opportunities and access to quality public services.

The country now had an opportunity to build on the foundation laid during the first term, turning it into broader prosperity for Zambians.

The next stage of scrutiny for Government will be whether the productivity and job-creation targets outlined translate into measurable improvements in household incomes over the coming months.

World.title: TECH Global University, the highest-rated university in the world by its students
World.content:
TECH Global University, the highest-rated university in the world by its students

The university has achieved the highest rating in the educational field, a 4.9 out of 5, after receiving more than 25,000 reviews on the top international opinion platforms





The leading global review platforms have positioned TECH Global University as the highest-rated university in the world by its students. In this regard, Google Maps, used by over 1 billion people according to official platform data, is one of the main sources of continuous praise for the institution. It has accumulated more than 4,000 positive reviews, achieving a rating of 4.9 out of 5. These reviews highlight the quality of its academic programs, the personalized attention given to each student, and the flexibility provided by online learning.

Similarly, the Trustpilot review website, which verifies and validates the authenticity of each published review, has awarded it the highest rating, establishing TECH Global University as the absolute academic reference at the international level. TECH Global University has received a score of 4.9 out of 5, based on more than 4,000 reviews.

This score corresponds to the “Excellent” rating, the highest a teaching institution can obtain on Trustpilot. The company explains that its methodology is based on evaluating various factors such as the quantity, quality, and age of the reviews received. In addition to the individual feedback from students, the frequency of reviews about the services provided is also considered. This evaluation considers the university’s commitment to obtaining constant feedback from its students.

On the other hand, on leading job search platforms like Indeed and InfoJobs, TECH Global University stands out for the positive reviews given by employees and collaborators, highlighting the professional environment and growth opportunities within the institution. As with other platforms, it holds the highest rating, 4.9 out of 5, and ranks as the highest-rated university after more than 6,000 reviews.

TECH Global University, a leader in employability with a 99% employment rate

There are several reasons behind the success of TECH Global University, the largest digital university in the world, on opinion portals. Susana Morales, an alumna of the Master’s in Neurosciences, highlights that “the university provides top-notch content, ensuring superior quality in the acquisition of skills.” In this context, thousands of reviews emphasize the quality of the institution’s teaching, as well as its personalized and effective attention.

Other graduates, such as Alessandro Pellegri from Rome, note the possibility of “studying at one’s own pace.” Similarly, Elizabeth Henderson, an alumna of the Master’s in Aesthetic Medicine, claims that the best feature of the program is its “professional orientation, addressing the current needs of each clinical area.” These opinions align with the numerous recognitions received by TECH Global University, which has also been recognized as a Google Partner Premier, a distinction awarded to only 3% of companies.

In a digitalized world, more people are choosing to take advantage of online platforms to specialize or update in high-demand areas that were once confined to rigid classrooms with fixed schedules. According to the latest reports from Research and Markets, the e-learning market is projected to generate approximately $701 billion in revenue by 2030, with an estimated compound annual growth rate of 14.6% for the period from 2026 to 2030.

These figures confirm the growing preference for online education over traditional models. In this context, user ratings are a decisive factor when choosing one university over another. According to a study by Trusted Shops, 97% of users look for reviews from other consumers before purchasing a product online, a trend that also holds true in the education sector.

TECH Global University, the largest digital university in the world

TECH is the world’s largest online university. With an impressive catalog of more than 14,000 educational programs available in 11 languages, it is positioned as a leader in employability, with a 99% job placement rate.

It is officially recognized in America, such as TECH Universidad (Mexico). It also has a strong presence in Africa, with TECH RUCU University (Tanzania) and TECH Euromed University (Morocco), and in Europe through TECH Global University (Andorra) and TECH Universidad (Spain).

Thanks to its international scope, TECH has a presence in more than 150 countries and has twice been recognized by the Financial Times as one of the 250 fastest-growing companies in Europe in recent years.

On the other hand, the prestigious Forbes magazine has distinguished it as the “world’s best online university,” highlighting its innovative learning methodology, Relearning, as well as the implementation of the Harvard Case Method.

In addition, it boasts an Ivy League faculty, at the level of Harvard or Stanford. Its more than 6,000 professors work in the best companies, organizations and institutions in the world. The largest multinationals (Amazon, Apple, Google, Nike…), the best hospitals (Mayo Clinic, MD Anderson Cancer Center…) and the best sports institutions (Boston Celtics, Dallas Cowboys…) collaborate with their best professionals to lead TECH’s academic programs.

The quality of its digital infrastructure and its high educational standards have been recognized by Google with Google Premier Partner status, a distinction reserved only for the top 3% of online institutions.

TECH is also considered the top-rated university by its students, with an average rating of 4.9 out of 5 in more than 25,000 public ratings on leading international portals.

World.title: Borrowed Majesties: Why Paramount Chiefs Are Afraid of Chief Mukuni
World.content:
By Kapya Kaoma

Judge Pixie Yangailo’s refusal to grant Chitimukulu, the Litunga, and Undi joinder in Chief Mukuni’s petition seeking paramount-chief status is a major blow to the “traditional” establishment. The chiefs have reasons to be nervous: this case could be revolutionary. It has the potential to transform the very definition of paramount chieftainship.

It is telling that the trio’s anxiety hinges upon how “junior chiefs” might interpret Mukuni’s victory—it would “destabilize traditional governance.” What they omit, however, is that the creation of paramount chiefs by colonial rulers was itself an act of social destabilization.

Until the colonial era, the concept of a “junior chief” did not exist among the Tonga. The same is true for the Chishinga and other tribes. Every paramount chief in postcolonial Zambia is a product of colonial policy of divide et impera (divide-and-rule) often associated with Frederick Lugard. The trio is deeply afraid because someone is finally questioning an injustice passed off as ancient tradition. Yet nothing socially constructed remains scrutinized. What was constructed can be deconstructed and reconstructed.

Reading Chief Mukuni’s petition, it seems his claim rests primarily on “tradition” rather than ethno-history. It is unclear whether this legal strategy is deliberate, given that tradition is manufactured over time. Yet the claims of the Litunga, Chitimukulu, and Undi over vast territories similarly lack ethno-historical foundation. Instead, their status rests on an assumed history of conquest and the subjugation of neighboring groups. Paramount chieftainship historically had less to do with organic tribal conquest than with fulfilling the colonial administrative agenda.

As a Tonga, for example, Chief Mukuni cannot claim his ancestors defeated other Tonga groups in battle to establish political hegemony. Traditionally, the Tonga were acephalous societies–they never had kings or chiefs. Instead, authority was decentralized around sikatongos (or bami ba mfula)—“owners of rain”—whose responsibility was rainmaking.

Because Tonga life depended on balanced rainfall for their two season harvest, sikatongos whose lands received better rains attracted larger communities, as was the case with Monze and Mweemba. Yet, because a sikatongo’s authority was derived from local ancestors (basangu), his influence didn’t extend beyond his immediate neighborhood. In Tonga cosmology, ancestral reach is strictly bound to ancestral land—a principle still celebrated during the Lwiindi ceremony. Moreover, historically, the Tonga were known for their resistance to any centralized monarch.

Two historical forces disrupted this sociopolitical organization: slave raiding and colonialism. Because the Tonga lacked centralized military structures, they were vulnerable to slave raiders. In response, charismatic sikatongos began organizing defensive alliances. Then came European colonialism. David Livingstone was among the first to label Mweemba and Monze as Tonga “chiefs,” even though the title and its political implications were alien to Tonga society. The term sikatongo does not translate to “king” or “chief.”

Colonial authorities later codified select sikatongos into official chiefs, granting them arbitrary authority over neighboring communities. Today, that administrative convenience is celebrated as authentic Tonga culture. Mukuni’s claim rests in this frame. Yet, like the office of paramount chief itself, Mukuni’s current area of authority was codified by the state as opposed to unbroken lineage.

No doubt Mukuni is making a clever calculation. With Hakainde Hichilema in power, he sees a window for elevation. This is what Chitimukulu, the Litunga, and Undi fear most–the very state system that elevated their offices could now elevate others or dismantle their exclusive status.

They have enjoyed unchecked top-tier authority for over a century, but Mukuni is stubborn enough to challenge the setup. If he succeeds, other leaders may seek to undo these social imbalances. Hence they are losing sleep–”official” history could be rewritten in a courtroom—ending in the creation of “Paramount Chief Mukuni.”

I believe Chief Mukuni would likely strengthen his claim by grounding his case in the political history of Zambian chieftainship rather than relying solely on “tradition.” As I have noted, cultural experts can easily contest traditional claims due to a lack of ethno-historical evidence. However, the political argument can hardly be refuted: no Zambian paramount chief historically exercised total control over all the territories and sub-chiefs currently assigned to them. Those regional monopolies were constructed by colonial and postcolonial bureaucracies.

So just as provinces, districts, and constituencies are regularly redrawn to reflect modern realities, there is no logical reason to treat colonial-era paramount titles as immutable. There is nothing ancient about the office of paramount chief—a reality symbolized even by the Litunga’s colonial-British-inspired ceremonial uniform.

Because tradition is fluid, paramount chieftaincy was meant to support narratives of domination. Over time, these constructs were ritualized to marginalize and subordinate other traditional leaders.

Who doesn’t know that history is written by the powerful, while truths remain buried with the powerless? If paramount chieftainships were created by colonialists, shouldn’t contemporary realities invite modernized structures? This question extends beyond Chief Mukuni. It is an issue all “junior” traditional leaders could bring before the Constitutional Court.

Even if Chief Mukuni loses, he is forcing us to question whether colonial structures should be treated as sacred texts. Is it time to re-evaluate the institution of paramount chieftainship today?

It takes stubborn people to expose the blind spots of cultural assumptions. This is what Chief Mukuni is doing.

World.title: Farmers cautioned against selling their entire harvest
World.content:
BuyZed Campaign Founder and Chief Executive Officer Evans Ng’oma says Zambians could face higher food prices if the impending El Niño disrupts local food production.

Mr Ng’oma has implored the government to put in place measures aimed at safeguarding the country’s abundant food stocks, following a bumper maize harvest of close to five million metric tonnes.

He told the media in an interview today, that farmers should resist the temptation to sell off their entire harvest and instead retain sufficient maize stocks for household and national food security.

Mr Ng’oma noted that Zambia is currently enjoying a bumper harvest of close to five million metric tonnes, giving the country an opportunity to build reserves before possible El Niño-induced production challenges emerge.

He has urged small-scale and commercial farmers to keep adequate stocks, while calling on the government to increase the Food Reserve Agency’s (FRA) maize purchases from the current 500,000 metric tonnes, to about three times the said quantity.

Mr Ng’oma explained that stronger reserves would help stabilise food supplies and cushion consumers from possible price shocks if local production declines.

He has also called for improved storage facilities by the FRA, saying reduced post-harvest losses is critical to ensuring that the country has sufficient food reserves to withstand possible disruptions, as well as ensuring that more of the country’s maize remains available for both local consumption and export.

Meanwhile, Mr Ngoma has urged farmers to prepare for the anticipated erratic rainfall by planting drought-tolerant and early-maturing crop varieties and adopting water-conserving practices such as potholing.

He encouraged farmers to also seek guidance from agricultural camp officers on measures to mitigate the effects of the El Niño.

BuyZed Founder has further called for greater diversification away from maize, particularly through increased production of sorghum, which he says is better suited to extreme weather conditions.

Mr N’goma has since urged the government to consider providing small-scale farmers with sorghum seed through the Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP), to help strengthen food security and reduce dependence on maize.
