World.title: Falklands Post Office celebrates 10th Anniversary of the Blue Belt Program
World.content:
Falklands Post Office celebrates 10th Anniversary of the Blue Belt Program

14th Monday, September 2026 - 02:55 UTC Full article

The UK Overseas Territories (OTs) are home to 90% of the UK’s biodiversity. Since its launch in 2016, the UK Blue Belt Program has worked in partnership with OTs’ Governments to enhance the protection and sustainable management of these unique marine environments, marking a decade of collaborative ocean stewardship. In total, 4,309,000 km² of the world’s oceans are protected by the Blue Belt Program. That is an area 18 times the size of the UK. Falklands Post Office celebrates such an achievement with the release of specific stamps issues.

Operating in some of the most remote and biologically rich regions on Earth, the Program brings together science, monitoring, compliance and capacity building to support long-term ocean management. Through this partnership approach, it has helped establish and strengthen large-scale Marine Protected Areas (MPAs), improve fisheries sustainability, and develop the evidence base needed for adaptive, ecosystem-based management.

This work reflects a shared commitment to safeguarding marine ecosystems while supporting sustainable use for future generations. Over the past ten years, the Blue Belt Program has continued to evolve, strengthening its focus through three key pillars: climate, nature and people. Together, these priorities support the protection of marine ecosystems, improve resilience to environmental change, and ensure that science and management underpin sustainable use of the ocean.

This work continues to be supported by leading UK delivery partners, including the Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (Cefas) and the Marine Management Organization (MMO). The South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands Marine Protected Area (SGSSI MPA), one of the largest in the world at 1.24 million km², is home to some of the planet’s most biologically rich marine ecosystems. Established in 2012 and strengthened through regular review, the MPA was further enhanced in 2025 with a major expansion of No Take Zones, now covering over 470,000 km², alongside additional closures that ensure krill fishing is now prohibited across more than half a million km². Supporting a highly productive and biodiverse Southern Ocean ecosystem, the SGSSI MPA sustains species from plankton to whales and serves as a natural laboratory for climate research. Evidence-based management, including a complete ban on bottom trawling, extensive No-Take Zones and strictly regulated, MSC certified sustainable fisheries, ensure this is one of the most effectively protected ecosystems globally.

These stamps celebrate the Blue Belt Program’s three pillars through examples from South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands. £1.25 - Climate: Glacier Glaciers are a defining feature of South Georgia’s landscape and are highly sensitive indicators of climate change. Rapid glacial retreat across the island reflects wider warming trends in the Southern Ocean, influencing freshwater input, coastal habitats and ocean circulation. Monitoring these changes helps improve understanding of how climate-driven processes affect marine ecosystems and the species that depend upon them. £1.40 – Nature: Northern Giant Petrel The northern giant petrel is a wide-ranging pelagic bird and an important higher predator within the Southern Ocean ecosystem. Breeding at South Georgia in significant numbers, these birds play a key ecological role in nutrient cycling and food web dynamics. Long-term monitoring of their populations provides valuable insight into ecosystem health and the availability of prey species. £1.55 – Nature: Southern Elephant Seal South Georgia supports one of the largest breeding populations of southern elephant seals globally. They are important consumers of fish and squid, undertaking long foraging migrations across the Southern Ocean.

As top predators, their population trends and foraging behavior may act as key indicators of changes in the marine environment, particularly in relation to prey availability and climate variability. £1.85 – People: Science at King Edward Point Scientific research is critical to the effective management of the SGSSI MPA. At King Edward Point, scientists from the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) conduct long-term monitoring and research programs that underpin evidence-based decision making. This work includes studying predator populations, tracking ecosystem change, and assessing the potential impacts of fisheries and climate change, ensuring that management measures remain robust and adaptive.

World.title: Taste of Mexico: The curious history and myths of chile en nogada
World.content:
September, known as the “mes patrio” or patriotic month, has begun. This is the month when Mexicans commemorate the consummation of our independence, which took place in 1821. During the official celebration on Sept. 15, the president reenacts the way the independence movement began with what we call the “grito” — the cry of independence.

We also celebrate the grito at home, accompanied by family and friends. We dress up to look even more Mexican with sombreros, fake mustaches and braids. We drink tequila, sing Mexican songs, shout “Viva México” and, of course, eat.

Perhaps the most famous seasonal dish, and the one that generates the most intrigue for me, is chile en nogada.



The dish is essentially a stuffed poblano pepper covered in a walnut sauce. The stuffing is a mixture of beef with fruits such as apple, peach, banana and pear, along with almonds, pine nuts, walnuts, onion and garlic. Its flavor profile, combining sweet and salty, is outstanding.

And now, the intriguing part

As a historian, I am fascinated by how official history is shaped, and I find it puzzling that chile en nogada is included in September’s menu as the quintessential Mexican dish.

According to information from an official government page, on Aug. 28, 1821, the Augustinian nuns of the Convent of Santa Mónica in the state of Puebla welcomed the first Emperor of independent Mexico, Agustín de Iturbide, with a newly created dish that represented the colors of the new national flag: green, white and red. This, the tale goes, is how chile en nogada came to be.

The historical records, however, tell a different story: Agustín de Iturbide did travel to Puebla in 1821, but he arrived on Aug. 5. The list of supplies purchased for the emperor’s reception shows that the ingredients needed to make the chile en nogada weren’t acquired, so it is highly unlikely that he ever tried the dish. Nevertheless, he did enjoy a splendid banquet.

The idea that the nuns created the dish for Iturbide is a myth: Historical records indicate that the recipe was already being prepared in the early 1800s. Researcher Lilia Martínez has discovered that nogada is a European sauce with documented origins going back to the 15th century.

It’s important to note that without the Spanish Conquest, this dish would be impossible, since most of the ingredients used in chile en nogada originate in Spain or were brought over in the intercontinental trade of the time. These ingredients include the English walnut, a protein option of pork, beef or chicken, pomegranate, almonds, apples, pears, peaches and bananas.

The poblano pepper is the sole ingredient native to this land — a huge and vital contribution, if I may add.

So why is it considered the quintessential Mexican dish?

“Je ne sais pas,” the French would say. Wouldn’t it make much more sense if we ate a mole madre or a “tlacoyo?” Or maybe we eat it because it’s the conjunction of two great culinary traditions. Regardless of the reason, I can promise you two things: first, it is one of the most delicious dishes in Mexican cuisine you’ll ever try. Second, once I find out when it became the quintessential Mexican dish, I will create a video and write an article about it.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mexico News Daily (@mexiconewsdaily)

Where can you eat it?

Any Mexican restaurant will have its version of chile en nogada. However, in my opinion, the best chiles I’ve had are found in Puebla. If you can’t go there, look for a thick, ivory-white sauce on your plate, and you’ll probably have an amazing chile en nogada.

I considered sharing the recipe, but every family has its own version, and I don’t want to offend anyone by claiming that mine is the ultimate recipe. This recipe is over three centuries old, from a time when people had the luxury of peeling walnuts with their fingernails and taking time to appreciate the landscape, so it requires a lot of time and patience; as in, two whole days. My parents had two comadres who prepared chile en nogada for the entire family, a party of 80 including us. A group of six women had to spend a whole week in the kitchen. We were fortunate, no doubt.



Do you have a good chile en nogada recipe to share with us, or is the one you use a family secret? Do you know where the best chile en nogada can be found? Share in the comments below.

María Meléndez is a writer and art historian. She works at the Mexican Cultural Institute of the Embassy of Mexico in Washington, D.C.

World.title: El Jalapeño: Dairy war between Chiapas, Oaxaca escalates over ‘world’s biggest cheese ball’
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

PIJIJIAPAN, Chiapas — Relations between southern regional neighbors in Mexico reached a historic low Thursday following a massive front-line fromage offensive by Chiapas cheesemakers, who ambushed Oaxaca by constructing a 1,611-kilogram ball of quesillo to reclaim their Guinness World Record for the “world’s biggest cheese ball,” escalating a long-simmering border dispute into an all-out dairy arms race.

The offensive in the coastal town of Pijijiapan neutralized Reyes Etla, Oaxaca’s 2024 record of 636.2 kilograms, effectively tripling the tonnage and signaling a strategic shift toward heavy-artillery curd production. Defense analysts confirmed the deployment required 15,500 liters of milk and four hours of continuous tactical winding on a custom-built metal platform designed to prevent structural failure under heat and humidity.

“This is no longer a matter of culinary pride; it is a full-scale declaration of dairy war,” said Chiapas cheesemaker Roberto Morales, addressing reporters near the massive sphere. “For over a year, Chiapas citizens lived under the psychological weight of a superior Oaxacan cheese ball. With this 1.6-metric-ton retaliation, we have fundamentally altered the balance of dairy power in southern Mexico.”

Defense officials in Oaxaca have yet to issue a formal surrender, though intelligence reports indicate high-level emergency meetings are underway in Reyes Etla. Observers spotted local agricultural logistics teams inspecting dairy reserves and evaluating blueprints for a potential 2,000-kilogram counter-ball ahead of the upcoming festival season.

Meanwhile, municipal officers in Pijijiapan face the formidable task of maintaining victory conditions before environmental factors intervene. “While our victory on the culinary battlefield is complete, we are now managing the post-battle logistics,” Morales added. “Specifically, the unraveling, portioning and consumption of 1.6 metric tons of high-density string cheese before ambient humidity forces a tactical retreat.”

World.title: Red threads, witches and upside-down tortillas: Mexican folk wisdom from our grandparents
World.content:
On Aug. 28, Mexico celebrated Grandparents’ Day, an annual tradition since 1983 that recognizes not only our grandparents’ boundless love, experience and wisdom, but also the invaluable contributions they make to Mexican families and communities.

In a country where many parents and caregivers work, grandparents often play a fundamental role in raising children, including picking them up from school, preparing their meals, and keeping them company or supervising them while their parents are away from the home. In fact, according to the University of Colima’s El Comentario, 30% of children in Mexico are cared for by their grandparents.

While capturing the full scope of their impact is nearly impossible, Mexico News Daily did its best, collecting stories from folks across Mexico about the lessons they learned from their grandparents. Some are amusing and quirky, while others are unexpected and confounding.

No matter their essence, though, each word chronicles the everyday wisdom and legacy of those who have left a deep and abiding impression for generations to come.

Pregnancy and babies

If you are pregnant and there is an eclipse, you must wear a safety pin on your belly to protect the baby.

If a pregnant woman has a craving and does not satisfy it, the baby will be born with the face of whatever she avoided eating.

Newborn babies should wear a red bracelet so that a witch will not suck on them.

Alicantes — a type of snake — hypnotize women who have recently given birth to steal their breast milk.

If a baby has a cough, fever or hiccups, the mother must stick a red thread to the baby’s forehead with saliva so it will go away.

If a baby has droopy cheeks, it is because they were made to sit up too early.

If you shave your baby’s head and rub tomato on it, their hair will grow back curly.

If a pregnant woman’s belly is egg-shaped, she will have a boy; if it is round, she will have a girl.

If you are pregnant and go to the beach, your child may be born with blue eyes.

Food

You should not eat watermelon at night because it bloats the stomach and is hard to digest.

If you do not eat what you are craving, you may get a sore on your tongue.

If you get up from the table before you have finished eating, your mouth may become crooked.

If you do not satisfy a craving, you may develop bile.

If you do not plant with enthusiasm, your harvest will not come in.

You must save the best ears of corn from the harvest to attract abundance.

You must rub the ends of a cucumber to remove “the poison:” meaning, its bitterness.

You should not drink plain water on an empty stomach when you are hungover, because it is harmful.

If you eat tortillas upside down, your insides will turn upside down.

Eat pozole with soda or tea, never with fruit-flavored water.

You have to scold or hit fruit trees so that they bear fruit.

To sleep better, drink warm milk before going to bed.

Witches and witchcraft

If you see red balls in the sky, they are witches . If they look close, the witch is far away; but if they look far away, she is close.

Rub an egg over your body to remove negative energy.

If La Llorona’s crying sounds close, it means she is far away; but if it sounds far away, it means she is close. La Llorona is an old legend about a mother who drowned her children in a river and, in sorrow, spends her nights crying for them. She is particularly associated with rivers, lakes and reservoirs.

Weather

If you bury a knife in the ground, you will prevent it from raining.

You should not bathe after an earthquake because the water has been “shaken.”

If you cross your eyes and a gust of air gets into them, they will stay that way forever.

You should not comb your hair, knit or embroider while it is raining, because lightning could strike you.

The first 12 days of the year predict what the weather will be like in each month: these are the famous cabañuelas .

Illnesses

To cure a sore throat, you have to rub roasted tomato on the chest and the soles of your feet.

To cure a cough, you have to iron some pieces of cloth, place them on the back and chest, and sleep with them warm.

Cold enters through the feet; that is why you should not walk barefoot inside the house.

You have to “cool” your eyes — by putting saliva in them — after watching television ; otherwise, you could go blind.

If you feel empachado — with indigestion or a blocked stomach — someone must massage your belly until that person begins to burp; that will relieve the bloating.

If a dog has a cough, you must put a necklace of limes around its neck so it will go away.

Death

If you are lying down, about to fall asleep, and a friend invites you out, you must say no; otherwise, you may encounter death.

If you hear an owl screeching, it means that someone you know will die.

Other beliefs

To cure espanto — a folk illness associated with fright — you must spit mezcal on the face of the person suffering from it while they sleep.

Espanto is cured by drinking a bitter beverage bought at the apothecary.

You should not buy underwear for your partner because it is bad luck: they might leave.

You should not sweep or do housework at night, because negative energy can enter or money can leave.

If you are going on a trip, you must leave a light on to prevent thieves from breaking in.

Stretching at the table is a way of thanking the devil.

You should not cut your hair after eating because it is harmful.

To make visitors leave soon, you must place a broom upside down behind the door.

Tell us in the comments: Did your grandparents have beliefs similar to these? Which ones do you think are true, and which ones are part of Mexican folklore?

María Ruiz is the Director of Digital Marketing at Mexico News Daily. She enjoys photographing her hometown of San Miguel de Allende in her spare time.

World.title: When Mexico bursts into bloom: A wildflower guide
World.content:
Mexico’s wildflowers astounded me … as if Mother Nature had rolled out the red carpet. Traveling through the central highlands in Querétaro and Guanajuato last September, the roadsides, fields and hillsides were covered in colorful blooms. It was a wow moment. Entire mountainsides shone in a patchwork of vibrant yellows, oranges, reds and pinks. Yet, six months earlier, when I passed through, the same mountainsides were dry, arid and sparse.

However, in September, an entirely different ecosystem lay before my eyes. So much so that I asked the driver to stop along the highway beneath the hillside of Mexican sunflowers. The blooms blanketed the landscape in a cheery yellow; he picked some for me after I shared that I was a botanical artist.

When to see the wildflowers

There are two wildflower seasons in Mexico. The first is in spring, from March to May, when arid regions like Baja California and northern deserts bloom after winter rains. These winter rains cause superblooms where desert plants bloom en masse and carpet the landscape.

The second wildflower season is in autumn, from September to November, after the rainy season throughout Mexico. Native plants put on a brilliant flowering display, bursting into bloom.

Of course, wildflower season may start a little earlier, or end a little later depending on the weather. Having been in Queretàro and Guanajuato in September for the last two years during the autumn wildflower season, I can tell you September is a great time to visit states in Central Mexico.

What flowers can you expect to see?

Cosmos, marigold, Mexican sunflowers, globe mallows, morning glory, salvias, mirasol and many more. From tiny butter daisy flowers blanketing the ground at your feet to the huge blooming shrubs of Mexican sunflowers looking you in the eye. There is a wide variety, from light happy yellows to deep striking purples.

Some flowers were a surprise to me. Like the soft baby pink hues of globe mallows. Not a plant that I had seen before. So, seeing a big patch was quite the sight. Another surprise was massive patches of happy pink cosmos. A popular garden plant, grown for its flowers, it was delightful to find out it is native to Mexico.

Seeing the stunning beauty of wildflowers transform the landscape, I knew there had to be symbolic meanings attached to these flowers.

My top 5

Someone asked me what my favorite flower was. It’s almost impossible to choose, but these five left the biggest impression. Especially the white poppy.

Chicalote, or Mexican white prickly poppy

The Chicalote, a native white prickly poppy, won my heart. Its delicate papery petals shining under the sun were so dreamy and elegant that I painted one. The delicate white petals symbolize tranquility, peaceful dreams and quiet rest.

These white prickly poppy flowers stand for endurance and resilience, peace and sleep.

Because the spiny plant thrives in dry, harsh and disturbed soils where other plants fail, to many it represents the ability to survive tough conditions through deep inner strength.

Mirasol, or cosmos

In a show-stopping display of vibrant pinks, cosmos put on quite a show. Huge patches waved to us along the roadside. Swaying on long feathery stalks as we passed. Another beautiful member of the daisy family, cosmos represents balance, peace and tranquility.

Also, cosmos is believed to act as a bridge between life and the afterlife, linking the physical world with the spiritual realm.

Girasol, or Mexican sunflower

Cherry sunflowers were by far the most common. Entire fields and mountainsides radiated in cheery yellow everywhere I went. This member of the daisy family represents faith, loyalty, and adoration.

Some Indigenous populations associated the flower’s bright face with solar deities. Aztec and Mexica people treated the plant as sacred. Dried sunflower seeds were left as offerings at major ceremonial sites like the Templo Mayor in Mexico City.

Mexican passionflower

Walking the streets of Queretàro, Mexican Passionflowers were abundantly climbing up trees or along old gates. This one was growing outside a church, which I found fitting, as they symbolize the Passion of Christ and the crucifixion.

The 10 petals and sepals represent the faithful apostles, while the corona filaments (seen as the purple inner ring) represent the crown of thorns. Inside, the three stigmas represent the nails, and the five anthers represent Christ’s wounds.

Copper globemallow

New to me, this member of the hibiscus family had me stopping for a closer look. The soft baby pink petals are as delightful as the velvety feel of its leaves. Flourishing in dry, harsh desert heat, the flower symbolizes endurance and resilience. Also standing as powerful emblems of hope, gentle comfort and vitality.

The best way to see them

Take a drive. These flowers line highways and laneways, lowlands and mountain ranges. So, by driving, you will see the greatest variety. I loved them all so much I made a quick sketchbook page with the most abundant. I hope you enjoy them as much as I have over the last couple of years.

Mexico Correspondent for International Living, Bel Woodhouse is an experienced writer, author, photographer and videographer with 500+ articles published both in print and across digital platforms. Living in the Mexican Caribbean for over seven years now, she’s in love with Mexico and has no plans to go anywhere anytime soon.

World.title: From the archive: Are Mexicans really always late?
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in December 2024 — is a humorous look at a stereotype regarding Mexicans and punctuality.

Before we get into the nuts and bolts regarding Mexican punctuality — or lack thereof — it’s important to clarify one thing. Mexicans are not actually always late.

That said, all stereotypes have to come from somewhere, don’t they? But like everything in life, there’s nuance to it.

Just like people all over the world, there’s room for a great deal of variety. Some people are always on time, and some people never are. Most people are punctual for certain activities, and unpunctual for others.

My dad, for instance, has never been punctual; I remember my mother saying she was terrified he wouldn’t make it to their wedding on time. My ex-husband also has challenges with punctuality, as does one of my best friends; I’ve spent great chunks of my adult life waiting hours.

I’m always super duper on time for everything, though I might let myself get to a party up to an hour late. My kid is leaning unpunctual, but I’m doing my damnedest to lecture it out of her. Because if there’s one thing kids love and respond to, it’s a good lecture.

Linguistic flexibility

One of the problems about even defining “late” is the language around defining time. For a deep dive into this, check out Joseph Sorrentino’s excellent piece on this specific type of vocabulary. Ahorita, al ratito, mañana … None of these words specify an actual time, you see? So “ahorita” could mean right this minute, and it could mean in five hours, or never. Al ratito (in a while) might mean in a couple of hours, or it might mean in a few years, depending on who’s saying it. You get the idea.

And really, this kind of language is useful because it allows for flexibility. In this way at least, Mexico is a flexible country.

Really, it has to be. Things come up that need tending to. Public transportation can be unpredictable. The opportunity to have a meal or talk to a pretty girl might come up. Your mom tells you to go fetch some things from the store, and you don’t tell her, “Sorry, I have plans.” Really, you just never know what can happen!

Life is unpredictable, and Mexicans have a fairly high tolerance for it being unpredictable, which is lucky for all of us.

Sometimes, though, there are things you must be on time for. And a good indicator of what those things are is whether or not there’s a specific time attached to them.

The meaning of ‘tolerancia’

School is one of those things. At my daughter’s school, for example, 8 a.m. is the official time kids have to be in the door. As a courtesy to the perpetually-late parents, there’s a “tolerance” of 10 minutes. To me, this means my daughter must be there before 8 a.m. if we’re not to be seen as rude and irresponsible. To others, it means 8:10 or even 8:11 is the limit. If kids aren’t in by that time, they must wait to enter the 9 a.m. class.

It was like this when I taught school here, too; some things, I suppose, are non-negotiable.

The same goes for official appointment times, even if the official or doctor you’re meeting isn’t exactly on time. So if you have a meeting with, say, immigration, you’d better be there at your appointment time! Some places will let you know that they have a tolerancia (literally, tolerance) of 10-15 minutes. This means that if you’re more than that amount of time late, you lose the appointment!

For other things, usually involving celebrations, arrival and start times are more flexible. This is especially true of parties, to which you can show up rather late without causing a fuss. Unless you’ve promised to bring something essential for the party, they’re just glad to have you there at some point. This doesn’t mean they’ll wait for you to start in on the cake and piñatas, though, so beware!

Clocks vs. cultural norms

Concerts and plays typically start within 15 to 30 minutes of their “official” start time; rock concerts might start hours after they’re meant to. Oh, well!

And if you’re meeting friends, it might depend on the specific circumstances. Are you meeting someone busy who only has a few minutes? Are you meeting them alone? In my group of mom friends, we always know that things can come up. “I’ll text you when I leave” is a good, flexible bridge that keeps people updated but keeps plans flexible.

In my own conservative and somewhat strict view, being on time means showing respect for the other person. If you are not on time, then you do not care about them or their time. And if you are on time, not only are you showing respect for them, but you’re making things easier for yourself, avoiding fluster. My cultural chauvinism is showing, I know.

But for plenty of people here, that’s a ridiculous notion. Why stress so much about being on time when literally anything can happen to make you not on time? Perhaps there’s a message here too about avoiding blame and responsibility. “Se me durmió el gallo” (The rooster went to sleep on me; as in, the rooster didn’t wake me up).

But that’s for another article. For now, I’ll leave you with a cute little proverb, as well as its juxtaposed, more truthful meme:

“Al que madruga, Dios le ayuda.” (The one who rises early receives God’s help.) It rhymes!

“Al que madruga, encuentra todo cerrado.” (The one who rises early finds everything closed.)

Truer words were never spoken.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, https://sarahedevries.substack.com/

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Exports and gas production hit record highs as patriotic spirit swells
World.content:
Listen to this article

Bilateral communications were front and center in Mexico the week of Sept. 7, with developments running the gamut from encouraging to combative. U.S. President Donald Trump’s remark that Mexico has “nothing” the United States needs beyond “hot tamales” and “tomatoes” caught fire over the weekend, unleashing a fresh round of provocations from Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio in the days that followed.

Mexico, however, continued to highlight trade and security collaboration with its northern neighbor, though the PISA test results and next year’s midterm elections sparked more conversations at home. Meanwhile, the annual inflation rate ticked up to 3.26% — as expected according to Banxico, which forecasts inflation of 3.5% by the end of 2026. President Claudia Sheinbaum remained optimistic through it all, especially as her administration makes its plans for 2027. Overhead, punishing heat baked Mexico’s northern border states even as monsoon rains drenched the Pacific coast and center of the country.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

2027 budget takes shape

On Monday, Finance Minister Édgar Amador Zamora submitted a 10.6-trillion-peso (US $627.8 billion) budget proposal for 2027 to Congress, an increase of about 1% in real terms over this year. Amador framed the package around “five pillars” — economic growth, protecting government priorities, strengthening revenue, more efficient spending and fiscal discipline. The government is banking on those pillars to shrink the budget deficit to 3.9% of GDP next year from an estimated 4.1% in 2026, even as public debt climbs to 55% of GDP. No new taxes or fuel-price hikes are planned.

Health care gets a 10.9% real-terms boost to 1.1 trillion pesos, largely for IMSS-Bienestar infrastructure and medicine supply, while education rises about 7% to 1.3 trillion pesos to fund new schools. Pension and welfare programs get just over 1 trillion pesos, and debt servicing alone eats up 1.6 trillion pesos — roughly one of every seven pesos the government spends. Security agencies see an 11.6% bump to 331.4 billion pesos, while Pemex funding falls 69.2% as the state oil company pushes toward self-sufficiency.

The National Electoral Institute (INE) is the biggest percentage winner of all, with an 87.5% real-terms increase ahead of 2027 midterm elections, while the Energy Ministry, the National Human Rights Commission and the Federal Electricity Commission absorb the steepest cuts. Sheinbaum said the following day that she is “very satisfied” with the package and that growth could exceed the official forecast of 1.5-2.5%, citing anticipated stability in trade relations with the U.S. and Canada.

Homicides continue to fall

Security officials reported this week that daily homicides fell 53% in August compared to September 2024, the final month of the López Obrador administration, making it the least violent August since 2015.

More than 67,000 people have been arrested for high-impact crimes since Sheinbaum took office, though Security Minister Omar García Harfuch cautioned that “the job is not done.” Days later, from Tuxtla Gutiérrez, the president highlighted a 63% drop in Chiapas’s homicide rate since Gov. Eduardo Ramírez Aguilar took office, alongside nearly 10,000 arrests in the southern state. The same briefing revealed the discovery of a clandestine hospital the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) used to treat injured members.

Olmeca Refinery notches record month

Pemex’s Olmeca Refinery in Tabasco posted its best month yet for fuel production in July, averaging 252,498 barrels per day, a 78.8% jump over June. Gasoline output rose even more sharply, up nearly 128% month-over-month, after equipment fires forced repairs earlier in the year. Despite the milestone, the plant — which began operating approximately two years ago — is still running at roughly two-thirds of its 340,000-bpd capacity.

Fox and PRI’s Alito Moreno join forces

In a striking political reunion, former President Vicente Fox met with PRI leader Alejandro “Alito” Moreno to discuss “the need to build a strong opposition” ahead of 2027 midterms — 26 years after Fox became the first opposition candidate to sweep the once-dominant PRI out of the presidency, and years after he called the party “black vipers, vermin and tadpoles.”

Morena, for its part, dismissed the pairing as “the reorganization of the power elite,” saying in a statement that “they change the names, they invent new organizations, but behind the facade, it’s the same old faces.” The PRI, which ruled Mexico for 71 years, now holds just two of the country’s 32 governorships — the same number as the much smaller Citizens Movement (MC) party.

At her Monday press conference, Sheinbaum branded the reunion “PRIAN” politics dating to the “neoliberal” era of former President Carlos Salinas de Gortari, and called Fox a “traitor of democracy” — a jab tied to his role in Mexico’s disputed 2006 election.

Bilateral high points

Trade and security cooperation produced some of the week’s more encouraging bilateral news. Mexico’s exports to the U.S. hit a monthly record in July: US $60.55 billion worth of goods were sent north, pushing Mexico’s share of the $332.92 billion U.S. import market above 18%.

Along the border, Mexican and U.S. forces carried out “High Eagle,” a binational operation to detect and disable drones cartels use to surveil authorities near Tijuana and San Diego. And though bad weather grounded Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s flight to Mexico City on Wednesday, he and Sheinbaum still held a video call on USMCA negotiations that Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard described as “cordial” and “very useful,” with talks on steel, aluminum and automotive tariffs continuing ahead of a fourth bilateral review round.

Bilateral low points

Other exchanges were considerably more combative. Over the weekend, Trump proposed to rename New Mexico “New America,” despite having no legal authority to rename a U.S. state, drawing pushback from the state’s Democratic leaders. Later in the week, from Ecuador, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio doubled down on claims that cartels control “vast territories” of Mexico, hinting the threat may eventually have to be “confronted one way or the other.” Sheinbaum shot back on Thursday morning, telling Rubio to keep Mexico out of U.S. midterm politics and calling his remarks electorally motivated. Rounding out the week, U.S. Vice President JD Vance labeled the Mexican flag “a symbol of the far left” after a protester interrupted his convention speech in Dallas, telling the man to “get your ass over there” if he loved Mexico so much.

Poor PISA scores spark a debate over screens

New results from the OECD’s Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), given to 7,843 students across 297 Mexican schools, showed that four in 10 15-year-olds — 41.8% — scored below the basic level in science, math and reading, more than double the 19.7% OECD average and Mexico’s worst showing since 2009.

Mexican students averaged 388 points in math, 408 in reading and 414 in science, all well below OECD averages of 463, 461 and 482, and the country has shed seven points in both math and reading since the 2022 test. The decline wasn’t unique to Mexico — the OECD’s education director called it part of a “dramatic” global drop, particularly in reading — and Mexican students still reported unusually high curiosity (80%, versus a 24% global average who called school “a waste of time”). Education International, the global teachers’ federation, pinned the broader slide on shrinking attention spans, heavy AI use and a worldwide teacher shortage. China, Singapore, South Korea, Estonia and Canada topped the rankings.

Education Minister Mario Delgado blamed excessive screen use for the drop in reading comprehension — arguing that “screens make it easy to ‘read’ or consume images” — while defending the New Mexican School curriculum model and promoting traditional games like yo-yos, marbles and spinning tops as a substitute for phone time. He conceded the PISA sample was “statistically representative” even as he questioned whether the test amounts to a comprehensive evaluation of Mexican education. Sheinbaum later told reporters Mexico will roll out new math and reading textbooks next year, including poems and short stories, and push a “return to pencil and paper,” tying the effort to new national guidelines already restricting cellphone use in schools.

Education Ministry, UNESCO team up on AI in schools

Also this week, Mexico’s Education Ministry signed a letter of intent with UNESCO to guide the “responsible” rollout of artificial intelligence in classrooms, with the U.N. body offering technical assistance, teacher training and research support. Officials said the goal is to ensure AI supports, rather than substitutes for, teaching and critical thinking, and the deal also opens the door to new rules on cellphone use in schools.

Mexico prepares for El Grito and Independence Day

With the country’s 216th independence anniversary approaching, more than 18,000 members of Mexico’s armed forces are readying for the Sept. 16 military parade through Mexico City, featuring drones, horses, dogs and a float marking the country’s World Cup hosting duties this past June and July. The holiday kicks off the night before, with Sheinbaum leading the Grito de Independencia from the National Palace balcony and Tejano band Intocable headlining a concert in the Zócalo.

Festivities and gritos will ring out from cities across the country, including in Sinaloa, whose capital city of Culicán will hold a public celebration of Independence Day for the first time in two years.

Points of 🇲🇽 pride

A 20-year-old engineering student from a Chihuahua farming family, Luis Ángel Robles Morales, won a national innovation award for an irrigation filter that is already helping 500 drought-stricken farmers use water more efficiently.

Forward Julián Quiñones and Club América’s Scarlett Camberos earned historic Ballon d’Or nominations, marking the first time two Mexican players — and a Mexican club — have featured on the shortlist for world soccer’s top individual honor.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Los Cafres Bring Nearly Forty Years of Reggae to Lima on 19 September
World.content:
PERU · LIVE MUSIC

Key Facts — The date Saturday 19 September 2026. The show is expected to begin at 8 p.m. Lima time.

— The venue Circulo Militar del Peru, Sede Salaverry, in Jesus Maria. It is an open-air field.

— The tickets Teleticket sells Campo B at 220 soles and Campo A at 360, about US$65 and US$107.

— The band Formed in Buenos Aires in 1987 and fronted by Guillermo Bonetto. Fifteen albums.

— The set Billed as a retrospective across more than thirty-five years, not a single-album tour.

— The catch Standing only, no seating tier, and no re-entry. Dress for Lima’s damp September nights.

They recorded the first roots reggae album sung in Spanish. Nearly four decades later they are still touring it.

Jesus Maria. The venue is a military club’s grounds, a short walk from the Campo de Marte. (Photo: “2017 Lima – Jardines del Campo de Marte” by Felipe Restrpo Acosta, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

Los Cafres play Lima on Saturday 19 September 2026. The venue is the Circulo Militar del Peru at its Salaverry site, in the district of Jesus Maria.

The show is expected to start at 8 p.m. Lima time and to run about four hours. Teleticket has not published a separate doors time.

Tickets are sold in two zones. Campo B costs 220 soles, about US$65, and Campo A costs 360 soles, about US$107.

Why This Band Matters

Los Cafres formed in Buenos Aires in 1987. The singer Guillermo Bonetto has fronted them for almost the whole of that time.

Their 1994 debut Frecuencia Cafre was mixed at Tuff Gong Studios in Kingston, the studio Bob Marley built. It is credited as the first roots reggae album conceived by an Argentine band.

It is also widely described as the first roots reggae record sung in Spanish anywhere. That claim is why the band occupies the position it does.

Rolling Stone named their 1995 album Instinto the best record in the history of Argentine reggae. The 2004 album Quien da mas took them from a scene to the mainstream.

Fifteen albums have followed, with three gold certifications and one platinum. The Lima show is billed as a career retrospective.

The Ticket Prices That Changed

A price range of 154 to 288 soles has circulated since the concert was announced in June. It is no longer what anyone pays.

The 154-soles figure was a thirty per cent presale price for Campo B. The 288-soles figure is the discounted rate for holders of a Peruvian disability certificate.

Current regular pricing is 220 soles for Campo B and 360 soles for Campo A. Those are about US$65 and US$107.

Neither zone had sold out as of Monday. Teleticket releases electronic tickets two days before the event, not at purchase.

Miraflores. Most visitors stay here, about twenty minutes from the venue by taxi. (Photo: “Lima, Peru – Modern Highrises (Miraflores)” by Stvabod

What the Venue Is Actually Like

The Circulo Militar is a military club, and the Salaverry site is a large open ground rather than a theatre. Concerts there are held on the field.

That has one consequence visitors regularly miss. Both ticket zones are standing, and there is no seating tier at any price.

There is also no re-entry once you are inside. Plan food and anything else you need before you go through the gate.

The entrance is at the junction of Jiron Pachacutec and Avenida Cayetano Heredia. Jesus Maria is a walkable middle-class district just inland from the historic centre.

Dressing for a Lima September

September falls inside Lima’s garua season, the coastal fog that sits over the city for much of the year. Nights run damp and grey.

Expect something between fifteen and eighteen degrees Celsius, roughly sixty to sixty-five Fahrenheit, once the sun is down. It rarely rains, but the air holds moisture.

For an open field with no cover, that means a layer. Visitors arriving from the Andes or from Brazil consistently underdress for it.

A Second Show the Same Day

The Peruvian singer Milena Warthon plays the Parque de la Exposicion the same Saturday, starting at 4.30 p.m. Lima time. The two venues sit ten to fifteen minutes apart by taxi.

That makes both possible in one afternoon and evening. It is an unusual overlap and worth knowing if you are planning a weekend.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where do Los Cafres play in Lima?

Saturday 19 September 2026 at the Circulo Militar del Peru, Salaverry site, in Jesus Maria. The show is expected to begin at 8 p.m. Lima time.

How much are tickets?

Campo B costs 220 soles, about US$65, and Campo A costs 360 soles, about US$107, through Teleticket. Both zones were still available as of Monday.

Why do I see lower prices quoted elsewhere?

The 154 to 288 soles range published in June mixed a presale discount with the rate for holders of a Peruvian disability certificate. Neither is the current regular price.

Is there seating?

No. Both zones are standing on an open field, and there is no seating tier at any price. There is also no re-entry once you are inside.

Who are Los Cafres?

An Argentine reggae band formed in Buenos Aires in 1987. Their 1994 debut is credited as the first roots reggae album sung in Spanish.

World.title: The Cast of La Reina del Flow Plays Buenos Aires Tonight
World.content:
ARGENTINA · LIVE MUSIC

Key Facts — The dates Monday 14 and Tuesday 15 September 2026, both at 9 p.m. Buenos Aires time. Monday sold out in June.

— The venue Movistar Arena, Humboldt 450, Villa Crespo. It holds roughly 15,000 people.

— Who performs The series cast, including Carlos Torres and Majo Vargas. Carolina Ramírez appears as a guest.

— The tickets Sold through the arena’s own site. Face value starts at 70,000 pesos, about US$46.

— The tour It opened in Santiago on 7 September 2026 and reaches Caracas in November.

— The catch Resale sites quote three to six times face value. Buy from the arena, not a reseller.

It is not a musical and not a tribute act. The people who played the parts sing the songs.

The Movistar Arena sits in Villa Crespo, a residential pocket west of Palermo. (Photo: “Estadio Malvinas Argentinas” by Fozza, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.)

Buenos Aires gets a show tonight that is easy to describe wrongly. La Reina del Flow en Concierto starts at 9 p.m. local time.

It is not a musical with a replacement cast. It is not a tribute act either.

The actors from the Colombian telenovela perform the series’ songs themselves, wrapped in narrative, choreography and large-format video.

Who Is Actually on Stage

Carlos Torres, who played Charly Flow, and Majo Vargas, who plays Yeimy Montoya on stage. Juan Manuel Restrepo, Kevin Bury, Juan Palau and Jay Torres complete the line-up.

Carolina Ramírez played the adult Yeimy in the series. She appears as a special guest rather than as the lead.

That distinction matters and has caused confusion. In February it was reported she would skip the world tour altogether.

Caracol Televisión later confirmed a special participation, restated in Argentine press on 9 September 2026. She is confirmed for Buenos Aires, Córdoba and Mar del Plata.

Why a Telenovela Fills an Arena

La Reina del Flow ran on Caracol from 2018 and became one of the most exported Colombian series of the decade. Netflix carried it worldwide.

Its plot runs on original reggaeton and urban tracks rather than on a licensed soundtrack. The songs became hits in their own right.

That is the difference. A drama with a score does not tour, a drama that generated a catalogue can.

Expect Perdóname, Reflejo, Fénix and Que arda el fuego. The reunion of Yeimy and Charly is the marketed centrepiece.

Villa Crespo. The streets around the arena are residential, so plan your exit before the encore. (Photo: “BarraCasaTinta-1” by Ezarate, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

Tickets, and the Resale Trap

Sales run through the arena’s own site, which opened on 10 June 2026. Official face value starts at 70,000 Argentine pesos, roughly US$46.

The full official price ladder is not published. Only the entry tier is advertised.

One resale site currently lists the same show between about 252,000 and 441,000 pesos, roughly US$167 to US$292. That is secondary pricing, not face value.

Monday sold out in June. Tuesday was added because of it and was close to selling out over the weekend.

If you are reading this on Monday, Tuesday is the realistic option. Buy from the arena.

Getting to Villa Crespo

The Movistar Arena is at Humboldt 450, in Villa Crespo. That is a residential neighbourhood west of Palermo, not a nightlife strip.

Subte Line B is the practical approach, from either Malabia or Ángel Gallardo. Both are a walk of roughly ten minutes.

The building is fully covered and mixes seating with a standing floor. September evenings in Buenos Aires still run cool, so the roof helps.

Because the surrounding streets are residential, taxi supply thins out after the show. Book before the encore.

What a Newcomer Should Know About the Venue

The Movistar Arena opened in 2019 on the site of an older stadium. It is run by the same operator as several arenas across the region.

Security screening is thorough and queues build from about an hour before. Doors times are not published for this show, which is normal here.

Bars inside take cards. Argentine venues have largely moved away from cash, which catches out visitors carrying pesos.

Where the Tour Has Been

The run opened in Santiago de Chile on 7 September 2026 at that city’s own Movistar Arena. It drew more than 12,500 and had sold out weeks ahead.

Lima followed on 12 September 2026. The Spanish leg earlier in the year drew a reported 120,000 across its dates.

After Buenos Aires the tour plays Córdoba on 18 September 2026 and Mar del Plata on 19 September. Mexico City, Guadalajara, Monterrey and Bogotá follow in October.

Caracas closes the Latin American run on 7 November 2026. For readers elsewhere in the region, there is time.

More: Argentina news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is this a musical or a concert?

A concert. The actors from the series perform its songs live, with narrative, choreography and video, rather than a staged book musical or a tribute act.

Does Carolina Ramírez perform?

Yes, but as a special guest rather than the lead. Majo Vargas plays Yeimy Montoya on stage for the tour.

Is it sold out?

Monday 14 September 2026 sold out in June. Tuesday 15 September 2026 was added in response and was close to selling out over the weekend.

How much are tickets?

Official face value starts at 70,000 Argentine pesos, about US$46. Resale listings run several times higher and are not face value.

How do I get to the Movistar Arena?

Take Subte Line B to Malabia or Ángel Gallardo and walk about ten minutes. The arena is at Humboldt 450 in Villa Crespo.

World.title: Balaclava Fest Doubles to Two Days in São Paulo on 26 September
World.content:
BRAZIL · LIVE MUSIC

Key Facts — The dates Saturday 26 and Sunday 27 September. Doors at 3pm, curfew at 11pm, over-16s only.

— The venue Tokio Marine Hall in Santo Amaro, southern São Paulo. Capacity is about 4,000.

— The headliners Blonde Redhead on Saturday. DIIV and Beach Fossils share Sunday, with sixteen acts across the weekend.

— The tickets Ingresse sells online. Takkø Café in Vila Buarque sells the same tickets without the booking fee.

— The stages Two stages, deliberately staggered. No act clashes with another, which is rare at this size.

— The catch Published prices come from one aggregator, not the seller. Check Ingresse before you budget.

Fifteen editions in one day each. The sixteenth takes two, and the line-up explains why.

Tokio Marine Hall. The room has been HSBC Brasil and Tom Brasil under previous owners. (Photo: “Sandy – Meu Canto Tom Brasil 31” by Teca Lamboglia, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.)

Balaclava Fest has run fifteen times as a single-day event. The sixteenth edition takes a whole weekend, on 26 and 27 September.

Doors open at 3pm both days and the site closes at 11pm. Entry is restricted to over-16s.

The venue is Tokio Marine Hall at Rua Bragança Paulista 1281, in Santo Amaro. It holds roughly 4,000 people.

The Line-Up, Day by Day

Saturday 26 September runs Blonde Redhead, Dry Cleaning, Pedro The Lion and bar italia. Wishy, Liv.e, Sharp Pins and Ludovic fill the rest.

Sunday 27 September brings DIIV, Beach Fossils, Wednesday and High Vis. Sudan Archives, Winona Riders, Adorável Clichê and Budang complete it.

That is sixteen acts across two stages. The organisers have staggered the set times so that nothing clashes.

Anyone who has spent a festival choosing between two bands will understand why that matters. At this scale it is unusual.

Why These Names Travel

Blonde Redhead have been running since 1993, formed in New York by an Italian brother pair and a Japanese singer. They are the closest thing here to an institution.

DIIV and Beach Fossils both come out of the Brooklyn guitar scene of the early 2010s. Their audiences overlap heavily, which is why they share a day.

Dry Cleaning arrive from London with spoken-word vocals over post-punk. Pedro The Lion is the long-running project of the American songwriter David Bazan.

The Brazilian acts are not filler. Adorável Clichê and Winona Riders both draw their own crowds in São Paulo.

Central São Paulo. The festival site is well south of here, in the Santo Amaro business district. (Photo: “Catedral da Sé em São Paulo” by Wilfredor, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.)

Who Runs It

Balaclava Fest is put on by Balaclava Records, a São Paulo independent label and promoter. It is not a corporate festival brand.

That shows in the booking. The bill favours acts with committed audiences over acts with radio play.

The move to two days doubles the size of the event. It is the largest thing the label has attempted.

Tickets and the Number We Will Not Vouch For

Online sales run through Ingresse. Tickets are also sold in person at Takkø Café, Rua Major Sertório 553, Vila Buarque, with no booking fee.

Reported prices run from about R$350 for standing, roughly US$68, up to about R$980 for a box, roughly US$191. Tiers rise as each batch sells.

We found those figures on a single festival-listings site rather than on the seller. Treat them as indicative and check Ingresse yourself.

Half-price entry is offered to students, people with disabilities and low-income young people. A separate discount applies to anyone donating a kilo of non-perishable food.

A two-day combo pass exists and includes priority entry. As of 10 September both day tickets and the combo were in their final batches.

Getting There Without a Car

Santo Amaro is not where visitors usually end up at night. It is a business district in the southern zone, well away from the bars of Vila Madalena or Augusta.

The useful detail is the train. João Dias station on CPTM Line 9-Esmeralda is a short walk from the venue.

Line 9 runs along the Pinheiros river and connects to the metro at Pinheiros and Santo Amaro. That makes the site reachable from most of the city.

Check the last train before you commit. An 11pm curfew and a late-running final act can leave you relying on a ride app.

What the Room Is Like

Tokio Marine Hall opened as HSBC Brasil in 2008 and spent seven years as Tom Brasil. The name changes with the sponsor, the room does not.

It is a covered hall with a mix of standing floor, raised seating and boxes. That structure is why the ticket tiers vary so widely.

For a September weekend in São Paulo, a roof is worth paying for. Spring here is wet.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is Balaclava Fest 2026?

Saturday 26 and Sunday 27 September 2026, at Tokio Marine Hall in Santo Amaro, São Paulo. Doors open at 3pm both days and the event ends at 11pm.

Who is headlining?

Blonde Redhead on Saturday, with DIIV and Beach Fossils on Sunday. Sixteen acts play across two stages, with set times staggered so that nothing clashes.

How much are tickets?

Reported prices run from about R$350, roughly US$68, to about R$980, roughly US$191. Those figures come from a listings site rather than the seller, so check Ingresse.

Where do I buy them?

Online through Ingresse, or in person at Takkø Café on Rua Major Sertório in Vila Buarque, where there is no booking fee.

How do I get to the venue?

Take CPTM Line 9-Esmeralda to João Dias station and walk. The venue is in the southern business district, not near the central nightlife areas.
