World.title: Retire in Mauritius as a Foreigner
World.content:
MAURITIUS · RETIREMENT

Key Facts — Age threshold 50 or above for the Residence Permit for Retired Non-Citizens.

— Financial test US$24,000 in a certified bank statement, or guaranteed income of US$2,000 a month.

— Permit term Ten years, renewable for another ten. A 20-year permanent permit becomes available after five years.

— The property number US$375,000. Above it, a qualifying purchase carries residency for the buyer and dependants.

— Income tax Zero on the first MUR 500,000, about US$10,650, then 10%, then 20% above MUR 1,000,000, about US$21,300.

— The American problem There is no Mauritius–United States tax treaty, and no Canadian one either.

Mauritius has built the most complete retirement offer in the Indian Ocean, and it is clearly designed with one group of retirees in mind. Working out whether you are in that group takes about five minutes and saves a great deal of trouble.

Retire in Mauritius as a Foreigner: Permits, Property and Tax

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesCost of living, safety, visas across Latin America › RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. × Best for expats Cost of living Safest places Easy visas Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Mauritius offers a ten-year retirement permit on a modest income test, no capital gains or inheritance tax on individuals, a tropical climate with a 4.3 degree gap between summer and winter, and a property route to residency. The fit depends almost entirely on which passport you hold.

The Retirement Permit, Precisely

The Residence Permit for Retired Non-Citizens is open to applicants aged 50 or above. The financial test at application is a certified bank statement from the country of origin or residence showing either a minimum of US$24,000 or a guaranteed minimum income of US$2,000 a month.

The permit runs for ten years and is renewable for a further ten. The renewal condition shifts in a way worth noticing: evidence is required of US$24,000 a year flowing into the applicant’s local bank account. At renewal the money must demonstrably have arrived in Mauritius, not merely have existed abroad.

The statutory fee is US$1,000, with a US$50 non-refundable application fee applying to all occupation and retired residence permit applications from 1 December 2025. Applying through the national e-licensing system is otherwise free and the Economic Development Board charges no processing fee.

The permit carries a right to invest but not to work. A holder may invest in any business provided he is not employed in it and derives no salary or employment benefit from it. Dependants covered are a spouse or common-law partner of the opposite sex, parents, and unmarried children not in gainful activity, each for the same duration.

Do Not Confuse It With the Premium Visa

The Premium Visa is a different instrument and the two are routinely conflated. It grants temporary visitor status for six months to a year, renewable, and is free to apply for, with no financial threshold. It is designed for people staying beyond 180 days in a calendar year whose main place of business and source of income remain outside Mauritius.

Its tax treatment is favourable: income earned remotely is taxed on a remittance basis, money spent through foreign credit cards does not count as remitted, and bank deposits are taxable unless taxes are declared as paid in the home country.

What it does not offer is permanence. There is no path from a Premium Visa to a permanent permit, no dependant framework of the kind the retirement permit provides, and no immigration status behind it. Anyone intending to buy property and settle needs the retirement permit, not the visa.

The Property Routes and the Magic Number

Property acquisition and residency are linked, and the figure that links them is US$375,000. Under the Integrated Resort Scheme, the Real Estate Scheme and the Smart City Scheme, an acquisition at or above that level brings a residence permit for the holder and dependants.

The Property Development Scheme, made under 2015 regulations, is the current vehicle. Projects must contain at least six residential units on freehold land of at least 0.4220 hectare, and there is no minimum price on the unit itself, but an acquisition exceeding US$375,000 grants a residence permit for as long as the property is held, extending to spouse and children under 24.

Apartments outside the approved schemes are also available, in condominium developments of at least two levels above ground. Here there is a purchase floor: MUR 6 million, about US$127,800, simply to buy. Residency still requires US$375,000.

The scheme that deserves more attention than it gets is the Senior Living Residence, a property development scheme variant for people aged 50 and over living independently in a peer environment with a clubhouse, health facilities and elderly-focused services. It has no minimum acquisition price. A retiree may acquire a unit or life rights and receives a permit for self and spouse until the property is no longer owned or occupied.

Holders under the resort, real estate and development schemes are exempt from needing an occupation or work permit to invest and work. The scheme pages also state that owners may rent the property, become tax resident, and face no restriction on repatriating sale or rental proceeds.

What the Transaction Costs

The duty structure is symmetrical and easy to remember. Buying from a development company, land transfer tax of 5% of property value is payable by the company at registration and registration duty of 5% is payable by the purchaser.

On a resale between private holders the same two charges apply, with land transfer tax of 5% falling on the seller and registration duty of 5% on the buyer.

So a foreign buyer pays 5% on the way in and 5% on the way out. Holders of a Mauritian diaspora scheme registration certificate pay no duty or tax on the deed of transfer.

The permit carries a right to invest but not to work, and dependants include parents.

Tax: The Part Worth Reading Twice

Individual income tax has three bands as of 1 July 2025. The first MUR 500,000 of chargeable income, about US$10,650, is taxed at zero. The next MUR 500,000 is taxed at 10%. Everything above MUR 1,000,000, roughly US$21,300, is taxed at 20%. This replaced an eleven-band structure and is a substantial simplification.

The solidarity levy remains in force. An individual whose leviable income exceeds MUR 3 million, about US$63,900, pays 25% of the excess. Leviable income means chargeable income plus dividends from a resident company and share of dividend from a société. Lump sums by way of commutation of pension, death gratuity or consolidated compensation for death or injury are excluded, which matters to a retiree taking a pension commencement lump sum.

Residence is established by domicile, by presence of 183 days or more in an income year, or by an aggregate of 270 days or more across the two preceding income years. Once resident, the practical position is that Mauritius-source income is taxed in full and foreign-source income is taxed to the extent it is remitted to Mauritius.

The revenue authority’s own pages are worded inconsistently on this point, with one describing worldwide taxation and another describing the remittance basis, so the sensible approach is to anchor on the remittance wording, note that pension treatment depends on the pension article of any applicable double taxation agreement, and obtain a ruling rather than an opinion.

Mauritius levies no capital gains tax, no inheritance tax and no wealth tax on individuals. The Registrar-General does administer a campement tax and campement site tax on coastal and holiday properties, with schedules updated in January 2026, which seaside buyers rarely hear about until the bill arrives.

The Treaty Question Decides Who Should Come

Mauritius has concluded 45 tax treaties, including the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, Belgium, Luxembourg, South Africa, India, China, Singapore, the United Arab Emirates and much of southern and eastern Africa. The India protocol was amended again in 2026.

There is no treaty with the United States. The United States appears only on the information exchange list. There is no Canadian treaty either, and the Australian treaty is partial. American and Canadian retirees therefore get no treaty relief on pension income, which is the single largest planning consideration for that readership and is usually buried at the bottom of retirement guides.

The absence of a treaty compounds a second problem. Air Mauritius flies to London, Paris, Geneva, Johannesburg, Cape Town, Perth, Kuala Lumpur, Mumbai, Delhi, Chennai, Antananarivo, Réunion, Rodrigues and Dubai. There is no direct service to or from the Americas, making it a twenty-four to thirty hour door-to-door journey from North America. Taken together, Mauritius suits European, South African, Indian and Australian retirees considerably better than North American ones.

Healthcare and the Medical Screening

The public system works on a universal-access principle with five regional hospitals, specialised institutions for cardiology, oncology, ophthalmology, ear nose and throat, mental health and respiratory disease, a nationwide emergency service, and a network of area and community health centres.

Private provision is substantial, with 29 private clinics regulated by the Medical Council of Mauritius. The facilities retirees are most often referred to include Wellkin Hospital at Moka, Fortis Clinique Darné at Floréal, Clinique du Nord at Tombeau Bay, La Clinique Mauricienne at Réduit, Clinique de Grand Baie and City Clinic in Port Louis.

Every non-citizen permit applicant faces compulsory medical screening: blood tests, urine and stool tests and a chest X-ray, with results less than six months old. Three of these must be done in Mauritius. Yellow fever vaccination is not required from Europe, North America, Oceania or Asia and there is no malaria risk. Medical insurance premium relief is capped at MUR 25,000, about US$530, for the taxpayer and the same again for a first dependant.

The plateau is cooler, wetter and cloudier than the coast, which should shape where retirees buy.

Climate, Cyclones and Where to Buy

The climate is mild tropical maritime with two seasons, a warm humid summer from November to April and a cool dry winter from June to September, with October and May as transition months. Mean summer temperature is 24.7 degrees and mean winter 20.4 degrees, a gap of only 4.3 degrees, which is why the island reads as comfortable rather than seasonal.

Long-term mean annual rainfall is 2,010 millimetres, of which 67% falls in summer. Coastal regions get seven and a half to eight hours of daily sunshine, against about five on the central plateau in winter. Curepipe and Vacoas are markedly cooler, wetter and cloudier than the coast, and that difference should shape where a retiree buys more than the price does.

Cyclone season spans the austral summer. Warnings are keyed to gusts of 120 kilometres an hour: Class I is issued 36 to 48 hours ahead, Class II to allow twelve hours of daylight, Class III six hours of daylight, and Class IV when such gusts are actually recorded. Any coastal purchase should be assessed for cyclone exposure and insured accordingly.

Cost of Living, With a Caveat

The Economic Development Board publishes indicative costs in dollars, and they read as somewhat stale, so treat them as a shape rather than a price list. A two to four bedroom house of 100 to 200 square metres is put at US$500 to US$1,000 a month, and a larger villa with garden and pool at US$1,200 to US$2,400.

Electricity runs US$20 to US$100 a month, water US$3 to US$6, and internet about US$30. A bus fare is US$1.00 and the metro US$1.25. Petrol is US$1.45 a litre and a mid-range dinner for two starts around US$30.

One cost is routinely missed and it is large. Car purchase carries 100% excise duty, which doubles the price of the vehicle. Anyone planning to run a car in Mauritius should budget for that before budgeting for the house.

For macro context, the Bank of Mauritius key rate stood at 4.75% in August 2026 and the overnight interbank rate at 3.40% in September.

The Route to Permanence

After five consecutive years on the retirement permit, a holder becomes eligible for a twenty-year permanent residence permit, itself renewable for another twenty. The retired non-citizen criterion requires having held the permit for at least five years and having transferred, by instalments or otherwise, an aggregate of at least US$200,000 over the five consecutive years immediately preceding the application.

An investor, professional or self-employed permanent permit holder may switch into the retired category for the remainder of validity on showing disposable annual income of US$40,000. Dependants covered include spouse, common-law partner, children and parents.

Applications go to the Residence Permit Section at the Prime Minister’s Office in Port Louis. For a retiree arriving at 50 with the intention of staying, the sequence is a ten-year permit, a five-year qualifying period with money genuinely flowing into the island, and then a twenty-year status that outlasts most retirement horizons.

More: Africa guides and news, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the requirements to retire in Mauritius?

Age 50 or above, plus a certified bank statement showing US$24,000 or guaranteed income of US$2,000 a month from outside Mauritius.

How long does the retirement permit last?

Ten years, renewable for a further ten. After five years a twenty-year permanent residence permit becomes available.

How much property must I buy to get residency?

US$375,000 under the resort, real estate, development and smart city schemes. The Senior Living Residence scheme has no price floor.

Is foreign pension income taxed in Mauritius?

Broadly, only to the extent it is remitted to Mauritius, and subject to the pension article of any applicable treaty. Get a ruling.

Is there a tax treaty with the United States?

No. Mauritius has 45 treaties but none with the United States or Canada, and the Australian one is partial.

Does Mauritius tax capital gains or inheritance?

No capital gains tax, inheritance tax or wealth tax applies to individuals. Coastal properties may attract campement tax.

Sources: Economic Development Board (residency.mu), Mauritius Revenue Authority, Bank of Mauritius, Mauritius Meteorological Services, Air Mauritius.

World.title: Buying Property in Belize as a Foreigner
World.content:
BELIZE · PROPERTY

Key Facts — Can a foreigner own freehold Yes, on the same terms as a national. There is no alien landholding licence in force.

— The currency risk None on paper. The Belize dollar has been pegged at BZ$2.00 to US$1.00 since May 1976.

— Transfer cost Stamp duty at 8%, with the first BZ$20,000, about US$10,000, exempt.

— Two title systems The Registered Land Act gives a state-backed Land Certificate. Older deeds property does not.

— Annual property tax Very low. Ceilings of 1% to 2% of value depending on the authority, set annually.

— The trap nobody mentions Retirees under the QRP programme are expressly barred from holding foreign currency accounts at domestic banks.

Belize sells itself to foreign buyers on English common law, a dollar peg and no restriction on ownership. All three are real. What the brochures leave out is exchange control, and it is the part that decides how easily money leaves again.

Buying Property in Belize as a Foreigner: Title, Tax and Exchange Control

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

RT Ask Rio Times Latin American markets, currencies and companies. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesMarkets, currencies and the economy › RT Ask Rio Times Latin American markets, currencies and companies. × Markets today The currency Rates & inflation Economy outlook Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Belize is the only Central American country where a foreigner can buy freehold land on the same footing as a citizen, conduct the whole transaction in English, and price it in a currency that has not moved against the dollar in half a century. The complications sit elsewhere.

Ownership Is Genuinely Unrestricted

Foreigners may hold freehold on the same terms as nationals, and there is no alien landholding licence in operation. The Central Bank of Belize frames its own procedure around the transfer of real property between a resident and a non-resident and imposes a notice requirement rather than a consent requirement, which is a meaningful distinction.

The Belize Tourism Board goes further and lists ease of purchasing land among the benefits of its retirement programme. Read together, the official position is that nationality is not a barrier to title.

One caveat belongs here for honesty. The statute repealing the old alien landholding regime could not be verified against primary text, because the official Belize statute website has been abandoned and its domain now serves unrelated content. The practice is clear; the citation is worth confirming with a Belizean attorney before you rely on it in a contract.

Two Title Systems, and Only One of Them Is Safe

Under the Registered Land Act, Chapter 194, Belize operates a Torrens-style register that produces a Land Certificate. This is the modern system and the state stands behind what the register says. If the certificate names you, you own it.

Alongside it sits the older General Registry, a deeds system in which conveyances are recorded as documents. That is a record of paperwork, not a guarantee of title, and establishing ownership requires an abstract tracing the chain back through prior deeds. Much of the mainland and older Belize City property still sits in this system.

The practical answer to the deeds problem is title insurance, and it exists here. Barrow and Williams in Belize City states that it is approved and registered with Stewart Title, RF and G Insurance and First American Title Insurance for the provision of title insurance. Two United States underwriters and a local insurer write Belize policies, placed through approved attorneys. On a deeds-system purchase, treat a policy as mandatory rather than optional.

What the Transfer Actually Costs

In Belize stamp duty is the transfer tax. There is no second, separately named property transfer tax layered on top, which trips up buyers arriving from jurisdictions that have both.

The headline is 8% on conveyance, with the first BZ$20,000 of value, roughly US$10,000, exempt. That much is consistently reported. A separate and unresolved question is whether nationals pay less: one Belizean news report states that transfers from Belizeans to foreigners attract 8% against 5% for Belizeans.

Both versions cannot be casually reconciled and the Stamp Duties Act itself is not currently retrievable from any government domain. Budget on 8% of the full price less the exemption, and have your attorney confirm the applicable rate in writing before you sign. This is the single most-cited number in every Belize property guide and it deserves more scepticism than it usually gets.

Annual Property Tax Is Close to Trivial

Outside the municipalities, land tax under the Land Tax Act is assessed on unimproved value. Inside town boundaries, the Towns Property Tax Act applies, and in Belize City a 1994 amendment assesses market value whether the property is occupied or not, with the rate set annually by the Minister on the recommendation of the city council and capped at 2% of market value.

Those are Revised Edition 2000 ceilings rather than current rates, and the actual figures are fixed each year by ministerial order or council recommendation. San Pedro Town Council, Placencia Village Council and Belize City Council all differ. In absolute terms the bills are small, and annual carrying cost is rarely what makes or breaks a Belize purchase.

Capital account transactions between residents and non-residents require central bank notice.

Exchange Control Is the Real Constraint

This is Belize’s most under-reported buyer risk, and the sourcing on it is strong. The Central Bank of Belize states that its approval and confirmation of notice are required for all capital account transactions involving residents and non-residents. Current transactions require a foreign exchange permit.

Foreign currency accounts are where it bites. The central bank’s Exchange Control Direction 10/2014 grants them primarily to entities in the export-earning sector and explicitly not for the purpose of accumulating foreign currency. Domestic banks are not permitted to open foreign currency accounts for non-residents at all, who are directed instead to institutions licensed under the International Banking Act. Banks set ceilings on account balances and excess must be sold to the bank.

And then the line that cuts directly against how the retirement programme is marketed: the central bank states in terms that retirees under the Qualified Retired Persons Incentives Act do not qualify to operate foreign currency accounts. A retiree whose income arrives in dollars, and who assumed it would sit in a dollar account locally, needs to rethink the plan before buying.

The QRP Programme, Read Properly

The Qualified Retired Persons programme is administered by the Belize Tourism Board under the Retired Persons Incentives Act, Chapter 62. Applicants must be 45 or over, prove income of US$2,000 per month or US$24,000 per year from a source outside Belize in United States dollars, sterling, euros or Canadian dollars, and undertake to deposit that amount with a Belizean financial institution.

The residence requirement is light, at a minimum of thirty consecutive days in the country annually. Benefits include a renewable resident card, multiple visa-free entry, import duty and tax exemption in the first year on household effects, a vehicle, a light aircraft and a boat, and exemption from tax on income from sources outside Belize as well as from capital gains and inheritance tax.

On property, the entitlement is to purchase land to build a home or to buy a home for residential use only. A QRP wanting to carry on business in Belize must apply separately to the tourism board and show residence of at least ninety non-consecutive days.

Ambergris Caye, Placencia and Belize City are separate markets with little in common.

Financing and Market Conditions

Local credit is available but not cheap by regional standards. The Central Bank of Belize reported new lending rates of 8.77% in May 2026, two basis points lower than a year earlier, against new deposit rates of 1.74%. Excess cash in the banking system stood at BZ$481.1 million, about US$240.6 million, more than double the level at the start of the year.

That combination, liquid banks and high lending rates, tells you the constraint on Belizean mortgage lending is appetite rather than funding. Most foreign buyers pay cash or finance abroad.

There is no official house price index in Belize and no recorded-sales database, so anyone quoting you market averages is quoting listing asks. Ambergris Caye, Placencia and Belize City are separate markets with little in common, and the only defensible approach is dated asking prices from two or three named brokerages, treated as asks rather than as transactions.

What to Do, in Order

Establish which register the property sits in before anything else, because that single fact determines how much due diligence the purchase needs and whether title insurance is essential.

Instruct a Belizean attorney independently of the seller and the agent, and have the stamp duty rate confirmed in writing. Then deal with the money question early rather than late: understand exactly which accounts you will be permitted to hold, in which currency, before you commit funds into the country.

The ownership rules in Belize are as open as the marketing says. The exchange control rules are not, and the gap between those two facts is where foreign buyers get caught.

More: Belize guides and news, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can foreigners own land in Belize?

Yes. Foreigners hold freehold on the same terms as nationals and no alien landholding licence is in force.

What does it cost to transfer property?

Stamp duty of 8% on conveyance, with the first BZ$20,000, about US$10,000, exempt. Confirm the rate with an attorney, as the treatment of nationals is disputed.

Is the Belize dollar pegged?

Yes, at BZ$2.00 to US$1.00 since May 1976, and the peg has held.

Is title insurance available?

Yes. Stewart Title, First American and local insurer RF and G write Belize policies through approved attorneys.

Can a retiree hold a US dollar account in Belize?

No. The central bank states that QRP retirees do not qualify to operate foreign currency accounts, and domestic banks cannot open them for non-residents.

What income does the QRP require?

US$2,000 a month or US$24,000 a year from a source outside Belize, plus a minimum stay of thirty consecutive days each year.

Sources: Central Bank of Belize, Belize Tourism Board, Registered Land Act Cap. 194, Towns Property Tax Act Cap. 65, Land Tax Act Cap. 58, Barrow & Williams, Breaking Belize News.

World.title: Investing in Chile as a Foreigner: Rules, Rates and What Changed
World.content:
CHILE · INVESTING

Key Facts — The market The Santiago exchange, now part of the nuam group with Lima and Colombia.

— The index The IPSA passed to MSCI on 1 September 2026 and is now the MSCI IPSA, with 31 starting members.

— The registration rule Foreign capital inflows above US$10,000 must be registered with the central bank. It is notification, not approval.

— Withholding on dividends The additional tax at 35%, with credit for corporate tax already paid.

— The policy rate 4.50% in September 2026.

— The unit to understand The UF, an inflation-indexed unit worth about 40,926 pesos, roughly US$43.50.

Chile is the easiest market in South America for a foreigner to put money into and the one where the registration paperwork matters most. Getting the second part right is what allows the money out again.

Investing in Chile as a Foreigner: Rules, Rates and What Changed

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

Chile offers investment-grade credit, an open capital account and a stock exchange in the middle of the largest structural change in its history, and the mechanics of entering it are more specific than most guides suggest.

What nuam Has and Has Not Delivered

nuam is the holding company integrating the Santiago, Lima and Colombia exchanges, announced in 2023. Common equity-trading technology is now complete across all three markets, with Chile’s platform launching in July 2026 as the final piece, and institutional access running through a point of presence at a Santiago data centre.

Index convergence is also complete. Colombia migrated in 2021, Peru in 2025 and Chile on 1 September 2026, with the IPSA and IGPA handed to MSCI, which now calculates, publishes and administers them under its global methodology. The index becomes the MSCI IPSA, keeping its name and its history.

Membership moved from a fixed thirty-company cap to a size and liquidity screen, starting at 31 companies, with rebalancing now quarterly rather than twice a year. The first review is announced on 11 November 2026 and takes effect on 1 December.

What has not happened is a genuine single regional order book or a unified securities depository. Settlement moves from two days to one in the second half of 2027. Anyone told the three markets trade as one book today is being told something that is not yet true.

What Is in the Index

Roughly 31 names concentrated in mining and materials, banks, retail and utilities. SQM is usually the busiest stock by turnover, alongside Falabella, Cencosud, Banco de Chile and Enel Chile.

The drivers are what you would expect: lithium and copper prices, the disruption of the domestic car market by Chinese manufacturers, cautious household spending and pension reform headlines.

That concentration is the risk as much as the opportunity. An investor buying the Chilean index is buying a commodity position with a consumer overlay, not a diversified economy.

Registration is a notification mechanism, not an approval requirement.

Chapter Fourteen and Why It Matters

Chapter XIV of the central bank’s foreign exchange compendium governs credits, deposits, investments and capital contributions from abroad. Foreign investors must register capital contributions with the central bank where inflows exceed US$10,000.

The crucial point, and the one most often misstated, is that this is a notification mechanism rather than an approval requirement. Nobody is deciding whether you may invest. What the registration does is create the record that allows capital and its returns to leave again through the formal exchange market.

Transactions must run through that formal market, meaning banks and authorised entities. Money that arrives outside it is money whose exit is complicated.

The Tax Position for Non-Residents

Dividends and profit remittances to non-residents are subject to the additional tax at 35%, with credit for corporate tax already paid at the company level. Chile operates a partially integrated system, so the credit is not always complete and the effective burden depends on the shareholder’s treaty position.

Investors resident in a country with a Chilean double taxation treaty generally receive full credit for the corporate tax, which brings the effective rate back toward 35% rather than above it. Investors without a treaty can face a materially higher combined burden. This is the single most important question to settle before structuring an investment.

Capital gains treatment varies by instrument, with a specific exemption regime for shares with sufficient market presence traded on the exchange. Take advice on the instrument rather than assuming a general rule.

The Pension System Is the Local Market

Chile’s private pension funds have historically been the dominant domestic buyers of Chilean assets, and the 2025 pension reform changed how contributions are split and managed.

That matters to a foreign investor because the local bid for Chilean equities and bonds is largely institutional and largely one set of institutions. Changes in how those funds allocate move the market more than retail sentiment does.

The 2027 budget assumes copper at US$5.37 a pound against a higher spot price.

Copper, Lithium and the Fiscal Picture

Copper traded around US$6.45 a pound in mid-September 2026, having touched US$6.60 in the preceding week, while the 2027 budget assumes US$5.37. Output fell 9.4% in July after storms.

A budget written on a conservative copper price against a higher spot price is a fiscal position with room in it, which is part of why Chilean credit remains investment grade through a difficult growth period. Monthly output was down 1.5% in July and unemployment stood at 9.53%.

Lithium is the other resource story, and the arrangement between the state copper producer and SQM is the structure through which the state takes a larger share of it. Anyone investing in Chilean lithium is investing in a public-private arrangement rather than a purely private one.

The UF, Again

The unidad de fomento is an inflation-indexed unit revalued daily, worth about 40,926 pesos or US$43.50 in mid-September 2026. Mortgages, long leases, insurance and a large share of corporate debt are denominated in it.

For an investor that means a nominal peso return and a UF return are different things, and a contract quoted in UF carries automatic inflation indexation. It is the most important piece of Chilean financial vocabulary.

The Risks

The political cycle is the one most often cited. President Kast took office on 11 March 2026 and the direction of tax, mining and pension policy under a full term is not yet established.

The peso traded near 941 to the dollar in mid-September against a year’s weakest of 965.50. Chilean assets are a commodity-linked position in a currency that moves with copper, and hedging that is a decision to take deliberately rather than by default.

More: Chile guides and news, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can foreigners invest in Chile?

Yes, freely. Inflows above US$10,000 must be registered with the central bank, which is a notification requirement rather than an approval.

What happened to the IPSA?

It passed to MSCI on 1 September 2026 and is now the MSCI IPSA, with 31 starting members, a liquidity screen instead of a fixed cap, and quarterly rebalancing.

Do the three nuam markets trade as one?

No. Common technology and common indices are in place; a single order book and unified depository are not. Settlement moves to one day in the second half of 2027.

How are dividends taxed for non-residents?

At the 35% additional tax, with credit for corporate tax already paid. The effective burden depends on whether your country has a treaty with Chile.

What is the UF?

An inflation-indexed unit revalued daily, worth about 40,926 pesos or US$43.50. Mortgages, long leases and much corporate debt are denominated in it.

What are the main risks?

Concentration in commodities, a currency that moves with copper, and a political cycle whose tax and mining direction is not yet settled.

Sources: Banco Central de Chile, nuam, MSCI, mindicador.cl, Chambers Banking Regulation 2026.

World.title: Investing in Uruguay as a Foreigner: What Is Actually Available
World.content:
URUGUAY · INVESTING

Key Facts — The rating Investment grade across the board: BBB+ at S&P, Baa1 at Moody’s, BBB at Fitch, all stable.

— The equity market Effectively non-existent. Fixed income and real estate are the market.

— The policy rate 5.75% as of August 2026.

— The currency The peso appreciated more than 12% against the dollar in 2025 and the central bank has not intervened in five years.

— The unit to understand The Unidad Indexada, a daily inflation-linked accounting unit that underpins the tax code and most government debt.

— The free zones Zonamerica, Aguada Park and the World Trade Centre free zone, with a distinct tax regime.

Uruguay is the highest-rated sovereign in South America with almost nothing to buy on its stock exchange. What you are buying is stability, and it comes as bonds and buildings.

Investing in Uruguay as a Foreigner: What Is Actually Available

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

RT Ask Rio Times Latin American markets, currencies and companies. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesMarkets, currencies and the economy › RT Ask Rio Times Latin American markets, currencies and companies. × Markets today The currency Rates & inflation Economy outlook Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Uruguay attracts foreign capital for its predictability rather than its returns, and understanding what is genuinely investable there saves a great deal of time.

The Credit Story

Uruguay is rated BBB+ by S&P, Baa1 by Moody’s, BBB by Fitch and BBB by Morningstar DBRS, all on stable outlooks, with unsolicited A minus ratings from two Asian agencies. That makes it the region’s highest-rated sovereign alongside Chile.

Net public debt stood at about 59.5% of output against a self-imposed anchor of 65%. The consolidated public-sector deficit was around 4.6% of output in 2025 and growth has been sluggish, at 0.9% year on year in the first quarter of 2026, with the economy ministry projecting 2.1% for 2027.

There Is No Equity Market Worth the Name

The Bolsa de Valores de Montevideo trades equities, corporate bonds, financial trusts, investment funds and international securities. The electronic exchange BEVSA handles the institutional fixed income, money market and interbank foreign exchange business.

The honest assessment is that Uruguay’s domestic equity market is negligible. There is essentially no liquid local stock to buy. Anyone expecting to build an equity portfolio in Uruguay should plan to do it through international securities accessed from Uruguay rather than in Uruguayan companies.

Government Bonds Are the Core Instrument

The debt management unit publishes a domestic issuance calendar and auctions treasury notes in nominal pesos, in inflation-indexed units and in a pension-linked unit. A recent example is a September 2026 series in indexed units worth about US$52 million equivalent, carrying a 2.55% annual coupon and maturing in 2030.

Foreigners buy domestic notes through a local bank or a registered broker, and the dollar-denominated global bonds through international clearing. The debt office publishes investor presentations and a medium-term financing strategy, which is more disclosure than most of the region offers.

Interest on Uruguayan public debt is generally treated as exempt for non-residents. Confirm the current position with the tax authority before committing, because the treatment depends on the instrument.

Understand the Indexed Unit Before You Buy Anything

The Unidad Indexada is a daily-published inflation-linked accounting unit, worth about 6.64 pesos or roughly US$0.165 in early September 2026. It is the backbone of Uruguayan finance: the tax code, residency thresholds, investment promotion thresholds and a large share of government debt are denominated in it.

The practical choice for an investor is between dollar instruments, which give currency certainty and pay around 2.5% to 3% at banks, and indexed-unit instruments, which protect purchasing power in local terms but carry currency risk against a dollar-denominated life.

Given that Uruguayan rents and property are priced in dollars, most foreign residents find the dollar side of that trade easier to live with, and the indexed side more interesting as a genuine investment.

Property is what most foreign capital in Uruguay actually buys.

Real Estate Is the Default

Property is what most foreign capital in Uruguay actually buys, concentrated in Montevideo, Punta del Este and increasingly in the interior for agricultural land.

Foreigners may own property on the same terms as nationals, including agricultural land, which is not the case in neighbouring Argentina. Purchases are made through a notary, who carries substantially more legal responsibility in the Uruguayan system than a conveyancer does in a common-law country.

Yields are modest and the case is capital preservation in a stable jurisdiction rather than income. Anyone underwriting Uruguayan property on rental yield alone will be disappointed.

The Free Zones

Zonamerica, Aguada Park and the World Trade Centre free zone operate under a distinct regime that exempts qualifying activities from most national taxes in exchange for local hiring and investment commitments.

They are the reason a substantial services and technology sector operates from Montevideo serving clients abroad, and they are the structure through which most foreign operating businesses enter Uruguay.

The investment promotion regime run through the executive’s investment commission offers corporate tax credits against qualifying capital expenditure outside the zones, scored on employment, decentralisation, exports and clean technology.

The central bank has not intervened in the currency market for five years.

The Currency Position

The peso appreciated more than 12% against the dollar in 2025 and the central bank had not intervened in the foreign exchange market for five years as of September 2026. The policy rate was 5.75% in August.

A strong peso compresses exporter margins and makes Uruguay expensive in dollar terms, which is the current complaint of the agricultural and industrial sectors. For a foreign investor holding dollars, it means entry prices are high by historical standards.

The central bank has separately begun requiring banks to warn dollar depositors about exchange-rate risk from October 2026, citing the loss of purchasing power on dollar sight deposits over twenty-five years. That is a statement about policy direction as much as about consumer protection.

More: Uruguay guides and news, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can foreigners invest freely in Uruguay?

Yes. There are no restrictions on foreign ownership of securities or property, including agricultural land.

Is there a stock market worth using?

Not really. Uruguay’s domestic equity market is negligible. Fixed income and real estate are the market.

How do I buy Uruguayan government bonds?

Domestic notes through a local bank or registered broker; dollar-denominated global bonds through international clearing.

What is the Unidad Indexada?

A daily inflation-linked accounting unit worth about 6.64 pesos, or roughly US$0.165, that underpins the tax code and much of the government debt.

What is Uruguay’s credit rating?

BBB+ at S&P, Baa1 at Moody’s and BBB at Fitch, all stable. It is the region’s highest-rated sovereign alongside Chile.

What are the free zones?

Zonamerica, Aguada Park and the World Trade Centre free zone, which exempt qualifying activities from most national taxes in exchange for local commitments.

Sources: Ministerio de Economía y Finanzas Unidad de Gestión de Deuda, Banco Central del Uruguay, Bolsa de Valores de Montevideo, rating agency actions.

World.title: Opening a Bank Account in Bolivia as a Foreigner
World.content:
BOLIVIA · BANKING

Key Facts — Can tourists open an account No. You need at least temporary residency and a foreigner’s identity card.

— The banks Banco Nacional de Bolivia is the most accessible to foreigners. Mercantil Santa Cruz is the largest.

— Initial deposit Typically US$50 to US$1,000, commonly around US$100.

— The event that changed everything Bolivia ended its fifteen-year dollar peg on 26 June 2026.

— Where the rate went From about 6.96 to 9.73 overnight, a peak of 12.64 on 9 September, and 11.53 by mid-September.

— The constraint Dollar availability. The central bank has intervened repeatedly and immobilised 3% of certain deposits for 180 days.

Opening a Bolivian bank account is a paperwork problem. Getting dollars out of one is a different problem, and it is the one that decides whether the account is useful.

Opening a Bank Account in Bolivia as a Foreigner

Bolivian banking changed more in three months of 2026 than in the preceding fifteen years, and anyone arriving with an expat guide written before June is working from a different country.

You Need Residency

Tourists and non-residents cannot open accounts. You need at least temporary residency and a foreigner’s identity card issued by the identification service, and opening is done in person.

One source suggests a basic savings account may be possible on a passport alone at some banks, with debit cards, online banking and dollar accounts requiring legal residency. Treat that as contested rather than as a plan.

The documents are the foreigner’s identity card, a passport, the visa or residency permit, proof of a Bolivian address, proof of income, a tax number, which takes one to two days to obtain, and an initial deposit of typically US$50 to US$1,000.

Which Bank

Banco Nacional de Bolivia is generally the most accessible to foreigners and has reliable online banking and dollar accounts. Banco Mercantil Santa Cruz is the largest and strongest in Santa Cruz.

Banco BISA is the most forward-leaning on digital assets. Banco Unión is state-owned with the widest distribution and the fewest international features. Banco Ganadero, Banco FIE, BancoSol and BCP Bolivia complete the main list, with BancoSol generally the most flexible on documentation.

The Float Is the Story

Bolivia ended a fifteen-year peg on 26 June 2026 by ministerial resolution and central bank board resolution, adopting a flexible managed float. It went live on 29 June at 9.73 bolivianos to the dollar, a devaluation of roughly 30% to 40% in a day. The parallel rate had reached around 20 at the crisis peak.

The rate is now set daily from the weighted average of banks’ dollar purchases, published by the central bank and applied the following business day, and banks may not sell foreign currency more than ten United States cents above it.

The path since has been volatile: through 11 bolivianos on 24 July, a peak of 12.64 on 9 September, then 11.53 by 12 to 14 September. A rate that moves 8% in a week is not a currency you can plan household finances around without thought.

The central bank immobilised 3% of certain deposits for 180 days.

The Dollar Shortage Has Not Gone Away

In September 2026 the central bank offered dollars to the financial system, temporarily suspended new dollar purchase operations, and from 8 September required banks to immobilise 3% of certain local-currency deposits for 180 days.

That last measure is the one to understand. It reduces the volume of bolivianos available to chase a limited supply of dollars, which is its purpose, and it also means a portion of the banking system’s deposits is not available for lending.

In practice banks still rarely dispense physical dollars at the official rate, withdrawal limits apply and commissions are charged. Dollar accounts exist; dollars in hand are a separate matter.

How Money Actually Moves

International transfers into Bolivia work but are slow and expensive by regional standards. Transfers out are more constrained, and the practical workarounds long-term residents use are foreign accounts, international dollar debit cards, and stablecoins.

Digital assets moved from prohibited to permitted in 2024 and the central bank has since reported substantial growth in their use for cross-border payments. Banco BISA is the institution most engaged with that.

Anyone planning to live in Bolivia on foreign income should keep their primary banking outside the country and treat the Bolivian account as a spending account rather than a store of value.

The Regulator and the Programme

Banking is supervised by the financial system supervisory authority. The central bank had seen reserves fall below US$2 billion before the float, and exchange-rate flexibility was the International Monetary Fund’s precondition for a programme now reported at US$2.5 billion to US$2.8 billion, with more than half earmarked to rebuild those reserves.

Fuel subsidies were cut in parallel and are scheduled to move toward cost recovery from January 2027. A banking system operating inside that adjustment is one where rules can change at short notice.

Keep dollars abroad and treat the Bolivian account as a spending account.

What to Do in Practice

Open the account once residency is settled rather than before, because the paperwork cannot be completed without the identity card.

Hold a boliviano account for daily spending and keep dollars abroad. Assume that cash dollars will be difficult to obtain locally and plan around card and transfer rather than around withdrawal.

Read the rate before large local payments. At 11.53 against a 12.64 peak nine days earlier, timing a transfer has mattered more in Bolivia this year than negotiating a price.

More: Bolivia guides and news, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a tourist open a Bolivian bank account?

No. You need at least temporary residency and a foreigner’s identity card, and you must open in person.

Which bank is best for foreigners?

Banco Nacional de Bolivia is generally the most accessible, with reliable online banking and dollar accounts.

Is the boliviano still pegged?

No. Bolivia floated on 26 June 2026. The rate moved from about 6.96 to 9.73 overnight and stood at 11.53 in mid-September.

Can I withdraw dollars?

Often not at the official rate. Withdrawal limits and commissions apply and banks rarely dispense physical dollars freely.

What is the initial deposit?

Typically US$50 to US$1,000, commonly around US$100.

How do expats move money?

Through foreign accounts, international dollar cards and, increasingly, stablecoins. Digital assets were permitted from 2024.

Sources: Banco Central de Bolivia, Ferrere, Opinión, Autoridad de Supervisión del Sistema Financiero.

World.title: Diesel hits $15.96 per gallon as concerns grow over cost to Belize businesses
World.content:
Diesel hits $15.96 per gallon as concerns grow over cost to Belize businesses

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Concerns are growing over the cost of doing business in Belize following another increase in the price of diesel.

A social media post circulating this weekend highlighted that diesel has risen to $15.96 per gallon, describing the increase as another blow to the country’s business sector.

The higher price of diesel has implications beyond motorists filling their tanks.

Businesses that depend heavily on transportation, generators, construction equipment and delivery vehicles can face higher operating expenses when fuel prices rise. Those costs can eventually affect the prices consumers pay for goods and services.

The transportation sector is particularly exposed since buses, trucks, taxis, tour operators and other commercial vehicles depend on fuel to operate.

Businesses involved in agriculture and construction can also face additional pressure because diesel powers much of the heavy equipment used in those industries.

The latest increase comes amid growing public discussion over fuel and energy costs in Belize.

Opposition Leader Tracy Taegar Panton also criticized the latest diesel increase this weekend, arguing that businesses and working families are being placed under increasing financial pressure.

The price of diesel has therefore become another focal point in the wider debate over Belize’s cost of living and the cost of doing business.

World.title: Woman says electricity bill soared from $340 to $1,040, sparking questions online
World.content:
Woman says electricity bill soared from $340 to $1,040, sparking questions online

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A social media post questioning a sharp increase in a household electricity bill is generating discussion among Belizeans.

The woman behind the post says she normally paid approximately $340 per month, but a recent amount due reached $1,040.55.

She publicly questioned the steep increase and expressed frustration over the financial burden.

A screenshot accompanying the post shows the amount due, but does not include enough information to determine why the balance increased so significantly.

Factors such as higher consumption, unpaid balances, adjustments or other billing issues could potentially affect the total, but the exact reason is not known.

There has been no independent confirmation that the bill was incorrectly calculated.

The complaint comes at a time when the cost of electricity and household expenses remain major concerns for many Belizean families.

Customers who notice unusual increases on their electricity bills are encouraged to review their consumption history and seek an explanation directly from BEL.

World.title: Should Belize ever have taken independence, the forbidden question, argued both ways
World.content:
Should Belize ever have taken independence, the forbidden question, argued both ways

By Horace Palacio:

There is a sentence some Belizeans only say after the third drink, or the third blackout, and lately they have begun saying it in daylight, on timelines, under news posts.

Belize should never have taken independence.

It usually arrives with company. That the whole affair was a scheme by politicians to inherit a territory as their private milking cow. That a nation this small can never staff a real army, a real police force, a real fire service, or tax itself into greatness. That anyone comparing us to El Salvador understands neither history nor demographics.

The usual response is outrage, a lecture about the flag, and the conversation dies. Today this column will do something different, because a country that cannot examine its own founding is fragile, and readers know my rule. I have argued that Belizeans should examine what they inherit, whether creeds or constitutions. The founding itself cannot be exempt. So, as with the Speednet deal and the minimum wage, here is the full ledger, both cases argued at their strongest, and the verdict left where it belongs, with you.

First, the case against independence, and let me argue it properly, because it is not stupid.

Begin with the arithmetic. In September 1981 this territory held roughly 145,000 souls, fewer people than a single district of the nations around us. The skeptic asks a fair question. Can a tax base that size, even grown to today’s 430,000, genuinely fund a modern army, a proper police service, fire coverage, hospitals, pensions, and roads? And he does not need to invent his evidence. This column supplied it all year. A government budget where seventy cents of every dollar is spoken for before a single wire is bought. A Prime Minister flying to ask a neighbor not to cut our electricity. Ten dollars imported for every one exported. Our brightest boarding planes. The skeptic simply gathers my own receipts and asks, is this what nationhood was for?

Then his counterfactual. Look, he says, at the territories that declined the flag. Cayman, Bermuda, the British Virgin Islands, still under the Crown, today rank among the wealthiest places in this hemisphere, with British passports, British courts, and a superpower’s treasury behind them when hurricanes or volcanoes strike, ask Montserrat. We chose the anthem, he says, they chose the safety net, and compare the results.

And then his sharpest blade, the milking cow. Independence, on this argument, did not end extraction. It localized it. The flag changed, and a domestic political class inherited the machinery, the ministerial contracts, the politicized public service created in 2000 and lovingly preserved by both parties, the procurement darkness that finally exploded into scandal this year. From London’s milking, the skeptic says, to Belmopan’s. That is his case, and stated honestly, parts of it draw blood.

Now the case for independence, argued with equal strength, and it begins by demolishing a myth hiding inside the skeptic’s counterfactual.

The comfortable-colony option was never truly on the menu. By the 1970s Britain was closing its empire with both hands, and the United Nations voted repeatedly for Belize’s independence. The micro-territories that remained are special cases, offshore finance islands of a few tens of thousands, a model no farming mainland territory of 150,000 could copy. And staying under London carried a danger the nostalgic forget. Colonies do not control their own fate, and in 1968 mediated proposals would have handed Guatemala sweeping influence over this territory. It was Belizeans in the streets who killed that bargain. The lesson is brutal and clear. A colony can be negotiated away over its own head. A nation cannot. Independence, with its UN seat and its access to the world court, is precisely the armor that kept every inch of Belize Belizean, Guatemala’s recognition in 1991, the claim now before the ICJ, not one acre lost in 45 years. Sovereignty’s hardest test, passed without a single tank division, which brings us to the army question. Costa Rica abolished its military entirely in 1948 and became the most stable country in Central America. Iceland, our size, keeps no standing army at all. Small nations are defended by law, legitimacy and alliances, not by battalions they cannot afford, and Belize’s borders are the proof.

As for the milking cow, the ledger must record a documented fact. George Price died in the same modest family home he had always lived in, famously austere, daily mass, no mansion, no fortune, nothing offshore. If independence was his scheme for personal enrichment, he forgot, across sixty years of opportunity, to collect. The extraction critique is real, this column has spent a year documenting it, but it indicts the political culture that followed, not the founder’s bank account. Judging independence by its worst administrators is judging marriage by its worst husbands.

And weigh what the young nation did buy. While El Salvador, Guatemala and Nicaragua drowned those very decades in civil wars and coups, this improbable little country held peaceful elections and handed power back and forth without a shot, again and again, a regional rarity worth more than its size. It used its small voice on principle at the United Nations. It clawed its debt down from the cliff. And above all it bought the right to make its own mistakes, and therefore the right to fix them. A colony’s errors are made for it, forever.

There is the ledger, both columns full. And now notice something remarkable before you vote.

Strip the anger from the skeptic’s post and what remains is a demand, for services that work, taxes that build, a state that serves rather than milks. Strip the romance from the patriot’s reply and what remains is the identical demand. Both sides of this forbidden question want exactly one thing, a Belize worthy of its flag. The quarrel was never really about 1981, which no verdict can reverse. It is about whether we have used what 1981 gave us, and that question, unlike the first, still has a living answer, being written by this generation, in scorecards and megawatts and classrooms, right now.

So decide for yourselves, Belizeans, what you believe about that September morning. This column, for once, casts no vote.

But it does offer one closing observation, free of charge.

You are reading a Belizean newspaper, freely questioning the founding of Belize, under the byline of a Belizean, judged by Belizean readers, with no governor’s censor in sight.

Colonies do not get to hold this debate.

Only free people audit their own birth.

Whatever your verdict, you just exercised the inheritance.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: BEL says Westlake emergency generation helped prevent load shedding
World.content:
BEL says Westlake emergency generation helped prevent load shedding

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize Electricity Limited says its temporary generation facility at Westlake is already helping to support the national electricity system as testing and commissioning of new emergency generation units continue.

According to BEL, the Westlake facility is currently operating at approximately 40 percent of its planned capacity.

The company says the additional local generation has provided greater flexibility in meeting Belize’s electricity demand, particularly when imported electricity from Mexico is unavailable.

BEL reported that during periods over the past two days when electricity supply from Mexico’s Comisión Federal de Electricidad was unavailable, generation from Westlake helped sustain the system and avoid load shedding during those periods.

Testing and commissioning will continue as additional generating units are brought online.

Once the facility is fully commissioned, Westlake is expected to provide 20 megawatts of emergency generation capacity.

BEL says the additional capacity will provide support when other sources of electricity supply are interrupted.

The company thanked customers for their patience as work continues to strengthen the reliability of Belize’s electricity supply.

World.title: Belize should consider Warren Buffett’s radical rule for controlling government deficits
World.content:
Belize should consider Warren Buffett’s radical rule for controlling government deficits

By Horace Palacio:

Belize should consider adopting its own version of a fiscal accountability idea famously proposed by billionaire investor Warren Buffett: if politicians allow the national budget deficit to become too large, they should risk losing the ability to seek reelection.

Buffett made the proposal during a 2011 CNBC interview, saying he could end the United States deficit in “five minutes.” His suggested rule was straightforward: if the federal deficit exceeded 3 percent of GDP, sitting members of Congress would become ineligible for reelection.

The principle behind the idea deserves serious consideration in Belize.

Governments routinely make decisions about borrowing, spending and taxation whose consequences can extend years beyond an election cycle. Yet the politicians approving those decisions may face little personal political consequence if public finances deteriorate.

A Belizean version of Buffett’s proposal could change those incentives.

Instead of treating fiscal discipline simply as a campaign promise, Belize could establish a clear deficit threshold tied to GDP. If a government exceeds that threshold without a legitimate national emergency, elected officials responsible for approving the budget could face serious electoral consequences.

There would have to be safeguards. Hurricanes, pandemics, recessions and other emergencies can require governments to borrow heavily. Buffett himself has acknowledged that deficit spending can be appropriate during extraordinary economic crises, including the 2008 financial collapse.

Belize therefore should not blindly copy a 3 percent rule. It should examine a framework suited to the country’s economy, accompanied by independent fiscal reporting and clearly defined emergency exceptions.

The larger lesson from Buffett is powerful: politicians respond to incentives too.

If Belize wants governments to take deficits, borrowing and public debt more seriously, fiscal responsibility should carry consequences that elected leaders cannot easily ignore.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: Make San Ignacio your Independence Day getaway this September
World.content:
Make San Ignacio your Independence Day getaway this September

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize Independence Day is one of the most exciting times of the year to experience the country, and San Ignacio is one of the best places to celebrate it.

Every September, Belize comes alive with flags, music, parades, cultural events and a strong sense of national pride. In San Ignacio, that energy blends with the charm of the Cayo District, giving visitors a celebration that feels festive, authentic and close to the heart of Belize.

The town offers a lively atmosphere without losing its laid back character. Visitors can enjoy Independence Day activities, explore local restaurants and bars, visit the market, and experience the warmth of the community during one of the country’s most important national holidays.

San Ignacio also makes it easy to turn the celebration into a full Belize vacation.

Between Independence Day events, travelers can explore ancient Maya sites such as Xunantunich, go cave tubing, visit waterfalls, take a jungle tour or simply spend time discovering the natural beauty of western Belize.

For accommodations, Cahal Pech Village Resort is an excellent place to stay.

Perched above San Ignacio, the resort offers sweeping views, a peaceful setting and convenient access to the town below. Guests can enjoy comfortable accommodations, swimming pools, onsite dining and a relaxing atmosphere after a busy day of Independence Day celebrations and sightseeing.

Its location also makes it a great base for exploring the Cayo District, with many of Belize’s top inland attractions within easy reach.

Celebrating Independence Day in San Ignacio gives visitors the chance to experience more than a holiday. It is an opportunity to see Belizean culture, pride and hospitality at their strongest while also enjoying some of the country’s best adventure experiences.

If you are planning a September getaway, make San Ignacio part of your Independence Day plans and stay at Cahal Pech Village Resort for the perfect combination of celebration, culture and relaxation.
