World.title: Sigh of relief
World.content:
ARCHIBALD... had been identified by investigators as one of the main organisers of robberies and break-ins targeting automated teller machines, remittance agencies, and other cash-intensive businesses

THE Chinese business community is breathing a sigh of relief after the fatal shooting of Dewar Archibald — who police sources say was part of an organised criminal network operating across several parishes — during a reported gun battle with cops in St Andrew early Sunday morning.

According to a highly placed source, Archibald, otherwise called Max, was a thorn in the side of several Chinese individuals as he preyed on their businesses and homes.

“He and his cronies were on their way to hit the home of a Chinese man in the Corporate Area when they were intercepted by the police Sunday,” the Jamaica Observer source said.

Police reported that Archibald, whom they described as a “high-risk criminal target linked to two murders and a series of major robberies and break-ins across Jamaica”, was among three people fatally shot during an operation by members of the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s Specialised Operations Branch along Red Hills Road about 1:45 am.

According to the police, the Specialised Operations team was on patrol in the Red Hills area when information was received that a group of armed men travelling in two vehicles — a red Honda HR-V and a white Toyota Probox — was allegedly preparing to carry out criminal activity in the St Andrew North Police Division.

A preliminary police report said the cops attempted to intercept the vehicles but the drivers did not stop. The Probox eluded the police.

“Police subsequently intercepted the Honda HR-V in the vicinity of Knightsdale Drive. Occupants of the vehicle reportedly opened fire at members of the police team, who then discharged their service weapons,” the police said.

Three people, one of them a woman, were subsequently found with gunshot wounds. The two men were identified as Archibald, 44 years old of Mountain View, Lincoln, Manchester; and Damian Byfield, 39 years old of Fraser’s Content, St Catherine. Police sources said the woman, who was unidentified at press time, was of brown complexion, approximately 5 feet seven inches tall, with braided hair, and was clad in a black dress.

Two firearms along with ammunition were recovered, the police said.

Police said Archibald was a member of the Speculation Gang and had been identified by investigators as one of the main organisers of robberies and break-ins targeting automated teller machines (ATMs), remittance agencies, and other cash-intensive businesses.

According to police sources, the woman is critical to the criminals’ modus operandi as “they use her as a lookout or a distraction”.

Archibald has also been implicated in two murders committed within the past nine months — Chevardo Messam at Galleon Beach in Crawford district, St Elizabeth, on December 21, 2025; and Kemar Brown, otherwise called Mars, in Bristol, Alexandria, St Ann, on January 9, 2026.

A woman was shot and injured during the second incident.

Police also reported that Archibald had been linked to a shooting during an attempted theft of an ATM in Drax Hall, St Ann, in April.

Additionally, investigations had further implicated him in a series of robberies and break-ins in Linstead, St Catherine, in February and June; Kingston in April; and Croft’s Hill, Clarendon, in May.

World.title: Ministry targets book list abuse
World.content:
There have been mounting complaints annually about lengthy and expensive book lists.

JAMAICA’S education authorities are moving to rein in controversial school book lists after a special review found that some lists issued to parents do not match those approved by the ministry.

Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon says an electronic system is being developed to prevent such discrepancies, amid mounting complaints annually about lengthy and expensive book lists.

The issue has dominated the news over the past few weeks, resulting in the ministry indicating that it would review schools’ textbook lists to ensure that only essential, high-quality texts are required, given agitation about escalating back-to-school costs.

Following on those indications Morris-Dixon, in a recent interview with the Jamaica Observer, said the measures contemplated will address not just the expense but also waste.

“Sometimes the books are not used. I have seen it too where you look through the book at the end of the year and you are like ‘Wait a minute, I spent all this money on this book and it was not being used’, and so I sympathise with parents,” Morris-Dixon said.

“I spoke to the ministry team, they put together a team to relook the book lists — because book lists have to be approved by the ministry — and we have seen some instances where the book list that the parent gets is not necessarily looking like what we have approved, so we are actually putting in place an electronic system that the schools will have to upload their book lists to. We will go through it and we will make the necessary adjustments,” Morris-Dixon disclosed.

She said the ministry is also mulling whether it could further absorb more of the costs which parents now bear.

“We are also looking at whether or not it is possible — we already spend about a billion dollars on books — to add some more books in terms of the [government-provided book] programme to support students, but obviously that’s another financial expense,” the education minister told the Observer.

Noting that the ministry, at present, provides textbooks for core subjects for grades four to six students in primary schools, Morris-Dixon said the intent is to explore whether or not it “could add to the number of books that are already provided”.

“So we are exploring it, and we are looking at all different methods that we can use, but what we are thinking is: The approval process for the book list, it’s important that we tighten that up and change the process so that we in the ministry review it prior to it getting to the parents, and we can look to see whether it’s an unnecessary burden, and also looking at the extent to which we could probably give more books to the schools,” she explained.

Recently, Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness addressed the issue, saying that he had received complaints from parents.

“Many parents have said, ‘Prime Minister, why am I being asked to purchase so many books that my child who is in the grade below… when I purchased them last year… didn’t use at all? When I see the book list for this year, it’s a totally different book list and I can’t use those books again,’ ” Holness said during the Office of the Prime Minister and Office of the Cabinet Primary Exit Profile Awards Ceremony.

“Then there are other parents who said to me, ‘Prime Minister, I have family who live overseas and nobody’s using books. All the books are on tablets and computers; they’re all e-books.’ So there has to be a consideration of a more economical approach without losing the value of books,” he added.

The prime minister emphasised that books remain an essential part of the learning process and stressed that the Government is not seeking to diminish their importance in education.

The education minister, in the meantime, told the Observer that the use of the electronic books sourced by the Government in 2022 has also been contemplated in the search for solutions, but said this measure would need more thought.

“We do have e-books but what we found, we did some work and the e-books are not being used, and so we know probably the students don’t have the devices to use it, and we also want to limit device use in schools, so it’s a delicate balance. We know the e-books could solve one problem, but you may create other problems, so we are obviously trying to be very balanced in the way we move forward,” Morris-Dixon told the Observer.

World.title: Gun law credited with decrease in murders, says Chuck
World.content:
CHUCK... the mandatory minimum sentence is under consideration, but firearms are a major problem in our country and that is why we don’t want to send a signal that we are going to relent on the enforcement to condemn the possession and the use of firearms

JUSTICE Minister Delroy Chuck signalled Sunday that while legislators are set to review the mandatory minimum sentences under the 2022 Firearms Act, a repeal is unlikely as security forces and other key stakeholders are crediting the law for the sharp decline in murders and shootings in recent times.

According to the Serious Crimes Report published by the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF), up to July this year Jamaica recorded 275 murders, 23 per cent less than the 335 reported during the same period in 2025. It said overall, Category One crimes declined by 15 per cent, with 322 fewer major crimes reported than last year.

According to the JCF, the reduction in murders formed part of a broader decline in serious crimes, with shootings falling by 27 per cent, robberies by 25 per cent, while both rapes and break-ins declined by 10 per cent over the comparative period.

In January this year the country reported its lowest monthly murder figure since national crime data collection began in 2001 with 33 homicides, representing a 55 per cent reduction when compared to January 2025 which recorded 74 murders.

“I am aware that in the Firearms Act you have mandatory [minimum] sentences. It is a matter that is being examined but I can tell you that ,from where I sit, the security forces and a number of my colleagues feel that the Act is working and it is bringing down murders and shootings. It is under consideration, but firearms are a major problem in our country and that is why we don’t want to send a signal that we are going to relent on the enforcement to condemn the possession and the use of firearms. But it is under consideration,” Chuck told members of the judiciary attending the 2026 Assize Church Service at East Queen Street Baptist Church.

The Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022, which prescribes a mandatory 15-year sentence for violations, took effect in November 2022 and, among other things, provides penalties ranging from 15 years to life imprisonment for possession of illegal weapons, and establishes a dual regime — distinguishing between prohibited weapons or unregulated firearms and connected activities, and firearms that are duly authorised or registered.

However, members of the bench have telegraphed that the provision is problematic. In 2024, Appeal Court President Marva McDonald Bishop revealed that there would be a full court sitting soon to hammer out issues with aspects of the new Act which, she said, have been proving a pain to lawyers and judges alike.

“The Firearms Act is giving problems to prosecutors, it’s giving problems to trial judges, and surely at the Court of Appeal. We might have seen other cases where the court might seem inconsistent in its approach, and we have taken the decision that we have to take steps to put the court in a position where we can declare conclusively what the position of the court is on a particular area of the law so to avoid confusion,” the Appeal Court president said in presiding over a special sitting of the court marking the opening of the Michaelmas Term — her first since being appointed in July that year.

Additionally, concerns have been that the mandatory minimum provisions in the Act counteract the Plea Negotiations and Agreements Act (plea bargaining legislation), with many accused opting to head to trial rather than plead guilty at their first appearance.

On Sunday, the justice minister’s remarks about the provision came in the course of his comments about the deluge of criminal matters awaiting trial before the island’s circuit courts.

Said Chuck: “Probably one of the main criticisms of our justice system is not access to justice but the inordinate and unnecessary delays in the delivery of justice. In truth, there are non-contentious matters which really should be dealt with in weeks rather than months and years, and it’s a major complaint which we need to address. And then… there are trials that must be heard and must be determined… we cannot try all cases, it’s just impossible, and so over the next many months I will be, literally, not only advocating but on a missionary zeal to urge persons in dispute to really settle matters by mediation.

World.title: Newcomers Tru Juice ambush Mt Pleasant for historic JPL win
World.content:
In this file photo, Tru Juice FC's Daniel Roberts attempts a shot as he is being closed down by Reno FC's Raheem Kerr in the semi-finals of last season's Jamaica Football Championship at Llandilo Sports Complex in Westmoreland. Tru Juice won the game on penalties after playing out a 0-0 regulation and extra time score. (Photo: Paul Reid)

ST CATHERINE, Jamaica – Daniel Roberts and Rodave Murray both scored braces as newly promoted Tru Juice FC stunned Mt Pleasant FA 4-0 in their first-ever Jamaica Premier League game, which was held at the Bramwell Clarke Complex in Linstead on Sunday.

Roberts created Tru Juice history when he gave them the lead in the 10th minute, their first goal at this level. He then added a second in the 42nd minute. Murray then scored in the 50th and 57th minutes to complete a brilliant start to the season for the newcomers.

Tru Juice had earned promotion to the JPL after qualifying for the final of the Jamaica Football Championships last season, after losing in the previous three semi-finals.

Fellow promoted club Humble Lion, who had been relegated from the JPL after the 2024-25 season, were not so lucky on Sunday, as they were beaten 3-0 by Tivoli Gardens.

Last season’s losing finalist, Cavalier FC came from a goal down to beat Dunbeholden FC 2-1 while semi-finalists Montego Bay United blanked Chapelton Maroons 2-0 at Jarrett Park.

At Jarrett Park, Deonjay Brown scored in the first half and then assisted Dwight Merrick in the second half as Montego Bay won their opening game for the second straight season.

Devontae Campbell created the opening goal after he dribbled circles around two Chapelton defenders on the left of the 18-yard box before proving a delicate cross for Brown to head past goalkeeper Roje Williams in the 22nd minute.

Brown then provided the assist for the second goal when he found Merrick, who came on at the start of the second half, putting a left foot volley just out of the reach of Williams’ outstretched left glove in the 85th minute.

Sunday’s games

Dunbeholden-1, Cavalier FC-2

Tru Juice FC-4, Mt Pleasant FA-0

Montego Bay United-2, Chapelton Maroons- 0

Tivoli Gardens-3, Humble Lion-0

-Paul A Reid

World.title: Alleged ‘high risk’ serial robber among three killed in reported confrontation with police
World.content:
file photo

KINGSTON, Jamaica — An alleged member of the Speculation Gang who the police have linked to two murders and a series of major robberies and break-ins across Jamaica was among three persons fatally shot during an operation in St Andrew early Sunday.

Dead is Dewar Archibald, otherwise called “Max”, described by police as a high-risk criminal target.

Reports are that a team from Specialised Operations was on patrol in the Red Hills area around 1:45 am when they received information that a group of armed men travelling in a red Honda HR-V and a white Toyota Probox were allegedly preparing to carry out criminal activities in the St Andrew North Police Division.

According to the preliminary police account, officers attempted to intercept the vehicles, but the drivers failed to stop. The driver of the Probox managed to elude the police.

The police report that they intercepted the Honda HR-V in the vicinity of Knightsdale Drive where occupants of the vehicle reportedly opened fire at members of the police team, who then discharged their service weapons.

Three persons were subsequently found suffering from gunshot wounds. The identities of the other two persons have not yet been released.

The Independent Commission of Investigations has been notified.

Archibald had been identified by investigators as one of the main organisers of robberies and break-ins targeting automated teller machines (ATMs), remittance agencies and other cash-intensive businesses. He was also implicated in two murders committed within the past nine months.

Archibald was linked to the murder of Chevardo Messam at Galleon Beach in Crawford district, St Elizabeth, on December 21, 2025.

He was also implicated in the January 9 murder of Kemar Brown, otherwise called “Mars”, in Bristol, Alexandria, St Ann. A woman was shot and injured during that incident.

READ: Man killed, woman injured at shop in St Ann

Archibald had also been linked to a shooting during an attempted theft of an ATM in Drax Hall, St Ann, in April. Investigators had further implicated him in a series of robberies and break-ins in Linstead, St Catherine, in February and June; Kingston in April; and Crofts Hill, Clarendon, in May.

Investigators believe Archibald was part of an organised criminal network operating across several parishes.

Investigations are continuing.

World.title: Surge in road deaths; at least 40 killed in crashes in last 28 days
World.content:
This file photo shows the motorcycle that collided with a Honda motorcar.

KINGSTON, Jamaica — At least 40 people were killed in motor vehicle crashes in the 28 days between August 14 and September 11, according to an analysis of the daily crash reports of the Island Traffic Authority (ITA).

According to the daily crash reports, 202 people were killed as a result of 174 fatal crashes as at August 14. Those figures included 49 motorcyclists. They also represented a 15 per cent decline or 36 fewer deaths when compared to the similar period in 2025. Fatal crashes were also down 16 per cent at that time.

Fast forward to Friday, September 11 and some of those gains have been eroded as is seen in the 242 deaths from 209 fatal crashes now being reported by the ITA. According to the ITA, fatalities have decreased by 10 per cent when compared to prior year while fatal crashes are down 10 per cent when compared with similar period in 2025. Overall, there are 26 fewer deaths when compared to the similar period in 2025.

As of September 11, motorcyclists account for 63 or 26 per cent of fatalities since the start of the year. Private motor vehicle drivers account for 55 or 23 per cent, while pedestrians account for 53 deaths or 22 per cent of all fatalities this year.

The ITA is also reporting that private motor vehicle passengers, account for 33 deaths or 14 per cent of fatalities, commercial motor vehicle passengers account for deaths 14 deaths or six per cent, and pillion passengers account for eight deaths or three per cent of fatalities since January 1.

Meanwhile, the group of road users determined to be the most vulnerable – pedestrians, pedalcyclists, motorcyclists and pillion passengers combined – account for 53 per cent of fatalities. Overall, passengers account for 24 per cent of all road deaths this year, while males and females account for 86 per cent and 15 per cent respectively of fatalities since the start of the year.

In the meantime, Westmoreland parish has recorded the highest number of fatalities, accounting for 13 per cent of fatalities since the start of 2026.

— Lynford Simpson

World.title: ‘Really, really sad’
World.content:
An undated picture of seven-year-old Keriecia Hutchinson and her four-year-old brother Samson Cameron, who died in a house fire in Smith Lane, Central Kingston, on Saturday.

GRIEF and anger were palpable in the Central Kingston community of Smith Lane on Saturday as it was confirmed that seven-year-old Keriecia Hutchinson and her four-year-old brother Samson Cameron had perished in a mid-morning house fire.

Residents remembered the two children who they said were promising and full of life while anger surged as people assigned blame for their deaths.

Keriecia was a grade one student at Calabar All-Age School, while Samson was a student of Calabar Basic School.

“The mother locked them up in the house and gone to a wholesale. She could have just left them out and asked any of wi to look on them,” charged one neighbour who, like her colleagues, refused to give their names.

“The mother do nothing wrong, the [son’s] father was here and him run go up there [to the room] before the fire get wicked and him run down back and say him can’t reach the children,” charged another neighbour.

Police on the scene refused to speak with the media to confirm or deny either claim, but the contention morphed into a physical battle between one woman — who was defending the children’s grandmother — and another female resident who was chastising the parents.

Police on the scene fired a number of shots in the air to separate the combatants and at least three people were later taken into custody.

But for most residents in Smith Lane the death of the two children was their main concern.

“Right yah now me feel really, really sad that the two kids lose them lives,” said one of the few residents willing to speak to the media on condition that she not be named.

“What I get to understand, the mother wasn’t here, she gone to the wholesale, but why did she lock the children inside? And when people call out and the father run inside, the door lock, and is like him forget the key so him panic. So when the door finally open and people a throw water — even me a throw out water — it did not save the children. It really, really sad,” said the woman.

She told the Jamaica Observer that Keriecia moved to live with her mother in Smith Lane when she was about two years old, while the son, “him a must be about four or five years old now, and him born right here so inna mi hand”, added the neighbour.

She said many residents tried to put the blaze out before the Jamaica Fire Brigade team arrived but they were unsuccessful.

Residents also had praise for a neighbour who they said soaked himself in water before entering the burning house after being told that the children were inside, but he was unable to rescue them.

“He is a hero, man. Him really try, but the children were not in the front room, they were in the back, and the little girl died hugging her brother trying to save him. You could see she was trying to help him,” said one man, who, like others, refused to give his name.

At press time Saturday the fire brigade had not determined the cause of the blaze, while there was no word on whether the people involved in the physical altercation had been charged.

An unofficial count by the Sunday Observer has shown four children have died in fires across the island since the start of this year.

World.title: ‘Why did my parents forsake me?’
World.content:
A 17-year-old boy is searching for answers, guidance, and assistance to turn his life around after a series of unfortunate events saw him moving in and out of five children’s homes without a solid plan for his future.

The recent high school graduate said he does not have a relationship with his parents, with both reportedly choosing not to play an active role in his life when he was just a few months old. He is being raised by his paternal grandmother who, he said, struggles to make ends meet and wants help to get him on the right track.

The young man shared that while in primary school he was bullied daily because he seemingly did not have any parents. He said he grew frustrated with the bullies and decided to fight back. During an altercation he said he accidentally damaged the car of a staff member of the institution.

He said attempts were made to contact his parents and grandmother, but they were unsuccessful. He ended up in State care.

“I went to five boys’ homes. I went to one in Clarendon, St Mary, Kingston, Spanish Town and Old Harbour [both in St Catherine]. The first three homes were nice, because I had friends there and people didn’t do anything to me, but the last home I didn’t like it because they started to molest me,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

“I was sleeping in my dorm and this boy molested me. They held me down in my sleep. It was five boys who did that to me…I was very scared,” he recounted, his voice filled with sadness.

He said the incident was reported to a staff member, who contacted his case worker. The young man said he was taken from that home and provided counselling. Another attempt was made to contact his grandmother, who eventually agreed to take him back in her care.

He said financial struggles were heightened when the house they were living in was destroyed by fire, leaving them with little to nothing to recover.

“I lost most of my clothes and things that I had. It was a rental house, so we had to find somewhere else to live,” recalled the 17-year-old.

He said they eventually found a new place to stay but lost a lot of things that they still need to replace, such as clothes and other household items.

Now out of high school, the 17-year-old said he is seeking assistance to turn his life around. However, his greatest wish is to have a relationship with his parents, especially his mother.

“Every day I get up I just feel sad, and I don’t know why. I don’t know why I didn’t get to meet my mother…When I get up and I see a parent with a son or daughter, I always say to myself, ‘Why did my parents forsake me?’ because I never do them anything. Whenever I see children with their mother, I just start to cry and just feel sadness. I cry every single day,” he told the Sunday Observer.

The 17-year-old said he is still in contact with a counsellor who encourages him that better days are ahead, but he is still left with more questions than answers about why his life had to be this way.

“I would be happy if I had a relationship with them. I just want a relationship with my mom. People always trouble me that I don’t have any mother,” he said.

Now a high school graduate, he is uncertain about where life will take him, and needs some guidance and assistance.

“I would love to get some help to get my driver’s licence and maybe some clothes, because I want to get a job and go to work. I also want to go to school. I was thinking of applying to HEART [Human Employment and Resource Training/National Service Training Agency Trust] and learn a skill, but I need some help.

“I need support, because I’m going to be 18 soon and I want to learn how to drive and stuff so that I can take care of myself. I just want support,” he said.

His grandmother said that, over the years, she has tried her best, but with ageing and a lack of resources there is only so much she can do.

“I get help from my sisters, but that is it. Otherwise, it’s just him and me alone,” she said.

She added that the situation is made worse by the fact that she is often left with questions she cannot answer.

“Almost every day him get up and ask me what happened with his parents, and if somebody did something to run them away. I don’t know the answer. His mother just left him with me, and his father is not around,” she said.

She, too, pleaded for assistance for her grandson, wanting him to have a better future than his past.

“I would love it if him can get some assistance to go to HEART and learn a skill. He needs clothes and other things, too,” she pleaded.

World.title: EU to propose KIDS Act on social media safety
World.content:
The new proposal comes after intense pressure by government leaders like France's Emmanuel Macron to put minors' safety on social media platforms at the top of the political agenda. The French government is pushing ahead with a national law to restrict kids' access to platforms like TikTok and Instagram.

The EU's new proposal will apply to social media, video-sharing platforms, online games and AI chatbots and AI companions, but it will excluding educational tools and will also come with some tools for parents and guardians, the documents said.

The proposal will come with a new enforcement architecture similar to those of the Digital Services Act and the Artificial Intelligence Act, including supervisory fees to be paid by companies, the documents said. These landmark laws centralize enforcement of the highest-risk companies and services to the European Commission.

The text is still subject to change before it is announced and will have to be negotiated with EU governments and lawmakers.

World.title: Finland joins France’s nuclear deterrence push
World.content:
“The initiative is first and foremost about strengthening European security,” said Finnish President Alexander Stubb.

PARIS — Finland is joining France's plans to cooperate more closely with other European countries on nuclear deterrence, the two countries announced Monday.

"Today, we took a new step forward as Finland joined the French forward deterrence initiative. The initiative is first and foremost about strengthening European security," Finnish President Alexander Stubb posted on X. "It reinforces Europe’s responsibility for its own defence and helps prevent escalation."

The Nordic country's decision is the latest example of Europeans rethinking their defense posture amid Russia’s escalating hybrid attacks across the continent and doubts about the reliability of U.S. security guarantees. Finland joined NATO in 2023 after decades of neutrality, and its embrace of closer European defense cooperation reflects how Russia’s war against Ukraine has reshaped Europe's security architecture.

World.title: Left edges ahead in Swedish election thriller
World.content:
An official familiar with the matter said Kristersson intends to play hardball — he is expected to try to tempt the small, liberal Center party to leave Andersson’s camp and join his side, before forcing a vote in the new parliament on whether he can stay on as prime minister. That vote is likely to be at least two weeks away.

The finely balanced contest is bittersweet for Andersson and her allies on the left. For months, her bloc had been leading comfortably in the polls, but the race tightened dramatically in the last two weeks of the campaign.

Speaking around midnight, she said the votes counted so far pointed to an “even” outcome. “But right now we are leading and if this holds up, Sweden will get a new government,” she said, to cheers from supporters packed into her party’s glitzy election night reception.

The election is a watershed moment for Sweden: An Andersson victory would restore center-left rule, while a Kristersson win could bring the far-right Sweden Democrats — a strongly anti-immigration party founded in the 1980s by neo-Nazis — into government for the first time. The result will also be watched closely elsewhere in Europe, where nationalist movements are gaining ground.

Kristersson has been governing for the past four years with support from the Sweden Democrats in parliament, but without giving them a formal role in the coalition.

He said the closeness of the result would make forming a government “complicated,” but insisted the left had failed to win a majority for its “socialist” economic program. “Where it ends remains to be seen,” he told his supporters at the Moderates’ election night party in central Stockholm. “But we are not in a hurry.”

World.title: EU fails to agree Russia sanctions rollover with one day to spare
World.content:
Slovakia has demanded that the bloc remove Alisher Usmanov from the list. | Igor Ivanko/AFP via Getty Images

BRUSSELS — EU capitals failed to extend one of the bloc’s Russia sanctions schemes on Monday, five EU diplomats told POLITICO. Three of them said EU ambassadors will reconvene later Monday for further discussion.

Ambassadors meeting in Brussels needed to reach unanimous agreement on Monday because the regime — which governs the asset freezes of about 3,000 individuals and companies — expires Tuesday.

Slovakia has demanded that the bloc remove two rich Russian businessmen from the sanctions list: Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman. France has reportedly attempted to create a compromise by suggesting only Usmanov be delisted.

Most other capitals were unwilling to consider delisting anyone while Russia is firing record numbers of missiles at Ukrainian civilian targets. One of the diplomats said that “against the backdrop of rising hybrid threats and Russian drone attacks only 1 kilometer from the Polish border, it's hard to believe that France is actually asking for this.”

Another part of the discussion revolves around whether to extend the measures by six months, as has been customary since 2014, or renew them for 12 months. Slovakia is understood to be unwilling to back the longer period.

World.title: Carney eyes ‘unique alliance’ with EU as Trump trade war strains Canada’s ties with US
World.content:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney wants to forge much closer ties with the EU. | Andrej Ivanov/AFP via Getty Images

“We share the same values, we have the same priorities and we have very complementary strengths,” the Canadian prime minister told reporters in Toronto.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Sunday that he is not seeking full EU membership but wants to forge much closer ties with the bloc, as he prepares to travel to Strasbourg amid an escalating trade war with the U.S.

“We’re not looking to become a member of the European Union,” Carney told reporters at the Toronto International Film Festival. “What we are looking — and will begin discussions for — [is] a unique alliance with the European Union.”

“We share the same values, we have the same priorities and we have very complementary strengths,” he added.

World.title: Why Reform’s donation will change British politics
World.content:
Will a record breaking £72 million change the face of British politics?

After receiving two of the biggest political donations in history – £36m each from crypto billionaires Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne.

Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy examine the political fallout – are the donations legal, will the government legislate to stop them and how does this vast sum of money influence British politics?

Elsewhere at the TUC conference in Brighton, the unions are ramping up the pressure on the government to deliver more for workers.

Plus, could former prime minister, Liz Truss, really be plotting a return to frontline politics?

World.title: The EU’s plan for ‘weaponized’ migration
World.content:
When Commission President Ursula von der Leyen gives her big State of the European Union speech on Wednesday, the topic of migration is likely to feature heavily.

On today’s show, Zoya Sheftalovich and Nick Vinocur discuss the EU executive’s proposed new tool to counter “weaponized” migration — like we saw in Ceuta this summer. Plus, what do the results of the Swedish general election mean for the country’s migration policy?

Next, a group of European leaders and senior EU officials are in Finland today, part of Brussels’ broader push to deepen its engagement in the Arctic as the region assumes greater geopolitical importance. Expect the Arctic to stay high on the EU agenda throughout the autumn.

World.title: Italy eyes nuclear power comeback by 2035
World.content:
In an interview with POLITICO, Pichetto Fratin said the energy shocks linked to Ukraine and the Persian Gulf had exposed Italy’s “excessive dependence” on foreign supplies, making nuclear power a matter of “national security.”

The push reflects Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s ambition to make Italian industry more competitive amid Europe’s drive for energy independence. The European Commission unveiled a strategy in March to accelerate small modular reactors.

Pichetto Fratin cited forecasts of sharply rising electricity demand over the next 10 to 15 years as transport and industry electrify and data centers expand to support artificial intelligence.

Generational change was also softening resistance, he argued. “Young people today are much less ideologically driven and much more pragmatic ... They are determined to get to the bottom of things and realize that nuclear power can be a safe source of energy that can help achieve decarbonization,” he said.

Modular model

Italy’s plans focus on small modular reactors. Pichetto Fratin said serial production by the end of this decade could cut construction to three or four years, allowing generation in 2034 or 2035.

The current legislation will not immediately authorize construction but will lay the groundwork for an independent nuclear safety authority, establish waste management rules and advance plans for a national repository for radioactive waste.

World.title: Houthis capture more Yemeni Red Sea islands, tightening grip on Bab el-Mandeb
World.content:
Yemen's Tehran-backed Houthis captured more islands in the southern Red Sea, government and Houthi officials said Monday, strengthening their control of a major maritime shipping route.

 

The capture of the islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish is the latest in the group's swift advance around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key passage for oil shipments that has become even more crucial during the Iran war as the Strait of Hormuz remains under US and Iranian blockades.

Like Hormuz, located at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula — is a chokepoint that connects the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea, making it a key waterway for cargo traffic to the Mediterranean Sea.

For more than a month, the Houthis have been striking Saudi oil infrastructure and shipping in the Red Sea, stepping up pressure on global oil prices and boosting Iran's leverage in its war with the US.

Forces of the internationally recognised Yemeni government have been attempting to rally and fight back, but the Houthi gains have seemingly come with little resistance.

The Houthis deployed on the Hanish islands, 160 kilometres north of Bab el-Mandeb, after hundreds of government-allied forces withdrew from the archipelago, according to two government officials and a Houthi official.

The group officially known as Ansar Allah captured the archipelago after seizing the nearby mainland port city of Mokha and the island of Perim, inside the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

In parallel, they waged an offensive further inland, particularly in the longtime battleground province of Taiz.

FILE: People read a newspaper to follow the war news at a shop in Sana'a, 8 September 2026 AP Photo

The Houthis also launched a fresh barrage of missile and drone attacks on Saudi military targets on Monday.

The Houthis said they fired dozens of drones and missiles at the kingdom — which backs the Yemeni government — prompting the Saudi Civil Defence to issue brief alerts in the neighbouring cities of Khamis Mushait and Abha.

The Saudi Civil Defence overnight said a Houthi projectile fell in a different area near the border with Yemen along the Red Sea, injuring two people and damaging a mosque and several other buildings.

Riyadh did not announce any new attacks targeting the Houthis.

Thousands fleeing fighting in Yemen

The Houthis came to power in late 2014 after storming Sana'a and seizing the presidential palace and key military sites, forcing Yemen's government into exile.

The group triggered a return to hostilities in Yemen's civil war in July after a UN truce that had largely maintained quiet since 2022, when they let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace.

Riyadh retaliated by striking the airport, prompting the Houthis to declare a blockade on the kingdom targeting its oil trade in July.

Some 150 civilians have been killed in fighting since 3 September, the government's Human Rights Ministry said. More than 200 civilians have been wounded, it said.

Thousands of families have fled their homes in Taiz and nearby provinces in the past day alone, said Khanzad Shah, acting head of Islamic Relief, a charity that operates in the area.

"Many of them don't have enough food or water as they had to flee with whatever they could carry. In some areas, whole villages have reportedly emptied," he said.

Displaced Yemenis rest at a temporary shelter in the Dar Saad district of Aden, 12 September 2026 AP Photo

The UN has estimated that more than 80,000 people have been displaced in the past two weeks, including over 2,000 people who fled by boat to Djibouti.

The fighting threatens to reignite a war that for more than a decade brought disaster to Yemen, killing more than 150,000 people and driving the country to the brink of famine.

The internationally recognised government supported by an array of disparate militias controls the south and east, including the key southern port of Aden.

The Hanish islands, newly captured by the Houthis, had been controlled by the UAE-backed allies. However, the UAE dismantled its military infrastructure there earlier this year.

For years, Saudi Arabia waged an air campaign against the Houthis, while backing the government and allied militias, yet it has appeared reluctant to throw itself fully back into the war, despite the Houthi attacks on oil infrastructure and shipping.

The Houthis are tied to Tehran's so-called Axis of Resistance — a loose network of militant groups in several countries in the region including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and militias in Iraq, all backed, trained and equipped by the IRGC to varying degrees.

Yemeni government forces to regroup?

On Sunday, the Yemeni government's military said it launched airstrikes on Houthi positions in the port city of Mokha, the coastal town of Dhubab and elsewhere in Taiz province.

The Houthis reported strikes by the Saudi-backed forces in Taiz province and artillery shelling in Saada province, the birthplace of the Houthi movement on Yemen's northern border with Saudi Arabia.

Sultan al-Arada, a member of the government's presidential leadership council, described the collapse of government forces in Mokha, about 80 kilometres from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and elsewhere on Yemen's west coast as "painful and regrettable."

He said in a televised interview aired late Saturday that forces "are currently regrouping and will return to the battle."

Rashad al-Alimi, who leads the presidential council, sought on Sunday to downplay the defeats as "incidental," according to comments published by the country's state-run SABA news agency.

The government "will remain clear and fixed on the goal of retrieving institutions and of reclaiming sovereignty over all national territories," al-Alimi said.

World.title: SoftBank shares plunge as calls grow to slow AI development
World.content:
Shares in Japanese investment conglomerate SoftBank Group, a major investor in OpenAI, plunged more than 10% on Monday, alongside other technology shares, after executives at some of the world’s leading AI companies backed calls to prioritise “caution over speed and prudence over profit”.

 

The phrase was used by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who called on Saturday for AI companies to “pace the frontier” through a coordinated slowdown in the development of their most advanced models, allowing more time to understand and manage the risks.

Among his main concerns is so-called “recursive self-improvement”, in which AI systems help to build the next generation of AI models.

“Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all,” Amodei wrote.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and xAI CEO Elon Musk publicly backed his warning, with Musk saying: “Dario is right.”

Altman also told Fortune in an interview published on Saturday that OpenAI would not proceed with an initial public offering this year, as the company focuses on safety.

OpenAI and Anthropic are both privately owned. Anthropic is reportedly preparing for a possible stock market listing in the coming months.

The comments followed the resignation of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who warned that the technology could escape human control.

Evan Hubinger, another Anthropic researcher who remains at the company, subsequently wrote: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” He said he believed the probability was greater than 10% within the next decade.

US President Donald Trump rejected the warnings on Sunday, calling AI critics “very negative forces” and saying the scenarios they raised would not happen. House Speaker Mike Johnson also urged people not to panic.

Investors nevertheless sold technology shares on Monday.

SoftBank’s decline “probably reflects the possibility that AI development may be slowed by regulators to try to avoid the worst-case outcomes that Anthropic and OpenAI have discussed,” said Dan Baker of investment research firm Morningstar.

“And maybe [it] also reflects the possibility that any further examples of loss of control of newer AI models could also slow AI development,” he added.

Other AI-related shares in Asia also fell. South Korean memory-chip maker SK Hynix lost 5.3%, while Samsung Electronics dropped 2.8%. Japanese chip-equipment manufacturer Tokyo Electron fell 0.9%, while memory-chip maker Kioxia Holdings sank 6%.

The race with China

Amodei also called for tighter restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips and semiconductor-manufacturing equipment, arguing that chips would largely determine the country’s AI capabilities.

However, he acknowledged to CBS News that the “toughest dilemma” was that China might not join a coordinated slowdown.

China’s state-backed Global Times described his position as “short-sighted” and accused him of trying to restrict China’s development through an “AI Cold War”. Meanwhile, President Xi Jinping has proposed a BRICS open-source AI zone to deepen cooperation on AI models and training.

World.title: Could astronauts get cataract surgery on Mars? Scientists test eye implants in space
World.content:
A trip to Mars could take months. So what happens if an astronaut develops a serious eye problem halfway there?

 

A team of researchers in the United States sent artificial lenses used in cataract surgery outside the International Space Station to find out whether the implants needed for future operations could survive the journey to places such as Mars.

Researchers behind the study believe someone will need cataract surgery on Mars in his lifetime.

“A Mars transit can require almost a year, and returning to Earth for a vision-limiting cataract, injury, or other surgical eye problem may not be realistic,” said Morgan Micheletti, an ophthalmic surgeon and director of research at Berkeley Eye Center in the US.

“Eventually, treatment will need to happen where the patient is.”

A cataract develops when the eye's natural lens becomes cloudy. During surgery, doctors remove that lens and replace it with a clear artificial one called an intraocular lens.

Doing the same thing millions of kilometres from Earth would require someone capable of carrying out the operation, as well as equipment, sterile supplies and implants that survive the journey.

The idea also grew out of a fascination Micheletti has had since childhood.

“I have been fascinated by space for as long as I can remember,” he said.

“Once I became an eye surgeon, that fascination evolved into a more practical question. Could I perform surgery in space?”

What happened to the lenses in space?

For the project named JAMES, the team sent 135 unpackaged artificial lenses to the International Space Station.

They spent around six months outside the station in three positions, exposing them to different conditions — One faced highly reactive atomic oxygen, another received substantial ultraviolet radiation from the Sun and a third was partly shielded from both.

Another 45 unpackaged lenses remained on Earth for comparison.

After the space lenses returned, a team at the Intermountain Ocular Research Center at the University of Utah examined 61 of them alongside 20 of the lenses kept on Earth.

Most of the space-exposed lenses, 42 out of 61, showed no notable changes.

Of the other 19, eight acrylic lenses developed cracks and surface roughness consistent with erosion from atomic oxygen, while five developed yellow discolouration and let less light through at some wavelengths.

All six light-adjustable lenses, which can be fine-tuned with ultraviolet light after implantation, developed an unusual cobblestone or “bubble-wrap” appearance. Researchers do not yet know why.

That does not mean cataract implants would necessarily be damaged on a journey to Mars, researchers caution.

The lenses were deliberately unpackaged and exposed directly to the harsh environment outside the station to identify how they might fail. In reality, they would travel protected inside a spacecraft.

The next step is to work out how much packaging and shielding they need without adding unnecessary weight and volume.

How realistic is cataract surgery in space?

Cataract surgery beyond Earth remains a distant prospect.

The experiment tested how the artificial lenses withstand space conditions, not whether surgery itself could safely be performed there. Researchers also do not yet know whether the changes found in some lenses would affect vision or make them unusable.

Micheletti next wants to test the machine used in cataract surgery during short periods of microgravity on parabolic flights.

It uses ultrasound and fluid to break up and remove the eye's cloudy natural lens.

If that works, he hopes to move towards longer microgravity tests and eventually a surgical experiment in orbit.

“The progression has to be deliberate. First the materials, then the equipment, then the procedure and, ultimately, the surgery,” he said.

“My long-term hope is to help make the first eye surgery beyond Earth possible.”

Findings from the experiment were presented at the European Society of Cataract and Refractive Surgeons congress in London on Sunday.

Researchers believe it is the first controlled experiment to expose multiple types of modern artificial eye lenses directly to the environment outside the International Space Station and return them to Earth for laboratory analysis.

World.title: Poland and Ukraine slam Russian strike on train near their border as 'escalation'
World.content:
Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he expected Moscow to escalate the war in "in the coming weeks", following Russian strikes that hit a Warsaw-bound train in Ukraine, just two kilometres from its border with Poland.

 

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said she believed Russia's strike to close to the Polish border was designed to "scare" Western countries backing Kyiv.

"It is clearly meant to scare Western countries from supporting Ukraine, from going to Ukraine to show support," Kallas said, urging Kyiv's supporters to do "the opposite".

Meanwhile the country's foreign minister Radoslaw Sikorski urged allies to "double" their support for Ukraine, following what he also called an "escalation".

The train was at Yahodyn station when the strike occured. According to reports, only the train's engine was hit. Ukrainian authorities said all passengers were evacuated and no casualties were reported.

Poland's prime minister Donald Tusk responds to the strikes just 2km from the border

Shortly before the train was hit, a different train carrying senior EU officials and the former British prime minister Boris Johnson, passed through Yahodyn on the same line towards Poland on their way back from a conference in Kyiv.

At the time of the attack, on board a different train at the same station was the former CIA director David Patraeus. He told the New York Times that he heard Russian drones overhead and a subequent explosion, describing it as "terrifying".

Former UK prime minister Boris Johnson was travelling on the same line on a different train shortly before this strike hit a locomotive

Russia said it had hit "railway infrastructure used to transport military cargo" from European countries.

Ukraine's president Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Moscow of "deliberately" striking the locomotive.

"It is precisely to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe that Ukrainian men and women fight every day, give their lives, and do not allow the aggression to expand," Zelensky said.

Elsewhere, Russia's strikes on Ukraine on Sunday killed at least two people in the city of Kramatorsk.

Ukrainian officials also reported that 20 people, including two children, had been injured in the southern port city of Odesa.

World.title: 'Wind turbines cause animal malformations': True or false?
World.content:
Norway made history on 6 March 2024 when it settled on a new deal for peaceful coexistence between the Sámi community and one of Europe's largest onshore wind power sites.

 

The agreement granted Sámi reindeer herders more winter grazing land, partly free electricity and the right to veto potential future wind farm concessions in exchange for allowing 151 turbines operated by Roan Vind to remain in the coastal Fosen district.

Nevertheless, two years later, the story was turned on its head by a false social media narrative with hundreds of thousands of views, which claimed that Norway's Supreme Court had ordered the turbines to be removed.

The posts alleged that the court had done so because the wind turbines were causing the birth of deformed reindeer.

As is often the case with fake stories, there was a grain of truth in it: the court did rule in 2021 that the operating licences for the wind farm were invalid, but only because the project violated the Sámi people's cultural rights, not because of any health issues in animals.

Where did the deformed reindeer conspiracy come from?

This conspiracy feeds into a bigger theory claiming that the turbines cause health problems related to their infrasound and low-frequency noise, generally between 35 and 45 dB.

For example, some allege that they cause tinnitus, ear pain, vertigo, and even back pain and accelerated ageing.

However, a large body of scientific work says that there is no evidence linking living close to properly installed wind turbines with adverse health effects.

Wind turbines pictured near Halle, in Germany AP/Matthias Schrader

"Based on the findings and scientific merit of the research conducted to date, it is our opinion that the weight of evidence suggests that when sited properly, wind turbines are not related to adverse health effects," says a paper published in the National Library of Medicine.

"This claim is supported (and made) by findings from several government health and medical agencies and legal decisions," it continues. "Other hypotheses suggest the stress could be connected to unpleasant visual cues, or even a general sense of concern about the turbines."

Indeed, some people living near wind turbines have reported headaches, stress and sleep disruption, but researchers suggest that these are caused by annoyance, visual cues or even the nocebo effect (where people experience real symptoms because they expect something to be harmful), rather than the sound that wind turbines may make.

In any case, there are no scientific reports of any deformed reindeer being born in Norway or elsewhere because of wind turbines.

World.title: Swedish centre-left holds slim election lead, but final result still too close to call
World.content:
Preliminary results in Sweden's general election show the left-led bloc of opposition parties holding a three-seat majority over the incumbent right-wing alliance led by Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson. Nevertheless, the final result remains too close to call.

 

Opinion polls had given the left-wing opposition a comfortable lead for much of the campaign, but the gap narrowed significantly in the final days before the vote.

The four opposition parties are led by Magdalena Andersson, leader of the Social Democrats. Her party is on around 28% of the vote and appears to be heading for its worst result in more than a century. Andersson said that if her opposition bloc’s lead is confirmed, she would be ready to form a new government. She has pledged higher taxes on banks and high earners, shorter healthcare waiting times and measures aimed at improving education.

Social Democrats party leader Magdalena Andersson votes at a polling station in Nacka, Sweden, on Sunday Stefan Jerrevång/TT News Agency via AP

Kristersson, whose Moderate Party had around 19.9% of the counted vote, said he would respect Andersson’s attempt to form a government if the result holds.

While the centre-left parties in the lead, for the individual parties, both the far-left and far-right parties have lost support.

The far-right Sweden Democrats have lost support compared with the 2022 election, with initial results showing their vote share falling from 20.6% to 17.6%. Party leader Jimmie Akesson nevertheless argued that the result showed the party had become more accepted in Swedish politics. “There are now so many more people around our country who no longer find it difficult to say that they are Sweden Democrats,” Akesson said.

Leader of the Sweden Democrats party Jimmie Akesson votes in Rinkeby, a suburb of Stockholm Claudio Bresciani/TT via AP

Since 2022 Kristersson’s government has relied on parliamentary support from the Sweden Democrats, giving the party significant influence over policy. He had promised the party key cabinet posts if the right-wing alliance won.

A Social Democrat-led coalition would end four years of right-wing government under Ulf Kristersson. His government came to power four years ago amid a growing concern over gang shootings and organised crime.

A change of government would not necessarily mean a reversal of Sweden’s tougher stance on migration. The Social Democrats have said a restrictive migration policy would remain under an Andersson-led government.

Still the final result may several days away. Late-arriving votes are due to be counted from Wednesday, while all ballots are automatically recounted by regional authorities.

World.title: France and Germany struggle to get their act together on European defence
World.content:
Paris and Berlin have never agreed on how far the EU should go in building up its own defence industry versus keeping the market open to outside partners. Now, as Europe's defence needs to grow more, that disagreement is coming to a head.

 

With Washington gradually pulling back from Europe, Russian pressure mounting on the eastern flank and China's geopolitical ambitions growing, the EU has rarely faced a more urgent moment to build up its own defence capabilities. But France and Germany cannot agree on how to do it.

Ever since Donald Trump returned to the Oval Office in January 2025, Europe's defence spending has surged, spurred by an administration that rarely misses a chance to accuse its allies of free-riding on American military power.

The fifth year of Russia's war against Ukraine, combined with Washington's announced troop withdrawal from Europe, has further fuelled concerns in EU capitals about the need to scale up defence readiness, both to support Kyiv and to boost deterrence.

But while there has never been more money on the table for European defence, there is still no shared vision at EU level on how that capability should be built: through purely domestic industry, or in partnership with allies.

"It's really a disagreement within the pro-European camp on what the best strategy is to build a strong industry in Europe, and especially, as far as defence is concerned, to be independent from all the great powers of the world," MEP Jean-Marc Germain (France/S&D) told Euronews.

Opposite visions

After Friedrich Merz became German Chancellor last year, there initially seemed to be growing alignment between Paris and Berlin on how to tackle their shared security challenges.

"We have decided to work together to ensure European preference in essential and critical industrial production sectors, including in our public procurement. Until recently, this was a European taboo," President Emmanuel Macron said at a joint press conference in August 2025.

But despite that early commitment to a European preference in public procurement, with defence contracts as the primary testing ground, deep-rooted strategic divergences soon resurfaced.

Since the Second World War, Paris has championed the idea of strategic autonomy: that Europe should act as an independent power, distinct from both superpowers, building a sovereign nuclear arsenal and a matching military-industrial complex.

By contrast, post-war Germany has traditionally kept its economy open, treated its trade surplus as close to inviolable, and kept defence spending relatively low, relying on NATO for its security.

Since the start of the second Trump administration, however, Berlin has abandoned its historical fiscal frugality, exempting defence and security spending from its constitutional debt brake and setting a target of 3.5% of GDP for defence spending by 2029.

Yet Germany's repositioning in the military sphere has not brought it closer to its closest European partner — instead, it has exposed a deep-rooted tension between the two countries' mentalities.

"We work very closely with the American defence industry, and we intend to continue doing so. There are simply systems that we don't yet have, or that we don't currently have. But we urgently need them in the next five to ten years," Germany's Federal Defence Minister Boris Pistorius said at a press conference in July.

As the traditional driving force behind European integration, the EU rarely advances without France and Germany moving in tandem. Yet that partnership has seldom faced such visible strains as in the ongoing negotiations over the bloc’s next long-term budget.

European preference

The European Commission's initial proposal earmarked €131bn for defence, security and space under the new European Competitiveness Fund, a fivefold increase on the previous budget period.

France wants that money to support a genuinely European defence-industrial base, while Germany wants to preserve its freedom to work with companies from NATO partners such as Norway, Canada and the UK.

Elements of European preference have already been written into EU defence policy. Under the Security Action for Europe (SAFE), the European Defence Industry Programme and the Ukraine Support Loan, at least 65% of procured defence products must be produced in Europe.

But these programmes also include exceptions for cases where European production cannot meet the required timing, volume or cost, exemptions France has been pushing to phase out, including for items such as ballistic interceptors and drone components.

Ultimately, the EU is trying to balance two objectives at once: meeting the immediate demands of boosting Europe's deterrence and supporting Ukraine's war effort, while ramping up domestic production to cut off strategic dependencies in the long run.

"France and Germany come from very different corners," an EU diplomat told Euronews, adding that they "don't always see eye to eye, but this tension is good because it helps to move the discussion forward."

But while Brussels tries to reconcile short-term pragmatism with long-term strategy, the fallout in Franco-German relations is already being felt, undermining joint projects and fuelling national fragmentation across the EU.

Faltering collaboration

Earlier this year, Berlin announced a €10bn satellite-based communication system for its military, directly competing with the EU's IRIS² secure connectivity network and prompting concerns about duplication.

In June, France and Germany formally abandoned plans to build a next-generation fighter jet under the Future Combat Air System (FCAS), a €100bn programme, after industrial disputes proved unsolvable.

The collapse of FCAS has also called into question Franco-German collaboration on tanks under the Main Ground Combat System (MGCS), with Berlin reportedly looking for more national autonomy and alternative options.

Meanwhile, the German government has been pushing Washington to allow the licensed production of advanced American weapons systems in Germany, in particular Patriot interceptors and Tomahawk cruise missiles.

For Paris, these are all signs that Berlin is pursuing a 'Germany first' approach: localising defence production at home with large-scale licensing deals with American companies; making massive national investments while pushing for cuts to the next EU budget.

Berlin, by contrast, considers France the outlier in this debate, isolated in pushing for very strict European preference rules that would advantage French companies, while most of the EU's defence industry openly collaborates with NATO partners.

"It has to be taken seriously because it's a real blockage," MEP Germain said. "The positions are not only far apart, but they rely on completely different strategies for European competitiveness and defence."

World.title: Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies
World.content:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan is signalling a move to expand nuclear power cooperation with Russia, just as his country’s first Russian-built nuclear station prepares to go live later this year. The deepening partnership is likely to unsettle Turkey’s western allies.

Advertising

On the sidelines of a recent gathering of regional leaders in Kyrgyzstan, Erdogan told his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, that Russia and Turkey “will take steps together to open some new power plants, along with the opening of the Akkuyu nuclear power plant”.

The Akkuyu nuclear power plant, built by Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, is due to go online later this year.

Erdogan’s announcement comes amid strained ties with Russia, as the Turkish leader has deepened relations with United States President Donald Trump.

Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, head of the Ankara office of US think tank the German Marshall Fund, describes Erdogan’s move as a “gesture” to Putin.

“Although Turkey is competing with Russia geopolitically, and although Turkey is firmly anchored in NATO and is improving its relationship with the United States, it does not intend to sever all ties with Russia,” Unluhisarcikli explained.

“Indeed, Turkey sees the Turkey-Russia relationship as a long-term strategic one. And this is, by the way, consistent with Turkey's balancing act.”

Trump tests Turkey's energy dependence on Russia with lure of US power

Nuclear lifeline

For Ankara, nuclear energy promises to help it break free from its heavy reliance on imported power. Once operational, the Akkuyu plant in southern Turkey will supply as much as 10 percent of the country’s electricity.

Rosatom owns the Akkuyu power plant and will recoup the estimated €21.5 billion construction costs by selling electricity to Turkey, generating annual income of around €2-3 billion.

Such income could be a vital tool for Moscow to mitigate tightening sanctions by both the European Union and the United States.

“The Akkuyu nuclear power plant allows Russia to build itself various state-to-state payment channels to store liquidity in Turkish banks without necessarily interfering with any sanctions regulations,” according to George Voloshin of Acams, a global organisation dedicated to anti-financial crime, training and education.

Voloshin believes that, given the project's 60- to 80-year lifespan, Turkey’s commitment to Russian nuclear power will shape bilateral ties for the long term, with consequences.

“It will be a source of scrutiny from western partners of Turkey. At the same time, nuclear energy has been so far shielded from any sanctions, so for Russia it is clearly a kind of lifeline,” he said.

The Akkuyu plant, currently under construction, will be Turkey's first nuclear power station. © AFP/Dogan News Agency/Ibrahim Mese

Turkey seeks Black Sea shipping deal as attacks threaten grain trade

Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Ankara has maintained that it is not bound by EU or US sanctions on Moscow. Yet behind the scenes, it has quietly followed many restrictions and secured crucial waivers, especially for Russian gas.

By leveraging its pivotal location near Syria and Iran, Ankara has walked a diplomatic tightrope between its western partners and Moscow.

However, deepening nuclear cooperation with Russia threatens to complicate the already difficult balancing act.

“It would reinforce the already existing distrust between Turkey and Europe and Turkey and the United States,” warned Unluhisarcikli.

“But at the same time, Turkey is in talks with other countries, the United States and South Korea. These are the main two competitors for Russia.”

Mutual dependency

Turkey’s dependence on Russian fossil fuels has stirred unease at home, and the idea of doubling down with Russian nuclear energy only heightens the sense of anxiety. “It is a dilemma,” Unluhisarcikli conceded.

Yet with Russia willing to shoulder the hefty construction costs, cash-strapped Ankara has a strong incentive to continue the partnership.

Russia expert Zaur Gasimov of Istanbul’s Turkish-German University points out that more than a decade of joint investment makes it tough for Turkey to turn to alternative suppliers.

"It's quite a profound project,” said Gasimov, “Russia conducts the training of Turkish specialists in the field of nuclear energy, which started 15 years ago. We now have three or four waves of Turkish engineers who stayed for longer periods in Russia; they learn the Russian language for two years, and you have an infrastructure of specialists.”

However, Gasimov stresses that, given the scale of investment by both sides, it has created an important mutual dependency. “Its importance makes the two sides, somehow, at the end, interested in preserving a certain level of the relationship,” he said.

This shared reliance might help keep Turkish-Russian rivalries in check, from North Africa to the Middle East, the Caucasus and the Black Sea.

Yet any step toward deeper nuclear cooperation is bound to invite sharper scrutiny and rising suspicion from Ankara’s western allies.
