A drone has struck a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw, around two kilometres from the Polish border, amid the latest round of mass Russian attacks on Ukraine. In a separate incident, a truck was also hit in Ukraine around 800 metres from a border crossing with Poland. “This is Putin’s terror ‘knocking’ directly on the doors of the EU and NATO,” wrote Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha. “Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners.” 🚨 BREAKING: Russian drone targeted a passenger train on the border with Poland. "Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners. Act now: throw the full weight of your sanctions at Putin’s aggressive regime," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Sybiha wrote in response. pic.twitter.com/VsgQ2UGtPb — UNITED24 Media (@United24media) September 13, 2026 “Today in the Volyn region, two kilometres from the Polish border, the enemy struck the locomotive of a passenger train,” announced Ukrainian Railways in a statement. “A monitoring group warned the train crew of the threat in advance, ensuring that no one was injured.” Ukrainian media outlets report that the train in question was a service running between Kyiv and Warsaw. They shared a video purportedly showing the strike, in which passengers are seen fleeing a train as an explosion is seen and heard in the background. Ukrainian Railways’ deputy director for communications, Oleksandr Shevchenko, was quoted by media outlet Suspilne confirming that the strike had been carried out by a Russian drone. Meanwhile, Poland’s border guard on Sunday morning confirmed to news website Interia that a drone had struck a truck in Ukraine around 800 metres from the Dorohusk-Jagodzin border crossing between the two countries. Earlier reports and images shared on social media had indicated that a petrol station at that location had been hit, causing a fire. The spokeswoman for Poland’s interior ministry, Karolina Gałecka, said that no injuries had been reported on the Polish side of the border. The border guard said that traffic at the crossing was proceeding normally. 🚨 BREAKING: Russian drones struck a gas station near the Yahodyn checkpoint on the Polish border, setting off a massive fire that engulfed parked cargo trucks. Border guards suspended processing and sheltered visitors during the air alert. pic.twitter.com/SSUiXayBYS — UNITED24 Media (@United24media) September 13, 2026 The interior minister himself, Marcin Kierwiński, condemned the two “Russian terrorist attacks” near the border and declared that “Russia is the enemy of the free world”. Sybiha, meanwhile, said that the incidents highlighted why the world must take “uncompromising, powerful steps…[to] make Moscow feel the consequences of its terror”. “Full trade embargo. Full entry bans. Full sanctions on the military-industrial complex,” wrote the Ukrainian foreign minister. “Putin needs to understand that his barbarism will be met with decisive action that increases the cost of war for him to an unacceptable level. Act now: throw the… — Andrii Sybiha 🇺🇦 (@andrii_sybiha) September 13, 2026 On Sunday morning, the operational command of Poland’s armed forces confirmed that it had activated defence and reconnaissance systems in response to Russia’s overnight drone attacks on Ukraine, but that no violations of Polish airspace had been recorded. Poland’s Government Security Centre (RCB) sent alerts overnight to residents in two provinces bordering Ukraine, while alarm sirens also went off in some areas right on the border. Deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk said that the latest incidents emphasise why it is necessary to provide military support to Ukraine. “Every missile destroyed and every drone shot down [in Ukraine] is a threat that doesn’t fly any further,” he wrote. In July, a Russian missile entered Polish airspace and crashed in the east of the country during a previous round of mass Russian attacks on Ukraine. World.title: Poland issued EU’s third most residence permits to immigrants in 2025
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland issued first residence permits to almost half a million immigrants in 2025, which was the third-highest figure in the European Union, behind Spain and Germany but ahead of Italy and France. However, the number of permits issued by Poland fell for the fourth year running, as the country continued to tighten its migration rules. Previously, between 2017 and 2022, Poland had led the EU figures for six years running, reaching a peak of almost one million permits in 2021. The new data, released on Friday by Eurostat, the EU’s statistical agency, show that Poland issued 467,314 first residence permits to immigrants from outside the EU in 2025. As was the case last year, Spain (635,438) issued the most, followed by Germany (605,292). Poland was then followed by Italy (433,099) and France (377,462). However, whereas in those four other countries the number of permits rose in 2025 (by 13.1% in Spain, 11.1% in Germany, 25.0% in Italy and 9.2% in France), in Poland the figure fell by 4.4%. That decline has come amid a tougher new migration strategy by the current government, a coalition that ranges from left to centre right, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Ahead of elections in 2023, Tusk, then in opposition, accused the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which had ruled Poland since 2015, of allowing “uncontrolled” migration, including through widespread abuses of the visa system. Shortly after coming to power in those elections, Tusk, a former president of the European Council, declared that the “survival of Western civilisation” depends upon preventing mass migration. His government has since introduced tougher entry requirements for foreign workers and students, suspended asylum rights for migrants who irregularly cross the border from Belarus, and stepped up deportations of immigrants who have committed crimes or entered the country unlawfully. Poland has introduced tougher new rules regulating the entry of foreign students and immigrant workers. “This is another step towards regaining control over migration and increasing the safety of Poles," says the government https://t.co/gYdikpc6pL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 2, 2025 The new 2025 data show that, in relative terms (the number of permits issued in relation to countries’ populations), Poland was only ninth in the EU (12.8 permits per 1,000 people), behind Malta (56.9), Cyprus (46.7), Portugal (27.3), Lithuania (18.5), Ireland (13.4), Croatia (13.2), Luxembourg (13.1) and Spain (12.9). That marks a significant decline since 2021, when Poland issued 967,345 permits, which was the highest in the EU in absolute terms but also second-highest in relation to population. In 2025, as in previous years, Poland issued the most first residence permits to Ukrainians (241,126, 51.6% of the total), who are by far the country’s largest immigrant group. They were followed by Belarusians (128,468, 27.5%), Georgians (10,249, 2.2%), Indians (9,230, 2%) and Turks (7,533, 1.6%) – the same top five nationalities as in 2024. Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians https://t.co/hNiOqmeUfX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2026 Following a decade of unprecedented mass migration, the number of foreigners with residence permits in Poland this year passed two million for the first time, making up just over 5% of the country’s population. Around 1.5 million of those are Ukrainians. In June, the number of foreigners working in Poland reached 1.14 million, making up almost 7% of the workforce. While Ukrainians constitute two thirds of the total, the fastest-growing nationalities are Colombians and Indians, who are now the third- and fourth-largest groups of foreign workers. The rise in migration has come as Poland’s economy has boomed but the country has also faced a demographic crisis, with a shrinking, ageing population and one of the lowest birth rates in the world. In 2023, the state Social Insurance Institution (ZUS) calculated that, in order to maintain its ratio of working-age population to retirees, Poland would need to attract almost two million immigrant workers over the following decade. However, it admitted that that target was “unrealistic”. World.title: Poland and other V4 countries will block EU climate policies that raise energy costs, warns Tusk
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has warned that the Central European Visegrád Group (V4) would seek to block any European Union climate policies that push up energy prices. Speaking after a meeting with the leaders of the other V4 countries, Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic, Tusk said that they could not accept policies that further weakened competitiveness at a time when they were already facing high electricity costs. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk w #Bratysława ⤵️ Polska i grupa #V4 nie pozwoli na żadne zmiany i na żadne propozycje instytucji europejskich, czy innych państw, które mogłyby wpłynąć na pogorszenie sytuacji energetycznej w naszych państwach. Ceny energii w tym regionie muszą spaść. pic.twitter.com/BFnRx8Clse — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 10, 2026 In recent months, Poland and some other member states have been pushing for a softening of the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), a cap-and-trade scheme launched in 2005 that makes polluters pay for carbon emissions in sectors such as power generation and heavy industry. They have also secured a postponement of the introduction of ETS2, which will cover emissions from road transport and buildings. “Whether we are talking about ETS1, ETS2, or other proposals, anything that brings a risk of more expensive energy for us will be blocked by us,” said Tusk on Thursday at a press conference alongside the other V4 prime ministers, as well as Ireland’s Micheál Martin. “Poland and the V4 will not allow any changes or any proposals from European institutions or other countries that could worsen the energy situation in our countries,” he added. “Energy prices in this region, including in Poland, must fall.” Poland has recorded the EU's third-fastest rise in household electricity prices this year. The country now also has the bloc’s second-most-expensive electricity, when taking cost of living into account https://t.co/WNLdCfOP16 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2025 Tusk argued that high energy prices pose a threat not only to Central European economies but also to the competitiveness of the EU as a whole. “We can forget about any dreams of competing with China or the United States if our energy prices remain as they are right now,” warned Tusk. Slovakian Prime Minister Robert Fico likewise said the V4 countries were united in their approach to the emissions trading system. “We will be very active, and we will also engage in discussions outside the meetings of the European Council and the Council of Europe to discuss what steps to take to bring down these energy prices,” he said. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš also expressed frustration with rising energy costs. “All of us in our industrial region pay a lot of money for emissions allowances. And what did the commission tell us in 2020? That the price of this allowance in 2030 will be €26.50. Right now, it’s €80,” he said. According to the Eurostat data, households in Poland paid €27.09 per 100 kilowatt-hours (kWh), including taxes and levies, for electricity in the second half of 2025. That was the 11th highest figure in the EU and below the figure of €28.96 across the bloc as a whole. However, when adjusted for purchasing power standards (PPS), which account for differences in costs of living, Polish households faced the second-highest electricity prices in the EU, at 37.15 PPS per 100 kWh, behind only Romania (49.52 PPS) and the Czech Republic (39.16 PPS). The effects of ETS on electricity bills has moved to the centre of political debate this year after the main opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), called for Poland to unilaterally withdraw from the system, saying it makes “Poles a cash machine for the EU’s absurd leftist climate policy”. The opposition-aligned conservative president, Karol Nawrocki, has also twice sought to call national referendums on rejecting EU climate policies, including ETS, arguing they are too expensive. Both his efforts were rejected by the government’s majority in parliament. While the government has rejected the idea of withdrawing from ETS – which it says would result in large, ongoing fines being levied against Poland – it has pushed for reforms to the system. In July, the European Commission outlined proposals to soften ETS in response to pressure from countries such as Poland, allowing industries to continue emitting CO2 for longer while providing more financial support for investment in clean technologies. Yet there are also a number of other EU member states that argue against weakening ETS, saying it would penalise those who moved early to cut emissions. Poland's right-wing opposition wants to withdraw from the EU Emissions Trading System, saying it makes Poles "a cash machine for absurd leftist climate policies"@PStrzalkowski explains what costs ETS really brings, and what prospects there are for reform https://t.co/UxpMWpG1pE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 4, 2026 Just before the European Commission unveiled its proposal in July, Poland’s climate minister, Paulina Hennig-Kloska, said she had assembled a coalition of 10 countries calling for ETS reform and a more realistic emissions-reduction path. They also want ETS funding mechanisms to account for national differences, including energy mixes and GDP per capita, to ensure a fairer transition for lower-income countries starting from a more challenging position. Poland, for example, has a historical reliance on coal, which it still uses to produce around half of its electricity, helping make it one of the EU’s biggest emitters. Renewables generated 29.4% of Poland's electricity in 2025, almost exactly the same figure as in 2024, ending a period of strong growth since 2021. Coal (52.2%) remained the dominant source, though its share declined. For more, read our full report: https://t.co/XjD9hfhabo pic.twitter.com/WklP7dYL78 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 2, 2026 However, the country has made significant progress in expanding renewables in recent years, particularly solar and onshore wind. In 2025, renewables accounted for just over 29% of Poland’s electricity generation, almost three times the share recorded a decade earlier. Further progress is expected this year, after Poland began to generate electricity from offshore wind farms for the first time. Under a national energy and climate plan approved by the current government in June, it plans by 2040 for Poland to generate 18-21% of power from offshore wind and 22-27% from onshore wind. A further 15-16% will come from nuclear, 14-18% from solar, 7-8% from gas and 0-5% from coal. Poland’s first offshore wind farm has begun to deliver electricity, with Prime Minister @donaldtusk celebrating the development as a "key element of our energy security and sovereignty". The government wants 20% of power to come from offshore wind by 2040 https://t.co/EodvInFmrn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 10, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish far-right leader Braun vandalises Ukrainian monument with hammer
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has published a video of himself using a hammer to attack a monument in Poland dedicated to soldiers from the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a World War Two partisan formation that fought against the Soviet Union but was also responsible for massacring Poles. Braun declared that the monument, which was also recently vandalised by other unknown perpetrators, should be removed as it “insults the memory of victims of the Ukrainian genocide against Poles” and “glorifies Nazism”. The incident comes amid recent tensions between Warsaw and Kyiv over World War Two history, and in particular the fact that the UPA continues to be honoured in Ukraine. Pomnik UPA w gminie Dołhobyczów w powiecie hrubieszowskim do likwidacji❗️ Obelisk obrażający pamięć ofiar ukraińskiego Ludobójstwa na Polakach powinien zostać usunięty profesjonalnymi narzędziami natychmiast po udokumentowaniu przestępstwa banderyzmu!#StopBanderyzacjiPolski… pic.twitter.com/8Q4QZ2z5vJ — Grzegorz Braun (@GrzegorzBraun_) September 10, 2026 The monument in question is located in the village of Liski, a few kilometres from the border with Ukraine, and marks the burial site of 41 UPA soldiers killed while fighting against the NKVD, the Soviet secret police, in 1946, in the aftermath of World War Two. The area previously had a large ethnic-Ukrainian population. The memorial was vandalised last month, when it was sprayed with black paint and its arch was damaged. On Monday this week, further damage was discovered to the inscription on the monument. Police announced that they had launched an investigation into vandalism, property damage and ethnic hatred, but had not yet identified the perpetrators, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). On Wednesday evening, Braun published a video showing himself and another man using a hammer to repeatedly strike the front of the monument, causing visible damage to the stone, which contains the names of the killed UPA soldiers. They also appear to attempt to remove a separate plaque. During the video, Braun, who is a member of the European Parliament and finished fourth in last year’s Polish presidential election, claimed that local residents are “afraid they would be set on fire” if they attempted to remove the memorial themselves. It is not clear when the video was recorded. Shortly after Braun published it, local police in Hrubieszów county, where the monument is located, issued a statement saying that officers were investigating damage to the monument. Interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka shared their statement and declared that “the perpetrators will not go unpunished”. Sprawcy zniszczenia pomnika w Białymstoku nie pozostaną bezkarni. Policjanci zabezpieczają dowody i przesłuchują świadków. https://t.co/7HCApuhPZ1 — Karolina Gałecka (@K_Galecka) September 10, 2026 Braun, who regularly carries out stunts intended to demonstrate his anti-Ukrainian, antisemitic and anti-LGBT views, and is already facing multiple legal cases over such incidents. He is currently on trial for attacking a celebration of the Jewish festival of Hanukkah in parliament using a fire extinguisher. Last month, he was charged with the crime of denying Nazi crimes for claiming that the gas chambers at Auschwitz are “fake”. He was also charged with theft over incidents in which he tore down Ukrainian and European Union flags, and with vandalism of an LGBT+ exhibition. If convicted, some of the crimes Braun is charged with carry potential years-long prison sentences. Braun’s Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party, which recently called for a “normalisation of relations with Russia”, enjoys support of around 8-9%, according to polling averages. That could make it a key player in deciding who can form a government after next year’s parliamentary elections. Figures from Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun's party celebrated Russia Day at the Russian embassy and presented a letter hailing Russia's development, blaming "globalists" for the Ukraine war and calling for normalisation of Polish-Russian relations https://t.co/SU3gEdVod0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 13, 2026 At the time of writing, there had been no response from Ukrainian authorities to Braun’s latest stunt. However, when the same monument was vandalised last month, the Ukrainian embassy in Warsaw issued a statement expressing its “deep indignation”. “Regardless of the difficult and tragic chapters of our shared history, burial and memorial sites should remain outside the realm of political disputes and be treated with respect,” they wrote. The embassy also expressed “particular concern that this incident occurs against the backdrop of a rising number of hostile acts toward Ukrainians in Poland, including reports of aggression and attacks on Ukrainian citizens” “Any attempts to shift historical disputes into the realm of vandalism, intimidation or hostility toward modern Ukraine and Ukrainians are dangerous and must be met with an appropriate legal response,” they added. Poland and Ukraine have been embroiled in a diplomatic dispute since May, when President Volodymyr Zelensky named a military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. His Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, responded by stripping Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour. Tensions have since cooled, and Ukraine has made moves to defuse the crisis. However, significant differences remain, in particular over memory of the so-called Volhynia massacres, in which the UPA led the killing of around 100,000 Polish civilians. Poland regards the episode as a genocide. Ukraine strongly rejects that label, and also continues to honour the UPA for its role in fighting against Moscow-imposed Soviet rule. Recent months have also seen a rise in anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland, including a series of cases of verbal or physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are by far Poland’s largest immigrant group. Reported anti-Ukrainian hate crimes were up 30% in the first half of this year. Demonstrations took place in 25 Polish cities on Sunday against the “growing wave of hate and violence” against Ukrainians, who are Poland’s largest immigrant group. Reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland are up 30% this year https://t.co/gGAEc6QZWT — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 10, 2026 In 2017, Ukraine responded to the dismantling of a UPA monument in Poland by introducing a ban on exhumations of Polish victims of the Volhynia massacres on its territory. It is believed that tens of thousands still remain buried in unmarked mass graves. However, last year, in a diplomatic breakthrough, Kyiv allowed such exhumations to resume, and since then the remains of dozens of victims have been found, researched and reburied. Earlier this month, Poland also granted Ukraine permission to conduct a search for the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by Polish resistance fighters during World War Two. Following a crash between a train and a truck at a rail crossing that left one passenger dead and both drivers with serious injuries, Poland’s main train drivers’ union has announced a go-slow protest that will take place on Friday. They note that they have long been warning about a lack of sufficient safety measures at rail crossings, and say that a “red line has now been crossed”. In the wake of Wednesday’s tragedy, Prime Minister Donald Tusk has pledged that the government will introduce “very tough” new punishments for those who violate regulations at crossings. Poczułam takie jakby silne hamowanie, takie bardzo silne i nagle takie bujanie i do człowieka dociera, że zaraz się wykoleimy – mówiła pasażerka pociągu Intercity "Koziołek", jadącego z Lublina do Szczecina, który wykoleił się w miejscowości Sokolniki Suche w Mazowieckiem.… pic.twitter.com/enyjD2Wo6K — tvn24 (@tvn24) September 9, 2026 On Wednesday morning, a train travelling between the cities of Lublin and Szczecin partially derailed in the village of Sokolniki Suche in central Poland after colliding with a heavy goods vehicle that, initial findings suggest, had entered the tracks at a rail crossing despite warning lights flashing. The crossing had no barriers. The train was carrying at least 114 people, including three crew. One passenger in the first carriage, a 39-year-old woman, died in hospital from her injuries, prosecutors announced later on Wednesday. Four others, including the drivers of both the train and the truck, remain hospitalised in serious condition. Prosecutors say that, from the evidence collected so far, they will launch an investigation into the crime of unintentionally causing a rail disaster, which carries a prison sentence of six months to eight years. However, they have not yet been able to interview either driver due to their health conditions. On Thursday, the head of the Polish train drivers’ union, Leszek Miętek, announced that a protest would begin at midnight and last through the whole of Friday. “We are appealing to train drivers to travel at a safe speed of 20 km/h (12.4 mph) across every level crossing in Poland,” he said, adding that he had “received reports from across the country” that “there’s full support for this type of action”. Miętek noted that the Polish labour code allows employees to refrain from work if they believe it poses a threat to their life or health. While drivers would not go that far, they want to demonstrate in a bid to prompt “action from those responsible for safety.” He warned that train delays should be expected on Friday. Związek Zawodowy Maszynistów Kolejowych mówi "dość" i ogłasza ogólnokrajowy protest po tragicznej katastrofie w Sokolnikach Suchych. W piątek, 11 września, pociągi w całej Polsce będą zwalniać na przejazdach kolejowych do zaledwie 20 km/h. Więcej o tym: https://t.co/jj6jKm40X2 pic.twitter.com/ThqfLx3dEc — TVN Warszawa (@tvnwarszawa) September 10, 2026 The union chief said that Wednesday’s accident “was not a surprise to us, considering that statistically we have an accident at a railway crossing every two days”. However, “a red line has [now] been crossed”, he added, quoted by news website Interia. Miętek noted that, for over 18 months, the union has been running a campaign, titled “I Want To Live”, focused on safety. Just two days before the accident, it had issued a special appeal to drivers over “growing safety concerns on Polish railways”. “We have been doing everything we can in parliament and at the infrastructure ministry to make sure this problem is noticed,” added Miętek, who also welcomed the fact that, following Wednesday’s accident, Tusk has pledged to take action. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Katastrofa kolejowa w Sokolnikach miała miejsce na przejeździe kolejowym, dlatego natychmiast rozpoczniemy prace nad zaostrzeniem przepisów dla tych, którzy wjeżdżają na przejazdy kolejowe, mimo zapór i czerwonych światel. pic.twitter.com/BgaZQLEPbR — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 9, 2026 In those remarks, the prime minister lamented that the accident in Sokolniki Suche was “yet another case of such a catastrophe happening at a rail crossing”. “We must immediately begin urgent work on tightening regulations,” he continued. This would include “very tough” punishments “for those who, unfortunately, quite systematically drive onto railway crossings despite barriers and red lights”. Infrastructure minister Dariusz Klimczak later confirmed that they were working on “radical” measures to toughen penalties for those who violate the rules at rail crossings. He revealed that one proposal being considered is suspending for three months the licence of any driver who ignores red lights at rail crossings. However, critics noted that the ministry had already announced such plans in July 2025, and had failed to implement them since then. – Chcemy wprowadzić przepis, na podstawie którego każdy kierowca, który wjedzie na przejazd drogowo-kolejowy kiedy jest zapalone czerwone światło, straci prawo jazdy, zostanie mu ono zatrzymane na trzy miesiące. Chcemy także zmienić kodeks karny we współpracy z ministrem… pic.twitter.com/RhE8pcvlJ9 — Ministerstwo Infrastruktury (@MI_GOV_PL) September 9, 2026 The latest data from Eurostat, the European Union’s statistics agency, show that in 2024 Poland recorded the second-highest number of rail accidents, 220, among all member states, behind only Germany (366). However, 24% of Poland’s accidents took place at rail crossings, compared to 16% in Germany. In total, Poland had by far the highest number of deaths caused by accidents at rail crossings (45), ahead of Germany (26), France (20) and Hungary (18). When taking into account the size of countries’ rail networks, Poland had 4.3 rail deaths (from all causes, not just accidents at crossings) per thousand kilometres of track, which was the fifth-highest figure in the EU, behind Portugal (6.2), Hungary (5.8), Slovakia (5.7) and Lithuania (4.6). Last week, in dramatic scenes captured on camera, a train carrying almost 300 passengers hit a truck at a rail crossing in Gdańsk, luckily resulting in no injuries. The driver of the truck, who is from Bosnia and Herzegovina, has been charged. A train crashed into a lorry stuck on a railway crossing in Gdansk, Poland, after the barriers closed while the vehicle was still on the tracks. World.title: Almost 80% of Poles support helping Baltic states if Russia attacks
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Almost 80% of Poles say that they would want their country to come to the aid of the Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – if they were attacked by Russia. The new poll follows a controversy over comments by a senior opposition figure, former defence minister Mariusz Błaszczak, in which he refused to confirm his support for Poland fulfilling its NATO obligations by coming to the aid of the Baltic states if they were invaded. In a survey for broadcaster Radio Zet, the IBRiS agency asked: “In the event of Russian aggression, should Poland help Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia?” In response, 77.8% of those polled said that it should, while only 16.1% were opposed. Among respondents who identified as politically centrist, 92% were in favour. The figures were lower for those with left-wing (75%) or right-wing (73%) views, though in both cases a large majority still supported coming to the Baltic states’ aid. Commenting on the findings, Radio Zet wrote that “the survey shows that Poles feel responsible for the military security of their NATO allies – contrary to what some politicians have said”. That was a reference to remarks last week by Błaszczak, who is the head of the parliamentary caucus of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s largest opposition group. Between 2018 and 2023, Błaszczak served as defence minister in the former PiS-led government. In an interview with Radio Zet, Błaszczak was asked if, in the event of a Russian attack on the Baltic states, Poland should come to their aid. “Polish soldiers should defend Poland,” he responded. “We need to be strong in our alliances…We should prioritise cooperation with the United States.” The interviewer pointed out that Article 5 of the NATO treaty requires members of the alliance to come to the assistance of another member that is attacked, and again asked if Poland should help the Baltic states if such an attack occurred. “We border Russia directly, and we border a Russia that has effectively taken over Belarusian territory. So we’re also on the front line,” replied Błaszczak. “This article, of course, speaks of solidarity, but the point is that the government that governs Poland should establish the best possible relations with the United States.” With the interviewer continuing to press the question, Błaszczak simply said that “it all depends on the circumstances” and “it’s not a straightforward issue”. Błaszczak’s comments were criticised by figures from Poland’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. They accused him of calling into question the validity of Article 5, on which Poland would rely if it were attacked. “A former defence minister who undermines the sanctity of Polish security, i.e. NATO’s Article 5, is a moron,” wrote deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk. Interior minister Marcin Kiewiński said that Błaszczak had “undermined the very purpose of NATO’s existence”. In response to the criticism, Błaszczak wrote on social media that, during the PiS government’s time in power, it had significantly enhanced security ties with the Baltic states, including stationing Polish forces in Latvia and contributing Polish F-16s to NATO’s air policing mission. “NATO’s Article 5 is activated collectively, and alliance commitments are binding, but every [Polish] defence minister’s priority should be the defence of Poland and ensuring the safety of Poles,” he added. Błaszczak to stan umysłu. Mało im było niszczenia SAFE, to dziś były szef MON podważył sens istnienia NATO wskazując, że Wojsko Polskie nie powinno bronić Litwy, Łotwy czy Estonii. Przyjaźń tego skompromitowanego środowiska z Orbanem to nie był przypadek… — Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) September 1, 2026 On Wednesday, Poland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, visited Latvia, including the base in Ādaži where a Polish military contingent has been based since 2017 as part of a multinational NATO brigade. “Poland and Latvia face similar threats in the security domain,” said Sikorski. “We must speak with one voice and take our security seriously. Only such actions can guarantee effective protection against the threat from Russia.” “We do not want an escalation of the conflict, but Putin must know that we are not going to sit idly by and wait for his next step,” he continued. “We understand that the defence of our allies also contributes to Polish security. We stand ready to share the burden of defending the eastern flank.” 📍 Ādaži 🇱🇻 Continuing visit to Latvia, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs @sikorskiradek visited the base of the Polish Military Contingent. World.title: Polish school pupils second best at maths in EU
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish schoolchildren are the second best in the European Union at mathematics, the third best at reading comprehension, and the fifth best at science, according to the latest results from a major international study of pupils’ abilities. The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) is carried out every three years by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and measures the performance of 15-year-olds. The latest instalment, based on tests taken in 2025, was published on Tuesday this week. It includes results from 91 countries and territories across the world. A total of 760,000 pupils were assessed, including 7,103 in 217 Polish schools. In maths, Polish pupils obtained a mean score of 484, which was the 12th highest in the world. The top seven places were taken by Asian countries and territories. But the only other European Union country to exceed Poland’s score was Estonia (508). Poland was just behind the United Kingdom (488) and Canada (485), but ahead of the likes of Finland (469), Germany (464) and the United States (463). In reading comprehension, Poland’s mean score of 482 was 14th in the world and third best in the EU, behind Ireland (500) and Estonia (499). Polish pupils performed slightly worse, in relative terms, in science, where their mean score of 495 was 18th in the world and fifth best in the EU. A number of Polish media outlets and Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrongly reported that Poland was third best in the EU for science. In fact, it was significantly behind Estonia (527) and Finland (504) and marginally below Ireland (500) and Austria (497). Poland’s latest results continue its recent history of performing strongly in PISA. In the 2018 instalment, Polish pupils were the third best in the EU in both maths and science, and fourth best in reading. In 2022 (when PISA took place a year later than planned due to the Covid pandemic), Poland was fourth in the EU in maths and fifth in both science and reading. In 2021, a separate assessment of reading comprehension among fourth-grade pupils – called PIRLS and carried out every five years by the International Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achievement – found Poland had the joint best result among EU countries, equal with Finland Following the announcement of the new PISA data, Polish education minister Barbara Nowacka welcomed the fact that “Poland has maintained its high ranking among European Union countries”. However, she added a note of caution, pointing to the fact that, overall, test scores have been declining, both in Poland and globally. That shows “Polish education still has a lot of work ahead of it”. Nowacka said that her ministry’s efforts to reform the school curriculum had been based on results and recommendations from previous PISA reports. World.title: From Sri Lanka to Prague: How Tharusha Brought Coconut Culture to the City
World.content:
Tharusha De Silva, originally from Sri Lanka, has spent much of his life between different countries.

Today, he is bringing a taste closely associated with home to Prague through his beverage brand, The Coconut Culture which is also available at select cafés and restaurants across Prague.

We spoke to him about his journey to the Czech Republic, navigating life between cultures, and the story behind The Coconut Culture.



Journey to Prague

Prague was never part of a long-term plan for De Silva. He first came to the Czech Republic in 2016 to study mechanical engineering, after growing up in Sri Lanka and spending his teenage years in Dubai. By his own account, his decision to come here was almost entirely random.

“We had a counselling office that used to help us with university applications, and one day they changed the wallpaper to a map of Prague. I just went into the room, pointed at it and said, ‘Hey, what is that?’ They told me a little bit about Prague, and that’s how I got here.”

At first, Prague was simply where he planned to spend his university years. “I always thought that I would leave after university,” he says. But the longer he stayed, the less certain leaving became.

“It’s very difficult to give you a straight answer to what made me decide to stay. But I think the city has its way of keeping you.”

Freedom and opportunity were part of what made the city difficult to leave.

“You could really make something of yourself here if you really want to,” he says.

Eventually, staying stopped feeling like a temporary decision. “In a way, I found a part of home here. That was enough to make me stay.”

The Coconut Culture

King Coconut, a variety native to Sri Lanka, became the starting point for The Coconut Culture.

Unlike varieties grown primarily for their meat or oil, King Coconut has a more specific purpose. “The other coconuts have multiple uses. Some are used to get the desiccated coconut from the inside, to make milk out of it, to make coconut oil, even some kind of biofuel. But this variant, the King Coconut, has one use: it is to drink it.”

It is sweeter and lighter than regular coconut water, with a taste he compares to subtly sweet spring water.

For De Silva, however, the connection with King Coconut goes back to his childhood. He remembers his grandfather taking him and his sister out on his scooter. On the way back, they would stop beside a road running between paddy fields and have a King Coconut together.

Years later, that childhood ritual became part of the reason he wanted to introduce King Coconut to people who had never encountered it.

“I want to bring King Coconut out more, make more people be aware of it, and give it its place in the world.”

The name The Coconut Culture came later, during a conversation with a friend about Czech and Sri Lankan culture. De Silva remembers describing his background almost casually: “I come from the coconut culture.” The phrase stayed with him.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by @coconutculture.eu

Living Between Cultures

Having grown up in Sri Lanka, spent his teenage years in Dubai and lived in the Czech Republic since 2016, De Silva has spent much of his life between different cultures.

There are, of course, things he still misses about Sri Lanka.

“I come from an island, a very fairly simple life. I get to walk around without any shoes. We have the sea, we have the ocean. We have the sun, so many fruits, so many wild animals, forests, mountains.”

But perhaps the biggest difference is language and the sense of belonging that comes with it.

“The most important thing is I communicate in my own language back home. Here, I am the expat. I either communicate in English or with the little Czech I know.”

“Back home, it’s my language. I speak in my language, I’m more comfortable. I feel like I’m a fuller version of myself.”

Distance has also changed the way he sees the place he came from.

“The place that I will make home or call home in the future is just going to be a mix of the cultures that I’ve experienced. It’s going to be some of the things that I picked up from Dubai, some of the things I’ve picked up living in the Czech Republic or Europe, and then, of course, where I come from, my roots.”

Finding a Home in Prague

Prague, naturally, has become part of that mix. After years in the city, De Silva says one of the things he values most is the openness he finds here.

“I think here, Prague is one of the places where you could just walk out feeling or looking any way you want. And it’s very rare that anyone would tell you anything because people accept you as you are.”

Part of that openness, he says, also comes from the people who have made Prague their home from elsewhere.

“Prague has many, many expats and the city is filled with expats. Therefore, all of these expats bring different cultures into Prague.”

Beyond the bigger things that make Prague feel like home, it is also the everyday details that have become part of his life here.

“I would definitely miss the café culture. I love to sit in a café in the mornings, in the evenings, have coffee, read, do some work.”

A First Taste

The first real test came at the launch event, held before The Coconut Culture had even received its full stock. De Silva and his team brought in a small number of bottles specifically for the occasion and invited friends to try the drink.

“We had a launch event with some of our friends, and we got a lot of good feedback about the drink, especially about its taste, about the way it’s packed, about the branding that we’ve done.”

For the team, it was an early indication that the idea could work in Prague.

“This was maybe where we thought, okay, this is actually something that the people of the Czech Republic, all the expats and the locals, will enjoy.”

Beyond King Coconut

King Coconut is only the first of the discoveries De Silva hopes to bring to Europe. He describes The Coconut Culture as “an exploration company”, where “the fruit is the vehicle”.

The idea is to keep the range deliberately small, with the company eventually aiming for five to seven products.

“The Coconut Culture has a very simple vision: to find native fruits. We want to have between five to seven products, and be very specialized in them: find these native fruits that are specific to countries or communities. And we want to go there, we want to discover it, and we want to bring it to the European market and give it to the people here.”

For De Silva, however, the products are also a way of introducing the places they come from.

“We want to find these cultures, tell their story to the world here and, hopefully, respect, as we always try to, where it comes from and also respect the place that it’s being sold at.”

World.title: Czechia Considers One Million-Crown Reward for Second Child as Births Hit Record Low
World.content:
Prime Minister Andrej Babiš is considering a million-crown reward for families who have a second child, along with lifelong tax relief for parents of a third child.

The proposals are among several measures being discussed, including support for parents who are studying, childcare services and more affordable housing. Babiš said he would bring together the relevant ministers to discuss the issue.



The Czech Republic recorded just 77,600 live births in 2025, the lowest figure since statistical records began in 1785. Births fell in every region compared with the previous year.

The country’s total fertility rate also dropped to 1.28 children per woman, while the average age of women having their first child rose to 29.2 years.

Million-crown reward for a second child

Babiš said the government was examining several proposals to encourage families to have more children.

“One million crowns for a second child,” he said, describing a possible incentive for women who already have one child.

He also mentioned a lifelong tax break for a third child, support for studying parents, nurseries and children’s groups.

Babiš also criticized mortgage costs, questioning why Czech interest rates remain 1.5 percentage points above those in the eurozone. He has repeatedly criticized the Czech National Bank, while cheaper mortgages were among ANO’s key election promises.

Debate over assisted reproduction

Babiš also addressed a proposal from the Ministry of Health that would allow single women to undergo assisted reproduction without a male partner.

Responding to criticism from the Alliance for Family, he acknowledged the importance of fathers but pointed to divorce and child-support disputes.

“I know that. But what is the divorce rate here? Fathers leave families and then sometimes do not even pay child support,” he said.

Babiš added that he did not want to comment extensively on the issue because of possible accusations of having business interests in reproductive clinics.

“It’s nonsense. A woman can choose the clinic she wants. If she hates Babiš, then let her not go there. I don’t decide on that at all,” he said.

World.title: Czechia Ranks Fourth Among Russia’s “Enemies” in New Propaganda List
World.content:
Czechia has been ranked among Russia’s top five “enemy” countries in a new list published by Vzglyad, a Russian outlet widely regarded as a Kremlin propaganda mouthpiece.

Czechia has been ranked as the fourth-most “hostile” country toward Russia in a new ranking published by Vzglyad, scoring 65 out of a possible 100 points.



The list places Czechia alongside Romania, Poland, the United Kingdom and Canada, all of which received the same score.

Italy topped the ranking with 80 points, followed by Germany, Lithuania and Finland, which tied for second place with 75 points each. The United States, Latvia and France shared third place with 70 points apiece.

Japan makes the list for the first time

Most of the countries in the top ten appear regularly in the ranking. This time, however, Japan was included for the first time.

According to Vzglyad, Japan’s inclusion was prompted by Tokyo’s “firm protest” over Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to Iturup.

Iturup is part of the southern Kuril Islands, which Japan claims as its “Northern Territories.” Russia considers the islands an integral part of its territory.

The territorial dispute dates back to the final days of World War II, when Soviet forces occupied Iturup and neighboring islands in 1945.

Czechia remains a regular presence

Czechia has consistently appeared among the top ten countries in the ranking.

The list was first published in November last year, when Czechia also placed fourth. In May, however, the country briefly dropped to the bottom of the ranking.

The index assigns countries a maximum of 100 points based on six criteria. According to Vzglyad editor Evgeny Pozdnyakov, the most important factor is military-political activity against Russia, which accounts for up to 30 points. Sanctions pressure contributes a further 20 points.

The ranking reflects the perspective of Russian state-aligned media and should not be interpreted as an official assessment of international relations or a measure of actual hostility between countries.

World.title: EU Moves to Curb Airbnb-Style Rentals to Boost Long-Term Housing
World.content:
The EU has introduced a framework to support long-term rentals in tourist-heavy cities. Airbnb warns it creates regulatory uncertainty without improving long-term housing outcomes.

The EU has announced an affordable housing plan aimed at encouraging long-term rentals and making housing more accessible for Europeans.

Unveiled on Wednesday, the plan aims to create clarity and predictability in how rules are applied by local authorities, particularly in neighbourhoods popular with tourists where short-term rentals have displaced residents.



“Lack of affordable housing is a matter of concern for so many of our European citizens,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a press statement. “Essential workers and students cannot afford to live where they serve and study. But most importantly, it is about fairness. Today, we are delivering for all Europeans.”

“The new rules are designed to help competent authorities identify ‘areas under housing stress’ using a common methodology,” a Commission press release explains.

Housing in Europe is getting worse

The latest data on access to accommodation across Europe are worrying, and have pushed the Commission to intervene.

Recent Eurobarometer data shows that 50 per cent of European city dwellers think that housing is an urgent problem they experience. House prices have skyrocketed faster than local incomes across most European capitals, rising 64.9% between 2015 and 2025 and rents 21.8%, according to EU data.

Even people who cannot afford to buy are facing rising rents, which consume 40% of household income, and middle-class families are also increasingly facing a reality where they can’t afford to buy or rent, but also aren’t eligible for social housing.

Many residents in cities like Lisbon, Barcelona and Prague complain that short-term rental platforms like Airbnb have removed homes from the market and pushed prices up, often forcing them to move.

Short-term rentals represent only 1.2% of the EU’s total housing stock, but they can account for up to 20% in some tourism hotspots. With too few homes being built where demand is strongest, Brussels estimates it needs more than 2 million new homes every year to fix the problem.

Airbnb, the largest worldwide platform for short-term rentals, has criticised the plan as not sufficiently clear.

“Airbnb shares the Commission’s ambition to make housing more affordable. But as drafted, the Affordable Housing Act will not add a single home to the long term rental market, while adding regulatory uncertainty for hosts across European cities,” the company wrote in a press statement after the Commission’s announcement.

The plan must now be negotiated by the EU co-legislators before being approved.

World.title: Prague’s Industrial Palace to Reopen to the Public for Guided Tours
World.content:
After a major renovation costing more than CZK 3 billion, Prague’s Industrial Palace at the Výstaviště exhibition grounds will open its doors to the public in two weeks.

From September 25 to October 11, visitors will be able to explore the history and architecture of the landmark and see how it has been transformed during the renovation on guided tours organised by Výstaviště Praha and Prague City Tourism.



According to Výstaviště Praha, the palace will not remain open to the public on a regular basis after the tours. Instead, it will serve as a venue for exhibitions, trade fairs and other scheduled events.

The renovation of the Industrial Palace, including the reconstruction of its fire-damaged left wing, began in February 2022, more than 13 years after the wing was destroyed by a fire in October 2008.

The approximately one-hour guided tour costs CZK 91. Organisers say the symbolic price refers to 1891, the year the Industrial Palace first opened. Tickets are available through the Prague City Tourism website. Places are limited, and some tour dates have already sold out.

The first major event scheduled at the renovated palace will be the Designblok festival in early October.

Built in Just Ten Months

The Industrial Palace was built for the 1891 Jubilee Provincial Exhibition based on designs by architect Bedřich Münzberger. It is considered an important example of both artistic and technical heritage. The building was the first in the Czech lands to feature an architectural design based on a prefabricated iron structure.

Contemporary records show that 450 workers completed the building in just ten months, despite flooding and severe frosts affecting the exhibition grounds during construction.

From the beginning, the palace served as a venue for exhibitions and cultural events, although it was originally intended as a temporary structure.

Between 1952 and 1954, the communist government decided to repurpose the building, ordering its main hall to be converted into a social and dance hall. The building was also renamed the Congress Palace and became part of the Julius Fučík Cultural and Recreation Park, which operated at the site at the time.

One Wing of the Palace Was Destroyed by Fire

On October 16, 2008, a fire destroyed the left wing of the Industrial Palace after items left on an electric hot plate caught fire. The person responsible was never identified.

The renovation did not begin until early 2022. Under the original plans, the work was supposed to be completed last year.

However, once the foundations, floors and suspended ceilings of the right wing were uncovered, it became clear that the condition of the historic building was worse than expected, leading to additional work and delays.

World.title: New York Inspired New Residential Project in Prague’s Smíchov
World.content:
A new seven-story residential building planned for Prague’s Smíchov district has moved closer to construction after securing a zoning decision.

The project, known as Smíchovská Žehlička, is being developed by BPD Partners and Top Estates and is expected to be completed in 2029.

The building will contain 66 apartments as well as eight commercial units for shops, services and restaurants. It will also include shared coworking and community spaces. The total gross floor area is expected to be close to 8,000 square meters.

The project is planned for a wedge-shaped site between Kováků and Na Zatlance streets, directly below Mrázovka Park. The unusual shape of the plot and the significant difference in elevation between the two streets have made the site particularly difficult to develop.

The project has been in preparation for more than a decade. BPD Partners, the investment group owned by Czech businessmen Vasil Bobel, Petr Pudil and Jan Dobrovský, began working with architect Patrik Hoffman on the scheme in 2010.

Inspired by New York’s Flatiron Building

The shape of Smíchovská Žehlička is largely determined by the site’s narrow, wedge-shaped plot and surrounding streets. The design also takes inspiration from New York’s Flatiron Building, whose distinctive triangular form became a response to an equally unusual urban site.

The Prague project aims to use the constraints of its location in a similar way. Rather than attempting to conceal the site’s difficult geometry, the design makes it a defining feature of the building.

The residential units and commercial premises will all be offered for sale. The development will also provide shared areas intended for coworking and community activities.

If permitting and construction follow the current schedule, Smíchovská Žehlička could be completed by the end of 2029.

World.title: Award-Winning Holocaust Documentary to Premiere in Prague
World.content:
Award-winning Holocaust documentary UnBroken will have its Czech premiere at Prague’s Edison Filmhub on Friday, September 25.

The screening will take place alongside the opening of the new “Rescuers of Children” exhibition at the National Pedagogical Museum.

Director, producer and writer Beth Lane will attend the Prague screening.



The documentary tells the story of Lane’s mother, Ginger Lane, and her six siblings, who survived the Holocaust after being hidden for two years by German farmers Paula and Arthur Schmidt.

The seven Jewish children were sheltered on the couple’s farm in Brandenburg, about 60 kilometers east of Berlin. They survived the war and emigrated together to the United States in 1946.

They are believed to be the only known family of seven Jewish siblings to have survived the Holocaust and later emigrated together as a family. Ginger Lane, now 86, is one of two surviving members of the family.

Paula and Arthur Schmidt were later recognized by Yad Vashem as Righteous Among the Nations, an honor given to non-Jews who risked their lives to save Jews during the Holocaust.

Their story is also featured in “Rescuers of Children,” the new exhibition at the National Pedagogical Museum. The exhibition examines the experiences of children and other vulnerable people during the Holocaust and presents stories of individuals who risked their lives to help those facing persecution.

The Prague screening follows the documentary’s German premiere in Dachau on July 17, where UnBroken received the inaugural Lichtbrücke Prize for Human Rights in Film.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by UnBroken (@unbrokenthefilm)

The film premiered in 2023 at the Heartland International Film Festival, where it won Best Documentary Feature Premiere. It has since been screened in more than 50 cities, including at the United Nations in New York and Vienna, the Museum of Jewish Heritage in New York and the Pilecki Institute in Warsaw.

UnBroken was released on Netflix in the United States in April 2025 and has since surpassed 1.5 million streams there.

The Czech premiere will take place at Edison Filmhub in Prague on September 25, 2026.

World.title: GALLERY: One of Europe’s Largest Aquariums Set to Open in Czechia in 2028
World.content:
A new public aquarium costing around CZK 700 million is planned for the Brno Exhibition Centre, with construction expected to begin in 2027 and the first visitors arriving in the second half of 2028.

The project, called Green Planet: National Aquarium, will occupy Pavilion C at the Brno Exhibition Centre. It is expected to contain around 100 aquariums and water tanks holding more than four million liters of water.



The facility will be home to about 400,000 animals representing roughly 500 species, including rare species. Developers say the project will rank among the largest aquarium complexes in Europe.

Brno Mayor Markéta Vaňková said the aquarium could attract around 500,000 visitors during its first year of operation, including people from across the South Moravian Region and neighboring countries.

The main attraction will be a 2.5 million-liter ocean tank featuring a 55-meter underwater tunnel.

Visitors will be able to walk through the tunnel while observing marine life around and above them. The aquarium will also feature hundreds of other aquatic species across its various tanks.

The developers say the number of animals will put the complex among Europe’s largest aquariums. They estimate that it will contain around 36 times as many animals as the Barcelona Aquarium.

The project is also designed around reducing water consumption.

According to the plans, recirculation systems will clean and treat water before returning it to the tanks. The developers say efficient water management will be one of the project’s priorities.

Czech and international specialists are involved in preparing the aquarium, which is expected to include both educational and visitor-focused elements.

World.title: Flydubai resumes Budapest flights as airline expands network to more than 125 destinations!
World.content:
Flydubai has resumed its direct Budapest–Dubai flights as the airline restores most of its network and expands to more than 125 destinations across 56 countries. The service is currently operating three times a week, with daily flights planned from late October.

Budapest flights resumed at the end of July

The Dubai-based carrier restarted its direct flights between Budapest Ferenc Liszt International Airport (BUD) and Dubai International Airport (DXB) on 31 July 2026.

The Budapest route currently operates three times a week on Wednesdays, Fridays and Sundays. From 25 October, flydubai plans to increase the frequency to a daily service.

The airline operates the route with Boeing 737 aircraft. The service also forms part of flydubai’s partnership with Emirates, giving passengers access to a much wider combined network via Dubai.

According to flydubai, passengers travelling on connecting Emirates flights can benefit from a single booking and checked baggage transferred through to their final destination.

Flydubai network grows to more than 125 destinations

The Budapest service comes as flydubai continues to rebuild and expand its international network. In a press release issued on 14 September, the airline said it had restored operations to 85% of its network and now serves more than 125 destinations in 56 countries, with an average of 2,200 flights per week.

In recent months, flydubai has resumed or launched services to several destinations, including Aleppo, Benghazi and Bangkok. The airline has also increased its Bangkok service to three daily non-stop flights, citing strong demand.

Flydubai is due to add another destination on 23 September, when it launches flights to Pokhara in Nepal, its second destination in the country after Kathmandu.

The carrier said it expects travel demand to remain strong during the upcoming winter season, with Dubai continuing to attract visitors while passengers use the city as a hub for travel elsewhere.

Flydubai’s Boeing 737 MAX 9 in Greece. Photo: depositphotos.com

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Budapest offers connections to destinations beyond Dubai

Flydubai said back in July that the Budapest route also strengthens connections between Hungary and the United Arab Emirates while giving Hungarian travellers easier access to destinations in the Middle East, Africa and Asia.

The airline has previously highlighted destinations such as the Maldives, Thailand, Sri Lanka and Kenya as examples of places that can be reached through Dubai.

The wider Emirates and flydubai network now offers access to more than 214 unique destinations in over 100 countries, with more than 4,600 possible connections through Dubai.

“Despite the challenging operating environment, we have remained focused on restoring our network safely and efficiently, adding capacity where we see demand while opening new markets,” flydubai Chief Executive Officer Ghaith Al Ghaith said.

He added that the airline was encouraged by strong customer demand during the summer and remained positioned to further restore its network in the coming months.

Read more travel news: Good news for passengers: Wizz Air restarts popular flights to multiple destinations from Budapest

Daily Budapest service coming in October

For Hungarian travellers, the most important change will come in late October, when the Budapest–Dubai route is scheduled to become a daily service. Flydubai said it is continuing to add capacity to its year-round routes as more aircraft become available. The airline currently operates an average of 2,200 weekly flights and aims to increase this frequency further.

World.title: The fast and easy-to-use qualified electronic signature your lawyer will approve
World.content:
Digital administration is becoming increasingly popular. However, those seeking to achieve high-level digital trust in full compliance with legal requirements have so far had to use several systems in parallel. One provider identifies them and issues their qualified electronic signatures, another platform enables user-friendly contract management, while their customers are identified through an external service provider. The renewed Netlock is now putting an end to this fragmented approach. Led by András Somkuti, former President of Docler Holding, and Bálint Lévai, owner of the BioTechUSA Group, Netlock’s new service integrates essential digital trust functions into a single, closed ecosystem, serving not only individuals but also large enterprises such as banks, insurers and media companies, as well as players in the SME sector.

Collaborative content

Netlock Democratizes Digital Contracting

Netlock’s 2026 story does not begin from scratch. As one of Europe’s first qualified trust service providers, the company has been offering qualified electronic signature services for 25 years. These services comply with the strictest EU regulations and, from several legal perspectives, provide greater security than a standard electronic signature. The newly launched Netlock provides digital identity, KYC services, and qualified electronic signatures in an easy-to-use, authentic and secure environment. Its range of functions is going to be expanded with contract lifecycle management, known as CLM, as well as content authentication and advanced cryptographic solutions. Together, these capabilities may provide a significant competitive advantage in any sector.

“With the two decades of expertise, we merged the best of our business-supporting services into a single, closed platform using one unified credit system. As a result, Netlock has become a comprehensive service provider capable of guiding our clients through the entire lifecycle of a contract, from preparation, approval and signing to tracking and archiving. We do all this while ensuring that our system is easy to use, authentic and secure at the same time. It can even support international copyright disputes by verifying the origin of media files, making it possible to prove that a given piece of content has existed in unchanged form since authentication and to identify who it is linked to,” said András Somkuti.

Media attestation in a convenient way

As AI-generated media becomes increasingly difficult to distinguish from authentic content, Netlock shifts the focus from detecting what is fake to proving what is trusted, authorised, and legally defensible. By combining C2PA content provenance with qualified electronic signatures, timestamps, electronic seals, verified identities, and embedded rights documentation, Netlock creates a cryptographically secure and legally meaningful trust layer that travels with the content itself. Organisations can certify origin and authorship, bind agreements and permissions directly to specific media files, preserve provenance throughout distribution and monetisation, and produce verifiable evidence in disputes or audits. Advanced fingerprinting can also reconnect altered or redistributed content to its original certified record even when metadata has been removed. Designed to support scalable rights management, compliance, and emerging requirements such as the EU AI Act, Netlock transforms digital content into a trusted, verifiable asset backed by human accountability and legal infrastructure.

Digital Identity in 1 Minute

Until now, the wide adoption of paperless contracting has been hindered by several overlapping challenges. Previously, no contracting party could be certain whether their partner had an electronic signature or whether they were able to use it properly. If they did not, obtaining a trusted signature usually involved a slow and costly identification process. In addition, document management systems and trust service providers typically operated on two separate platforms, and integrating them could have created an inconvenient user experience in everyday use. Furthermore, electronic signature and document management systems were usually priced on a per-user basis, which could make the process disproportionately expensive for partners who only sign documents occasionally. Together, these factors have led users in two main directions: either they have used electronic signatures that have long been available on the market but are not qualified from a legal standpoint, or they have reverted to “old-school” paper-based contracting.

“We have applied UX/UI solutions that allow anyone to use Netlock intuitively in everyday situations, regardless of their level of digital competence. Obtaining the right to use a qualified electronic signature, from identification to issuing the first trusted signature, takes no more than one minute. With this new service, users can begin digital administration not only quickly, but also on a reliable, authentic and legally robust foundation,” added András Somkuti.

Unique Business Model With Transaction-Based Pricing

Unlike the industry standard, Netlock’s business model is not user-based but transaction-based. This means a company does not need to maintain unnecessary monthly subscriptions for colleagues who merely sign only once or twice. Instead, they need to pay only after transactions. The platform also allows one party to “sponsor” the other party’s signing cost, meaning any external partner can be included in the signing process without requiring expensive licenses for those who sign only rarely.

“A business that is able to centralize trust functions in a single system can significantly reduce trust-related risks and losses arising from administrative errors. Clients using Netlock can more easily enter the world of fully digital contracting without having to compromise between usability and a reliable trust framework. European regulation is also moving in this direction: the future of digital administration will be built on more unified, secure and better-controlled trust services,” said Bálint Lévai.

Simple Electronic Signature Platform vs. Qualified Trust Service Provider

The ecosystem provided by Netlock is based on the company’s status as a Qualified Trust Service Provider, or QTSP. Qualified trust service providers are organizations that are officially audited and registered by international authorities. “The fundamental difference compared to a simple platform is that, in this case, it is not merely software recording that someone has participated in a process. Instead, a legally accountable and regulated organization ensures that the signer really is who they claim to be, that the time of signing is authentic, and that the document has remained unchanged. As a result, the Netlock signed documents can also be interpreted in court or administrative proceedings,” added András Somkuti.

“In the case of financing documents or multinational contracts, the stakes are high, and the question is always the same: if something becomes disputed, how can be proved that the signature was valid? Through a qualified trust service provider, this is never a matter of retrospective reconstruction. Fast signing is now available from many providers, but far fewer are capable of ensuring that behind the signature there is a regulated and audited trust framework. We have entered the market at the right time, and there is enormous international interest in Netlock, particularly from the financial, enterprise and legal sectors. Our mission is to establish the fundamental conditions of trust in the digital world for everyone,” said Bálint Lévai.
