World.title: [OPINION] No good immigrants: Lessons from the win of far-right party in Germany
World.content:
Current and prospective overseas Filipino workers all over the world can take important lessons from the AfD’s victory in this region

The citizens of Saxony-Anhalt, a small federal state in eastern Germany, elected their Parliament recently. The result, a disappointment but not a surprise to poll watchers, was a resounding victory for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD). It secured 43.8% of the state’s vote, ending up just three seats short of an absolute majority in the Parliament of Saxony-Anhalt.

But what does this mean for Filipinos? Germany has just 45,000 or so overseas Filipino workers (OFW), and Saxony-Anhalt is home to only a few hundred (current) Filipino passport-holders, being poorer and more conservative than most other German states.

I argue, however, that current and prospective OFWs all over the world can take important lessons from the AfD’s victory in this region.

In the run-up to the election, the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt published a detailed campaign platform that devoted much attention to migration and asylum policy. The proposed crackdowns on irregular migration and social welfare support for immigrants and refugees were expected. In response, the TGD, a non-government organization representing Germany’s community of Turkish immigrants, has asked the federal government not to send incoming refugees into Sachsen-Anhalt, out of concern that they will become targets of extreme new policies.

In addition, however, the AfD proposed drastic reductions to in-migration of health professionals, including a virtual ban on those coming from outside Europe. The AfD reasoned that doctors and nurses from foreign backgrounds would endanger patients because of their purported limited German language skills, lower-quality training, and alien cultural values.

This is a more extreme position than earlier assertions, where the party claimed to be targeting foreigners with irregular residency status, or who had committed criminal offenses. It also flies in the face of the party’s attempts to portray itself as being friendly to the “right” kind of immigrant: the party’s co-leader at the federal level, Alice Weidel, is famously married to a woman born in Sri Lanka but adopted into a European family as a small child.

Of course, the AfD’s proposal to forbid entry to non-EU nurses and doctors received widespread critique in German media (to be fair, as did most of its platform, since German mainstream media is hostile to the AfD). Germany has an aging population, and has trouble retaining the nurses it either imports or trains.

Refusing to admit trained health professionals into the country would drastically undermine its health system. Around 14% of all practicing doctors in Germany have a foreign passport. Well-traveled observers might also note that Germany can hardly accuse foreign health workers of being less trained: unlike many countries from which it imports nurses, Germany gives its own nurses vocational training instead of full university degrees.

And there’s the rub.

Weaponizing one group vs the other

Health professionals are supposed to belong to the vaguely-defined category of “good immigrants,” as essential workers that the aging populations of the Global North can’t do without. Filipino nurses, in particular, are often the standard-bearers of the Pinoy diaspora, a welcome asset to their host countries as among the most sought-after nurses in the world.

Rising bilateral cooperation between Germany and the Philippines is bringing more and more Pinoy nurses and doctors to Germany. But in 2026, they and other international professionals are accused of being a potential threat to the health and lives of patients. What kind of social and political climate awaits these new arrivals in the coming years?

Many Filipinos abroad believe that they are safe from xenophobic and racist hate because they follow the rules, offer essential services, and even accept mistreatment — all with the signature Filipino charm and cheer. This self-concept, along with a healthy dose of internalized racism, is why some diaspora Filipinos support xenophobic policies. The assumption is that these proposals will apply to the “other” immigrants. “Good” immigrants need not worry.

The AfD’s proposals show that their agenda was never really about separating the “good” immigrants from the “bad” ones. It was about weaponizing one group against another, and discarding minorities according to their own political convenience.

Saxony-Anhalt’s election might not be as exceptional as we would like to think. The AfD’s popularity is rising all over Germany, nowadays polling as the country’s most or second-most popular party, and it is even able to attract a share of votes from immigrants — especially those who consider themselves “good” immigrants distinct from “bad” ones.

Efficient collaborators

Far-right parties are rising in power all over Europe and other regions, and are proving to be efficient collaborators, as shown by the mutual support between the AfD and the American MAGA movement. Hence, there are many places in the world where immigrants can learn this painful lesson: for true haters, there is really no such thing as a good immigrant.

In the face of all this unpredictability, the most constructive mindset for immigrants is to maintain a healthy sense of self-love and kinship, especially with like-minded locals and a diverse set of other newcomers. Take pride in your international heritage and your courage to embrace change, and respect these traits in others who have also made the leap.

Adhering to conservative distinctions between good and bad immigrants is only playing into the far right’s strategy to divide and conquer minorities. If you are globally-minded enough to cross continents to build your future, you can also be open to partnering with other communities of internationals. Self-advocacy is also important. Those immigrants who can safely take part in public civil society actions could do so more often.

As for those who are still in their homeland and thinking about going abroad, they should take on a global mindset early in their migration process. Even before leaving the country, it is important to be informed about potential destinations.

What are the specific opportunities and challenges in each destination? Knowing that, are you still ready to make the journey, and how do you plan to prepare yourself? Are you aware of all your options, so that you can choose the best possible way to arrive at a new home?

Last but not least, Filipino government authorities and representatives should consistently do their utmost to negotiate a fair deal for OFWs and raise the country’s global standing. OFWs are not simply “labor export” or “good immigrants,” but have dignity and rights no matter what the locals in a destination country might think of them.

In an unpredictable and sometimes hostile world, people should be able to count on their homeland’s leadership as a stable source of identity, integrity, and strength. This rootedness is a key factor in being able to make a good home anywhere in the world. – Rappler.com



Jamina Jugo is a research officer at the Darmstadt University of Applied Sciences, and a lecturer in European Studies at the Ateneo de Manila. She received her doctorate in Political Science from the University of Göttingen in Lower Saxony, Germany. She is a naturalized German citizen.

World.title: FACT CHECK: Comelec debunks claim of ACMs altering votes in Lanao del Sur
World.content:
The Commission on Elections said the post, which circulated amid the BARMM polls, is malicious and baseless. The poll body added that an automated counting machine cannot manipulate a ballot’s results.

Claim: An automated counting machine (ACM) in Butig, Lanao del Sur altered the ballot cast during the first Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) parliamentary elections.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: The claim was posted on Facebook on September 14 by a user named Zeddie DM.

The post shows an alleged photo of the voter receipt produced by an ACM, which supposedly reflected a vote mismatch. The user wrote, “BGC ang lumalabas kahit UBJP ang binoto.”

([Bangsamoro Grand Coalition] appeared on my receipt even though I voted for [United Bangsamoro Justice Party].)

The post later gained traction after the Facebook page Boss Mil reposted the claim. As of writing, it has amassed over 1,400 reactions, 200 comments, and 600 shares.

Comments on the post speculated fraud in the elections and called for manual counting of results.

The facts: The Commission on Elections, in a Facebook post on September 14, said that the circulating post is false, has no basis, and is a malicious imputation meant to mislead the public about the voting process.

“Palaging binabanggit ng Comelec sa bawat voter education campaign na ang Automated Counting Machine (ACM) ay hindi kayang manipulahin ang resulta ng balota. Kung ano lamang ang shinade na bilog sa balota ay iyon lamang ang babasahin ng ACM at i‑record sa voter receipt,” the poll body said.

(In every voter education campaign, Comelec consistently emphasizes that the Automated Counting Machine cannot manipulate election results. The machine reads and records on the voter receipt only the circles actually shaded on the ballot.)

Comelec also reminded the public of the implications of spreading false information under the Omnibus Election Code. The poll body said that those undermining the integrity of the elections may face imprisonment of one to six years.

BARMM polls: The post circulated amid the historic BARMM parliamentary elections, which marks a historic milestone in the region’s transition from the 2014 peace agreement between the Philippine government and the MILF to a functioning parliamentary system. (LIVE UPDATES: First BARMM parliamentary elections)

During the September 14 polls, election watchdogs flagged alleged violations, including reports of pre-shaded ballots, vote-buying, voter coercion and unauthorized assistance, and the presence of armed people inside voting centers. – Lourence Angelo Marcellana & James Bones/Rappler.com

James Bones is a Research and Data volunteer at Rappler. He is a fourth-year Bachelor of Science in Industrial Engineering student at the Polytechnic University of the Philippines – Manila.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: Watchdogs flag ballot violations, vote-buying as BARMM polls near end
World.content:
PRE-SHADED BALLOT. The Commission on Elections reports ballots in several voting precincts in Maluso, Basilan, have been pre-shaded ahead of the Bangsamoro parliamentary elections on September 14, 2026.

Namfrel and LENTE raise alarm over reports of pre-shaded ballots, vote-buying, voter coercion, and armed people at voting centers as the first BARMM parliamentary election progresses

CAGAYAN DE ORO, Philippines – By early afternoon, the first parliamentary election in the Bangsamoro region was still hours from closing, but election watchdogs were already compiling a troubling picture.

Reports of alleged pre-shaded ballots, voters being told how to vote, money changing hands, and armed people inside voting centers raised questions about whether some voters in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) were able to cast their ballots freely and in secrecy.

The National Citizens’ Movement for Free Elections (Namfrel) and Legal Network for Truthful Elections (LENTE) both reported irregularities as voting progressed, although they said polling was orderly in many places.

Namfrel, in an early afternoon bulletin, cited allegations of pre-shaded ballots, unauthorized handling of ballots, attempts to bypass voting procedures, and the blocking of accredited observers.

The election monitor said it was “deeply concerned by reports of violence, ballot fraud, and obstruction of accredited observers in several localities” even as it called on candidates, security forces, and elections officials to “help ensure that the remainder of the electoral exercise is peaceful and calls on voters and volunteers alike to remain vigilant.”

LENTE, in a 2 pm bulletin, reported vote-buying, ballot secrecy violations, unauthorized assistance and firearms inside voting centers as voting progressed in the first BARMM parliamentary elections.

The allegations could not be immediately independently verified. The Commission on Elections (Comelec), however, earlier ordered the replacement of ballots in Maluso, Basilan, and placed the town under its control after pre-shaded ballots were discovered.

Assisted voting was among the most widespread concerns. LENTE said 187 of 501 reports involving voter assistance, or about 37%, concerned assisted voting. It warned excessive or unauthorized assistance could compromise ballot secrecy and allow those helping voters to substitute their own choices.

“A major issue to emerge from the BARMM elections thus far is the vulnerability of voters’ ability to freely choose their own representatives, with the sanctity of the ballot repeatedly violated and the assisted voting process abused across several areas LENTE monitored,” the group said.

LENTE added, “In its worst form, an assistor is no longer assisting the voter at all but substituting their own choice for the true will of the electorate.”

In 137 of 492 reports, or 28%, voters did not personally feed their ballots into automated counting machines. Electoral board members were reported to have done so in 119 cases, contrary to election rules.

In Maguindanao del Norte, some voters reportedly left polling places before their ballots were fed into machines, allowing watchers to complete the process. In 41 reports, people assisting voters had helped more than the legal limit of three voters, LENTE said.

The watchdog also recorded 19 reports of vote-buying and 27 cases of partisan political activity by electoral board members.

Security concerns included seven reports of people carrying firearms inside voting centers, including three incidents each in Talitay, Maguindanao del Norte, and Marawi City, Lanao del Sur.

Namfrel separately reported an intimidation and shooting incident at Pilot Central School in Cotabato City, where a volunteer also witnessed pre-shaded ballots.

In Sultan Kudarat, Maguindanao del Norte, a Namfrel volunteer reported seeing an electoral board member shade multiple official ballots and feed most of them into a vote-counting machine without voters present. Another volunteer reported receiving a pre-shaded ballot in Datu Abdullah Sangki, Maguindanao del Sur.

Namfrel also reported delays in election materials in Al-Barka, Basilan, because of security concerns involving armed people along transport routes. Some electoral boards were still being deployed as late as 10:20 am.

Despite the reports, Namfrel said most polling places it observed opened on time, with electoral boards, voting machines and election materials in place.

Voting is scheduled to end at 7 pm, followed by counting and canvassing. The elections are the first parliamentary polls in BARMM since the autonomous region was created in 2019. – Rappler.com

World.title: Meet Joaquin Tovera, the La Salle rookie who looks like UAAP’s next big thing
World.content:
ROOKIE. Joaquin Tovera in action for the La Salle Green Archers in the UAAP Season 89 men's basketball tournament.

Rookie guard Joaquin Tovera shines in his debut for defending champion La Salle, wasting no time making his mark with his scoring prowess

MANILA, Philippines – Joaquin Tovera did not take long to make his presence felt in the UAAP.

In his first game for defending champion La Salle, the 18-year-old guard looked right at home, exploding for 22 points to go with 3 steals in just 14 minutes as the Green Archers escaped the NU Bulldogs, 89-87, in their UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball tournament opener on Sunday, September 13.

For much of the game, Tovera looked like the best player on the floor, repeatedly blowing past NU guards Reinhard Jumamoy and Tebol Garcia, both of whom tried to get under his skin.

“At first I was nervous, but when I stepped on the court, I just wanted to show what I got,” said Tovera.

Play Video

“I think he was a bit nervous, but he got his bearings. It’s his first time playing in front of a crowd like this,” La Salle head coach Topex Robinson said. “I guess he just soaked up the experience. It’s going to get a lot tougher from here on, but he knows that.”

Tovera’s debut was impressive on its own, but his resume suggests there is much more to come.

Chino Hills product

The Filipino-American guard attended Chino Hills High School in California, the same basketball program that produced NBA stars Lonzo and LaMelo Ball.

Tovera made a name for himself with his explosive scoring, including a 47-point outburst against Etiwanda High School in a Baseline League game.

He also played for Fil-Am Nation Select on the competitive youth and travel circuits alongside fellow Filipino-American players based in the United States.

Representing Fil-Am Nation in this year’s NBTC tournament, Tovera averaged 27.7 points, 6.3 rebounds, and 5.7 assists per game.

Gilas Youth star

Tovera also represented the Philippines internationally, emerging as a major force in the Gilas Pilipinas Youth program.

He won tournament MVP honors in the FIBA U18 Asia Cup SEABA Qualifiers after averaging 16.4 points, 4.0 assists, and 3.0 steals per game.

According to Robinson, it is what Tovera is expected to do with La Salle in the UAAP.

The La Salle coach has been particularly impressed by how quick the teenager has embraced the challenge of learning the team’s championship-proven system.

“I guess what really kind of stood out is the way he’s really been coachable,” Robinson said. “He was asking questions, especially with the veterans and other coaches. I guess we could see that he’s really making his way to adapt to our system. We don’t have to force him to do that, but he was the one asking those questions. That’s really huge for us.”

Tovera’s ability to contribute, even as a rookie, has also given La Salle another dynamic piece alongside its veteran core.

“Him scoring that much and contributing a lot on both ends helped us a lot. Having a young guy [playing well] together with our veterans is really going to be a big help for us moving forward,” Robinson added.

Brief UP stint

Before enrolling at La Salle, Tovera initially committed to play for the UP Fighting Maroons.

He even saw action for UP in the FilOil EcoOil Preseason Cup in June, serving as a backup to Rey Remogat.

Tovera averaged 5.0 points, 1.7 rebounds, and 3.3 assists during his brief stint with the Fighting Maroons. On his 18th birthday, however, he de-committed from UP and made the surprising move to La Salle, which caught many in the league by surprise.

Tovera was once viewed as the heir apparent to Remogat, who will leave UP at the end of Season 89. Instead, he landed at La Salle, where he is now being groomed as a potential successor to Jacob Cortez and the future leader of a program that has won two of the last three UAAP championships.

Robinson knows Tovera is still developing, though, and the La Salle coach is giving the teenager room to learn, make mistakes, and understand the game at the collegiate level.

“He’s young. He’s only 18. He’s going to make those young mistakes,” Robinson said. “What we just try to remind him is that everybody is allowed to make a mistake. You’ll get the support that you need. Hopefully, it’s going to lighten the process and the load on his shoulders.” – Rappler.com

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.
