World.title: Iran envoy: Georgia not the only destination for Iranians
World.content:
Iranian envoy to Georgia makes pointed remarks

Iranian Ambassador to Georgia Seyed Ali Moujani has responded to a statement by Georgia’s Civil Aviation Agency saying the country would fully comply with sanctions against Iranian airlines imposed by the United States. The ambassador said Georgia had been one possible destination for Iranians, but was not the only one.

On 8 September, the United States imposed sanctions on 27 Iranian airlines. Six of them — Sepehran Airlines, Varesh Airlines, Qeshm Air, Fly Kish Airlines, Taban Airlines and AVA Airlines — also operate flights between Georgia and Iran. “As the expanded sanctions list announced by the US State Department includes airlines that currently operate flights between Georgia and Iran, the Georgian side, as in other cases, will act in full compliance with the international sanctions regime,” the Civil Aviation Agency said.

In turn, the Iranian embassy published a map of the Black Sea region showing only half of Georgia. When the Georgian service of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty asked the Iranian ambassador whether the map was intended to convey a political message, he replied:

“Sometimes a diplomat can say nothing, write nothing and simply share a picture… Water knows no borders; the Caucasus and Iran need a common, interconnected future.”

Map published by Iranian ambassador to Georgia

What Iran’s ambassador said

Seyed Ali Moujani said Iranian tour operators had contacted the embassy’s consular section in recent days with questions about whether tourist trips to Georgia would continue.

“Georgia has undoubtedly been one of the important Black Sea tourist destinations for Iranians,” Moujani wrote, noting that the country had attracted many Iranian tourists in recent years.

He also said Iran respected Georgia, the Georgian people and the country’s independent decisions.

“Georgia’s recent decision to introduce certain restrictions in connection with Western sanctions is one that we must respect as the country’s choice. However, respecting the choices of others does not mean disregarding our own right to choose,” the Iranian ambassador wrote.

Moujani said Iranian tourists, like citizens of other countries, considered a range of factors when choosing a holiday destination, including safety, convenience, cost, mutual respect and dignity.

The ambassador also noted that tourism generated mutual economic benefits.

“The arrival of tourists does not simply mean travellers entering a country. Hotels, restaurants, transport providers, shops, tour guides, craftspeople, public services and dozens of other sectors of the economy all benefit,” Moujani wrote.

He said travellers had also historically played an important role in building links between cultures and peoples, and sometimes in creating new opportunities for cooperation and development.

“If a new situation has emerged today, we should not view it solely as a restriction; every restriction can become an opportunity to find new paths,” the ambassador said.

Seyed Ali Moujani said there were other coastal destinations in the Black Sea region besides Georgia that could serve as alternatives for Iranian tourists.

“There are other destinations — other countries worth visiting, other cultures worth discovering and other peoples worth engaging with,” Moujani wrote.

The ambassador described Iran’s respect and friendship for Georgia and the Georgian people as unwavering, but stressed that Iran and the Iranian people’s right to choose also deserved respect.

World.title: Second chance: South Ossetia revives efforts to promote Ossetian amid leadership change
World.content:
South Ossetian Education and Science Minister Aslan Lolayev has announced plans to open a specialist class offering advanced study of the Ossetian language and literature.

Lolayev said the class would accommodate more than 30 pupils, but did not specify which school it would be based at or which year group it would be for.

“The authorities plan to open another three such classes in the next academic year — two in Tskhinvali and one in one of the districts,” Lolayev added.

He said the authorities hoped the introduction of classes offering advanced Ossetian-language study would “become one of the stages in developing a national Ossetian school system and expanding the use of the native language in education”.

Russian and Ossetian are South Ossetia’s official languages, but administrative work and education are conducted only in Russian. Russian is dominant overall, and is also the language predominantly used by the local population in everyday life.

However, Zarema Ts, a schoolteacher from Tskhinvali, says there is demand among young people for greater promotion of the Ossetian language. She believes the younger generation should therefore be encouraged to study the Ossetian language and literature, as well as Ossetian history and ethnography.

“There should be more opportunities, clubs and classes for studying Ossetian, not only within the education system but also outside educational institutions. For example, why not organise Ossetian-language classes for visitors and Russian specialists working here?”

North Ossetian experience not fully embraced

Zarema says, however, that proficiency in Ossetian is considerably higher in South Ossetia than in North Ossetia. Statistics appear to support her claim: in North Ossetia, which is part of the Russian Federation, the situation surrounding the Ossetian language has been recognised as critical, prompting the local authorities to take serious steps to preserve it.

The Alan Gymnasium, a multilingual Ossetian-Russian boarding school, has been operating in Vladikavkaz for nine years, with most subjects taught primarily in Ossetian. The school was established at the initiative of then North Ossetian leader Vyacheslav Bitarov, who continues to provide it with financial support.

South Ossetian officials, however, have been slow to adopt this model.

In early 2026, Aslan Lolayev was preparing to present a project for a national school in Tskhinvali modelled on the Alan Gymnasium. Reports said the project had already been agreed with the relevant Russian authorities and only needed to be implemented.

Lolayev was subsequently dismissed as education minister, and acting minister Rimma Pliyeva said the North Ossetian gymnasium model was unsuitable for South Ossetia. She argued that South Ossetia’s education system was already “perfectly fulfilling its role in teaching the Ossetian language”.

Second chance

Several months later, however, there was another twist: South Ossetian President Alan Gagloyev resigned early and Prime Minister Marat Kambolov took over as acting president.

Kambolov reinstated former Education Minister Aslan Lolayev, giving him another opportunity to implement at least part of his programme to expand advanced study of the Ossetian language and literature.

How successful the initiative will prove remains unclear, with South Ossetian experts so far reluctant to make predictions.

Three years ago, in September 2023, Aslan Lolayev raised concerns about a shortage of Ossetian-language textbooks.

“These textbooks cannot be purchased commercially because they were published under a state procurement programme. All copies were distributed to educational institutions. Moreover, the textbooks were published in 2019 and, if handled with care, have a lifespan of five years. After that, they need to be replaced,” he said at the time.

Lolayev added that the republication of the textbooks was included in a three-year programme that was due to be submitted to parliament and the government for consideration.

“I hope it will receive support and that we will be able to resolve this issue,” Lolayev said in 2023. There have been no reports of new textbooks since then.

South Ossetia is due to hold a presidential election on 18 September. Whether the change of leadership and the arrival of a new team, which includes Aslan Lolayev, will alter the situation remains to be seen, although there are hopes within society that it will.

Madina Valiyeva, a finalist in the Team of the Future personnel programme, for example, says that if she is appointed to an official post, one of her goals will be to establish a South Ossetian version of the Alan Gymnasium.

“There is a very apt saying: ‘No language, no nation.’ We must preserve our native language and pass it on to future generations. That is the future of our people,” Valiyeva said.

World.title: Abkhaz president voices blacksmith in cartoon
World.content:
Abkhaz President Badra Gunba has voiced a character in the animated film Nart Sasrykva, dedicated to a hero of the Abkhaz epic. Gunba provided the voice of one of the film’s characters, the blacksmith Ainar.

Work on the 36-minute animated film, which has taken five years to complete, is nearing its end, with its official premiere due in a month. Director Astamur Kvitsinia adapted the heroic epic, which has several versions, into a format designed to be engaging and accessible to children.

It is unclear why the president became involved in voicing the film. One possible explanation is the longstanding friendship between Badra Gunba and Astamur Kvitsinia, dating back to Gunba’s time as Abkhazia’s culture minister from 2011 to 2014.

Astamur Kvitsinia is widely regarded as the father of Abkhaz animation and has created more than a dozen animated films based on Abkhaz fairy tales and myths.

Versions of the Nart epic, about warrior brothers who battle giants, are found among many peoples of the Caucasus. Most scholars date the epic to the 8th-7th centuries BC.

Each people’s version has its own distinctive features and reflects its particular worldview. In the Abkhaz version, the Narts are a family of 100 brothers and their only sister. Sasrykva, the youngest of the brothers, is the epic’s main hero.

World.title: “Injustice prevails under oligarch Ivanishvili” — video podcast “Protests in Georgia”
World.content:
For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society.

Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms.

For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti.

In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years.

To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

World.title: Opinion: ‘Arresting a person in Georgia over their views on a 34-year-old war is a legal absurdity’
World.content:
Opinion on Giorgi Baramidze’s arrest

“Arresting someone over an opinion expressed in a historical programme about a 34-year-old war — especially when he has since apologised for the statement — is a legal absurdity,” said Tamta Mikeladze, director of the Social Justice Center, commenting on the arrest of Georgian opposition leader and former defence minister Giorgi Baramidze.

On 11 September, Giorgi Baramidze was arrested on charges of treason against the state, specifically sabotage. His arrest followed an interview on the programme “Birth of Georgia”, in which he said that at the beginning of the 1992–93 Georgian-Abkhaz war, the Georgian side had no prisoners because they were “shot”.

Tamta Mikeladze: “Arresting someone over an opinion expressed in a historical programme about a 34-year-old war — especially when he has since apologised for the statement — is a legal absurdity.

The prosecutor’s argument that the statement damaged Georgia’s international standing and image, offended the honour of war veterans and so on has no basis in criminal law. If specific individuals believed Baramidze had defamed them, they could have taken him to court in a civil case.

Claims that the statement could be used in international legal proceedings are also unfounded. There are no international legal proceedings concerning the war in Abkhazia, and Baramidze was not a decision-maker at the time. His words therefore could not carry the kind of weight that would affect any legal consequences.

Arresting someone for expressing an opinion – even if that opinion is unfounded, foolish, offensive or unacceptable – is therefore an unimaginable departure from the rule of law.”

Mikeladze also examines the alleged offence in detail and points to a mismatch between the charge and the statement, arguing that no remarks of this kind can legally constitute sabotage.

World.title: One of Georgia’s opposition leaders, Giorgi Baramidze, detained on ‘treason and sabotage’ charges
World.content:
Opposition figure Baramidze arrested in Georgia

Giorgi Baramidze, one of the leaders of the opposition United National Movement and Georgian former defence and interior minister, has been detained in Georgia.

Prosecutors searched his home before handcuffing him.

The detention stems from an interview Baramidze gave on the programme “Birth of Georgia”, in which he said that at the beginning of the 1992–93 Georgian-Abkhaz war, the Georgian side had no prisoners of war because they were “shot”.

On 7 August, the prosecutor’s office said it had opened an investigation into “treason against the state and sabotage” over the statement.

As of today, five former Georgian defence ministers are (!) in prison, while a sixth is facing criminal charges.

Giorgi Baramidze is now the seventh on the list.

What the prosecutor’s office says

Deputy Prosecutor General Amiran Guluashvili confirmed that Giorgi Baramidze was detained on charges of treason against the state, specifically sabotage. The charge carries a prison sentence of up to four years.

Giorgi Baramidze, one of the leaders of the opposition United National Movement and Georgian former defence and interior minister

The prosecutor’s office says its investigation found no evidence that prisoners of war were executed by Georgian armed forces or other participants in the conflict. It therefore described Baramidze’s claim as “baseless and fabricated” and said it was part of a targeted information campaign.

According to the prosecutor’s office, Baramidze’s statement could damage Georgia’s international image, the reputation of its defence forces and the dignity of those who took part in the war. It could also undermine efforts to reconcile with communities affected by the conflict and rebuild trust.

The prosecutor’s office says Baramidze’s remarks harmed Georgia’s peace and de-occupation policy and obstructed the work of state agencies, including the Office of the State Minister for Reconciliation and Civic Equality, which is working to restore trust and cooperation.

The prosecutor’s office will ask the court to remand Baramidze in custody. The investigation is ongoing.

What Giorgi Baramidze said

During the programme “Birth of Georgia”, Giorgi Baramidze recalled the exchange of prisoners during the Georgian-Abkhaz war and said: “We had no prisoners. Our side did not take prisoners — they were shot.”

Baramidze’s statement drew a strong reaction from government officials. He later explained several times what he had meant.

He said he was referring to the very beginning of the war, when the Georgian side still had no regular, organised army and some fighters, driven by grief after losing loved ones in the fighting, sometimes did not take enemy combatants prisoner.

“During the first period, this was the situation: people whose mothers, fathers or other loved ones had been killed were so consumed by anger that they did not take prisoners during fighting and killed them instead. They had been driven to despair. This is the bitter truth about the early stage of the war, which I know because I was personally involved in prisoner exchanges,” Baramidze explained.

He said the situation later changed, with the Georgian side beginning to take prisoners, making prisoner exchanges possible.

Baramidze also says he was personally involved in the process, which ultimately helped secure the return of around 200 Georgian prisoners.

World.title: Live from Gyumri, Armenia, in photos and videos
World.content:
Gyumri, Armenia, photos and video

Gyumri is the second-largest city in Armenia after Yerevan. The video was filmed during a journey from Georgia to Armenia, and the story follows this route.

As soon as you cross the Georgian border and enter Armenia, the road becomes mountainous. The plains and forest-covered mountains gradually give way to rocky slopes.

The road runs across the Ashotzk Plateau along the Akhuryan River gorge and around the Shirak Range. This is where Gyumri lies, at an altitude of more than 1,500 metres above sea level.

The air is noticeably cooler here, which is why both tourists and residents of the capital come here in summer.

Locals are particularly proud of their drinking water. It comes from mountain springs and is exceptionally cold and delicious.

Small drinking fountains can be found throughout the city. Locals call them “pulpulak”. They attract attention partly because of their distinctive designs, with no two fountains looking quite alike.

They are usually built from local stone — tuff or basalt — and decorated with national ornaments, crosses and various symbols.

There is also a tradition of building pulpulaks in memory of deceased loved ones.

A defining feature of Gyumri is its black stone. Almost all the city’s old buildings are made from local volcanic tuff.

Drinking fountain in Gyumri, Armenia. JAMnews photo.

In the city centre lies Vardanants Square. It was named in memory of the battle between the Armenian army, led by commander Vardan Mamikonian, and the Persian army in 450–451.

Vardanants Square in Gyumri, Armenia. JAMnews photo.

Churches of Gyumri

On either side of the square stand two churches: the Church of the Holy Mother of God, also known as the Church of the “Seven Wounds”, and the Church of the Holy Saviour.

The Church of the Holy Mother of God holds a special place in Gyumri’s history. During the Soviet period, when most churches in the city were closed and converted into warehouses or museums, the “Seven Wounds” Church remained one of the few still operating. It became a centre that preserved church traditions and a symbol of believers’ resistance.

Symbolically, the church courtyard contains a brass cross riddled with bullet holes. It commemorates the clergy who continued their service and supported believers during Stalin’s anti-religious campaign. Dozens of members of the Shirak Diocese clergy were arrested and executed.

Today, the bullet holes in the cross are clearly visible even from a distance. The names of clergy members who died during those years are engraved on its lower section.

On 7 December 1988, an earthquake almost destroyed the city in just 30 seconds.

The entire northern part of Armenia was affected. More than 27,000 people died, and 750,000 were left homeless.

A huge fragment of stone broke off the Church of the Holy Saviour in Gyumri during the earthquake. They left it lying beside the church. According to local residents, it serves as a reminder of that terrible day.

A bronze memorial, “To the Innocent Victims, the Compassionate Hearts”, was built nearby. The inscription appears on the monument in three languages: Armenian, Russian and English.

It depicts figures emerging from the rubble and helping one another.

The scale of the destruction clearly showed the difference in quality between older buildings and structures from the Soviet period.

Low-rise buildings in Gyumri made from traditional black tuff. JAMnews photo.

One- and two-storey buildings dating from before the Soviet era proved more resilient, while high-rise buildings constructed in the 1970s and 1980s were completely destroyed.

The tragedy fundamentally changed the city’s future development strategy. Based on the findings of seismologists and architects, Gyumri banned the construction of high-rise residential buildings.

The city returned to its historic style: low-rise, sturdy buildings made from local black and orange tuff.

Tourists often explore the city in these horse-drawn carriages, which are popular in Gyumri. JAMnews photo.

World.title: Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan move to streamline cross-border road transit
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 14. Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan agreed to step up efforts to streamline cross-border road transport, including by developing a "seamless transit" mechanism and expanding the use of digital procedures for freight and passenger transportation.

This was reflected in the statement by the Uzbek Ministry of Transport, following the meeting of the Joint Commission on International Road Transport between Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, held in Samarkand.

According to the Ministry, the meeting was chaired by Uzbekistan's First Deputy Transport Minister Mamanbiy Omarov and Kazakhstan Deputy Transport Minister Maksat Kaliakparov.

"The sides discussed measures to increase freight and passenger transportation between the two countries, improve the permit system and strengthen their transit potential. As part of the talks, the countries agreed to establish a bilateral working group to introduce a “seamless transit” mechanism for international road transport," the Uzbek Ministry of Transport said in a statement.

The mechanism is expected to simplify and digitize relevant procedures, reduce administrative barriers and gradually shift the sector toward electronic document processing.

The parties also reached a preliminary agreement to introduce electronic permit forms for irregular international passenger road transportation starting in 2027.

Particular attention was given to the development of road transport infrastructure and improving the efficiency of transport controls.

The move toward digital permits and electronic documentation could help reduce processing times and administrative burdens for carriers operating between Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, while supporting more efficient cross-border movement.

The countries are also seeking to strengthen their wider transport and logistics cooperation as they work to expand trade and improve regional connectivity.

"The introduction of seamless transit and digital documentation will help simplify cross-border procedures and create more efficient conditions for international road transportation," the Uzbek Transport Ministry said.

The talks concluded with both sides reaffirming their interest in further developing cooperation in the transport and logistics sector.

Furthermore, the parties agreed to ensure the practical implementation of the agreements reached during the meeting and continue coordination on measures to improve international road transportation between Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan.

World.title: Turkmenistan, Malaysia discuss oil and gas cooperation
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 14. Turkmenistan and Malaysia discussed cooperation in the oil and gas sector during talks with the leadership of the Malaysia Petroleum Resources Corporation (MPRC).

This was reflected in a post published by the Embassy of Turkmenistan in Malaysia following a meeting between Ambassador Muhammetnyyaz Mashalov and MPRC President and Chief Executive Officer Mohd Yazid Jaafar.

The meeting took place at MPRC headquarters and focused on cooperation in the oil and gas sector.

Diplomatic relations between Turkmenistan and Malaysia were established in 1992, but the relationship has been built primarily around energy cooperation. Malaysia's state energy company Petronas entered Turkmenistan in 1996 and remains one of the country's largest foreign investors, developing offshore projects in the Turkmen sector of the Caspian Sea, operating the Kiyanly gas processing complex and training hundreds of Turkmen specialists. Over three decades, the company has become the anchor of Turkmen-Malaysian economic ties, while cooperation has gradually expanded to education, engineering services and industrial technologies.

The partnership entered a new phase in 2026. During Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim's visit to Ashgabat in June, the two countries signed a framework agreement on long-term hydrocarbon cooperation that opened the way for Petronas to participate in the development of the giant Galkynysh gas field — one of the world's largest gas deposits. The agreements also covered opportunities in gas processing, gas chemicals and oil refining, broadening cooperation beyond the company's traditional Caspian operations.

World.title: AI MONTH 2026: Kazakhstan unites key artificial intelligence events into single tech program
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 14. As part of the Year of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence in Kazakhstan, AI MONTH 2026 kicks off on September 23, presenting a large-scale program of events in artificial intelligence and digital technologies. The initiative will unite the tech community, business sector, academia, startups, international experts, and regional initiatives across the country.

The central event of AI MONTH will be the international tech forum AI & Digital Bridge 2026, which will take place on October 1–3 in Astana.

In 2026, AI Week transformed into AI MONTH: the number of artificial intelligence initiatives has grown significantly, while the tech agenda expands across more industries, audiences, and regions nationwide. The new format brings these initiatives together into a unified program, showcasing the development of Kazakhstan's AI ecosystem on a national scale.

On September 23, AI MONTH will kick off with HackAlem AI powered by OpenAI, one of the world's largest hackathons focused on developing AI solutions. Teams of up to three members will build agentic AI solutions for 10 key sectors of Kazakhstan’s economy, with the mandatory use of Codex and OpenAI APIs.

The total value of prizes and technical resources for HackAlem AI stands at $1.1 million. This package includes a cash prize pool, API tokens, and OpenAI technical infrastructure, allowing participants to develop and launch their own AI solutions.

The winners of HackAlem AI will be awarded on the main stage of the AI & Digital Bridge 2026 International Technology Forum. The hackathon will bring together developers, students, young professionals, startups, and IT enthusiasts, offering participants the opportunity to turn an idea into a functional AI solution in a short period.

On September 29–30, Astana will host KazHackStan, Central Asia's largest international cybersecurity conference. Over 100 regional and international speakers will address DevSecOps, OSINT, data protection, malware analysis, and emerging cyber threats linked to artificial intelligence.

During the same days, Astana will host a C5+1 international platform dedicated to AI cooperation between Central Asian nations and the United States. Representatives from governments, international organizations, and the tech community will discuss AI regulation, infrastructure development, talent cultivation, and stronger international tech partnerships.

The investment agenda will continue with the LP Summit, the first summit in Eurasia for LPs and VC investors. It will unite institutional investors, venture capital and sovereign wealth funds, corporations, and family offices to discuss the development of the venture ecosystem and new investment opportunities.

A dedicated stream of AI MONTH will focus on healthcare technologies. At AI and MedTech Day, experts, physicians, developers, and startups will discuss the application of artificial intelligence in diagnostics and healthcare management, while collaborating on new MedTech solutions.

One of the most captivating tech components will be the Unitree Humanoid Robotics Hackathon. Teams will program actual Unitree G1 humanoid robots provided by the organizers, solving real-world challenges directly on hardware without simulators.

Technology will also extend beyond the traditional IT agenda. From October 1 to 3, Astana will host the Astana AI Film Festival, an international festival showcasing an emerging movement in cinema where artificial intelligence serves as a full-fledged filmmaking tool. The program features AI-generated films, public screenings, panel discussions, and workshops exploring how technology is reshaping directing, visual style, storytelling, character design, special effects, and voice acting.

The program also includes the FIRST Tech Challenge and FIRST LEGO League international robotics competitions, a UNICEF strategic foresight session on the impact of AI on the future of children and youth, corporate technology events, and other specialized formats.

Eurasia’s premier tech forum and one of the global IT industry's landmark events — AI & Digital Bridge 2026.

The forum will bring together executives from leading technology companies, global business founders, scientists, investors, entrepreneurs, startups, and representatives of international organizations. The program focuses on artificial intelligence, tech entrepreneurship, investments, human capital development, and new opportunities in the digital economy.

Tickets for the open program on October 2–3 are already available on the official forum website at https://digitalbridge.ai/.

On October 1, a special high-level program will take place, featuring heads of state, international delegations, and tech industry leaders. Participation in this session is by invitation only.

On October 2 and 3, AI & Digital Bridge 2026 will present its open program for forum attendees, bringing together representatives from global tech companies, international experts, entrepreneurs, startups, and investors under one roof.

Among the confirmed speakers and participants for AI & Digital Bridge 2026 are Rev Lebaredian, Vice President of NVIDIA; Balaji Srinivasan, Founder of Network School; Kai-Fu Lee, Founder of Sinovation Ventures and 01.AI; Greg Wyler, Founder and CEO of E-Space; William Ford, Chairman and CEO of General Atlantic; Sebastian Kurz, Co-founder and President of Dream; Richard Stirling, Co-founder and CEO of Oxford Insights; Eleanor Olcott, Financial Times Correspondent; Yerzat Dulat, Co-founder and CTO of Higgsfield AI; Jamie Beaton, Founder of Crimson Education; Murat Abdrakhmanov, Founder of MA7 Ventures; Bagdat Mussin, Chairman of the Board of Kazakhtelecom JSC; Ramil Mukhoryapov, Co-founder of Choco Holding; and other leading figures from the global technology and entrepreneurial ecosystem.

AI & Digital Bridge 2026 will serve as the premier platform for international tech dialogue, highlighting Kazakhstan's growth as a Eurasian AI hub—a destination for technology, talent, entrepreneurs, and investment.

AI MONTH extends far beyond Astana. Throughout the month, artificial intelligence and digital technology events will take place in regional tech hubs across Kazakhstan.

The lineup features workshops, bootcamps, hackathons, career meetups, pitch sessions, and startup battles. The events are open to students, educators, developers, entrepreneurs, startup teams, and professionals eager to learn and apply artificial intelligence in practice.

The regional program will engage participants from across the country in the tech agenda, enabling them to gain new skills, develop their own solutions, and present promising projects to the professional community.

Schedules, venues, and registration details for all regional events are available on the Astana Hub platform.

The month-long program will conclude with the Grand Final of alem.ai Battle, an AI competition organized by Astana Hub—an international innovation cluster dedicated to advancing tech entrepreneurship and the IT industry in Kazakhstan.

The final will bring together the strongest teams and young talent from Kazakhstan and Central Asia. Participants will showcase their developments across four categories, making the finale a premier platform for presenting promising AI solutions.

In this way, AI MONTH brings the entire AI development lifecycle into a single program, spanning education, talent cultivation, and product development to tech entrepreneurship, venture capital attraction, and international collaboration.

This month-long format captures the scope of the transformation taking place across the country, demonstrating that the AI agenda is advancing not only through landmark international events, but also across regional tech hubs, academic institutions, startups, and enterprise businesses.

AI & Digital Bridge 2026 will serve as the centerpiece international platform of AI MONTH, showcasing Kazakhstan's role as an emerging Eurasian center for artificial intelligence and digital technology development.

AI & Digital Bridge 2026 is organized by the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development of the Republic of Kazakhstan, Astana Hub, and the Astana City Akimat.

AI MONTH brings together partners supporting the development of artificial intelligence, tech initiatives, and Kazakhstan's AI ecosystem. The Gold Partners of AI MONTH are Freedom Bank, Kaspi.kz, and Samruk-Kazyna JSC. The Silver Partner is Halyk Bank. The Transformation Partner is Beeline Kazakhstan. The Official Partner of HackAlem AI is Firebird AI KZ Ltd.

World.title: Uzbekistan, South Korea anchor strategic partnership in $12B projects
World.content:
Photo: The Press service of the President of Uzbekistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 14. Uzbekistan and South Korea have prepared a portfolio of prospective projects worth about $12 billion and agreed on an $8 billion strategic partnership program with Korea’s Export-Import Bank.

This was reflected in the statement by the press service of the Uzbek president, following talks between President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and South Korean President Lee Jae Myung in Seoul, held in both a limited format and with the participation of delegation members.

According to the information, in the course of the meeting, Korean President described Mirziyoyev’s visit as an important event in the history of bilateral relations, which have traditionally been built on friendship and mutual respect.

Mirziyoyev, in turn, described South Korea as a reliable friend and one of Uzbekistan’s most important economic partners.

"The leaders welcomed growth in bilateral trade and investment and highlighted the presence of more than 700 joint ventures with Korean capital operating in Uzbekistan. Major Korean companies active in the Uzbek market include Samsung, LG, Lotte, Young One, BOMI and KIA," the press service said.

Total Korean investment in Uzbekistan’s economy has exceeded $8 billion, with major projects including KIA vehicle production in Jizzakh region, the National Children’s Medical Center and the Ustyurt Gas Chemical Complex at the Surgil field.

The leaders identified five priority areas for further economic cooperation: expanding trade, increasing investment, developing cooperation in critical minerals, and strengthening transport and infrastructure ties.

"The numerous Korean diaspora is an integral part of the multinational family of Uzbekistan and serves as a "spiritual bridge" between our countries and peoples," the press service noted.

The sides also agreed to build a stronger innovation and technology alliance combining South Korea’s advanced technologies with Uzbekistan’s industrial and resource potential.

The proposed alliance will focus on information technology, cybersecurity, advanced and digital technologies in medicine and health care, and pharmaceutical production.

Cooperation with the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA), Korea Eximbank and the Economic Development Cooperation Fund (EDCF) is already supporting dozens of projects in health care, industry, ICT, agriculture, water management, energy, infrastructure and education.

The leaders also emphasized the importance of stronger contacts between parliaments, government agencies, regional administrations and business communities.

Education and workforce development featured prominently in the talks. Four branches of South Korean universities currently operate in Uzbekistan, training specialists in education, IT, engineering, digital technologies and other priority fields. Five vocational training centers established with KOICA assistance also provide Uzbek youth with professional skills.

The sides highlighted the role of the University Presidents Forum in exchanging experience on workforce training and agreed to continue strengthening educational cooperation.

They also welcomed the first-ever Interregional Forum held ahead of the presidential talks and agreed to hold its next edition in Samarkand.

Cultural and humanitarian ties were another focus. Mirziyoyev emphasized the role of Uzbekistan’s Korean diaspora as a “spiritual bridge” between the two countries.

The sides agreed to designate 2027 as the Year of Culture and Mutual Exchanges, with a program of joint cultural and humanitarian events.

The leaders also noted the convergence of their positions on issues on the regional and international agenda and reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining close political dialogue.

World.title: Uzbekistan's Tashkent leverages CCCME to attract Chinese manufacturers
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 14. Uzbekistan’s Tashkent region is seeking to attract Chinese machinery, electronics and high-tech manufacturing companies through the China Chamber of Commerce for Import and Export of Machinery and Electronic Products (CCCME), which represents more than 10,000 businesses.

This was reflected in the statement by the Tashkent Regional Administration, following a meeting between Governor Zoyir Mirzayev and the leadership of the China Chamber of Commerce for Import and Export of Machinery and Electronic Products (CCCME) at the Embassy of Uzbekistan in China.

According to the Regional Administration, the meeting focused on the region’s industrial, investment and export potential, as well as opportunities available to foreign investors seeking to establish new production projects in Tashkent region.

The sides discussed cooperation in machinery and electrical engineering, high-tech manufacturing, industrial cooperation and the expansion of export and import operations. They also considered opportunities for Chinese companies to launch investment projects in the region.

“The CCCME’s extensive network can provide Tashkent region with an important platform for establishing direct contacts with leading Chinese manufacturers and exporters, attracting new partners and expanding the region’s export geography,” the Tashkent regional administration said.

Meanwhile, the CCCME, headquartered in Beijing, brings together more than 10,000 companies and operates through 22 industry divisions. Its activities include promoting trade and investment and supporting international industrial cooperation.

During the meeting, the Uzbek delegation presented investment opportunities in Tashkent region and highlighted the infrastructure and conditions available for foreign investors seeking to establish production facilities.

The sides also discussed ways to make greater use of CCCME’s capabilities in promoting trade and investment, developing international industrial partnerships, providing legal support and offering professional services.

The meeting concluded with agreements to take practical cooperation between Tashkent region and CCCME to a new level, jointly develop promising projects and work to attract major Chinese companies to the region.
