World.title: Uzbekistan, Palestine discuss prospects for deeper bilateral ties
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 14. Uzbekistan and Palestine discussed ways to strengthen bilateral relations and expand cooperation.

This was reflected in the statement by the Uzbek MFA, following a meeting between First Deputy Foreign Minister Bakhromjon Aloyev and Waill Ahmed Batrekhi, Palestine’s ambassador extraordinary and plenipotentiary to Uzbekistan.

According to the Ministry, in the course of the meeting, the sides reviewed key areas of bilateral relations and considered prospects for further developing cooperation between the two countries.

The talks covered opportunities to strengthen existing ties and identify additional areas for practical engagement.

"The important areas of bilateral relations were discussed, prospects for further developing cooperation were considered, and views were exchanged on a number of international issues," the ministry said.

Particular attention was given to maintaining regular political dialogue between Uzbekistan and Palestine and advancing cooperation through diplomatic channels.

The meeting comes as Uzbekistan continues to develop relations with partners in the Middle East and expand its diplomatic engagement on international and regional issues.

Uzbekistan and Palestine have maintained diplomatic relations and cooperate within international organizations, including the United Nations. Political dialogue remains an important component of their bilateral ties, while the two sides have also expressed interest in expanding cooperation in other areas of mutual interest.

The meeting concluded with the sides reaffirming their interest in further developing bilateral cooperation and maintaining contacts through diplomatic channels.

World.title: Azerbaijani delegation visits Altynken gold mine and gold refinery in Kyrgyzstan (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 14. A delegation led by Zakir Ibrahimov, Chairman of the Executive Board of AzerGold CJSC, visited the Altynken gold mine and the gold refinery operated by Kyrgyzaltyn in the city of Kara-Balta as part of a business trip to Kyrgyzstan.

In the Chuy Region, the delegation toured the Altynken mine and learned about its operations, production infrastructure and key stages of gold mining. Mine specialists provided information on the transportation of ore from the open pit to the processing facilities, as well as ore processing and other technological operations. It was noted that the Altynken gold mine has been operated since 2016 by a joint venture established by Kyrgyzaltyn and Zijin Mining, one of China’s major mining companies.

During the visit, the delegation toured the production facilities and reviewed the ore processing technology, technical solutions in use and industrial safety standards. The two sides exchanged experience in mining, gold production and processing operations, and discussed the application of modern technologies and opportunities for further cooperation.

The delegation then visited the Kyrgyzaltyn gold refinery in Kara-Balta. The hosts got acquainted with the refinery’s production infrastructure and technological processes, as well as its laboratory facilities, quality control systems, safety standards and environmental and operational requirements.

The delegation also toured the gold bullion production area and observed the main stages of the manufacturing process. Specialists explained the measures in place to ensure that gold products meet quality and safety standards.

The discussions also covered the use of advanced production technologies in the gold industry, the exchange of industry expertise and prospects for expanding cooperation between the two sides.

The visit was held under the Memorandum of Cooperation and Interaction signed between AzerGold CJSC and Kyrgyzaltyn OJSC.

World.title: Minister flies to Pilbara after report of up to 15 kids living unsupervised
World.content:
Western Australia's child protection minister has been dispatched to the Pilbara amid reports her department is failing to address the neglect of vulnerable Indigenous children.

Jessica Stojkovski flew into Port Hedland, 1,600 kilometres north of Perth, on Monday in the wake of reports in The Australian that up to 15 children, some as young as five, were living unsupervised in a home in South Hedland.

The newspaper reported WA's Department of Child Protection (DCP) had failed to take action, despite multiple complaints from residents, police and other agencies of the children's neglect, and failed to address separate complaints of sexual abuse of children in WA's East Kimberley.

The latest reporting followed claims the Department's Pilbara staff failed to heed warnings about the risk posed to the children of Port Hedland mother Margaret Dale Hawke, before she murdered them in 2022.

Jessica Stojkovski was picked up from the tarmac at Port Hedland Airport. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

Ms Stojkovski was picked up from the tarmac at Port Hedland Airport after touching down about 4pm on Monday and left the airport without taking questions.

In a written statement provided by a spokesperson, Ms Stojkovski said child protection was a "complex" issue.

"It is unacceptable that children in Western Australia are living this way," she said.

"No child should have their safety and wellbeing put at risk.

" I am seeking urgent answers in relation to the children concerned and what actions are being taken. "

The furore has sparked renewed questioning of the DCP's culture, resourcing and alleged failure to protect children at risk across regional and remote WA.

Elders say neglect a pressing issue

Kariyarra elder Pat Mason said children left alone to fend for themselves was a major issue in South Hedland.

"Children need to be in a home, and be safe in a home," Ms Mason said.

"If you can't feel safe in a home, then we as adults, no matter whose child it is, have to make sure they are safe, some way or somehow.

"We can't leave them like what's happening in South Hedland."

Pat Mason says neglect of children has become a consistent problem across the Port Hedland community. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

Ms Mason said the situation was the worst she had seen it, and that the system was failing.

"I reckon the perpetrator should be removed, not the child … the child should be left in the home, with the home that they love being in rather than taking them out," she said.

"When you remove them, they end up suiciding or turning to horrific things like stealing cars, destroying someone else's property because they haven't got a property of their own."

Nyamal elder Linda Doogiebee-Dridi (Milbugana) said the department needed to work with the community to address the problem.

"We don't have a place where my people can go to, to sit down and have a yarn and say, 'Look, I need help. Can you help me?'" she said.

Linda Doogiebee-Dridi (Milbugana) says a whole of community approach is needed to address child neglect in the community. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

"How do we make government departments change? By reaching out and saying, 'Let's co-design this department that has Aboriginal Affairs to the way that it's going to be culturally appropriate.'

"Until we actually have that talk with each other, we're not going to move on and create something that's beneficial to our people living in the Pilbara."

Latest concerns for under-fire department

Speaking earlier on Monday, Premier Roger Cook said the information that had come to light was "distressing".

"The Department of Child Protection works in very complex and difficult circumstances, made even more complex and difficult in a town such as Port Hedland," he said.

"We'll continue to ensure that we're doing everything we can to keep the kids of Western Australia safe."

The reports are the latest in a string of issues for the DCP and its care of vulnerable children across the state.

Child Protection falls under the Department of Communities, a so-called "super department" responsible to five separate ministers.

Roger Cook says the reports of neglect in South Hedland are distressing. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

More than 400 children in the department's care suffered emotional, physical or sexual abuse between 2020 and 2023, when the child protection and foster care system was described as being in "dire crisis".

An inquest into the suicide of a 15-year-old boy in the Kimberley heard the teenager had 30 different caseworkers prior to his death, while the timeframe for investigations of abuse or neglect had blown out to 60 days.

In 2024, the department left 170 vulnerable children without a dedicated caseworker.

Critics have accused the department of maintaining a nine-to-five culture in the face of a persistent problem, with the police union accusing it of outsourcing its functions to overstretched regional police officers.

Unveiling a journey of despair in WA's troubled child care system When a child isn’t safe with their family, they are placed into the care of the WA government. But some of these children and their foster parents are shining a spotlight on conditions they say are putting youth back in harm’s way.

Allegations taken 'seriously': department

The department did not answer specific questions about how it responded to the reported neglect in South Hedland.

A department spokesperson said it worked with multiple community and Aboriginal agencies to respond to at-risk individuals and families in South and Port Hedland.

"Communities' leadership also meets regularly with South Hedland and Port Hedland Aboriginal leaders, to listen to and address local concerns and discuss available supports," the spokesperson said.

"Where safety concerns for family visitations are raised, Communities engages with Police to ensure appropriate arrangements are put in place to allow contact visits to occur safely.

"Communities takes any allegation of child sexual abuse very seriously. Where concerns are raised, Communities will report to Police who are responsible for investigating alleged criminality."

World.title: Yemen's Houthi rebels seize more key islands in Red Sea to grip shipping route
World.content:
Yemen's Iranian-backed Houthi rebels have captured more strategic islands in the southern Red Sea, government and Houthi officials say, strengthening their control of a major maritime shipping route.

The capture of the islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish came as Saudi-backed government forces attempted to rally over the weekend, attempting to fight back after the rebels' lightning advances around the Bab el-Mandeb, a crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.

Members of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces react during what they say to be clashes with Iran-aligned Houthis in Al-Hazm, Yemen. (Reuters: Media Centre of the Yemeni Armed Forces)

The Houthi rebels deployed fighters on the Hanish islands, 160 kilometres north of Bab el-Mandeb, after hundreds of government-allied forces withdrew from the archipelago, according to two government officials and a Houthi official.

The officials spoke on condition of anonymity on Monday because they are not authorised to talk to journalists.

Grasp on shipping tightens

The Houthis' new gains further enable the group to threaten Saudi crude oil shipments, which have used the Red Sea as a substitute to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking shipping.

The escalation, especially Houthi attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure and its shipping endeavours across the Red Sea, adds to mounting pressure on global oil supplies and prices, which could give Iran leverage in its war with the United States.

Trucks explode during what the Houthis say was an attack targeting vehicles coming from Saudi territory, at the Al-Wadiah border. (Houthi Media Centre via Reuters)

The new capture of the Greater and Lesser Hanish islands comes after the rebels last week seized the port city of Mokha on Yemen's mainland, and the island of Mayun, located inside the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The Houthis' advances also put them just 32 kilometres from the US military base in Djibouti, on the other side of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

Saudi air base attacked

The Saudi Civil Defense sent an all clear early on Monday after issuing alerts for potential danger in the southern cities of Najran, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Abha. It also later issued warnings for Khamis Mushait and Abha a second time before lifting them again.

Yemeni civilians celebrate while riding in the back of a utility vehicle as they follow a convoy carrying Houthi prisoners freed in Mokha following the Houthi takeover. (STR via AP Photo)

On Sunday, Houthi officials released a statement claiming they had attacked the Saudi Khamis Mushait air base.

Renewed fighting between Houthis and Yemeni forces Renewed fighting has erupted between the Iran-backed Houthis and Yemeni government forces, supported by Saudi Arabia.

The advances came with little resistance from forces of the internationally recognised government. But over the weekend, those forces sought to regroup, and the Yemeni military advanced toward the strategic town of Dhubab, north of the strait.

The fighting is pushing Yemen back into full-fledged civil war, after a truce that largely proved to be successful during the past three years.

AP

World.title: The 'kooky' show that lured Celeste Barber back to the theatre
World.content:
Comedian Celeste Barber is set to return to theatre for the first time in 20 years in "kooky" comedy play The Book of Liz.

While her last stage role was in 2006, the comedian and actor, known for Wellmania and Colin from Accounts, told ABC Arts in 2023 working at Sydney Theatre Company (STC) was "on the bucket list".

As the company launches its 2027 season, she says starring in The Book of Liz is "a dream come true".

It's a full-circle moment for Barber, who worked at the theatre's restaurant back in 2003, the year after she finished drama school.

She recalls her then-roommate landing a role alongside Hugo Weaving in Tom Stoppard's The Real Thing that year.

"I was cleaning cutlery at the end of the shift and looking down the corridor at them in the green room together running lines," she says.

" I remember thinking, as I scrubbed crusty pasta off a fork, 'One day that will be me'. And now it's happening. "

STC artistic director Mitchell Butel was impressed by Barber's comedy and dramatic chops in Wellmania. (Supplied: Netflix)

Premiering Off-Broadway in 2001, The Book of Liz is a play by American siblings Amy and David Sedaris — Amy best known for Bojack Horseman and surreal sketch show At Home with Amy Sedaris, and David for his comic essays.

Barber will play the relentlessly positive Sister Elizabeth Donderstock, who decides to leave her cloistered community after she's forced to give up her treasured cheese ball recipe.

She soon finds a job as a waitress at a family-run restaurant, with help from a bizarrely Cockney-accented Ukrainian couple. They're just two of the eccentrics Liz encounters as she adjusts to life away from her community.

It was the opportunity to work on a play by the Sedaris siblings, who write together as "The Talent Family", that lured Barber back to the stage.

"I loved [The Book of Liz] as soon as I read it," Barber says. "It made me laugh.

"I feel like a Sedaris play about an Amish cheese ball maker who is on a quest to find herself is exactly what the world needs: something funny, with heart."

Stepping away from theatre for 20 years wasn't deliberate, the comedian adds, but a "pivot" because she "couldn't book a job or even get an audition".

To play Liz, Barber plans to draw on the skills in character comedy she's finessed over more than a decade as a stand-up, but is most excited by the chance to work collaboratively.

"My favourite part of performing is diving in and picking apart a character and finding out what makes them tick, what makes them laugh, cry, fart, scream," she says.

"That's where the juice is.

"I plan on approaching this play in the way I approach most things: panicked. Then as soon I step into the rehearsal room I'll take on the form of a human sponge.

"I love rehearsal rooms; I love working and performing with other people. I love actors and I love notes!"

The Book of Liz is one of 13 plays in STC's 2027 season, which also includes a Miss Fisher's Murder Mysteries play, and an adaptation of Jenny Hocking's The Palace Letters, starring Georgie Parker (Dalliance), about efforts to unseal papers about Gough Whitlam's dismissal in 1975.

The season is artistic director Mitchell Butel's second, with his leadership steering the company to its first surplus — of $765,759 — since 2022.

Butel says Whitlam's dismissal is still relevant in terms of "questions of nationhood". (Supplied: STC/Holly Ward)

That success is expected to continue, with ticket sales for 2026 already surpassing last year, thanks to new John Farnham musical Whispering Jack and An Iliad, starring David Wenham.

"There's always work to do and we have massive targets to keep the door open," Butel says.

" But hard as it is to produce theatre that's commercially successful, it's a great privilege and honour to do it, and we should celebrate it. "

Companies working together

An Iliad will tour Melbourne in 2027, with more cities expected to be announced. It's just one example of STC collaborating with theatre companies, festivals and venues across Australia in 2027 to extend the life spans of local productions.

In another modern adaptation of an ancient Greek text, Oedipus becomes a political thriller set on election night. It will star Richard Roxburgh and Heather Mitchell and will head to Adelaide Festival.

Roxburgh and Mitchell haven't shared a stage since 1992. Next year, they star together in Oedipus. (Supplied: STC/Holly Ward)

Keeping with the theme of reinterpreting classic plays, STC also co-produces John Proctor Is the Villain, with Melbourne Theatre Company (MTC), which interrogates Arthur Miller's The Crucible through the eyes of high school students.

In one of the season's literary adaptations, STC and State Theatre Company South Australia (STCSA) will collaborate on The Bookbinder of Jericho, about twin sisters working in a bindery during WWI, from the same team behind the sell-out success of The Dictionary of Lost Words.

Logan St, about an unlikely friendship between an Aboriginal woman and an Afghan cameleer in Adelaide in the 1940s, transfers from STCSA.

Co-produced by STC, Queensland Theatre Company (QTC) and Jones Theatrical Group, Miss Fisher's Murder Mysteries: Death by Deckchair is set on a boat and takes as its starting point one of the late Kerry Greenwood's novels not previously adapted for TV.

English writer Jack Thorne's reinterpretation of A Christmas Carol, which has played at Melbourne's Comedy Theatre every year since 2022, will come to Sydney for the first time, starring Tim Minchin in his first play since 2013.

A Christmas Carol will reunite Minchin with Matthew Warchus, the director of Matilda the Musical. (Supplied: STC/Holly Ward)

Butel says collaborations across Australian theatre like these are "really important".

"Because you're sharing costs, there's suddenly an ability to up cast sizes," he says.

"Bookbinder's a cast of eight, John Proctor is a cast of nine. Oedipus is a cast of 11, A Christmas Carol is a cast of 18. They're pretty large-scale shows for us."

A theatre for actors

Cast size isn't the only thing determining the scale of a production: The now-international "cine-theatre" hit The Picture of Dorian Gray will return to Australia, with Nikki Shiels (Colin from Accounts) playing all 26 characters.

STC's 2027 season Oedipus by Sophocles; adapted by Robert Icke

Logan Street by Jacob Boehme

Becky Shaw by Gina Gionfriddo

The Palace Letters by Melanie Tait

Amah and Nanna by Disapol Savetsila

Miss Fisher's Murder Mysteries: Death by Deckchair by Deb Cox

The Book of Liz by Amy and David Sedaris

The Picture of Dorian Gray by Oscar Wilde; adapted by Kip Williams

The Fifth Step by David Ireland

John Proctor Is the Villain by Kimberly Belflower

Vanya by Anton Chekhov; adapted by SImon Stephens

The Bookbinder of Jericho by Pip Williams; adapted by Verity Laughton

A Christmas Carol by Charles Dickens; adapted by Jack Thorne

It's not Shiels's first time in the role, having been the alternate performer, or understudy, since 2022. Next year she'll be taking over full-time from Eryn Jean Norvill, who originated the production.

Norvill will star in a one-woman show of her own as part of STC's 2027 season: Vanya, a new adaptation of Russian playwright Anton Chekhov's play, first brought to the stage by Andrew Scott (Fleabag).

Vanya is another example, along with The Book of Liz, of how Butel likes to program a season.

"I'm finding actors I love and want to be on our stage and asking 'What's going to float your boat?" Butel says.

That approach also led to Andrea Dimitriades (ABC TV's Return to Paradise) starring in the Australian premiere of Gina Gionfriddo's Becky Shaw, loosely based on William Thackeray's Victorian satire Vanity Fair.

Co-starring in Becky Shaw is Lincoln Younes (Last King of the Cross), in his first theatre role in a decade. He's just one screen star coming to STC, alongside Erik Thomson (Packed to the Rafters) in West End hit The Fifth Step and Gold Logie winner Lynne McGranger (Home and Away) and Annette Shun Wah in Disapol Savetsila's road trip comedy Amah and Nanna.

In 2017, at 23, Amah and Nanna writer Disapol Savetsila became the youngest-ever playwright to debut at STC. (Supplied: STC/Holly Ward)

Developed by Bathurst's Arbour Theatre Company, co-founded by Savetsila in 2020, Amah and Nanna was the winner of this year's Patrick White Award. Earlier play readings were hosted at Bathurst Memorial Entertainment Centre.

"It actually shows the benefit of funding regional arts centres to do this kind of work, because they have the ability to workshop stories that are of the regions," Butel says.

STC's 2027 season feels notable for its sheer breadth, which might account for the company's success since Butel took the reins.

"We're often accused of being elitist … but it's not all high art," he says.

"For every Uncle Vanya, there's also this kooky, Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt-like fall into the rabbit hole [like The Book of Liz].

"Some people like KFC; some people like caviar. We'll provide it all for you."

World.title: Prominent pork industry identity charged over alleged multi-million-dollar fraud
World.content:
A Queensland pork industry heavyweight has been named as one of the people charged over alleged large-scale financial crimes that authorities claim resulted in tens of millions of dollars being funnelled out of businesses for personal use.

Darren Gary Wilson, 63, alongside Cameron Ronald Wilson are alleged to have kept $10 million in sales records off the books for personal use and moved more than $30 million in cash between New South Wales and Queensland between 2017 and 2026.

The men are facing multiple charges each including receiving and possessing tainted property, destroying records, fraud, making false declarations and fraudulent omission of entry in record.

They have also been accused of fraudulently relabelling frozen meat products to alter production and best before dates.

Pork industry financial crimes charges Police allege about $10 million was funnelled out of businesses in the pork meat industry for personal use.

Authorities have confirmed the changes did not pose a risk to food safety.

The pair were not required to appear in person on Monday and their bail has been extended.

Darren Wilson is a prominent face in the pork industry, starting Wilpak wholesale meats in Ipswich in the 1980s.

The company has since expanded to include meat processing and pig farms in Queensland.

He is also widely known in the racing industry.

Darren and Cameron Wilson are to return to court in coming weeks.

The pair were charged following a joint investigation involving the Queensland Crime and Corruption Commission, the New South Wales Police Anti-Money Laundering Unit and the New South Wales Crime Commission.

World.title: Star Hawk's season over after ACL injury
World.content:
Three-time All-Australian Emily Bates will miss the rest of the AFLW season with a knee injury in a huge blow to Hawthorn's chances of snaring a maiden premiership.

Scans have confirmed Bates tore the anterior cruciate ligament in her right knee when the leg twisted awkwardly in a tackle during the Hawks' win over the Western Bulldogs on Saturday.

The 30-year-old club captain also damaged the meniscus and will undergo surgery.

"This is clearly disappointing news for Emily," Hawks AFLW general manager Keegan Brooksby said.

"The playing group and wider club will support her through the recovery journey.

"We have no doubt she'll approach her rehab with the diligence and professionalism she's always been known for.

Emily Bates played her 100th game for the Hawks against Adelaide. (Getty Images: Josh Chadwick)

"Although Emily won't return to the field in 2026, she will continue to play an important off-field role in our program, as our captain."

Hawthorn face a huge test against AFLW juggernaut North Melbourne in Cairns on Friday night without Bates and Laura Stone (concussion).

Fellow midfielder Daisy Flockhart also has to prove her fitness after suffering a knock to her chest against the Bulldogs.

"We've been playing different players through [the midfield] and trying to build some versatility in our side … we're confident in the players we'll have in there," Hawks coach Daniel Webster said post-match on Saturday.

"It'll be a good challenge next week with who we're playing.

"We'll probably have some sort of different look in there with different players and that's OK. We'll keep getting to work."

Hawthorn (3-2) sit eighth in their quest for another finals berth, while North Melbourne (5-0) are in familiar territory on top of the ladder.

AAP

World.title: 'Bittersweet' Swans captaincy call for Rampe
World.content:
Dane Rampe didn't think Sydney would still be here, let alone that he'd be tasked with leading the Swans to an unlikely AFL premiership again.

A heart-and-soul player, veteran defender Rampe will stand in for an injured Callum Mills and captain the club in Friday's preliminary final against Fremantle at the SCG.

Rampe had led the Swans to the eventual 2024 grand final loss when a luckless Mills suffered a hamstring strain before that year's preliminary final.

But the circumstances surrounding this year's premiership push wildly differ.

Mills's vice-captain Isaac Heeney is among five Swans players serving club-imposed bans after last month's post-match incident at the Pullman Hotel in Melbourne.

Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice are the other Swans who won't play again this season.

Many in the AFL world had written off Sydney in the lead-up to finals, with even club chairman Andrew Pridham believing their chances had been "torpedoed".

Swans show what 'Bloods' culture is supposed to look like Many questions were asked about Sydney's famed culture in the wake of the Pullman Hotel scandal. As the finals got underway, the players showed exactly what it is supposed to look like on the field.

A gutsy 53-point qualifying final win over Brisbane went some way towards rebuilding respect for the club, especially after Mills suffered an ACL injury in the first quarter.

Sustained by the grit displayed against the back-to-back reigning premiers, Rampe was given the nod by Mills, coach Dean Cox and club leaders.

The former Swans co-captain is chasing his maiden premiership after playing in four grand final defeats (2014, 2016, 2022 and 2024).

"It's a thrill. It's a privilege. And yeah, it's a little bit bittersweet," Rampe said on Monday.

"The overwhelming emotion is probably just gratitude to be back here.

"Probably a month ago, we weren't sure what was going to happen with the team and with the club and with the players.

"To be here and challenging in a prelim is just something, particularly being at the back end of my career, I'm really grateful for."

Callum Mills may miss all of the 2027 season, or at least a sizable portion of it. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Rampe's return to captaincy comes after being re-drafted as a rookie by the Swans with fellow defender Jake Lloyd at the end of last year.

While Lloyd has signed on for a 15th season, neither Rampe nor the Swans have made a call on whether he will continue next year.

But the door is open, with defender Mills facing the possibility of missing the entire 2027 season.

"I haven't had a chance to think about that. I don't think it [being captain] does much," Rampe said.

"We'll wait and see. I'm just happy to be where I am at the moment and to have that little bit of hope and belief is, I feel, a real luxury."

Drafted at age 22 in 2013, Rampe was named co-captain with Josh Kennedy and Luke Parker for the 2019 season.

The trio handed the reins to Mills at the end of 2023, but their successor endured a tough 2024 season pockmarked by injury.

Mills was restricted to seven games, hurting his shoulder in a "Mad Monday" wrestling contest with a teammate before being ruled out of finals.

Cox's selection conundrum for Friday's clash is further complicated, with key forward Joel Amartey (Achilles) and winger Justin McInerney (hamstring) near full fitness.

Rampe said the Swans were playing the cards they were dealt.

"You've got one or two ways you can go in these circumstances," Rampe said.

"You can get the 'poor me' and feel sorry for yourself, or you can do something about it."

AAP

World.title: HYROX Beijing sparks backlash after Aussie athlete soils herself mid-race
World.content:
The organisers of a viral sporting event in Beijing have faced backlash and criticism after an Australian woman was allowed to continue competing after soiling herself.

Athlete Joanna Wietrzyk was participating in the global indoor fitness race HYROX in the Chinese capital at the weekend when she suffered a bout of fecal incontinence.

Wietrzyk was allowed to finish the course and won her event, with videos and photos posted online showing her continuing through demanding exercises and using communal equipment while visibly soiled.

The incident has gone viral on Chinese social media and sparked debate about HYROX's health and safety standards, as well as athlete responsibility.

"She's so selfish — she kept running the whole way even though she had diarrhoea," one user on Weibo questioned. "What about the runners behind her?"

Another wrote: "The host is ultimately unprofessional!"

On Weibo, the hashtag #Hyrox incontinence female competitor has not been punished# has more than 27 million views.

HYROX is a global fitness challenge in which participants race to complete often gruelling stations, including sandbag lunges, burpees, sled pushes and rowing.

An article on the Beijing incident was the most-viewed story on Chinese state media website, the Global Times, on Monday.

Joanna Wietrzyk (middle in black top) is an elite HYROX athlete who holds the Women's Solo Pro world record. (Instagram: joannawietrzyk)

In a statement, HYROX China said the area was decontaminated after the race had finished.

"After the incident, the organising committee immediately closed off and isolated the affected area and track, and completed comprehensive disinfection," organisers said.

"Relevant equipment was removed from the venue, and waste was disposed of in accordance with municipal waste-management standards."

The organisers also said they would replace flooring at the venue to protect future athlete health.

HYROX World also issued a statement addressing the incident.

"HYROX has clear bio-contaminant and medical procedures in place," the statement said.

"In this instance, an unforeseen situation arose in which protocols designed for elite competition and mass participation became blurred, creating ambiguity in how they were applied and understood."

The incident went viral on Chinese social media at the weekend and triggered strong backlash to the organisers. (Weibo, RedNote and Douyin)

But social media users and other athletes at the event have attacked the response and questioned why Wietrzyk was allowed to finish the race, potentially risking the health and safety of other competitors.

"For people who were exposed to that situation, there could be genuine physical and psychological consequences," one competitor named johopalooza posted on Instagram.

"I paid HYROX to provide a professionally organised and safe event. So while I understand the athlete perspective, ultimately my contract and expectation is with HYROX.

"Protecting athletes is important, but showing the wider community that HYROX takes responsibility when its own procedures fail is just as important."

Loading Instagram content

'Organisers should assess the risk'

HYROX has also been accused of double standards over its hygiene rules, which punish athletes with time penalties if they litter on the course, spit or clear their nose onto the floor.

HYROX has been contacted for comment.

Wietrzyk, who is a HYROX world-record holder, was invited to compete at the Beijing event.

She has been contacted for comment.

Li Hongxin, an associate professor of sports management at China's Zhengzhou University of Light Industry, said the athlete should not be criticised or judged for experiencing a physiological problem.

"I think her determination and sportsmanship are very understandable," he said.

But he said the incident raised questions about the responsibility of event organisers.

"Organisers should assess whether such a situation could affect the health or wellbeing of other competitors," he said.

Dr Li said this was particularly important because HYROX was an indoor event.

"Take a marathon as an example. If a competitor is menstruating, organisers would generally respect their decision to continue because a marathon is an outdoor event," he said.

"They don't share equipment with other competitors, so it generally doesn't pose a public safety concern.

"But HYROX is an indoor event, where competitors share equipment. In that situation, I think the organisers should have staff step in and adjust the event, or take appropriate emergency measures."

World.title: 'Thinking about my ute': How 12yo passed time on 16-day walk to meet PM
World.content:
Twelve-year-old Dusty Langby has today made it to Canberra, completing a 500-kilometre, 16-day walk from his hometown in western New South Wales and raising more than $400,000 to deliver paediatric care to bush communities.

To top off the long journey, Dusty has a meeting locked in with the prime minister to discuss that same topic.

"When we were walking to Canberra today, we saw there were flags at the top of parliament," Dusty told 666 Canberra.

" And we all nearly started crying because we knew we were nearly there. "

Supporters line the path on day one, as the crew make their way to Trangie from Warren, NSW. (Supplied)

The trek began in Dusty's hometown, Warren in NSW, on August 30, his crew comprising his mum Sarah, local nurse Christine Letton, Little Wings nurse Nichole Callan, and Little Wings chief executive Clare Pearson.

The charity Little Wings provides free flights for children who are seriously ill, or who need specialist care in rural and regional NSW, ACT and QLD.

Both Dusty and his brother have flown from Warren to Sydney with Little Wings for specialist medical appointments.

"It's just such an amazing cause," Dusty said, wanting more children to be able to access the service.

Dusty said he wanted more children to access the services of Little Wings charity. (Supplied)

"The pilots and the volunteers are such kind people, and they all are just really kind, and I wanted to help," he said.

On his agenda for his appointment with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Dusty said, was asking the PM to match every dollar he's raised for the charity.

In total, he raised $423,000, which he said was "going to change heaps of rural family's lives" and "just help more kids".

Getting used to walking

For Dusty, committing to the mission meant slowing down and finding a hobby in walking.

"I don't really walk, I normally run. So it took me a long time to get used to walking, not running," he said.

At some stages, Dusty thought about his ute to pass the time. (Supplied)

That involved training since January on walks which overall ate through four pairs of shoes, he recalled.

Over the course of the trip, with each day ranging from a 19 to a 55 kilometre-long commute, the team's energy levels ebbed and flowed.

"At the start we were just chatting all the way, we weren't listening to music, we were just chatting away," he said.

The team set out on August 30, from Warren to Canberra. (ABC News)

"I had a couple of my friends join me, and we were chatting. I think it was the third day where we started to walk in silence," he said.

" Then we started playing music and we started to get in the groove. "

The family will go camping to 'decompress' and take in Dusty's achievement. (Supplied)

Sometimes he passed the time by planning upgrades to his 1999 Toyota Hilux ute.

"My pop has some lights I'm going to put on the ute, so I was just thinking about that: 'hm, how can I fix my ute', so I might sell some of my stuff in my bedroom and upgrade my ute, like, fix it," he said.

On one day, they felt a "little sprinkle" of rain and rushed to get their their gear on.

"We put all of our wet weather gear on, because we thought it was going to pour down with rain. 10 minutes later [or] five minutes later, it stopped and we were just wet as," he said.

"Every day has been different," his mum Sarah adds.

Dusty and his mum Sarah say each day varied from the next as they walked from town to town towards Canberra. (ABC News: Lish Fejer)

"But all rewarding in itself, each day and every community we enter just welcomed us so gracefully and so humbling, and we are just amazed."

Ms Langby said they had many supporters cheering them on, and offering them food at each leg.

She gave shout-outs to the people, pubs and inns of Yass, Murrumbateman, Parkes, and the Lake Cargelligo school which delivered the crew a Woolworths order.

"There's just so many we can't even [thank them enough], and express our gratitude for feeding us beautiful and nutritious food for the trip," Ms Langby said.

Family time to 'decompress'

Now in Canberra, Dusty said his feet have been spared from blisters and he was feeling "really good" after the 16 day mission.

Loading...

"But on the other hand, my mum and the rest of the team are not going so well," he added.

The family will go camping together, Ms Langby said, to take in Dusty's huge feat.

"We're going to decompress, just have a bit of time with Dad, my other son Angus, just being on the river fishing, motorbike riding, and just enjoy our company and reflect on what we've just achieved."

World.title: A cure for loneliness? Hayes Theatre backs the power of live performance as new season launches
World.content:
CultureTheatreStage shows A cure for loneliness? Hayes Theatre backs the power of live performance as new season launches Lenny Ann Low September 14, 2026 — 9:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“I’ve just realised,” says Victoria Falconer, co-artistic director, with Richard Carroll, of Hayes Theatre Co. “People are talking about the loneliness epidemic and this is a cure.” “You want connection? You want humans? Come to the theatre. We can give you that. It’s here. Why am I not yelling about this more?” Joel Granger in his Phar Lap costume, with Hayes artistic directors Richard Carroll and Victoria Falconer. Sitthixay Ditthavong Launching Hayes Theatre Co’s 2027 season, their final one as co-artistic directors, Falconer and Carroll have many thoughts about the power of theatre. As the arts industry grapples with the cost-of-living crisis, including recently curtailed seasons of several high-profile Australian musical theatre productions, new and original stage work remains vital. “In the hope for humanity, in the hope for learning, in the hope of connection,” Falconer says. “All of that is why we make art in the first place.”



Falconer says parts of the sector, including financial support and opportunities for artists, have been broken for some time. But she sees hope. “People have been struggling for ages,” she says. “People from non-privileged backgrounds find it very hard to get into the arts. That should have been the canary in the coal mine, always, but it’s not. Big things need to change. “But I feel that is coming. Whether that’s the government finally giving artists a living wage, or from something more grassroots. That’s where Hayes came from, a bunch of indie producers with no money persuading the council to give them a building and to put some shows in it. “That can never die. In the darkest times, for hundreds of years, people are drawn to theatre. Why would we be any different?” The 2027 Hayes season will be Richard Carroll and Victoria Falconer’s last as co-artistic directors. Sitthixay Ditthavong



Small but mighty, Hayes Theatre Co is known for a stream of successful new and reimagined musical theatre works and next year some of its shows will venture beyond the company’s Potts Point base. Under the banner Hayes in New Places, the soldout 2025 hit Phar Lap: The Electro-Swing Musical returns for an expanded production at Carriageworks and a multicity tour, including a Melbourne Theatre Company season. In October, Mack the Knife, a new work by Falconer and Carroll, transforms the Foundry Theatre inside Sydney Lyric into a multiroom, immersive rock-cabaret musical based on The Beggar’s Opera by John Gay and The Threepenny Opera by Bertolt Brecht and Kurt Weill. Carroll says Hayes Theatre Co’s Potts Point home remains integral to its identity but sharing work with wider audiences, in Sydney and beyond, has been a longtime aim. “This season reflects the journey that we want to be taking Hayes on,” he says. “It is a massive thing for us to be transferring and touring Phar Lap, a new Australian work that’s such a Hayes show in terms of its invention and being silly, funny but also weirdly moving. “And Mack the Knife, it’s important for us to make clear that although it’s based on The Threepenny Opera, it’s a whole new script with a new story and some different songs. It’s an original work with the first section a fully immersive [experience], where people will be making their own way through different spaces, before the show itself.”



Joel Granger as Phar Lap, which is showing at Carriageworks next month before heading out on the road. Sitthixay Ditthavong The 2027 season also features new productions of the musical farce Lucky Stiff, folk epic Swept Away and Pulitzer Prize and three-time Tony Award-winning rock musical Next to Normal, an exploration of family and illness, loss and grief. And then there’s a world premiere, Peter Allen: Not the Boy Next Door, a work honouring the acclaimed Australian singer-songwriter’s legacy and songs. “It’s a new cabaret-concert celebration similar to Barbra, this year’s smash sellout Hayes hit,” Falconer says. “It’s high time we celebrated such an influential person across musical theatre and cabaret.” Opera fans are catered for with director Matthew Barclay’s Bridgerton-style, reimagining of Mozart’s Così fan tutte: School for Lovers, before Sydney Theatre Award-winner Cameron Mitchell delivers coming-of-age sci-fi satire Be More Chill and Rachael Beck (Cluedo, Beauty and the Beast) stars in the Australian premiere of Flowers for Mrs Harris, based on the Paul Gallico novel which also inspired the 2022 feature film Mrs. Harris Goes To Paris.



House of Rot, starring Paul Capsis and Adam Noviello, returns as does the Festival of New Work, extended to three weeks, and the Winter Cabaret Festival now called Flare: Winter Cabaret Festival. Related Article Stage shows ‘A really stupid and fun idea’: There’s a Phar Lap musical, and it’s not horsing around “We ask our audiences what they love about Hayes and they always say, ‘I see things here that I’ve never seen before’,” Carroll says. “Being able to surprise, that’s something we don’t take for granted.” Falconer agrees. “People really just want to come to a space and watch another human do some stuff,” she says. “And the more thrilling, the more inventive, the more skilful that is, the better.”

World.title: No taffy for Albo
World.content:
In reflecting on then-transport minister Anthony Albanese’s gaffe in quoting a fictional character in a 2012 speech to the National Press Club – US president Andrew Shepherd, played by Michael Douglas in the movie The American President – Philip Cooney of Wentworth Falls wonders, “Which other fictional presidents and PMs might do well in today’s opinion polls?” For the record, Albo escaped censure from then-prime minister Julia Gillard because she loves Douglas and “he’s married to a Welsh woman”.

Janice Creenaune of Austinmer has more on the curbside nature break (C8): “While living in Oxfordshire, we had to drive the A34 north to school in Kidlington to the west of Oxford. Accidents were common and the two lanes were often blocked for sometimes four to six hours, depending on circumstances. Men found relieving themselves fairly easy. For women, not so much. I was advised that it was acceptable to open both car doors on one side and pee between them. Leaving the car to go elsewhere was not an option, but I did wonder about the MGs that were still very popular and once made in Abingdon-on-Thames where we lived.”

Granny wished she’d heard this piece of advice from David Prest of Thrumster a number of decades earlier: “My dad told me never to put a tyre valve cap in my mouth while inflating a tyre as you never knew if a dog (or a person) had peed on the tyre. ‘Always put it on the ground,’ he said.”

“Rumour has it that a prototype of a coffin (C8) made from toadstools was rejected because it was too small and could not cater for larger people,” reports Paul Taylor of Winston Hills. “Evidently, there was not mushroom inside.”

With golf cart-chasing US political aide, Natalie Harp, having a moment in the news, Kevin Hunt of Kenthurst notes that “the Daily Mail reports that Melania Trump’s ‘top spokesman’, Marc Beckman, in an interview with media host Stella Inger Escobedo, complained that the liberal press was obsessed with the first lady’s private life, as well as the ‘hardworking, very talented, very intelligent’ close aide to the president, aka ‘the human printer’. ‘The press,’ Beckman said, ‘just keep harping on with these subjects.’ If the pun was intended, it was quite a good one.”

World.title: ‘Not eliciting that duty of care’: AFLW player hit with three-game ban for jaw-breaking bump
World.content:
A Port Adelaide defender has been whacked with a hefty three-game ban over a head-high bump described by one expert as “probably one of the worst bumps I’ve seen” in women’s footy.

The incident in Saturday’s game between Melbourne and Port at Casey Fields left Melbourne defender Eliza McNamara needing surgery on a broken jaw.

Port player Ella Heads caught her opponent high early in the last quarter of Melbourne’s 51-point win. McNamara left the field immediately and was taken to hospital.

The front-on hit was deemed by the AFLW match review process to be careless conduct, high contact and severe impact, leading to the three-game suspension.

World.title: Parents of student killed in mistaken identity murder face ‘heartbreaking’ future
World.content:
Breaking NationalNSWCrime Parents of student killed in mistaken identity murder face ‘heartbreaking’ future Daniel Lo Surdo September 14, 2026 — 8:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The mother of the star Sydney university student shot dead in a case of mistaken identity has recalled the moment she held her “beautiful” son in her arms as he took his final breath. Marco Tapia, 23, was killed in bed at his Glen Alpine residence in the early hours of September 1 after a group of assailants stormed his family home and sprayed bullets at him. It would become the first of three underworld shootings in Sydney’s escalating gangland war. Sergio and Claudia Tapia say “hate came to our house” the night their son was killed. A Current Affair Parents Sergio and Claudia recounted the “nightmare” attack that claimed their son’s life, telling A Current Affair on Monday the violent onslaught happened “so fast”. “I remember him taking his final breath,” Claudia said. “There was hate that came to our house.”



Sergio said the attack had been forever etched in their memories: “It’s amazing I didn’t have a heart attack when that happened … when you close your eyes is when you see everything again and again, and again and again.” Marco’s sister, Cassie, will be without her “big little brother” when she gets married in November. Invitations for her nuptials were due to be sent the day he was killed. Marco Tapia was shot dead while in bed at his family’s Glen Alpine residence on September 1. Sam Mooy “He’s my best friend, and the fact he’s not going to be there as one of the groomsmen is heartbreaking,” she said. “He was just such a warm person.” But the Tapia family has chosen peace over anger, suggesting they could one day forgive the people behind Marco’s death.



“I thought in this situation I would be seeing fire and brimstone and looking for vengeance. Certainly, there’s no anger in our heart. If you have anger, you cannot have peace in your heart,” Sergio said. “Right now we are striving for peace, and forgiveness will come.” The Tapia family have chosen peace over anger following the death of Marco. A Current Affair Tapia was in his third year of a biomedical engineering degree at the University of Technology Sydney, where he had won awards and volunteered for Engineers Without Borders. His only known brush with the law was a minor traffic offence. Tapia’s death was the first of two mistaken identity murders orchestrated by Sydney’s underworld in as many days.



Joshua Macdonald, 40, was shot dead in the doorway of a Merrylands West duplex home one day after Tapia’s murder as he arrived at the home with two children. The owners of the residence, where Macdonald didn’t live, are known to police and are linked to organised crime. Joshua Macdonald was killed in a shooting at Merrylands West on September 2. Nine News The attacks triggered the NSW government’s third significant crackdown on organised crime in two years as it worked to stave off suggestions it had lost control of Sydney’s streets. The reforms, announced by Premier Chris Minns on September 7, promised tighter targeting of offshore kingpins and local middle men orchestrating violent attacks and tougher penalties for teenagers carrying out gang-related shootings and firebombings.



Louis Meehan, a 32-year-old boxing coach linked to the Alameddine crime family, was shot dead in an ambush at a Punchbowl carpark on September 9, two days after the suite of reforms was unveiled. Meehan, who was known to police, was sprayed with gunfire by an assailant who fled in a silver Lexus. Meehan died in the carpark while onlookers prayed for his welfare. Louis Meehan was shot dead in the latest attack linked to Sydney’s gangland violence. Janie Barrett Escalating underworld violence comes as the warring Alameddine crime family and the Coconut Cartel jostle for control of Sydney’s lucrative drug trade. Powerbrokers for both groups are living overseas, where they’re believed to be orchestrating criminal activities away from Australian jurisdiction. World.title: Frank, fearless, but not so free-style? Staff survey changes raise eyebrows
World.content:
NationalQueenslandPublic service Frank, fearless, but not so free-style? Staff survey changes raise eyebrows Matt Dennien September 14, 2026 — 7:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: a Working for Queensland survey prompt, “vacancy management” hits Child Safety, and wage ruling saga lands senior teachers on par with their juniors. It’s everyone’s favourite time of the year. No, not the seasonal change of spring – Working for Queensland survey month! By everyone, of course, we mean those with thoughts about their public sector employment they would maybe only dare lay out in the free-text general feedback box of the anonymised questionnaire. This year, however, it seems there could be a catch. Queensland public service HQ at One William Street. Matt Dennien Word has reached the Circus tent from multiple agencies the no-holds-barred rant box has disappeared from some surveys, or been replaced with a more restrictive prompt for others.



Since landing in inboxes from late August, some eager (only about 20 per cent of the 330,0000-strong workforce filled it out in 2025) and eagle-eyed public servants have clocked the curious changes. But it’s not uniform across the sector, with the separately collected free-text section included at the discretion of each agency and sent directly, unedited, to the boss. We’ve caught whispers some folks receiving surveys have this year found no open feedback section at the end. Other departments we’ve had intel from are said to have replaced the general feedback prompt with one asking what you’d tell someone considering a job there, or what is one thing you would change.



“It’s not as open-ended as it has been in previous years,” a department source said, speaking to us on condition of anonymity for perhaps the obvious reason of not being authorised to do so. Related Article Public service Returning kindness: The volunteers who emotionally rejuvenate Roma Street’s police They noted it seemed to be an attempt to steer staff away from airing more detailed or specific gripes. One former agency chief, also granted anonymity, told us they viewed it as one of the most important parts of the surveys because of the freeing, anonymised nature of the comments. They suggested any removal of or constraining of this would reflect a lack of willingness to “really hear what people think”.



With a couple of weeks left to complete, we imagine more will discover the changes as they open them closer to the due date – a practice Circus members are certainly not immune from on our workplace feedback forms, either. But what to do if you discover you’re cut off from the trauma dump you were hoping to give, or have already been confronted by such an injustice? We’ve got you covered. Fill out the form below (on a non-work device and network) and tell us instead. Drop contact details if you’re willing to talk more, anonymously, of course. We’ll even try and publish what we can in a future segment. Let the frank and fearless feedback flow!



‘Vacancy management’ comes for Child Safety frontline support roles Fresh on the heels of the state’s first credit rating downgrade in almost 20-years, Circus can add a seventh department to its list of those with various efforts in place to squeeze staffing budgets. The latest “vacancy management strategy” word (don’t call it a hiring freeze!) is from over at Belinda Drew’s Department of Families, Seniors, Disability Services and Child Safety. There, the strategy is said to review vacant roles across child safety, disability services and corporate support before they can be filled. Those not deemed “key frontline” require stricter approval. This includes sign-off by a deputy director-general and a documented rationale. So far, so similar to what we’ve heard from widely across the sector.



But the thing that has some child safety staff, and their union (Together), up in arms? What, exactly, is being classified as a frontline role under the exemption list. In particular, the lack of an exemption for administration and business officers in child safety service centres – who keep such centres, which support frontline child protection workers, running. “These roles are critical to frontline child protections, and they should be treated as critical workers when it comes time to fill them,” Together assistant secretary Dee Spink said in a statement. “The department says this isn’t a recruitment freeze, but for some workers it can feel like one.”



Comment has been sought from the department. For what it’s worth, we quizzed independent economist Saul Eslake about this vacancy management approach to belt-tightening while chatting to him on Friday about that credit downgrade. His view? “They’re a lazy way of trying to save money,” Eslake offered. “They’re fairly crude measures and not ones that I would ever support.” Eslake also reckoned the roughly 3 per cent staff expense growth projected from next financial year in Treasurer David Janetzki’s June budget (this year’s is 5.4 per cent) is only possible with a proper freeze on the size of the public service. Either that, or that slim surplus pencilled in for after the 2028 election might end up being kicked down the road – something we’re sure the ratings agencies will be watching closely.





The first band of this classification is available to those with two or more years of satisfactory service as a “senior teacher”. The second, EST 2, can be reached after three years at EST 1. That higher band was created in the 2019 agreement and is not reflected in the award. While EST 1 wages were set to lift through a safety net tied to the state wage case ruling, EST 2 wages were not. Then acting general secretary Brendan Crotty said the union clocked the issue weeks ago, raising it with Sharon Schimming’s apparently unaware department and Minister John-Paul Langbroek. Eventually, a departmental directive was issued to allow EST 2 teachers to get the higher award rate. This temporary fix, however, essentially leaves more senior teachers on an equal pay rate to those on a lower band until the difference can be sorted via the broader ongoing arbitration process. Yikes.



The issue has, as you might imagine, gone down like a tonne of lead pencils for teachers – some of whom have taken to the union’s social media comment sections to give an unfavourable report card of even some of the union process. Queensland teachers gather in Queen’s Park during the second of two Queensland Teachers’ Union strike days last year. Polina Levina/Getty Images “The QTU acknowledges that some members at EST 2 level may understandably feel frustrated that, for the time being, this means being paid at the same, if higher, rate as EST 1,” Crotty wrote to members last week. That “time being” is likely to still be some time yet, given arbitration hearings before the Queensland Industrial Relations Commission have now been given a start date of… April 6 next year. Have a curiosity for the Circus tent? Email on m.dennien@nine.com.au. For more security, sing out with a non-work device and network via Signal (mattdennien.15 or here) and mattdennien@protonmail.com. World.title: Transport minister accepts lifetime membership to Qantas platinum
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Transport minister accepts lifetime membership to Qantas platinum Nick Newling September 14, 2026 — 7:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Transport Minister Catherine King has accepted a lifetime membership to Qantas’ platinum frequent flyer rewards tier less than two years after MPs ceremonially handed over their membership to the airline’s VIP lounge following public backlash. The minister, whose responsibilities include aviation and the courting of airlines to make use of the new Western Sydney International Airport, quietly updated her register of interests on Monday to reflect the gift she received from the airline. Catherine King at the opening of Western Sydney airport in July. Wolter Peeters The airline’s second-highest tier, behind platinum one, offers free access to first and business class lounges across the globe, additional baggage allowance, priority check-in, boarding and baggage access. It also offers priority upgrades and seat selection. A Qantas frequent flyer would need to accrue 1400 status credits in a year to qualify for the platinum tier. A discount economy ticket between Sydney and Melbourne garners 10 points, meaning a traveller would need to fly between the capitals 140 times to reach the tier.



A lifetime membership to the tier requires 75,000 status credits, or 7500 Sydney to Melbourne flights. In November 2024, a raft of federal MPs including Community Strong Australia representative Allegra Spender quit the VIP lounges of Qantas and Virgin after a furore over flight upgrades and special treatment for politicians. Related Article Exclusive

Immigration Slash the intake: Majority of Australians demand deeper migration cuts The saga began after the publication of an extract of The Chairman’s Lounge by journalist Joe Aston, published in Good Weekend, claimed that Prime Minister Anthony Albanese had received at least 22 free Qantas upgrades over the past decade, and that he had liaised directly with former Qantas chief Alan Joyce over upgrades. Albanese admitted at the time that he spoke to Joyce about two non-commercial trips with Qantas but said these had also included Liberal ministers and media companies. He said he did not ever ask Joyce for an upgrade and his office said this denial meant there were no calls, texts, emails or other communications with the former Qantas boss.



In 2023, King was thrown into the spotlight for denying a Qatar Airways bid to double their flights into Australia, a move that many in the industry said would have lowered ballooning travel costs for Australians. The minister updated her register of interests with the alteration added under the title “gifts”. The membership came with a travel wallet and bag tag. King misspelled the tier’s name in her declaration, writing that she was a member of the “Platnium” tier. King’s office was contacted for comment. A spokeswoman for King told the Australian Financial Review – who first reported the gift – that the minister received the status by virtue of the extent to which she has travelled with the airline.
