World.title: ‘Moving at light speed’: Plug-in solar and batteries are coming to Australia
World.content:
EnvironmentSustainabilityRenewables ‘Moving at light speed’: Plug-in solar and batteries are coming to Australia Caitlin Fitzsimmons September 14, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Apartment residents could soon be able to buy plug-in batteries to store cheap or free power produced during the day to use in the evening even without solar panels. The plug-in home batteries for energy storage are part of reforms that would also usher in portable panels, broadening access to solar power to renters and apartment dwellers. Portable solar panels on apartment balconies in Freiburg, Germany. Alamy Stock Photo Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen said all states and territories had agreed to look at how plug-in solar and batteries could work in Australia to give apartment dwellers and renters more control over their bills. “A third of Australians have a solar panel on their roofs. It’s more popular than the backyard pool,” Bowen said.



“Now we’re taking the next step, by looking at how even more Australians can take advantage of free, abundant sunshine to cut their energy bills - even if they don’t have a roof.” As reported previously by this masthead, plug-in solar allows consumers to buy panels for about $500 each that hang in an outdoor area and plug into a socket to power any appliances, charge a battery or feed into the grid. The device does not need to be installed by an electrician and the owner can take it with them when they move home. The technology is widely used in Germany; increasing in other European countries such as France and Spain and many US states; and was recently legalised in Britain. It is currently unlawful in Australia, though the market is growing anyway and a number of online retailers already sell systems here. Tyler Peck, 24, rents an older home in Melbourne and could use plug-in solar to help lower his heating bills in winter. Justin McManus The federal and state climate change and energy ministers agreed on Friday to progress legal and regulatory reforms that would enable widespread adoption in Australia, with a key deadline by mid next year. New Zealand is separately working to enable plug-in solar.



Glen Morris, director of Smart Energy Lab and a member of the Solar Standards Committee, said Australia had been lagging but was now moving at light speed given it usually took years to develop new standards. “It went from zero to 100 in one day.” Morris said. “I was prepared for a very long campaign to get it through … but obviously, when there’s political will, things can move a bit faster.” The main change required was an amendment to the Australian standard for inverter systems, which could be fast-tracked by copying international standards, he said. “The products designed for the European market already have the safety features we like – it’s important that we don’t turn it into a very complex process, so that it can be done swiftly. “To some extent, the horse has bolted because people can buy these and the only thing stopping them plugging it in is that it’s illegal. But it’s not very obvious – certainly if you don’t have solar panels and just have a plug-in battery system, no one would know.”



Francis Vierboom, chief executive of Rewiring Australia, said the real game changer for apartment dwellers could be “suitcase batteries” because the panels required outside space but the batteries could be deployed separately to solar. Related Article Renewables Push to deliver solar to 2.5m apartment dwellers gains traction The plug-in panel technology is often called “balcony solar”, and panels hanging vertically off balcony railings are a common sight in Germany. However, Vierboom said the panels would be most useful in backyards in the Australian context. “The sun is a lot lower in the sky in northern Europe, and solar that’s actually on sideways on your balcony is going to generate more energy than it does in Australia, where the sun is a bit higher in the sky because we are closer to the equator,” Vierboom said. The batteries would charge up from the cheap daytime energy available on the grid, including three hours of free power available in the middle of the day on some plans, and then a household could use that energy in the evening peak.



“The less we all lean on the grid in that evening peak, the cheaper the energy system stays, and the more we can be using solar energy instead of fossil fuel generators in the evening,” Vierboom said. Related Article Electricity Bruce’s home was ‘like a tent’. A new energy rating is guiding upgrades Governments may need to look at strata law and tenancy law to consider whether owners’ corporations, strata managers and landlords could block plug-in solar and under what circumstances. Solar Citizens, an advocacy group for consumers to benefit from renewable energy, has been lobbying Bowen to push for plug-in solar. Chief executive Heidi Lee Douglas said the group would push for a clear timeline with a target deadline of July 1 next year, and to ensure renters, apartment dwellers and low-income households could benefit. “Renters shouldn’t be locked out of cheaper, cleaner energy simply because they don’t own the roof over their heads,” Douglas said. “They should have a fair right to request solar, batteries and energy-efficiency upgrades, and landlords shouldn’t be able to unreasonably say no.”



Tyler Peck, 24, rents an older home with his partner in Preston in Melbourne. While the home is affordable and close to transport, it is poorly insulated and the heating bills are high. Peck would like to have plug-in solar set up on his porch, which gets good sunlight, and says he is equally motivated by the electricity savings and the environmental benefit. But he would definitely wait for the official green light, rather than buying any of the systems already on the market. “With all the [public service announcements] that went out a while ago about dodgy scooter or e-bike batteries being fire hazards, I’m just very cautious about anything that isn’t official,” Peck said. Return on investment An 800-watt system with two panels would cost $450 to $850 based on German prices, which gives it a two to four-year payback with a 25-year warranty, Morris, of Smart Energy Lab, said. Adding a 1.6-2Kwh battery would be a combined cost of $1100-$1300, with a five to eight-year payback and batteries rated for 15 to 20 years of daily use.



Morris said Australian prices would probably start higher, and eventually fall. Bowen said on Saturday that if plug-in solar met safety standards, it would be automatically covered by the government’s existing rebates, the Cheaper Home Battery policy and the Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme for solar panels, adding “but we’ll work those details through”. However, Vierboom said the government should consider a change to legislation, since the Cheaper Home Batteries program does not cover small batteries, or the installation of batteries without solar, and the solar panel rebates required installation by an accredited electrician. Morris said he had been testing a small panel tilted 75 degrees from horizontal – only 15 degrees off being vertical – similar to how it was used in Germany. But to get a decent return on investment in Australia, it should be tilted more horizontally – from 37 degrees in Melbourne to 32 degrees in Queensland, with Sydney in the middle. On a balcony, “it would stick out a bit more, providing a bit more shade for your neighbour below”, Morris said. Other options for apartments



Karin Aubrey will get a shared solar system on the roof of her apartment building in the Sydney beachside suburb of Maroubra in October. The building received a Solar for Apartment Residents grant from the NSW government to reduce the cost, and will use the Allume SolShare 2 technology to fairly split the solar power between apartments. Karin Aubrey is getting shared solar on her Sydney apartment block but supports plug-in solar as an option in the market. Wolter Peeters Aubrey is happy about the panels and the grant, but said it took more than a year of advocacy to get everyone in the owners’ corporation on board given the cost of the panels and electrical rewiring required. She would like to add shared batteries in future, which the Allume technology allows, but in an old building that gets damaged by salt spray, “there are always competing needs”. Aubrey saw plug-in solar in action on her recent trip to visit friends in France and would support it becoming available here because it would allow households to make decisions independently, not just through strata. “They’re having crazy heatwaves [in France], and their apartment buildings are usually quite complicated with who owns them and how big they are, so balcony solar is taking off a little bit there,” Aubrey said.



“I heard it about it there because everyone’s trying to get air conditioning for the first time, and the load is just massive. It’s a good idea.” Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: We looked at staff salaries at 60 private schools. These pay the most
World.content:
NationalNSWEducation We looked at staff salaries at 60 private schools. These pay the most Christopher Harris September 14, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One Sydney private school will pay its most experienced teachers more than $160,000 next year, as principals warn a failure to attract high-quality talent to the profession is hindering students’ academic progress. Catholic Secondary Principals Australia said the quality of Australia’s teaching workforce, along with its lack of specialised mathematics teachers, is the “single most significant in-school factor impacting student progression and achievement”. The Sydney Church of England Grammar School in North Sydney will pay its most experienced teachers at least $160,000 next year. “Australia faces an acute crisis in attracting and retaining high-calibre educators, a challenge magnified exponentially in rural and remote locations. The shortage is particularly severe in specialised fields,” they said. Its former president Dr Stephen Kennaugh and executive officer Michael Egan made the remarks in a submission to a parliamentary inquiry probing declining academic achievement earlier this year.



“There is an urgent need to lift teacher qualifications, especially in pure mathematics and secondary sciences, where out-of-field teaching has become a necessity rather than an exception.” The latest global report card, released last week, showed Australia’s academic results have continued their long-term slide in English and mathematics, while science results are stagnant. The quality of the teacher in front of students makes the single most significant difference to academic outcomes, research shows. Last year, almost 500 students across the country were admitted to teaching degrees despite having an Australian Tertiary Admission score less than 50. The latest national figures show technology, arts, and mathematics subjects had the highest rates of out-of-field teaching. One-third of subjects were taught by a teacher with no relevant tertiary study in the subject, according to the Australian Institute for Teaching and School Leadership.



Separate data collected by the OECD’s Program for Student Assessment found in 2025 that 49 per cent of students in Australia were in schools whose principals reported that instruction was hindered, at least to some extent, by a perceived lack of teaching staff. The OECD average was 39 per cent. Shore School in North Sydney is set to pay its most experienced teachers $162,236 next year, with a spokeswoman noting the school was committed to attracting and retaining outstanding teachers who deliver exceptional educational outcomes. St Joseph’s Hunters Hill will pay its teachers $150,000 next year. Nikki Short St Joseph’s in Hunters Hill will pay teachers $150,000, according to its latest enterprise agreement, while Mount St Benedict College and Brigidine in St Ives will pay the most experienced teachers $145,000. By comparison, a public school teacher on step 7 will earn $133,422 next year. Most of Sydney’s high-fee independent schools are covered by a single enterprise agreement, but many institutions pay a premium, including at PLC Sydney, where staff are paid 5 per cent on top of the top band salary of $138,329 next year.



“This places PLC Sydney above all of our neighbouring competitor schools in terms of remuneration for staff,” principal Paul Burgis said. Separate data from the government’s Workplace Gender Equality Agency reveals average staff remuneration (which includes all employees, not just teachers) for several private schools hit $140,000 in the 2024-25 financial year, the latest data available. It is different from teacher wage data. The top-paying school on that metric was Sydney Grammar, where the average full-time employee was paid $178,000 in that financial year, up from $174,000 the year before. Its headmaster, Stuart McPherson, said the school wanted “to remunerate our teachers well for what they do”.



“I would also say that teachers are attracted to Grammar because they like teaching the kind of boys we have here – curious, hard-working, polite and well-behaved, interested in things beyond the curriculum – and because there’s a dynamic culture of learning and teaching community amongst the staff at this school.” The next top-paying schools, on an average employee basis, were Ascham, Waverley and Our Lady of Mercy College, each paying at least $144,000 that financial year. Some schools warn to approach the data with caution because it averages the salaries of all employees, including groundskeepers and executive staff, while some schools employ recent graduates as tutors on a casual basis, which can also skew the total employee remuneration figures. Association of Independent Schools of NSW chief executive Margery Evans. Rhett Wyman Independent Schools NSW chief executive Margery Evans said schools may use a range of strategies to attract and retain staff, including leadership pathways, flexible work arrangements and remuneration incentives.



“The real issue is Australia’s teacher workforce challenge. Every school sector is competing for specialist teachers. The focus should be on growing the number of high-quality teachers entering the profession and supporting them to stay.” The number of students completing initial teacher education degrees increased by 3.7 per cent, with 15,903 new teachers eligible to enter the workforce in 2025, according to the latest government graduate data. What schools said about staff salaries Stuart McPherson, headmaster, Sydney Grammar School: “I wouldn’t want to comment on Grammar’s salary scale other than to say that we want to remunerate our teachers well for what they do.” Shore spokesperson: “Teacher remuneration is one element of a comprehensive employment offering that reflects the wide range of responsibilities undertaken by staff, including teaching, student wellbeing, pastoral care, co-curricular programs and leadership responsibilities.” Brother Steve Hogan, principal, Oakhill College: “The Workplace Gender Equality Agency figure is an average remuneration amount across the workforce and shouldn’t be interpreted as the salary of a classroom teacher. This includes co-ordinator allowances, which are clearly stipulated within the Agreement and paid to co-ordinators on top of a teacher’s base salary.” Pittwater House principal Dr Steven Middleton: “In my three decades of experience as a teacher and leader in independent schools, I believe good teachers and other school professional staff aren’t necessarily making employment decisions solely on the highest salary available. “We keep hearing about a teacher shortage, but we believe we are an employer of choice, receiving many applications for advertised roles and also expressions of interest from Sydney, interstate and regional NSW, as well as a number of international teachers seeking to relocate from the UK, Canada, New Zealand and South Africa.” Rosebank College principal Iris Nastasi: “Please be aware in the instance of Rosebank, our data would also comprise coaches and tutors; these are recent school graduates.” Matt Macoustra, head of school, Newcastle Grammar: “As is the case across the entire education sector, there can be particular subject areas or specialist roles where schools need to work harder to find the right candidate. However, we continue to attract high-quality applicants who are drawn not only by remuneration and conditions, but by the opportunity to work in a supportive professional environment and make a meaningful contribution to the education and development of young people.” Presbyterian Ladies’ College Sydney principal Dr Paul Burgis: “PLC Sydney pays the CMEA, which is 3 per cent above the public school award. We then add a further 5 per cent above this. This places PLC Sydney above all of our neighbouring competitor schools in terms of remuneration for staff. “Further, PLC Sydney retains staff exceptionally well, as indicated by the number who qualify for long service leave each year.” Barker College spokesperson: “Barker College was recognised in The Educator’s 5-Star Employers of Choice 2026, an acknowledgement of excellence in workplace culture, employee satisfaction and people-first leadership across the Australian education sector. Our staff benefit from a modern approach to recruitment and retention which includes competitive remuneration and access to a vibrant and purpose-driven workplace.” Hunter Valley Grammar School principal Rebecca Butterworth: “Salaries are one component of what makes a school a great place to work. Equally important are opportunities for professional growth, the ability to retain excellent teachers, and a positive and supportive workplace culture. At HVGS, we are privileged to have highly accomplished educators teaching our students and a strong culture of care and belonging for staff and students.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: A cure for loneliness? Hayes Theatre backs the power of live performance as new season launches
World.content:
CultureTheatreStage shows A cure for loneliness? Hayes Theatre backs the power of live performance as new season launches Lenny Ann Low September 14, 2026 — 9:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“I’ve just realised,” says Victoria Falconer, co-artistic director, with Richard Carroll, of Hayes Theatre Co. “People are talking about the loneliness epidemic and this is a cure.” “You want connection? You want humans? Come to the theatre. We can give you that. It’s here. Why am I not yelling about this more?” Joel Granger in his Phar Lap costume, with Hayes artistic directors Richard Carroll and Victoria Falconer. Sitthixay Ditthavong Launching Hayes Theatre Co’s 2027 season, their final one as co-artistic directors, Falconer and Carroll have many thoughts about the power of theatre. As the arts industry grapples with the cost-of-living crisis, including recently curtailed seasons of several high-profile Australian musical theatre productions, new and original stage work remains vital. “In the hope for humanity, in the hope for learning, in the hope of connection,” Falconer says. “All of that is why we make art in the first place.”



Falconer says parts of the sector, including financial support and opportunities for artists, have been broken for some time. But she sees hope. “People have been struggling for ages,” she says. “People from non-privileged backgrounds find it very hard to get into the arts. That should have been the canary in the coal mine, always, but it’s not. Big things need to change. “But I feel that is coming. Whether that’s the government finally giving artists a living wage, or from something more grassroots. That’s where Hayes came from, a bunch of indie producers with no money persuading the council to give them a building and to put some shows in it. “That can never die. In the darkest times, for hundreds of years, people are drawn to theatre. Why would we be any different?” The 2027 Hayes season will be Richard Carroll and Victoria Falconer’s last as co-artistic directors. Sitthixay Ditthavong



Small but mighty, Hayes Theatre Co is known for a stream of successful new and reimagined musical theatre works and next year some of its shows will venture beyond the company’s Potts Point base. Under the banner Hayes in New Places, the soldout 2025 hit Phar Lap: The Electro-Swing Musical returns for an expanded production at Carriageworks and a multicity tour, including a Melbourne Theatre Company season. In October, Mack the Knife, a new work by Falconer and Carroll, transforms the Foundry Theatre inside Sydney Lyric into a multiroom, immersive rock-cabaret musical based on The Beggar’s Opera by John Gay and The Threepenny Opera by Bertolt Brecht and Kurt Weill. Carroll says Hayes Theatre Co’s Potts Point home remains integral to its identity but sharing work with wider audiences, in Sydney and beyond, has been a longtime aim. “This season reflects the journey that we want to be taking Hayes on,” he says. “It is a massive thing for us to be transferring and touring Phar Lap, a new Australian work that’s such a Hayes show in terms of its invention and being silly, funny but also weirdly moving. “And Mack the Knife, it’s important for us to make clear that although it’s based on The Threepenny Opera, it’s a whole new script with a new story and some different songs. It’s an original work with the first section a fully immersive [experience], where people will be making their own way through different spaces, before the show itself.”



Joel Granger as Phar Lap, which is showing at Carriageworks next month before heading out on the road. Sitthixay Ditthavong The 2027 season also features new productions of the musical farce Lucky Stiff, folk epic Swept Away and Pulitzer Prize and three-time Tony Award-winning rock musical Next to Normal, an exploration of family and illness, loss and grief. And then there’s a world premiere, Peter Allen: Not the Boy Next Door, a work honouring the acclaimed Australian singer-songwriter’s legacy and songs. “It’s a new cabaret-concert celebration similar to Barbra, this year’s smash sellout Hayes hit,” Falconer says. “It’s high time we celebrated such an influential person across musical theatre and cabaret.” Opera fans are catered for with director Matthew Barclay’s Bridgerton-style, reimagining of Mozart’s Così fan tutte: School for Lovers, before Sydney Theatre Award-winner Cameron Mitchell delivers coming-of-age sci-fi satire Be More Chill and Rachael Beck (Cluedo, Beauty and the Beast) stars in the Australian premiere of Flowers for Mrs Harris, based on the Paul Gallico novel which also inspired the 2022 feature film Mrs. Harris Goes To Paris.



House of Rot, starring Paul Capsis and Adam Noviello, returns as does the Festival of New Work, extended to three weeks, and the Winter Cabaret Festival now called Flare: Winter Cabaret Festival. Related Article Stage shows ‘A really stupid and fun idea’: There’s a Phar Lap musical, and it’s not horsing around “We ask our audiences what they love about Hayes and they always say, ‘I see things here that I’ve never seen before’,” Carroll says. “Being able to surprise, that’s something we don’t take for granted.” Falconer agrees. “People really just want to come to a space and watch another human do some stuff,” she says. “And the more thrilling, the more inventive, the more skilful that is, the better.”

World.title: No taffy for Albo
World.content:
In reflecting on then-transport minister Anthony Albanese’s gaffe in quoting a fictional character in a 2012 speech to the National Press Club – US president Andrew Shepherd, played by Michael Douglas in the movie The American President – Philip Cooney of Wentworth Falls wonders, “Which other fictional presidents and PMs might do well in today’s opinion polls?” For the record, Albo escaped censure from then-prime minister Julia Gillard because she loves Douglas and “he’s married to a Welsh woman”.

Janice Creenaune of Austinmer has more on the curbside nature break (C8): “While living in Oxfordshire, we had to drive the A34 north to school in Kidlington to the west of Oxford. Accidents were common and the two lanes were often blocked for sometimes four to six hours, depending on circumstances. Men found relieving themselves fairly easy. For women, not so much. I was advised that it was acceptable to open both car doors on one side and pee between them. Leaving the car to go elsewhere was not an option, but I did wonder about the MGs that were still very popular and once made in Abingdon-on-Thames where we lived.”

Granny wished she’d heard this piece of advice from David Prest of Thrumster a number of decades earlier: “My dad told me never to put a tyre valve cap in my mouth while inflating a tyre as you never knew if a dog (or a person) had peed on the tyre. ‘Always put it on the ground,’ he said.”

“Rumour has it that a prototype of a coffin (C8) made from toadstools was rejected because it was too small and could not cater for larger people,” reports Paul Taylor of Winston Hills. “Evidently, there was not mushroom inside.”

With golf cart-chasing US political aide, Natalie Harp, having a moment in the news, Kevin Hunt of Kenthurst notes that “the Daily Mail reports that Melania Trump’s ‘top spokesman’, Marc Beckman, in an interview with media host Stella Inger Escobedo, complained that the liberal press was obsessed with the first lady’s private life, as well as the ‘hardworking, very talented, very intelligent’ close aide to the president, aka ‘the human printer’. ‘The press,’ Beckman said, ‘just keep harping on with these subjects.’ If the pun was intended, it was quite a good one.”

World.title: ‘Not eliciting that duty of care’: AFLW player hit with three-game ban for jaw-breaking bump
World.content:
A Port Adelaide defender has been whacked with a hefty three-game ban over a head-high bump described by one expert as “probably one of the worst bumps I’ve seen” in women’s footy.

The incident in Saturday’s game between Melbourne and Port at Casey Fields left Melbourne defender Eliza McNamara needing surgery on a broken jaw.

Port player Ella Heads caught her opponent high early in the last quarter of Melbourne’s 51-point win. McNamara left the field immediately and was taken to hospital.

The front-on hit was deemed by the AFLW match review process to be careless conduct, high contact and severe impact, leading to the three-game suspension.

World.title: Parents of student killed in mistaken identity murder face ‘heartbreaking’ future
World.content:
Breaking NationalNSWCrime Parents of student killed in mistaken identity murder face ‘heartbreaking’ future Daniel Lo Surdo September 14, 2026 — 8:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The mother of the star Sydney university student shot dead in a case of mistaken identity has recalled the moment she held her “beautiful” son in her arms as he took his final breath. Marco Tapia, 23, was killed in bed at his Glen Alpine residence in the early hours of September 1 after a group of assailants stormed his family home and sprayed bullets at him. It would become the first of three underworld shootings in Sydney’s escalating gangland war. Sergio and Claudia Tapia say “hate came to our house” the night their son was killed. A Current Affair Parents Sergio and Claudia recounted the “nightmare” attack that claimed their son’s life, telling A Current Affair on Monday the violent onslaught happened “so fast”. “I remember him taking his final breath,” Claudia said. “There was hate that came to our house.”



Sergio said the attack had been forever etched in their memories: “It’s amazing I didn’t have a heart attack when that happened … when you close your eyes is when you see everything again and again, and again and again.” Marco’s sister, Cassie, will be without her “big little brother” when she gets married in November. Invitations for her nuptials were due to be sent the day he was killed. Marco Tapia was shot dead while in bed at his family’s Glen Alpine residence on September 1. Sam Mooy “He’s my best friend, and the fact he’s not going to be there as one of the groomsmen is heartbreaking,” she said. “He was just such a warm person.” But the Tapia family has chosen peace over anger, suggesting they could one day forgive the people behind Marco’s death.



“I thought in this situation I would be seeing fire and brimstone and looking for vengeance. Certainly, there’s no anger in our heart. If you have anger, you cannot have peace in your heart,” Sergio said. “Right now we are striving for peace, and forgiveness will come.” The Tapia family have chosen peace over anger following the death of Marco. A Current Affair Tapia was in his third year of a biomedical engineering degree at the University of Technology Sydney, where he had won awards and volunteered for Engineers Without Borders. His only known brush with the law was a minor traffic offence. Tapia’s death was the first of two mistaken identity murders orchestrated by Sydney’s underworld in as many days.



Joshua Macdonald, 40, was shot dead in the doorway of a Merrylands West duplex home one day after Tapia’s murder as he arrived at the home with two children. The owners of the residence, where Macdonald didn’t live, are known to police and are linked to organised crime. Joshua Macdonald was killed in a shooting at Merrylands West on September 2. Nine News The attacks triggered the NSW government’s third significant crackdown on organised crime in two years as it worked to stave off suggestions it had lost control of Sydney’s streets. The reforms, announced by Premier Chris Minns on September 7, promised tighter targeting of offshore kingpins and local middle men orchestrating violent attacks and tougher penalties for teenagers carrying out gang-related shootings and firebombings.



Louis Meehan, a 32-year-old boxing coach linked to the Alameddine crime family, was shot dead in an ambush at a Punchbowl carpark on September 9, two days after the suite of reforms was unveiled. Meehan, who was known to police, was sprayed with gunfire by an assailant who fled in a silver Lexus. Meehan died in the carpark while onlookers prayed for his welfare. Louis Meehan was shot dead in the latest attack linked to Sydney’s gangland violence. Janie Barrett Escalating underworld violence comes as the warring Alameddine crime family and the Coconut Cartel jostle for control of Sydney’s lucrative drug trade. Powerbrokers for both groups are living overseas, where they’re believed to be orchestrating criminal activities away from Australian jurisdiction. World.title: One Nation limbo: how low can they go?
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters One Nation limbo: how low can they go? September 14, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. POLITICS How abusive of Pauline Hanson to make a personal attack on Anthony Albanese, (″⁣Emotional PM defends late mother from Hanson’s attack”, 14/9). Her comments crossed a line from political debate into malice and shows her true character.

It seems that if she hasn’t got the understanding to strike high, then she strikes low. The personal nature of Hanson’s remark reflects cheap political tactic, and my hope is that voters will walk away from her.

Julie Ottobre, Brunswick East How will Hanson policy affect public housing?

While Pauline Hanson was making her poisonous comments about the prime minister’s mother, she also said that people should only be allowed to live in public housing for a limited period.

Is this a policy statement? Would she evict long-term public housing occupants if she was in power?

Public housing isn’t free housing. Occupants pay rent, and are subject to asset tests. It’s the same as a private rental except the rates are set to enable those who cannot afford alternatives to have a roof over their heads.

Damien Ryan, Berwick



Hanson’s vitriol an acid test

Sean Kelly (″⁣Is Hastie a hero for tackling Hanson? It’s complicated″⁣, 14/9) questions whether Pauline Hanson’s vitriolic attacks on her political opponents will alienate many of those voters who have recently gravitated to her side.

Pollsters have argued that many new One Nation supporters, far from being hard right ideologues, are ordinary decent Australians who have genuine concerns about immigration, cost of living and housing.

If that’s the case, we should expect to see a drop in One Nation support in the face of Hanson’s gratuitous nastiness. It would be the acid test.

Mike Smith, Sandringham So many targets for party’s anger

Anger, personal attacks and bad behaviour appear to be the stock in trade of One Nation. Immigrants, asylum seekers, Muslims are among the targets of anger. Veterans and politicians’ mums suffer ridicule and denigration, and evidently, it’s OK to display public drunkenness and take drugs if you are an MP or plan to become one.

Mike Reece, Doncaster Barnaby Joyce’s changing hue

Of all the politicians in parliament, Barnaby Joyce stands out as one who one would think would discourage family members being brought into any public discussion. There were some who hoped he would raise the standards of One Nation when he joined it. Barnaby, you have morphed from blushing One Nation newbie to a ruddy recalcitrant.

Adrian Tabor, Point Lonsdale Hanson unfit for her role

Apologise? Pauline Hanson should resign in disgrace. She is unfit to be the prime minister and unfit to be in the Australian parliament.

Philip Henseleit, Glenlee Try living on Newstart

I’m with Pauline. It’s a disgrace people live in public housing for decades. I look forward to seeing One Nation policy that ensures Newstart is enough to live on and workers can afford to rent or buy their own homes.

Christine Morris, Wyndham Vale



Hanson’s parliamentary record

I’m continually bemused by Hanson voters who believe this guff about her being an outsider. An ″⁣outsider″⁣ for 30 years? Can anyone tell me what piece of legislation she has shepherded through parliament in this time?

Carmel Boyle, Alfredton More burning issues

I am a few years older than One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, and spent most of my early years sleeping on the front verandah of a rented house in Windsor until 1951 when my parents were allocated a Housing Commission house in Jordanville. For the first time, I occupied a bedroom inside a house at the age of 16.

My father saw overseas service for the majority of the war, but without government housing being built, I am certain that my brothers and I would have been moved from pillar to post. After some years, my parents were able to purchase the home where they lived for the remainder of their lives.

Housing Commission houses saved a housing crisis back in the 1950s. There are more important things for government than chastising people who live in Housing Commission homes all over Australia.

Ken Clarke, Wangaratta THE FORUM End Brethren tax status

The Age is doing its job in covering the secret and effective efforts by the Christian Brethren to disrupt the 2025 elections (“Tail, Film, Heckle,” 14/9).

MP Jerome Laxale has also done a stand-up job of chairing the Parliamentary Joint Standing Committee on Electoral Matters and producing its report. This committee solicited and received many submissions and heard many people testify about the impact of deceptive and aggressive right-wing and neo-Nazi proxy organisations who did not have to reveal their funders or spending.

The government must take action now to cancel any tax benefits to the Brethren, and to change laws relating to proxy organisations. The broader public must also get involved. Democracy and fair elections are precious and worthy of protecting. There are clear examples of what happens when they go unchecked.

Amy Bachrach, McKinnon



Scotch’s privilege

My boys go to a government school on the Bellarine Peninsula. The school runs a breakfast club offering toasties, fruit and milk. This club is open to all, but it exists primarily to ensure that students from struggling families can start the day with a full stomach.

The article about Scotch College, ″⁣Preserving the cardinal thread″⁣ (14/9), describes a different world, divorced from the funding realities faced by most government schools. Scotch buys houses to bulldoze them for a staff car park. It rustles up $60 million to acquire a neighbouring property. School leaders talk of opportunity and possibility.

What goes unsaid is that these opportunities at Scotch and other private schools so often come at the expense of others. A few years ago, I wrote to Scotch College to suggest that the school might show leadership and forgo the millions it receives in federal and state funding. I received a reply, in which I was told that the school had as much right to public funding as any other.

I went to Scotch. The cardinal thread? Spare me.

Seumas Spark, Indented Head Pause AI race

Many technological developments over the past 100 years have provided, as a side effect, an increased possibility of killing living things. Cars, aeroplanes, and many chemicals are examples.

Obviously, developments in armaments are intended to achieve this goal. The atomic, and later hydrogen, bombs were the horrific ultimate achievements that continue to test our full range of human qualities to control them. While the technicalities of these inventions may not have been understood by most people, the negative consequences of their use could be envisioned.

Today, we are in the midst of technological developments in the digital world of which most people have no understanding.

Artificial intelligence, the latest area of innovation, operates in very important spaces impacting on the human condition: the distribution of information, the control of systems, and how we interact with each other.

It also makes huge demands on our most important resources, energy and water.

We need to stop and take a deep breath to learn more about what we are facing. Not just the experts or those who will profit obscenely or politicians, but all of humanity.

Howard Tankey, Box Hill North Trumps says relax

I’m not sure which is more frightening: the warnings from experts about out-of-control AI, or Donald Trump’s response that there’s nothing to worry about.

Bruce Watson, Belgrave Degrees of danger

Mark Gongloff is right. When it comes to climate change, humans are like frogs in a slowly boiling pot, except we keep reaching out to turn up the heat ourselves (″⁣Climate change effects are punching us in the face, yet we refuse to defend ourselves″⁣, 14/9). We simply cannot seem to turn off the coal, oil and gas taps. It is deeply frustrating.

Polls consistently conclude that most Australians want the Albanese government to take stronger action on climate change, but misinformation and the powerful vested interests of the fossil-fuel industry continue to stand in the way.

It may sound like a cliché, but every fraction of a degree of warming matters, for both humanity and the natural world.

The good news is that politicians do listen when enough people speak up. Silence won’t cool the planet.

Sarah Brennan, Hawthorn Please explain, Pauline

Pauline, Angus and Matt: Post the Nepal tragedy, how you can ignore the warnings of climate catastrophe by every reputable scientist?

Greg Curtin, Nunawading



Rules for trams

Re ″⁣Garry was trying to tap on when he fell on a tram. Three weeks later, he was dead″⁣ (13/9): As an octogenarian regular user of Melbourne’s wonderful trams, I make the following three comments.

The modern electric trams have such powerful acceleration that drivers should be instructed to take off more slowly.

The newer trams are not well-designed in that there are no overhead grips in the aisles. And, although I don’t really need one, for safety I now take a walking stick when I use a tram.

Kerry Breen, Kew Drive to conditions

Road safety is a personal responsibility and the armchair commentators should always wait for a full report before rushing to conclusions.

When anyone who is killed or injured in a road incident, it is a serious matter for the family and friends of the person involved, and justice for these people is crucial.

As a driver, motorcyclist, and pedal cyclist, I am always amazed at the disregard for the ancient law of riding or driving to the conditions. How often can you notice drivers speeding in conditions that demand caution?

How often do we witness motorcyclists riding close up behind a car (often in the driver’s blind spot) then weaving past cars? As a frequent bicycle rider along dedicated walking and cycling paths, do we notice Lycra-clad riders at a good pace not either carrying a bell or using it?

The road conditions of Victorian roads have taken a dive in quality. This is for a variety of reasons such as greatly increased traffic, heavier vehicles, and contractors taking shortcuts building roads.

Conditions may demand extreme caution such as not driving at or above the recommended or mandated road speed limit. Ride or drive to protect yourself from danger and don’t blame the conditions.

David Hassett, Noble Park Learn to swerve

Given the current potholed state of Victorian roads, the best way to avoid wheel damage is to leave sufficient ″⁣swerve time″⁣ behind the vehicle in front. Tailgaters stand no chance of seeing or avoiding road damage in time.

Keeping a slightly longer gap at highway speeds allows drivers enough visibility to straddle or steer around potholes safely.

Harley Powell, Elsternwick Ride as Dutch do

As both a cyclist and pedestrian, I agree with your correspondent (Letters, 14/9): Shared roads and paths do not work. The answer: separate. Sharing is dangerous.

On the roads, cyclists think car drivers are entitled (and dangerous), and on shared paths, pedestrians think cyclists are entitled (and dangerous).

If you have ever cycled in the Netherlands, you will know it is bike heaven. I wish.

But, as a Dutch woman once told me, ″⁣we all own bikes″⁣, and strict laws and separate bike paths favour cyclists.

I encourage your correspondent to become an honorary Dutch citizen and ride a bike. Then lead by example so that when we share paths and roads, consideration and care is numero uno.

Gryff Jamieson-Ballard, Castlemaine Train your Jack Russell

Re your correspondent’s advice to not buy a Jack Russell (Letters, 14/9): We always had a policy of adopt, not shop, and we took in a JR pup, who became a brilliant little dog – fun, lively, companionable, smart and loyal.

However, Jack Russells need to be trained, and work has to be put in to ensure there’s a clear understanding of rules, hierarchies and boundaries. This is not ideal for people who are inexperienced in training dogs.

Regardless of breed, dogs should never be left alone with babies or small children. We had our JR for almost 20 years and loved every minute.

Barbara Chapman, South Yarra



Postal code

Your correspondent from East Brighton (Letters, 12/9) draws attention to the issue of whether the adjectives north, south, east and west should be placed before or after the noun. The trend seems to be to place the adjective first. The two newest railway stations are East Pakenham and West Tarneit.

And Australia Post which delivers mail to me five times a fortnight should not worry because all should be fine as long as the postcode is correct.

Rod Watson, East Brighton AND ANOTHER THING Matt Golding One Nation

Pauline Hanson, if you want to disgracefully bring politicians’ mothers into play, that makes your own family fair game. Before you speak, maybe you need to consider the consequences of the gateway you are opening.

Mick Hussey, Beaconsfield Given One Nation leader Pauline Hanson’s anger at government support for a disabled, single mother (Albo’s mum), what are her thoughts and intentions towards the NDIS? And the disability pension?

Jennifer Beckett, Koroit



Pauline Hanson has criticised the PM’s mother for living too long in public housing. While one might assume Maryanne Albanese would have loved to purchase her own home but unfortunately, she wasn’t able to call on a billionaire friend to fund a less frugal lifestyle.

Kevin Bailey, Croydon It’s time for Pauline Hanson to ″⁣go back to where she came from”. And it’s high time for the Plymouth Brethren cult to lose its tax-free status as a church.

Anthea Hyslop, Eltham Furthermore

The ideal place for the police academy could be the army barracks in St Kilda Road.

Meg Biggs, Yarraville In reply to your correspondent regarding dog bites (Letters, 14/9): All breeds have the capacity to bite. It is how they are trained that makes the difference. I have owned two Jack Russell terriers who never bit anyone.

Karen McKay, Strathmore Well, I have had the pleasure of living with several Jack Russells, and they are the sweetest dogs ever – must be their owners who bite.

Mary Edgerton, Port Melbourne



On Sunday, I watched the NRL finals and if you looked at the jumpers, the contest was between Unibet and Picklebet. It says it all about the influence the gambling industry has on sport.

Peter Heffernan, Balaclava Finally

I am mortified that a story of a moneyed, private school for boys was featured on the front page (14/9). Is it still the 1950s?

Robyn Hodge, Alphington The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Frank, fearless, but not so free-style? Staff survey changes raise eyebrows
World.content:
NationalQueenslandPublic service Frank, fearless, but not so free-style? Staff survey changes raise eyebrows Matt Dennien September 14, 2026 — 7:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: a Working for Queensland survey prompt, “vacancy management” hits Child Safety, and wage ruling saga lands senior teachers on par with their juniors. It’s everyone’s favourite time of the year. No, not the seasonal change of spring – Working for Queensland survey month! By everyone, of course, we mean those with thoughts about their public sector employment they would maybe only dare lay out in the free-text general feedback box of the anonymised questionnaire. This year, however, it seems there could be a catch. Queensland public service HQ at One William Street. Matt Dennien Word has reached the Circus tent from multiple agencies the no-holds-barred rant box has disappeared from some surveys, or been replaced with a more restrictive prompt for others.



Since landing in inboxes from late August, some eager (only about 20 per cent of the 330,0000-strong workforce filled it out in 2025) and eagle-eyed public servants have clocked the curious changes. But it’s not uniform across the sector, with the separately collected free-text section included at the discretion of each agency and sent directly, unedited, to the boss. We’ve caught whispers some folks receiving surveys have this year found no open feedback section at the end. Other departments we’ve had intel from are said to have replaced the general feedback prompt with one asking what you’d tell someone considering a job there, or what is one thing you would change.



“It’s not as open-ended as it has been in previous years,” a department source said, speaking to us on condition of anonymity for perhaps the obvious reason of not being authorised to do so. Related Article Public service Returning kindness: The volunteers who emotionally rejuvenate Roma Street’s police They noted it seemed to be an attempt to steer staff away from airing more detailed or specific gripes. One former agency chief, also granted anonymity, told us they viewed it as one of the most important parts of the surveys because of the freeing, anonymised nature of the comments. They suggested any removal of or constraining of this would reflect a lack of willingness to “really hear what people think”.



With a couple of weeks left to complete, we imagine more will discover the changes as they open them closer to the due date – a practice Circus members are certainly not immune from on our workplace feedback forms, either. But what to do if you discover you’re cut off from the trauma dump you were hoping to give, or have already been confronted by such an injustice? We’ve got you covered. Fill out the form below (on a non-work device and network) and tell us instead. Drop contact details if you’re willing to talk more, anonymously, of course. We’ll even try and publish what we can in a future segment. Let the frank and fearless feedback flow!



‘Vacancy management’ comes for Child Safety frontline support roles Fresh on the heels of the state’s first credit rating downgrade in almost 20-years, Circus can add a seventh department to its list of those with various efforts in place to squeeze staffing budgets. The latest “vacancy management strategy” word (don’t call it a hiring freeze!) is from over at Belinda Drew’s Department of Families, Seniors, Disability Services and Child Safety. There, the strategy is said to review vacant roles across child safety, disability services and corporate support before they can be filled. Those not deemed “key frontline” require stricter approval. This includes sign-off by a deputy director-general and a documented rationale. So far, so similar to what we’ve heard from widely across the sector.



But the thing that has some child safety staff, and their union (Together), up in arms? What, exactly, is being classified as a frontline role under the exemption list. In particular, the lack of an exemption for administration and business officers in child safety service centres – who keep such centres, which support frontline child protection workers, running. “These roles are critical to frontline child protections, and they should be treated as critical workers when it comes time to fill them,” Together assistant secretary Dee Spink said in a statement. “The department says this isn’t a recruitment freeze, but for some workers it can feel like one.”



Comment has been sought from the department. For what it’s worth, we quizzed independent economist Saul Eslake about this vacancy management approach to belt-tightening while chatting to him on Friday about that credit downgrade. His view? “They’re a lazy way of trying to save money,” Eslake offered. “They’re fairly crude measures and not ones that I would ever support.” Eslake also reckoned the roughly 3 per cent staff expense growth projected from next financial year in Treasurer David Janetzki’s June budget (this year’s is 5.4 per cent) is only possible with a proper freeze on the size of the public service. Either that, or that slim surplus pencilled in for after the 2028 election might end up being kicked down the road – something we’re sure the ratings agencies will be watching closely.





The first band of this classification is available to those with two or more years of satisfactory service as a “senior teacher”. The second, EST 2, can be reached after three years at EST 1. That higher band was created in the 2019 agreement and is not reflected in the award. While EST 1 wages were set to lift through a safety net tied to the state wage case ruling, EST 2 wages were not. Then acting general secretary Brendan Crotty said the union clocked the issue weeks ago, raising it with Sharon Schimming’s apparently unaware department and Minister John-Paul Langbroek. Eventually, a departmental directive was issued to allow EST 2 teachers to get the higher award rate. This temporary fix, however, essentially leaves more senior teachers on an equal pay rate to those on a lower band until the difference can be sorted via the broader ongoing arbitration process. Yikes.



The issue has, as you might imagine, gone down like a tonne of lead pencils for teachers – some of whom have taken to the union’s social media comment sections to give an unfavourable report card of even some of the union process. Queensland teachers gather in Queen’s Park during the second of two Queensland Teachers’ Union strike days last year. Polina Levina/Getty Images “The QTU acknowledges that some members at EST 2 level may understandably feel frustrated that, for the time being, this means being paid at the same, if higher, rate as EST 1,” Crotty wrote to members last week. That “time being” is likely to still be some time yet, given arbitration hearings before the Queensland Industrial Relations Commission have now been given a start date of… April 6 next year. Have a curiosity for the Circus tent? Email on m.dennien@nine.com.au. For more security, sing out with a non-work device and network via Signal (mattdennien.15 or here) and mattdennien@protonmail.com. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Transport minister accepts lifetime membership to Qantas platinum
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Transport minister accepts lifetime membership to Qantas platinum Nick Newling September 14, 2026 — 7:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Transport Minister Catherine King has accepted a lifetime membership to Qantas’ platinum frequent flyer rewards tier less than two years after MPs ceremonially handed over their membership to the airline’s VIP lounge following public backlash. The minister, whose responsibilities include aviation and the courting of airlines to make use of the new Western Sydney International Airport, quietly updated her register of interests on Monday to reflect the gift she received from the airline. Catherine King at the opening of Western Sydney airport in July. Wolter Peeters The airline’s second-highest tier, behind platinum one, offers free access to first and business class lounges across the globe, additional baggage allowance, priority check-in, boarding and baggage access. It also offers priority upgrades and seat selection. A Qantas frequent flyer would need to accrue 1400 status credits in a year to qualify for the platinum tier. A discount economy ticket between Sydney and Melbourne garners 10 points, meaning a traveller would need to fly between the capitals 140 times to reach the tier.



A lifetime membership to the tier requires 75,000 status credits, or 7500 Sydney to Melbourne flights. In November 2024, a raft of federal MPs including Community Strong Australia representative Allegra Spender quit the VIP lounges of Qantas and Virgin after a furore over flight upgrades and special treatment for politicians. Related Article Exclusive

Immigration Slash the intake: Majority of Australians demand deeper migration cuts The saga began after the publication of an extract of The Chairman’s Lounge by journalist Joe Aston, published in Good Weekend, claimed that Prime Minister Anthony Albanese had received at least 22 free Qantas upgrades over the past decade, and that he had liaised directly with former Qantas chief Alan Joyce over upgrades. Albanese admitted at the time that he spoke to Joyce about two non-commercial trips with Qantas but said these had also included Liberal ministers and media companies. He said he did not ever ask Joyce for an upgrade and his office said this denial meant there were no calls, texts, emails or other communications with the former Qantas boss.



In 2023, King was thrown into the spotlight for denying a Qatar Airways bid to double their flights into Australia, a move that many in the industry said would have lowered ballooning travel costs for Australians. The minister updated her register of interests with the alteration added under the title “gifts”. The membership came with a travel wallet and bag tag. King misspelled the tier’s name in her declaration, writing that she was a member of the “Platnium” tier. King’s office was contacted for comment. A spokeswoman for King told the Australian Financial Review – who first reported the gift – that the minister received the status by virtue of the extent to which she has travelled with the airline. World.title: ‘Moving at light speed’: Plug-in solar and batteries are coming to Australia
World.content:
EnvironmentSustainabilityRenewables ‘Moving at light speed’: Plug-in solar and batteries are coming to Australia Caitlin Fitzsimmons September 14, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Apartment residents could soon be able to buy plug-in batteries to store cheap or free power produced during the day to use in the evening even without solar panels. The plug-in home batteries for energy storage are part of reforms that would also usher in portable panels, broadening access to solar power to renters and apartment dwellers. Portable solar panels on apartment balconies in Freiburg, Germany. Alamy Stock Photo Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen said all states and territories had agreed to look at how plug-in solar and batteries could work in Australia to give apartment dwellers and renters more control over their bills. “A third of Australians have a solar panel on their roofs. It’s more popular than the backyard pool,” Bowen said.



“Now we’re taking the next step, by looking at how even more Australians can take advantage of free, abundant sunshine to cut their energy bills - even if they don’t have a roof.” As reported previously by this masthead, plug-in solar allows consumers to buy panels for about $500 each that hang in an outdoor area and plug into a socket to power any appliances, charge a battery or feed into the grid. The device does not need to be installed by an electrician and the owner can take it with them when they move home. The technology is widely used in Germany; increasing in other European countries such as France and Spain and many US states; and was recently legalised in Britain. It is currently unlawful in Australia, though the market is growing anyway and a number of online retailers already sell systems here. Tyler Peck, 24, rents an older home in Melbourne and could use plug-in solar to help lower his heating bills in winter. Justin McManus The federal and state climate change and energy ministers agreed on Friday to progress legal and regulatory reforms that would enable widespread adoption in Australia, with a key deadline by mid next year. New Zealand is separately working to enable plug-in solar.



Glen Morris, director of Smart Energy Lab and a member of the Solar Standards Committee, said Australia had been lagging but was now moving at light speed given it usually took years to develop new standards. “It went from zero to 100 in one day.” Morris said. “I was prepared for a very long campaign to get it through … but obviously, when there’s political will, things can move a bit faster.” The main change required was an amendment to the Australian standard for inverter systems, which could be fast-tracked by copying international standards, he said. “The products designed for the European market already have the safety features we like – it’s important that we don’t turn it into a very complex process, so that it can be done swiftly. “To some extent, the horse has bolted because people can buy these and the only thing stopping them plugging it in is that it’s illegal. But it’s not very obvious – certainly if you don’t have solar panels and just have a plug-in battery system, no one would know.”



Francis Vierboom, chief executive of Rewiring Australia, said the real game changer for apartment dwellers could be “suitcase batteries” because the panels required outside space but the batteries could be deployed separately to solar. Related Article Renewables Push to deliver solar to 2.5m apartment dwellers gains traction The plug-in panel technology is often called “balcony solar”, and panels hanging vertically off balcony railings are a common sight in Germany. However, Vierboom said the panels would be most useful in backyards in the Australian context. “The sun is a lot lower in the sky in northern Europe, and solar that’s actually on sideways on your balcony is going to generate more energy than it does in Australia, where the sun is a bit higher in the sky because we are closer to the equator,” Vierboom said. The batteries would charge up from the cheap daytime energy available on the grid, including three hours of free power available in the middle of the day on some plans, and then a household could use that energy in the evening peak.



“The less we all lean on the grid in that evening peak, the cheaper the energy system stays, and the more we can be using solar energy instead of fossil fuel generators in the evening,” Vierboom said. Related Article Electricity Bruce’s home was ‘like a tent’. A new energy rating is guiding upgrades Governments may need to look at strata law and tenancy law to consider whether owners’ corporations, strata managers and landlords could block plug-in solar and under what circumstances. Solar Citizens, an advocacy group for consumers to benefit from renewable energy, has been lobbying Bowen to push for plug-in solar. Chief executive Heidi Lee Douglas said the group would push for a clear timeline with a target deadline of July 1 next year, and to ensure renters, apartment dwellers and low-income households could benefit. “Renters shouldn’t be locked out of cheaper, cleaner energy simply because they don’t own the roof over their heads,” Douglas said. “They should have a fair right to request solar, batteries and energy-efficiency upgrades, and landlords shouldn’t be able to unreasonably say no.”



Tyler Peck, 24, rents an older home with his partner in Preston in Melbourne. While the home is affordable and close to transport, it is poorly insulated and the heating bills are high. Peck would like to have plug-in solar set up on his porch, which gets good sunlight, and says he is equally motivated by the electricity savings and the environmental benefit. But he would definitely wait for the official green light, rather than buying any of the systems already on the market. “With all the [public service announcements] that went out a while ago about dodgy scooter or e-bike batteries being fire hazards, I’m just very cautious about anything that isn’t official,” Peck said. Return on investment An 800-watt system with two panels would cost $450 to $850 based on German prices, which gives it a two to four-year payback with a 25-year warranty, Morris, of Smart Energy Lab, said. Adding a 1.6-2Kwh battery would be a combined cost of $1100-$1300, with a five to eight-year payback and batteries rated for 15 to 20 years of daily use.



Morris said Australian prices would probably start higher, and eventually fall. Bowen said on Saturday that if plug-in solar met safety standards, it would be automatically covered by the government’s existing rebates, the Cheaper Home Battery policy and the Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme for solar panels, adding “but we’ll work those details through”. However, Vierboom said the government should consider a change to legislation, since the Cheaper Home Batteries program does not cover small batteries, or the installation of batteries without solar, and the solar panel rebates required installation by an accredited electrician. Morris said he had been testing a small panel tilted 75 degrees from horizontal – only 15 degrees off being vertical – similar to how it was used in Germany. But to get a decent return on investment in Australia, it should be tilted more horizontally – from 37 degrees in Melbourne to 32 degrees in Queensland, with Sydney in the middle. On a balcony, “it would stick out a bit more, providing a bit more shade for your neighbour below”, Morris said. Other options for apartments



Karin Aubrey will get a shared solar system on the roof of her apartment building in the Sydney beachside suburb of Maroubra in October. The building received a Solar for Apartment Residents grant from the NSW government to reduce the cost, and will use the Allume SolShare 2 technology to fairly split the solar power between apartments. Karin Aubrey is getting shared solar on her Sydney apartment block but supports plug-in solar as an option in the market. Wolter Peeters Aubrey is happy about the panels and the grant, but said it took more than a year of advocacy to get everyone in the owners’ corporation on board given the cost of the panels and electrical rewiring required. She would like to add shared batteries in future, which the Allume technology allows, but in an old building that gets damaged by salt spray, “there are always competing needs”. Aubrey saw plug-in solar in action on her recent trip to visit friends in France and would support it becoming available here because it would allow households to make decisions independently, not just through strata. “They’re having crazy heatwaves [in France], and their apartment buildings are usually quite complicated with who owns them and how big they are, so balcony solar is taking off a little bit there,” Aubrey said.



“I heard it about it there because everyone’s trying to get air conditioning for the first time, and the load is just massive. It’s a good idea.” Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Fundraiser launched for children of woman who died in Nelson
World.content:
A fundraiser has been launched to help secure a stable home and future education for the two children of a woman who died in a suspected murder-suicide in Nelson.

Tracey Schroder has set up a Givealittle page for her nephews, Ryan and Josh, following the death of her sister Nicola Yvonne Perry, 48.

Nicola and 49-year-old Brendon James Perry died at a property on Parkers Road in Tāhunanui on 4 September.

RNZ understands their deaths are being treated as a suspected murder-suicide.

Nicola Yvonne Perry, 48, was killed in a suspected murder-suicide in Nelson. NZ Police

The alarm was raised after a shotgun was stolen from Hunting & Fishing on Quarantine Road in Annesbrook.

In a message accompanying the fundraiser on Facebook, Schroder said her family was trying to cope with the loss of her sister, and she wanted to help her nephews.

"My family are trying to cope with intense grief from the tragic loss of my sister Nic Perry, and right now the best way I can support my nephews is to help their futures, Nic would have wanted us to."

The fundraiser page said the money raised would go towards providing Ryan and Josh with a safe and stable home, as well as supporting their future schooling and study.

The fundraiser has raised more than $12,000 for the family so far.
