World.title: Environmental imprint of new jeans 180 times higher than second hand pair - research
World.content:
The environmental cost of a new pair of jeans could be enough to make a shopper blue.

Brand new jeans can have an environmental footprint that is 180 times higher than pre-loved ones, according to new research.

The data from Planetary Accounting Network uses a dashboard to calculate the environmental costs of everyday purchases, breaking down environmental data for a product, such as the amount of carbon produced, water used and waste created.

Planetary Accounting Network says by 2030, carbon needs to be limited to six kilograms per person per day - and waste to 2kg.

Secondhand jeans far more eco-friendly than new pair - research Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

Recycling champions Wanaka WasteBusters commissioned the research and general manager Gina Dempster told RNZ they wanted the data to figure out a number for the environmental benefits of second hand jeans over new ones.

"And what they found is that if you look at your average per-capita budget for a healthy planet, buying a second hand pair of jeans from WasteBusters uses about three percent of my daily budget, whereas just the fabric for a new pair of jeans could use up to five full days of my planetary budget, which would leave me nothing for food, transport and all the other things I have to do every day."

She said the environmental cost of denim came from the water usage, the deforestation, and the use of nitrogen fertilisers in producing the denim.

"The reality is that if you buy a pair of jeans from an opshop, that pair of jeans has already been made, and then the environmental cost of just bringing those jeans into an opshop and running the shop and selling them is extremely low.

"So essentially they are kind of free for the environment."

Gina Dempster from Wastebusters. Wastebusters

She said it was well known that jeans used thousands of litres of water in their production, but knowing the footprint was 180 times higher "really makes you think about every pair of jeans that you've ever owned".

Wanaka WasteBusters receives a "massive" amount of jeans with a huge rack of available pants, mostly selling for about $10-$15, according to Dempster.

"If it was a really high quality pair of jeans in new condition you might be paying up to $30, but that would be a pair of jeans that you might be paying $300-$500 for new."

Dempster said it was hard for people to get a feel for the sheer amount of textile products that were going on to the second hand market.

"That's one thing for our team, working at the drop-off every day, we see the amount of textiles that come through one opshop in one small town in New Zealand, and it's honestly overwhelming.

World.title: Father of Dunedin party victim says supermarkets share blame for drinking culture
World.content:
Coroner describes death of student as 'senseless' Checkpoint Download MP3 8m

A man who's daughter died at an overcrowded party in Dunedin says it's devastating to hear a coroner's report into another alcohol-related death in the city.

A coroner described the death of an Otago University student, who died after choking on his own vomit in 2023, as a "woeful illustration" of the country's youth drinking culture.

Partygoers had carried him to a bedroom after he was found passed out and "pretty much unresponsive" in the kitchen.

A witness described people later trying to clear vomit from his throat. Emergency services were called and took over doing CPR, but the student could not be revived.

Sophia Crestani died at an overcrowded house party in Dundas Street, Dunedin in October 2019. RNZ

Bede Crestani, who's daughter Sophia was crushed to death at an overcrowded house party in Dunedin, told Checkpoint that supermarket companies Woolworths and Foodstuffs had some responsibility for the problem.

"I would like them to get into a room, in Selwyn College, where we met the tenants the day after Sophia died with other parents and family of people who have been victims of excessive drinking, and front us and say that what they're doing is legal and all OK."

He stopped short of saying supermarkets should not sell alcohol, but he said the supermarkets should look at their own part in the issues relating to binge drinking.

"They need to look at the problems and have a look at some of those streets down there - and look at some of the broken glass after different events ... and go 'what is their part of the damage that's resulting from that?'''

Crestani said New Zealand had a youth drinking culture which encouraged people over consume alcohol.

"There is a drinking problem in New Zealand where it's cool to drink too much. It's not victimless, people die and it causes many other health problems as well."

He said people needed to be responsible for their own and their friends drinking.

"There does need to be responsibility for people who hold parties or events ... and I advocated for prosecution of the tenants in Sophia's case."

A Foodstuffs spokesperson told RNZ their thoughts were with the family and friends of the man who died.

"We also acknowledge the advocacy of families who have experienced the loss of loved ones and understand why these issues are so important to them.

"This is a deeply sad situation, and we do not think it would be appropriate for Foodstuffs to comment on or debate the views expressed by grieving families. Alcohol harm is a complex issue involving a range of factors, individuals and organisations.

"We support efforts to promote the safe and responsible consumption of alcohol and comply with all applicable laws and regulations governing its sale."

The University of Otago extended its thoughts to the student's whanau and friends following the tragic loss..

A spokeswoman said safety and wellbeing of students remained top priorities.

She said as well as proactive and regular communication with students about responsible consumption of alcohol - the university had a range of dedicated services, including clinicians with specialist drug and alcohol harm expertise.

World.title: Dangerous copper, metals thefts causing millions in damage
World.content:
Spike in copper thefts causing millions of dollars in damage Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

The growing problem of the theft of copper and other recyclable metals is causing millions of dollars of damage to infrastructure and endangering perpetrators and the public.

Police said the thefts - which often occurred at night and in remote locations - could be hard to detect and urged the public to report any suspicious behaviour.

Thefts put KiwiRail projects back months

On a cold, windy night on the rail corridor near Featherston - north of Wellington - KiwiRail's Andy Lyon was overseeing crews working to replace cabling stripped from within steel pipes near the tracks.

He said nearly 5 kilometres of cable had been stolen from the Wairarapa network this year.

In July, police arrested a 36-year-old Featherston man in connection with a series of thefts of signalling power cabling in the area.

"We're right in the throes of installing a new signalling system so the damage that's been done here just puts the work back months. We're having to bring people in on night shifts to make repairs and be able to keep ourselves on target," Lyon said.

Lyon said - across KiwiRail's network - nearly 90 instances of intentional damage had cost over $2 million to repair this year.

Andy Lyon, Kiwirail General Manager Wellington Metro. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

He said people were putting themselves in extreme danger in their attempts to source recyclable materials for quick cash.

"The rail corridor is a hugely dangerous place. It can be a kilometre for a freight train to be able to stop. The cable can have high voltage running through it so it's incredibly dangerous and we really don't want to see anybody get hurt.

"But unfortunately, that's the risk people are taking when they chose to come into the corridor and steal cable."

Kiwirail workers repairing sections of the Wairarapa trainline damaged by thieves. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Further north, lines company Vector had logged 630 instances of vandalism and theft from their networks during the last eight months.

General manager operations and maintenance, Marko Simunac said staff were discovering tell tale evidence of high voltage discharges as thieves cut into live cables.

Danger signs included charred and scattered tools - where people are attempting to steal materials from their network. SUPPLIED

"We are finding hacksaws which have been melted into the cable because there was a flashover. We are finding tools just left scattered in a place charred. So those people, very likely, are presenting to the medical centres," Simunac said.

In March, a man died after he was electrocuted in what police believe was an attempt to take copper from a transformer in Christchurch's Red Zone.

But it wasn't just criminals who were at risk.

Simunac said some instances of tampering were shutting down network fail safes leaving homes open to appliance damage and fire risk.

Tubing, discarded by thieves, after they have removed the copper cables within RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Others were leaving powerful connections open to the public.

"They have stolen the locks from our transformers on the roads. [They] just walk away and you've got live electricity exposed on public walkways. Kids are curious ... I just don't want to even go that way cause that would be horrific so I can't even think about it," Simunac said.

Simunac said two recent - but unsuccessful - attacks on cables beneath a motorway overpass created more than $500,000 worth of damage.

"Ultimately it is a lost opportunity. This half million dollars - in this particular instance - we could have put into a resilience project or a community project. We could have put it into a community battery somewhere. We could address those climate change impacts as well," Simunac said.

Andy Lyon inspects where thieves cut open metal pipes to steal the copper cables within. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Both companies were investigating adding forensic tagging of cabling to better allow police to determine where items they recover had been stolen from.

Police director - prevention, Inspector Natasha Allan said police were working to bring district team's intelligence together develop a more detailed national picture of the problem.

A new scheme being trialled in Christchurch was also allowing police to analyse patterns and trends by having metal recyclers share details of their purchases with police en masse.

Operation Scrap was launched at the beginning of the year and involved monitoring transactions across all metal recycling businesses within the district.

But Allan said catching people in the act was a challenge for police.

Woodside train station, Wairarapa. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

"These offences often occur in remote or isolated locations and under the cover of darkness, which can make detection difficult.

"In some cases, offenders leave limited evidence, making identification and prosecution challenging. Successful investigations often depend on timely reporting, witness information, CCTV footage, and cooperation with infrastructure owners and industry partners," Allan said.

Allan urged the public to be on the lookout for individuals in restricted areas - handling equipment without obvious authority - and in locations or times that seemed out of place.

World.title: Two people dead, third in hospital after boat capsizes at Manawatū beach
World.content:
Two people have died and one is in hospital after a boat capsized near the Rangitīkei River mouth.

Emergency services rushed to Tangimoana Beach around 8am on Monday in response to reports of three people in the water.

Manawatū Area Commander Inspector Matenga Gray said one person sustained injuries and was taken to hospital.

"Sadly, two people have died."

Surf Life Saving New Zealand said the boat capsized about 200m offshore from the Rangitikei River bar, north of Himatangi.

It said six lifeguards responded immediately from the Manawatū-Tararua SAR squad with two inflatable rescue boats.

One person made it back to shore by themselves and the remaining two were brought to shore at Tangimoana Beach by Coastguard and police.

Police, Hato Hone St John, Coastguard, Fire and Emergency and a rescue helicopter all responded, Surf Life Saving said.

Hato Hone St John said two ambulances, an operations manager, and one rapid response vehicle attended.

"One patient has been transported to Palmerston North Hospital in a moderate condition."

Coastguard said its National Operations Centre was notified of the capsized vessel and responded after receiving reports of three people in the water.

"Volunteers from Coastguard Manawatū responded with their jet ski Blue Rescue and rescue vessel Kevin Morris II."

World.title: Wellington City Council apologises for library website overspend
World.content:
Wellington City Council has apologised for spending over $600,000 on a website to draw visitors to the newly reopened City Library.

An independent review found shortcomings in the oversight, procurement process and the value for money offered by the site.

Chief operating officer James Roberts - the senior responsible officer for the whole Te Ngākau Civic Square upgrade, including the library - said he took "full accountability" for the expense.

"It is clear from the review there are lessons we need to take from this and I've already started making changes to ensure it doesn't happen again.

"Managing projects of this size, scale and complexity - such as earthquake strengthening on reclaimed land - is enormously challenging. I accept that one of the implications of this is that I didn't pay enough attention to this element of the project," Roberts said.

In June, Wellington's deputy mayor Ben McNulty said he became aware of the bill for the website the day after the Council Grants Committee had been forced to decline $3m in community funding due to a record volume of applications.

McNulty said the fee was "an atrocious amount of money to be spent on this type of website".

Wellington's deputy mayor Ben McNulty RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Author of the review Colin MacDonald found an ambitious project scope, a rushed tender process and a lack of oversight - beyond the board overseeing the Te Ngākau Civic Square redevelopment - combined to see the website's reach up to half a million dollars more than would typically be spent on a comparable Government website.

MacDonald said typical government website costs ranged from $100,000 to $350,000 in comparison.

He said scope of the redevelopment Te Ngākau Civic Square informed the project leading to the decision to create a highly polished, stand alone site designed to attract visitors to the newly reopened library.

"The project team operated under a strong, high-level mandate approved in 2020 and 2021 by Council to drive the regeneration of Civic Square.

"They considered that the biggest risk facing them was that not enough people would turn up and use the new facilities and the regeneration outcome would not be achieved. This may have given tacit permission to always go for the best. I could find little evidence of wider perspectives (e.g. from the executive leadership team) being brought to bear on the project and its decisions," MacDonald said.

RNZ / Mark Papalii

The report said a rapid "procurement in-a-day" tender process - which used a closed panel to assess proposals across a single day - undermined the market competition for the contract.

The tender - which went to market on May 2025 and was scheduled for implementation four months later - saw only two applications from six service providers approached.

The successful applicant was determined on the basis of their pitch for the first phase of the project which amounted to an initial expense $75,000 - rather than the likely full project cost.

The vendor was then retained for the remaining phases of the project.

The report said website's cost represented less that 0.1 percent of the $614M Te Ngākau Civic Precinct programme - which the library redevelopment was a part of - and meant the cost of the site did not trigger further scrutiny beyond the board overseeing the project.

"Because website spending was within delegated authority and represented a small share of the overall budget, it was never discussed at the programme board, limiting oversight. The programme continued to be guided by its original 2020 and 2021 foundational documents," the report said.

MacDonald said the project was allowed to make decisions that had implications for other parts of the council without sufficient consultation.

He said - while project leaders believed they had "consulted widely" with other parts of the council - perceptions from outside were that it had become increasingly difficult to influence decisions relating to the project.

"Some subject matter experts felt side-lined. This became particularly relevant as the website development and implementation progressed," MacDonald said.

MacDonald said a council commission value for money appraisal pointing out the cost of the site was "in the premium price bracket" and could have been "an opportunity to pause and reconsider the scope and specification".

"A more moderated approach by the project could have delivered a less expensive site that was still fit for purpose in supporting the relaunch of the building, its facilities and services, and the wider Te Ngākau precinct," MacDonald wrote.

The report made eight recommendations including developing a Council web strategy, procurement planning based of "whole-of-life" costs for projects, creating a formal value for money framework, appointing independent chairs for major programme governance boards and updating project mandates when council priorities change.

Mayor Andrew Little said the council would work towards implementing the recommendations and improving council practises to provide better transparency of costs and value for money for ratepayers.

"I've been clear that under my mayoralty - when the Council organisation makes mistakes - we front up to the public, we fix those mistakes and we learn from them. That's why I asked for this review, and that's what is happening now.

World.title: Auckland's City Rail Link: 25,000 more train passengers on first weekday
World.content:
Matthew Theunissen live onboard CRL as morning commute begins Morning Report Download MP3 1m 26s

An estimated 72,500 passengers were counted on trains across the Auckland Transport network by 5pm today - 25,000 more than last Monday.

Auckland's City Rail Link has had its first full weekday in operation on Monday.

Auckland Transport chief executive Stacey van der Putten said passenger numbers stayed strong all day, following the morning's busy peak period.

"This shows Aucklanders are getting out there and exploring the new routes that CRL offers, and it's a fantastic new way for people to visit parts of the city they may not have had easy access to in the past," she said.

"Our ambassador staff have been supporting customers at Karanga-a-Hape and Maungawhau stations throughout the day to transfer from the East-West to the South-City or Onehunga-West lines," van der Putten said.

"These transfers will become second nature to Aucklanders in the weeks to come."

More than 100 customer service staff and ambassadors were at stations helping with travel and transfer information, and more than 100 security staff were also present, she said.

AT said the opening day on 13 September was the busiest Sunday on the rail network on record.

On Beresford Square outside the new Karanga-a-Hape Station, some were having a coffee at the nearest cafe, and others took a moment to stop and join a Waiata group singing Purea Nei and celebrating Te wiki o Te Reo Maori.

Bo Meng from the nearby bakery PieFee said in the past they didn't open on Sundays, but they opened yesterday to coincide with the CRL opening to the public.

He said Monday was also busier than usual.

"I've seen heaps of people walking around, and new faces, so yea pretty good," said Meng.

His colleague added that they're considering opening on future Sundays as they expect to get more customers coming through.

Bo Meng outside Piefee. Lucy Xia

Charlotte Ryan from the Karangahape Road Business Association said she had seen lots of new faces over the past few days, particularly on Sunday.

"I think I expected lots of our friends or lots of the K'rd community to come out, and they were, but it was actually majority people that I don't think have been here in 10 or 15 years or even longer.

"People were commenting where they thought old buildings were, it was really really interesting to see that people had returned."

Ryan said she was optimistic about the future, but added that some businesses were still waiting to see how many customers they would get before they made decisions around staffing.

Charlotte Ryan outside the Karanga-a-Hape station. Lucy Xia

"Do you bring on those extra staff, how quickly are people going to start using this as a thoroughfare, you know it's like a social experiment," she said.

Karanga-a-Hape Station is an interchange station, with a bus connection to Westgate, and a transit point for people hopping from the West-East line to the South City line.

Ryan said she expected people might be open to having a wander around Karangahape Road, or getting a drink in between transits.

Meanwhile, the mid-city Te Waihorotiu station was touted to become New Zealand's busiest train station, but Shobhana Ranchhodji from Roma Blooms - which is mere metres from the Victoria St West entrance - said she had barely noticed any change in the amount of foot traffic.

Shobhana Ranchhodji. RNZ / Nick Monro

"Nothing's changed, no more people than what it was last Monday ... I say give us a month, it is what it is," she said.

Commuters cut down on travel times, concerns over app for some

Key features of the new network include the Eastern and Western lines merging into one, as well as faster trains.

On the 5.27am East West train from Swanson, Craig said he's glad he no longer needs to wait for 5-10 minutes at the New Market Station as he did in the past.

He estimates that he can save about 15-20 minutes on his journey into town.

Johnny Waititi used to take the train to Britomart from Ōtāhuhu, then bus to Symonds Street to the kura where he works as deputy principal.

Johnny Waititi. RNZ / Nick Monro

He said he was now able to take the train directly to Karanga-a-Hape station then walk to work - saving about 20 minutes on each trip.

Waititi said overall, it was a good experience this morning, but he said the service he'd originally planned to take did get cancelled - although he said he was able to quickly find out in advance through the Auckland Transport app.

Waititi said he was worried for older people who don't have the app and won't be able to get timely updates on cancellations.

Johnny Waititi. RNZ / Nick Monro

Auckland Transport told Morning Report there was one train fault this morning which has caused a few cancellations.

Another worker who was travelling on the East-West line, trying to get to Auckland City Hospital, said she's disappointed her train got cancelled and she's having to take a bus to get to Grafton.

A family living on Vincent Street in the CBD, whose two children go to school in New Lynn, are stoked to be saving time on their daily school runs.

Arrenda Maryzona with her husband and two sons. RNZ / Lucy Xia

The family doesn't own a car, and mum of two Arrenda Maryzona used to spend four hours on the bus each day, with each return trip to the school taking two hours.

Now, she said it's just a three minute walk to the Karanga-a-Hape station, and she's saving about 15 minutes on each trip - adding up to an hour saved.

World.title: Are oil price hikes putting a pre-election OCR increase back in play?
World.content:
Recent spikes in global oil prices and bond yields appear to be increasing the possibility the Reserve Bank will need to hike the Official Cash Rate again in October.

While the Bank hiked the OCR earlier this month by 0.25 percent, to 2.75 percent, financial markets interpreted the commentary associated with the increase as dovish, with a pause in hikes in October looking likely.

The Reserve Bank is due to review the OCR again on October 28, just over a week before the election on November 7.

But the BNZ Economics team said in a research update today that the outlook has shifted.

"Things can change very quickly in this zany world that we now live in. The last few days have been a case in point with oil prices soaring, bond yields rising aggressively, central banks looking increasingly likely to push rates higher, the New Zealand dollar falling and, as a wee counterpoint to the unfortunate developments, New Zealand growth aggregates showing remarkable resilience," BNZ said.

Oil prices surged back over US$100 (NZ$172) a barrel last week on renewed fighting between Iran and the US and growing concern about the disruption to the Red Sea oil route from Houthi rebels.

The research note went on to say that a few days back, markets were pricing in little chance of a rate hike in October and almost no chance of two before the end of the year.

"Now, there's a near two-thirds chance of a hike priced for the first meeting and around an even chance of two rate hikes," BNZ said.

BNZ said it thinks the market assessment is entirely apt, pointing out that when the Reserve Bank put together its September Monetary Policy Statement it assumed the Dubai crude oil price would average US$83.70 (NZ$144.66) across the September quarter, falling to US$78.40 (NZ$135.50) in a year's time.

The economists note that the crude price is almost 17 percent higher than had been assumed for the next quarter and, in addition, the NZD on the trade-weighted index is currently sitting at 65.4 compared with a 66.9 estimate.

They say this not only puts further upward pressure on domestic fuel prices, but also on imported inflation generally.

BNZ said the full impact of the recently elevated oil prices will be a big shock to the fourth-quarter inflation reading.

World.title: Jordan Petaia returns to Wallabies squad after NFL stint
World.content:
Jordan Petaia has been selected in his first Wallabies squad since the 2023 Rugby World Cup as Les Kiss braces for the sternest test yet of his brief coaching reign.

A one-time teenage Test debutant, Petaia has been included in Australia's 34-man group for the upcoming showdown with back-to-back world champions South Africa in Perth.

The 26-year-old has been plying his trade in France and Japan since the end of the 2024 Super Rugby Pacific season, after seven seasons at the Queensland Reds.

He left the Reds in 2024 to pursue a career in the NFL, signing briefly for the Los Angeles Chargers in 2025, before being waived later that same year.

He then signed for Perpignan in the Top 14 before locking in a long-term spot at Urayasu D-Rocks.

Petaia made his Wallabies debut at just 19 at the 2019 World Cup in Japan, scoring a memorable try against Uruguay, and has since pulled on the gold jersey a total of 31 times.

With now just a year before Australia hosts the 2027 World Cup, Kiss says it's time to see if Petaia is ready to make a run at a third appearance at the global showpiece.

Jordan Petaia is set for a return to Wallaby gold. (Getty Images: PA Images/Bradley Collyer)

"Look, we've got a lot of good back-three players here in the country. We made sure we looked at all of them," Kiss said on Monday.

"It was just the ideal opportunity to see Jordan. He's been out of the system for a couple of years now. He has played in two World Cups. We just wanted to touch base with him, get him to come and work out with us, see how he's going.

"We haven't selected that team yet, but it was just a good opportunity to see Jordan back in the environment and him to have a good look at us with the new coaching structure and all those sort of things.

"From the team perspective, there was a lot of deep discussion about where we would go with that."

The classy utility back is one of three new faces in the squad that won back the Puma Trophy in an undefeated tour of Argentina earlier this month.

Another is Western Force recruit Harry McLaughlin-Phillips, who has been named in his first official Wallabies squad, replacing Carter Gordon who suffered a fractured calf bone in Mendoza.

Born in Toowoomba and raised in Gunnedah, the 22-year-old flyhalf was part of Australia's 2023 and 2024 World Rugby U20 Championships and has featured for the Reds on more than 35 occasions.

Queenslander Zane Nonggorr is back in the squad after completing a successful return to the field in Saturday's 2026 Super Rugby AUS opener having picked up a minor calf strain in Japan.

He replaces Wallaby number 1,000 Massimo De Lutiis, who is being managed after playing three straight Tests to kick off his international career.

Outside back Filipo Daugunu is also being managed due to a minor knee complaint.

"We've learned a bit more about ourselves as a group over the last four Tests and we know we still have a lot to work on to get to where we want to be," Kiss said of the Springboks challenge in Perth on September 27.

"South Africa have been the benchmark team in World Rugby for a long time and we're motivated by the challenge of meeting them in our own backyard in two weeks' time."

Wallabies Squad:

Forwards — Allan Alaalatoa, Angus Bell, Charlie Cale, Josh Canham, Tom Hooper, Isaac Kailea, Fraser McReight, Josh Nasser, Zane Nonggorr, Brandon Paenga-Amosa, Billy Pollard, Aidan Ross, Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, Lachlan Shaw, Carlo Tizzano, Taniela Tupou, Rob Valetini, Jeremy Williams, Harry Wilson (capt).

Backs: Jock Campbell, Ben Donaldson, Isaac Henry, Len Ikitau, Max Jorgensen, Ryan Lonergan, Tate McDermott, Harry McLaughlin-Phillips, Declan Meredith, Hunter Paisami, Jordan Petaia, Harry Potter, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, Kalani Thomas, Tom Wright.

World.title: World Athletics firm on Russia ban, Coe acknowledges need for solution
World.content:
World Athletics president Sebastian Coe has said the governing body's position on the exclusion of Russian athletes has not changed ahead of an upcoming Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) case, while acknowledging the need for a resolution.

Russian Athletics last month filed a fresh appeal with CAS challenging sanctions imposed by World Athletics, which has barred Russian and Belarusian athletes from international competition since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

"Our position hasn't changed, and this isn't about politics or passports. It's about the integrity of competition," Coe told reporters on the final day of the inaugural Ultimate Championship in Budapest.

Aussie athletics star shocked at massive pay packet for coming second Australia's Nicola Olyslagers finishes second in the high jump at the new Ultimate Championship competition.

"From the age of 18, I believe that every position I've taken … it's about integrity and it's about competition, and that matters to me."

Coe declined to discuss the federation's legal strategy ahead of the arbitration proceedings but said World Athletics would continue to defend its stance.

"So our position won't change," he said. "And look, yes, this does need to be resolved, and I'm acutely aware of that. (But) I don't think our legal teams would be particularly thankful if I laid out our approach on this."

The comments came a month after Russian Athletics confirmed a new CAS filing, following an initial filing in July, aimed at overturning sanctions it says prevent it from fully representing Russian athletes internationally and participating in World Athletics decision-making processes.

Despite reaffirming the federation's position, Coe said he recognised the importance of ultimately restoring full global participation in the sport.

"We want a full complement of people on a global level competing in our sport, and that has to be our overall objective. Of course, it does."

The Lausanne-based CAS serves as sport's highest arbitration body and is expected to hear Russian Athletics' challenge in the coming months.

World Athletics has maintained one of the toughest positions of any international federation since Russia's invasion of Ukraine, while some sports have gradually reintroduced Russian and Belarusian athletes under neutral status.

The International Skating Union has established a pathway for selected Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete as neutral competitors, although it confirmed earlier this week that Kamila Valieva and three other figure skaters had their neutral status revoked.

Russian state news agency TASS quoted Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev as saying that all the skaters affected by the ruling would appeal to CAS.

Reuters

World.title: Mas 'fulfils his destiny' to win historic Vuelta
World.content:
Enric Mas has finally delivered an expectant Spanish public an overall victory at the Vuelta a España, his win confirmed at the end of the final stage into Grenada on Sunday.

Mas finished safely in the peloton during the 21st and final stage of the race, won by Norway's Tobias Johannessen.

The 31-year-old from Mallorca held off four-time Vuelta champion Primož Roglič to become the first Spaniard to win the Vuelta since Alberto Contador in 2014.

Mas finished 2 minutes and 15 seconds ahead of Roglič overall, with Austria's Felix Gall finishing third at 2:44.

"It's just special," Mas told reporters after the race.

"It's been a day to remember, a special Vuelta, and it has been wonderful.

"There's always tension about what could happen, but you've seen it all went smoothly, so we're delighted and we enjoyed every kilometre today.

"It was a long wait and a long way to today. But to be honest, it was always special Vueltas, and this one I think is the special one."

Primož Roglič (left), has won four Vuelta's, while Enric Mas (centre) finally claimed his first aged 31. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

Five-time Tour de France winner Tadej Pogačar had come into the race as the overwhelming favourite for victory, building an ominous lead of 3 minutes 50 seconds by the end of the seventh stage.

The freakish Slovenian star had won three of the six completed stages at that stage and looked set to claim a win of unparalleled dominance in the modern era.

However, the two-time reigning world champion badly crashed on the eighth stage of the race, breaking his collar bone and fracturing his neck, ending his season.

From that point though, Mas, who had tested Pogačar on the mountainous fourth stage in Andorra, dominated the race alongside his much-maligned Movistar team.

Mas had finished second at his home grand tour three times, in 2018, 2021 and 2022, and also finished third in 2024.

When he finished second to Simon Yates in 2018, triumphing on the queen stage at that year's race, there was an expectation that Mas would become the heir to seven-time grand tour winner Contador as Spanish cycling's next big thing.

Mas even spent his junior years racing with the Alberto Contador Academy, indicating just how high hopes were that he would excel.

And although Mas has achieved plenty, finishing in the top six overall at grand tours eight times over the course of his career, the expected Contador-like dominance never eventuated.

It is telling that long-time AS reporter Juan Gutiérrez entitled his post-Vuelta piece: "Enric Mas cumple su destino", "Enric Mas fulfils his destiny".

Movistar switched their usual blue jerseys for red ones to honour Enric Mas's achievement. (Getty Images: Alexander Hassenstein)

Contador wrote in Spanish newspaper AS that he was "very happy and incredibly excited" to see Mas achieve his potential.

"I know how hard he's worked these past few years and how much criticism he's always faced," Contador said.

"Instead of letting it get him down, he turned it into motivation to demonstrate the talent he truly possesses.

"Every cyclist develops in their own way and, in Enric's case, it was fast because he finished second in the 2018 Vuelta a España.

"Then, when he didn't quite seal the deal, well, we all know how sports are — it seems like if you don't win, nothing has any merit.

"That's why cycling will be fair to Enric Mas for winning this Vuelta."

Contador acknowledged that Pogačar would likely had claimed victory had he remained in the race, but that Mas thoroughly deserved his victory.

" It's not a gift," Contador said. "It's thanks to his hard work and his form. He was the strongest. "

Santiago Buitrago of Colombia and Team Bahrain Victorious claimed the king of the mountains jersey, while British rider Oscar Onley won the white youth jersey.

Wout van Aert added some personal closure by claiming the green sprinter's jersey, and the super combative prize, after he crashed out while leading both the points and king of the mountains classifications in 2024.

"In a way this is finished business," van Aert said.

"After the near miss two years ago and the big injury I had afterwards, it was quite a disappointment.

"It makes it more special to be here, to come completely to the end, and to wear this beautiful jersey."

World.title: NRL hands down decision on Cleary after finals sin-binning
World.content:
Nathan Cleary has avoided a ban for dangerous contact, with the Panthers star now just sweating on a foot injury ahead of Penrith's NRL preliminary final.

On Monday, Cleary was handed a grade-one dangerous contact charge for collecting Hugo Savala's leg after the Sydney Rooster kicked in Penrith's 19-12 qualifying final win.

But that charge only carries with it a $1,000 fine with an early guilty plea, meaning Cleary can breathe a sigh of relief with no ban in place.

Had Cleary been handed a grade-two charge, the Penrith halfback would have been facing a one-game ban and the reality of being rubbed out of the preliminary final.

Manly prop Josh Aloiai and South Sydney forward Jacob Host received grade-two charges in 2024 for making contact with kickers.

Canberra's Zac Hosking was fined for a similar incident in last year's finals, while Melbourne's Harry Grant had a charge overturned at the judiciary in 2024.

Loading Instagram content

With the threat of a ban now out of the way, Cleary can focus on his foot and the two weeks he has to be fit to take on the winner of the Warriors and Newcastle.

Cleary was easily Penrith's best in the win over the Roosters, but his sin-bin at the end of the first half for the contact on Savala was only the start of his worries.

The 28-year-old limped through the final 10 minutes of the game with a sore right foot, and opted to give Dylan Edwards the Panthers' last conversion attempt.

Cleary also appeared to say to a Penrith physio after kicking the match-winning 72nd-minute field goal, "my foot is f***ed".

The star half did attempt to play down the injury to his right foot after the game, but his father and coach Ivan admitted there was "something wrong with it".

"I just copped a little bump on the foot," Nathan Cleary said on Fox League.

"It was a pretty important kick, so I just wanted Dyl [Edwards] to take it. I wasn't sure how it would hold up goal kicking.

"It was just precautionary."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: Antonelli edges closer to historic title as teammate concedes the fight
World.content:
Kimi Antonelli is on the brink of becoming the youngest F1 champion in history, while his nearest rival says he is out of the fight.

Antonelli's win in Madrid on Sunday night (AEST) was his eighth grand prix win of the season, extending his lead in the drivers' championship over teammate George Russell to 81 points.

Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton is a further 20 points adrift with eight or nine race weekends remaining, depending on whether F1 can race in the Middle East to end the season.

Piastri hit twice on first lap, Antonelli wins thanks to safety car luck Oscar Piastri and George Russell made contact with each other twice before the first corner, as Kimi Antonelli took full advantage of a fortunate safety car to win the Formula 1 Spanish Grand Prix.

Mercedes have lived up to pre-season expectation that they would be the best team in 2026 but Russell, in his eighth season, was expected to win a maiden drivers' championship.

But Antonelli, in just his second season, has been brilliant all season and has a massive lead in the championship.

After Sunday's Spanish Grand Prix, where Russell placed fifth and conceded a further 15 points to Antonelli, the British driver conceded his hopes of winning the title this year are all but gone.

"We [Mercedes] are in a great position to win the constructors' [championship]. Realistically, I'm not in the fight for the drivers'," Russell said in Madrid.

" That just allows me to focus on race-by-race, and try to focus on just getting some good results. "

Sebastian Vettel became the youngest F1 world champion in 2010 when he claimed his maiden title at 23 years, 133 days.

Antonelli took the mantle as youngest driver to lead the championship earlier this year — but when asked if he could relax with an 81-point lead, the young Italian said he would not be taking his foot off the gas.

"That's exactly what I don't want to do," he said.

"I want to keep pushing race by race, keep delivering and keep enjoying all the way."

F1 heads to Azerbaijan for a grand prix around the streets of Baku on Saturday, September 26.

World.title: 'It's for you, Mum': Cooney-Cross makes emotional Arsenal home return
World.content:
Matildas star Kyra Cooney-Cross has shared an emotional message from her late mother with fans as she made her return to the women's top flight in London.

The Australian star midfielder played her first Women's Super League game for Arsenal since late last year.

With the blessing of the club, she had taken personal leave early this year to be with her mother Jess.

Arsenal shows support for Cooney-Cross Arsenal players and supporters pay emotional tributes to Matildas star Kyra Cooney-Cross following her return to Australia to be with her mother, who has been diagnosed with cancer.

Cooney-Cross announced on January 8 via Instagram that her mother was diagnosed with terminal stage 4 bile duct cancer. She died on July 10.

Arsenal manager Renee Slegers confirmed on March 28 Cooney-Cross was granted indefinite compassionate leave and would remain in Australia after the Asian Cup to be with her mother.

Before the game against Crystal Palace, fans and teammates gave Cooney-Cross a big welcome.

In the end, Arsenal drew 0, leaving the club fifth on the Women's Super League table.

But it wasn't really about the result.

In the Arsenal match day program, Cooney-Cross wrote a personal note to the fans, thanking them for the "outpouring of love and support we received", saying it would never leave her or her family.

"Coming back to the UK was made easier because I have a family here," she wrote.

Cooney-Cross said her mum was very good at sending her messages before games, and so she shared a message from Jess "for all of us".

Loading Instagram content

"Kyra, try to remember what it felt like when you were little … when you just loved having the ball at your feet, playing with your mates, testing yourself against the boys or adults for the fun of it,' the message reads.

"Back then, it wasn't about proving anything … it was about the feeling, the freedom, the creativity, the joy of pushing yourself.

"Play because you love the ball at your feet, the rhythm of the game. Train because it feels good to move and challenge your body and feel strong.

"This is how you start doing it for you again — Mum."

Cooney-Cross finished her message with a simple line:

"It's for you, Mum. Love," and then her signature.

World.title: Ariarne Titmus among elite athletes dragging Sydney Sweeney betting ad
World.content:
Dozens of athletes have taken aim at a highly sexualised  for a betting company featuring actress Sydney Sweeney, accusing it of belittling women in sport.

The ad shows Sweeney in little to no clothing as she plays mock tennis, golf, baseball and ice hockey, holds basketballs, footballs and a soccer ball, and boasts about punters being able to bet on "just sports".

"So they wanted to show just sports," she says while perched topless on top of a basketball hoop.

After saying "sports" nine times, she appears topless on a pool table, before saying: "You can't trade this, I just look good here."

Sydney Sweeney appears topless for most of the . (YouTube: Novig)

The  has been widely criticised, particularly by female athletes, for setting back women in sport.

American gymnast Gracie Kramer was one of the first to respond with an Instagram reel reading: "idk what Sydney Sweeney was doing, but this is what a woman in sport looks like."

Loading Instagram content

"Because it really is that deep," she wrote in the caption, kicking off a trend among some of the best athletes around the world.

A slew of Australian Olympians are part of the chorus, with even the AIS posting: "THIS is sport", featuring several women athletes with the same backing track as the ad.

Swimming great Ariarne Titmus commented on the ad on Instagram, where it has been viewed over 33 million times, describing it as "an absolute joke".

Loading Instagram content

"I can't describe how infuriated I feel when I watch this," the four-time Olympic gold medallist wrote on her stories.

"Not only is it a kick in the face to every woman who has dedicated her life to perfecting her craft, but every woman who enjoys sports for what it really is — teamwork, friendship, dedication, excellence, unity … the list goes on.

"But how do we live in a world where monetising a woman's body and sexualising women's sport is still a thing? To take the mickey like this, I thought we were genuinely moving past this bullsh*t.

"What is this teaching young men and women of today? Sydney Sweeney, do better."

Loading Instagram content

Titmus's replacement as swimming's middle-distance queen, Lani Pallister, also posted that she had "truly no words", while Hockeyroos goalkeeper Joc Bartram said she was disappointed to see women's sport being sexualised.

"In a world where it just feels like women's sport is being recognised for the talent and skill that it involves rather than the sexualisation of women, this new add (sic) by @sydney_sweeney feels so out of touch," said Bartram, who was named goalkeeper of the tournament at the recent World Cup where the Hockeyroos finished fourth.

"There are so many different ways to get people's attention rather than sexualising women's sport once again. For another woman to bring female athletes down to such a level when we have fought so long to be recognised by our male counterparts and are still fighting to prove we belong every day, just leaves me speechless.

"There are so many incredible female athletes doing wonderful things for their sport and women's sport as a whole, please throw your support behind them rather than this tasteless campaign!"

Loading Instagram content

Australian Olympians like Bree Masters, Lauren Ryan and Liz Clay, and water polo silver medallist Tilly Kearns, were among those posting to highlight what women in sport actually look like.

"I absolutely fking hate Sydney Sweeney's new sports ad," Kearns said.

"Like what are we doing … so much worse than I imagined too."

Australian Olympic boxer and WBC bantamweight champion Skye Nicolson joined the trend while acknowledging the backlash was giving the company "exactly what they wanted".

Loading Instagram content

"But honestly these companies need to do better. Stop sexualising women in sport," she wrote.

In an apparent response to the criticism, Sweeney posted on her Instagram stories several images from ESPN's famous Body issue, showing numerous nude elite athletes, including tennis legend Serena Williams, UFC icon Ronda Rousey, NFL great Rob Gronkowski and NBA champion Karl-Anthony Towns.

This is not the first time Sweeney has faced criticism for an advertising campaign, including a 2025 American Eagle ad that boasted about her "great jeans" and was praised by US President Donald Trump.

The s received backlash for alluding to eugenics and the belief in genetic superiority of blonde-haired, blue-eyed white people.

When asked about the backlash and criticism that "specifically in this political climate white people shouldn't joke about genetic superiority", Sweeney was non-committal.

"I think that when I have an issue that I want to speak about, people will hear," she told GQ.

Just as this controversy has boosted an otherwise little-known company into the international spotlight, the American Eagle controversy boosted the company's stock, although the apparel retailer has slumped recently.

World.title: Team USA wins fifth straight Women's Basketball World Cup
World.content:
Breanna Stewart has scored 22 points and grabbed 10 rebounds to lead the United States to a comfortable 97-79 win over France and another FIBA World Cup title in Berlin.

Jackie Young added 18 points, six rebounds and five assists as the US used a dominant third quarter to close the door on France's chances.

The victory gave the US its 12th gold medal at an event it has historically dominated. No other nation has won more than six ‌golds, with the Americans taking the last five championships.

Team USA outscored France 30-12 in the third quarter to turn a 45-43 deficit into a runaway victory.

With ‌the score tied 47-all early in the third, Stewart, Kahleah Copper and Young scored baskets for a 7-0 USA run and a 54-47 edge. Then, with the US leading 58-53 with just over ‌2 minutes left in the quarter, it found another gear.

Chelsea Gray and Copper each scored a basket, and after ⁠a France free throw, Team USA ‌went on a 9-0 run ‌to go up 71-54. Copper made three free throws during the run, ‌which was punctuated by Aliyah Boston's lay-up with 40 seconds left in the period.

Caitlin Clark answered a ‌Migna Toure three-pointer with her ⁠own jumper to make it 73-57 going into the fourth.

Copper finished with 15 points, with Gray and Clark adding 12 apiece.

Dominique Malonga paced France with 21 points and ⁠six rebounds. Gabby Williams added 20 points and seven assists.

France held a 20-17 lead after ‌the first ‌quarter following a 3-pointer from Marine Johannes and a pair of Malonga free throws.

Spain, the USA's semifinal opponent, won the third-place game 81-58 against host Germany.

Tech.title: Trump and Mike Johnson think the AI industry is overreacting
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Yesterday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a lengthy open letter saying it was time to “pace the frontier” and slow down AI development. OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Elon Musk both agreed, publicly voicing their support on X. Even Alphabet’s Demis Hassabis offered tentative support for Amodei’s proposal.

Donald Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson, however, seem to think the AI executives are being overreactive and fear that a pause could lead to China outpacing the US in the AI race. According to the Financial Times, Trump said “Look, we’re leading China in AI ... and, frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.”

Johnson echoed those sentiments on CNN, telling Jake Tapper that rushing to place restrictions on AI development could be a “national security threat.” He urged people not to panic. “If Congress just races in and does some sort of emergency session to try and regulate AI, we will lose the race to China.”

Tech.title: Apple is reportedly working on iPhone game controllers
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says Apple is developing two game controllers for the iPhone and will likely sell them under the Beats brand. Rumors that Apple might enter the game controller business have circulated for some time. But last week, MacRumors reported finding two references in macOS 26.7’s code to two game controllers identified as first-party devices.

Despite the code being found in macOS, not iOS, Gurman says the controllers are designed for iPhones. Additionally, he says that it is Beats executives leading the charge on this product. Apple sometimes uses its subsidiary brand to experiment with new product categories and compete at lower price points without sullying its more premium Apple lineup. As Gurman notes:

For example, Beats now sells a range of iPhone cases and USB-C cables that don’t necessarily fit Apple’s usual approach to design. A controller makes sense in that context. To reach a broad audience, it has to be relatively affordable, which means avoiding some of the more expensive materials and finishes typically associated with Apple products. The culture and lifestyle around gaming controllers also could fit naturally under the Beats umbrella.

Tech.title: The Units’ Digital Stimulation is synthpunk perfection
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

The Units are a band I discovered in part thanks to No Dogs in Space. During their miniseries on The Screamers (another incredible band worth checking out), they mention synthpunk.org as one of their sources. And there’s no better way to get my attention than to combine two of my favorite things — punk rock and synthesizers. The site was down that day (it appears to be back up now), but I was able to access a version from July through the Wayback Machine. What greeted me was a bare-bones site with links for six bands, including The Screamers. But at the top was The Units, a band I’d never heard of and, after tracking down their 1980 record Digital Stimulation, I fell in love.

The production, especially on the Devo-esque vocals, feels distinctly of its time. But the sound palette and arrangements are more aggressive, dancier, and generally just more modern-sounding. Ignoring the vocals, album opener “High Pressure” could pass as an MSPAINT song. The title track, with its sped-up disco stomp, could have been released by DFA in 2003. And many of the later tracks would be at home on a Single Frame record.

The Units weren’t the first punk band to dabble with synths. Nor were they the first act to largely replace guitars with keyboards and lean into technology as a core theme of their songwriting. The Talking Heads offered a cleaner, artier take on punk, incorporating keyboards, non-Western percussion, and even tape loops. Devo’s first single, “Mongoloid,” has a distinctly punk edge that would have been right at home alongside The Units. But the band still leaned heavily on traditional guitar and bass, and always felt more at home in the art-rock and new wave scenes.

Husband-and-wife duo Scott Ryser and Rachel Webber, the primary songwriters of The Units, had a sharper edge to their sound. They were firmly grounded in the West Coast punk scene that made its DIY ethos a core part of its identity. Their contemporaries were the Dead Kennedys, The Mutants, and The Avengers. You can hear it in the lean arrangements that prioritize raw energy over perfection. That’s not to say songs like “Cannibals” and “Bugboy” are simplistic. Their bleak, slightly humorous critiques of an uncaring world are models of efficiency — unfussy and infectious.

Like a lot of Bay Area punk bands, there’s a melodicism to The Units’ work that is hard to shake. “Warm Moving Bodies” feels like a dancefloor anthem waiting to happen, and “High Pressure” is an undeniable earworm.

The band did record a second album in 1981, Animals They Dream About, but it remained unreleased until 2016. It’s also an excellent document of the under-represented synthpunk scene of the late ‘70s and early ‘80s. Though, it is far more polished and leans into poppier new wave arrangements that are a step removed from their bootstrapped punk roots.

The Units’ Digital Stimulation is available on Bandcamp and via streaming on Apple Music, YouTube Music, and Deezer.

Tech.title: Waymo pulls over, calls cops on riders with a ghost gun
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Two people were arrested in San Fransico while riding around in a Waymo robotaxi after the cab pulled over and called the cops on them. The riders were juveniles in possession of a loaded AR-style ghost gun and were taken to a juvenile hall. While the police report did not specify who was operating the autonomous car, Waymo later confirmed it was one of its vehicles to the Los Angeles Times.

A spokesperson told the LA Times that a “violation of our terms of service involving a firearm” was detected. At which point the car pulled over and alerted the authorities.

Earlier this year, a Waymo faked having mechanical problems to pull over when two passengers were drinking alcohol and firing a toy gun out of the back of the car. In that instance, the riders Waymo snitched on were also juveniles. So let this be a lesson to teens: if you’re gonna do dumb stuff, don’t do it in the back of a robotaxi.

Tech.title: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother will make you forget all about Marvel’s Blade disaster
Tech.content:
Marvel’s mishandling of its Blade reboot will likely go down as one of the studio’s biggest mistakes. There was a great actor in place to play the vampire hunter (Mahershala Ali), and a promising director set to take over the reins (Bassam Tariq). In retrospect, though, the disappointing demise of Blade might not be such a bad thing, because Tariq and Ali have collaborated on something much more interesting than a superhero reboot: the powerful hitman thriller Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.

That was one of five movies I was able to cram into a very hectic third day at the Toronto International Film Festival (you can see my previous reports here and here), and it was one of those days that drives home why events like TIFF can be so special. Each film I saw was drastically different from the last — there was everything from a drama about drifting cars to a throwback horror flick based on a famous Japanese ghost story — which was a great reminder that there are still plenty of new ideas left in the world of film.

So let’s get to it. Here are some rapid-fire reviews of everything I saw on day 3 at TIFF.

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother

In theaters in October

Latif (Ali) lives a life of contradictions: he’s a devout Muslim and loyal father, but he also works as a hitman, albeit one who works under a specific moral code (only kill bad guys; never use a gun). But both his faith and his code are tested when his wife dies and he’s forced to become a single father to three kids, including a newborn baby. At the same time, his blood-soaked past comes back to haunt him, putting everyone at risk. We’re in a great moment for pure action flicks like Furious or the John Wick franchise, but Your Mother offers something very different. It’s a powerful character study, one where the action is comparatively fleeting, but all the more powerful and impactful because of it. It’s a film that always left me guessing just how Latif was going to get through this, and, despite being very serious and often solemn, the story also has plenty of laugh-out-loud moments. Ali is excellent as the morally questionable righteous killer, but I was also really impressed by John Cho as the villain, a charismatically unhinged leader of a right-wing church group.

In Alaska

No theatrical date yet

A slow-burning crime thriller, In Alaska, co-directed by Jaap van Heusden and Vinnie Karetak., follows a suicidal teen named Woody (Leo Matthew Temela) who, after a tragic mishap, finds himself wanted by the FBI for causing millions of dollars worth of damage to an oil pipeline. It’s a film of two sides: Woody’s desperate attempts at survival, and veteran agent Susan (Noomi Rapace), the only who realizes the damage wasn’t caused by eco-terrorists. In Alaska is a moodier take on the genre, and one that asks some difficult and important questions about both its leads, particularly Woody, who constantly grapples with whether he even wants to live at all. What starts out bleak ends on a much more hopeful note.

Image: TIFF

The Face of Horror

No theatrical date yet

Conceptually, Anna Biller’s The Face of Horror is a mishmash of styles and influences. It’s based on the influential Japanese ghost story Yotsuya Kaidan, but adapts the tale for 14th century England. It then renders the whole thing in the style of Technicolor horror classics. That curious combination works, though, as the film has a campy sense of theatricality to it, with over-the-top performances and classic-style special effects — including some truly memorable make-up work — that lend its grisly tale of murder and betrayal a distinct vibe. And it’s all held together by two strong lead performances: Eleanor (Kristine Froseth), the jilted wife-turned-nightmare of Edward (Jonah Hauer-King), a smarmy and morally-dubious knight who is the kind of asshole you can’t wait to see get what’s coming to him.

Image: Image: Roadside / Vertical

Babies

No theatrical date yet

A film that explores that nagging question many long-term couples are forced to answer repeatedly: when are you going to have a baby? Written and directed by Lauren Miller Rogen, Babies is centered on Annie (Anna Kendrick) and Aaron (Seth Rogen), the only childless couple in their social circle. But Annie can’t stop thinking about the question — there’s a lot of her internal monologue debating the pros and cons of having kids — and the couple are forced to really confront the idea when a close friend and her young daughter come to stay with them, providing a taste of parenthood. Babies works for two reasons. First, it’s hilarious: Kendrick and Rogen have a blast together, and the supporting cast includes the likes of Issa Rae, Zach Cherry, and Ed Helm. But it also feels grounded in a way that makes it very relatable, whether you have kids or not.

Drifter

No theatrical date yet

If Good Will Hunting and The Fast and the Furious were smushed together, you might get something like Drifter. The film is directed by longtime Fast star Sung Kang, who also plays the lead role of Tree, the janitor of a smalltown race track who moonlights as a driver for a drug kingpin. But all he really wants to do is drift, and events conspire to bring him to an event where he’ll go up against the best drifters in the world. The challenges are much more than just on the track, though; Tree has spent most of his life alone, so he’s forced to learn to open up to others, and he also has to contend with extracting himself from the world of crime. Unfortunately, Drifter leans too heavily on the established formula of underdog sports stories, which makes most of its beats feel predictable, with the exception of its completely improbable ending. Worse still is that, with the exception of Tree, none of the characters feel developed at all, and the crime thriller aspect doesn’t gel well with the feel-good story. At least there are some beautiful sequences that make drifting a car feel like an artform.

Tech.title: Your car is selling your data
Tech.content:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on cars, data privacy, and autonomous vehicles, follow Andrew J. Hawkins. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

How it started

Earlier this year, the Federal Trade Commission issued an unprecedented penalty against General Motors: a five-year ban on selling customer data to consumer reporting agencies and third-party data brokers.

For years, GM had been collecting all sorts of data on its customers — such as how often they sped or whether they drove at night — and selling it to brokers to generate risk profiles for insurance companies. More often than not, drivers were unaware of the degree to which their data was being collected. Many had unknowingly consented to it by signing up for an OnStar connected services plan, which activated a feature called Smart Driver that collected their driving data.

GM was then turning around and sharing that data with two data brokers, LexisNexis and Verisk, both of which work with the insurance industry. In a 2024 blockbuster investigative report by The New York Times, some drivers said their insurance rates went up as a result of the data collection. The enrollment process was so confusing that many vehicle owners had no idea their data was being shared. Under the settlement with the FTC, GM has to make it easier for drivers to turn off location tracking, as well as enable them to access and delete their data collected by the automaker.

But GM isn’t the only automaker vacuuming up data on its customers. A team of researchers from the Mozilla Foundation spent months examining the privacy policies of all the major car companies for a report they were working on in 2023. Their conclusion: Every single one had “horrible privacy and security,” said Jen Caltrider, who helped author the study. Not only that, but customers were forced to accept overlapping policies for the car, the connected services, the smartphone app, and the financial services through which they received their loan — all of which included data collection provisions.

“And so it was really overwhelming trying to understand what was going on,” Caltrider said.

There has been plenty of corroborating evidence for this. Consumer Reports published its own investigation last year that concluded “nearly every automaker that sells cars in the U.S. is similarly collecting and sharing so-called ‘driver behavior data’ with other companies and continues to do so.”

Cars are particularly problematic compared to phones because the privacy controls are less intuitive. A smartphone owner can generally find and tweak their privacy settings. With a vehicle, the data collection is spread across multiple systems and policies, making it much harder for consumers to understand what is happening. It feels like a free-for-all because automakers are collecting enormous amounts of information without much public scrutiny.

How it’s going

After GM was penalized as a result of the Times investigation, the issue of data privacy and cars appears to finally be getting some scrutiny. But as is often the case, policymakers may be missing the mark on how to address it.

Last December, a trio of House Republicans introduced the Data Rights for Information and Vehicle Electronics in Real-time, or DRIVER, Act. According to these lawmakers, the bill “reaffirms a basic principle: if you own the vehicle, you should own the data it generates.”

But while the bill would give vehicle owners a bit more control over their data, it would also allow automakers to continue gathering and selling it to third-party data brokers, which makes it a nonstarter for privacy advocates. As Caltrider notes, access and deletion rights are not the same thing as preventing excess collection in the first place. If an automaker can collect enormous amounts of information and the consumer must then go through an arduous process to discover what was collected and request that it be deleted, the burden remains on the individual. Most privacy advocates would rather see a system in which automakers simply do not collect so much information to begin with.

The issue has even risen to the level of MAGA World. Last July, Donald Trump’s Transportation Secretary, Sean Duffy, sent a letter to Congress outlining the administration’s policy priorities for the upcoming surface transportation reauthorization bill. Tucked in the letter was a new concept called “the Freedom Car,” which Duffy described as Americans’ right to “drive disconnected and non-automated” vehicles. The proposal would ban the government from requiring that vehicles be equipped with automated driving systems or have the capability to transmit data wirelessly — which, to my knowledge, no one is trying to do.

What happens next

It’s unclear whether the DRIVER Act or the Freedom Car will ever clear the hurdles in Washington to become real policies. What is clear is that there is significant demand for simpler vehicles. People are asking why they can’t just buy a car without all the sensors and data collection. They look at new concepts like the Slate Truck and wonder whether they could also use something more bare-bones.

Sure, consumers may accept useful safety equipment such as backup cameras, but many don’t want their vehicle tracking everything they do — and they definitely don’t want to see ads on their vehicle screens. (BMW, I’m looking at you.) Nor do they want Flock cameras tracking their every movement while they drive down the street.

But automakers have every incentive to keep collecting data because there is money to be made from it. As long as the broader data economy rewards companies for gathering and monetizing information, there’s little reason for automakers to voluntarily abandon the practice.

By the way

Every automaker has its own privacy page where vehicle owners can submit requests, including opting out of data collection. Of course, they’re all buried under mountains of legalese, so good luck finding it.

Same goes for all the smartphone apps for connected car services. Changing your privacy settings in those apps is generally a little easier.

Read this

The New York Times ’ investigation into GM’s data collection program is worth a read, if just for the flabbergasted reactions from drivers who couldn’t understand why their insurance rates were going up.

Edmunds and Consumer Reports both did the work to ask every automaker for their data collection policies. There’s a lot of variety across the industry.

These Redditors are crowdsourcing a list of new cars (from 2019 onward) that aren’t digitally connected and/or transmitting data to the car company’s servers. Spoiler alert: It’s a pretty short list!

Screen Share

This week, I’m featuring somebody who I have been working with for a long time: Verge news writer Emma Roth. Emma is one of the smartest in the biz on all things streaming, can write something good on just about anything — just recently, she’s tackled topics like AI detectors and Meta child safety settlements and food recalls — and is a great person to team up on stories with. She’s a key part of our newsroom.

I asked her to share her homescreen and the apps and things she cares about. Here it is, plus some info on the apps she uses and why:

Images: Emma Roth

The phone: Samsung Galaxy Note 20 Ultra (the last Note created!).

The wallpaper: It’s a photo I took at a local inlet! It’s a great pelican-watching spot.

The apps: My homepage might be relatively bare, but it includes the essentials: Google Messages, Microsoft Edge, Samsung Mail, and my Phone, along with shortcuts to the Google Play Store and my Camera.

That sense of organization disappears as soon as I swipe into my app drawer. The first page has the apps I use the most, resulting in a chaotic mishmash of apps like Reddit, Slack, and Sam’s Club.

Maybe showing my messy app drawer to the world is a sign that I should tidy things up a bit. I can’t remember the last time I used any app inside the Samsung folder, or tapped into my Phone from this screen instead of using the shortcut in my dock.

I also asked Emma to share a few things she’s into right now. Here’s what she sent back:

I’ve recently gotten back into Project Zomboid . It’s a PC game that’s basically like a cross between a hardcore zombie game and The Sims — except you’re fighting for survival instead of managing a virtual household.

One app that’s not at the top of my app drawer (but probably should be!) is Yuka . You can use it to scan the food and beauty products across your home and grocery stores to see whether they contain risky additives. Yuka assigns a rating to everything you scan. It’s a quick and easy way to figure out whether something I’ve bought (or plan to buy) is actually harmful, without having to know exactly what azodicarbonamide or monocalcium phosphate are.

My modded PlayStation Vita has overtaken my Steam Deck as my favorite handheld. I’ve been playing an emulated version of Final Fantasy VII. I missed out on that classic when it came out, and I’m thoroughly enjoying it now.
